question: In 1993 an American mathematics professor invented a brand-new kind of game. Each player builds a custom deck of magical spells, creatures, and lands, then duels a rival to bring that rival from 20 life to zero. He called the game Magic: the Gathering, and it kicked off the whole trading-card-game craze that later included Pokemon and Yu-Gi-Oh! What was the mathematician's name?
context: Garfield earned his PhD in combinatorial mathematics at the University of Pennsylvania. He pitched the game to Peter Adkison's tiny Wizards of the Coast outfit in 1991.

question: Magic: the Gathering is a fantasy card game where every spell needs magical energy called mana. Every card belongs to one of five colors, and each color has its own feel. One color is peaceful and orderly and heals; one is clever, cold, and draws cards; one is dark, ruthless, and kills things; one is fast, angry, and burns; one is wild, green, and full of growing life. Which five colors are they?
answer: White, blue, black, red, and green
choices: White, blue, black, red, and green
Red, blue, yellow, green, and orange
Gold, silver, bronze, copper, and iron
Fire, water, earth, air, and spirit
context: The five colors form the Color Pie. Each color has a flavor identity: white law, blue knowledge, black ambition, red passion, green nature.

question: In 1990 a computer programmer named Peter Adkison started a small game company out of his garage in Renton, Washington, near Seattle. Three years later his tiny company published Magic: the Gathering, the very first modern trading card game. It quickly became one of the most famous game makers in the world and later bought the Dungeons & Dragons rules too. What is the company called?
context: Adkison founded WotC in 1990. Garfield brought him the prototype of Magic in 1991. WotC was acquired by Hasbro in 1999.

question: In Magic: the Gathering, red is the color of fire and fury. Its most famous cheap spell costs just one red mana and hurls a jolt of electricity that deals three damage to any creature or player. Every red beginner deck has run four copies of it since 1993. The card art shows a jagged yellow bolt splitting the sky. What is this spell called?
context: Lightning Bolt printed in Alpha at common. It became the gold standard for cheap red removal in every format that allowed it.

question: In Magic: the Gathering, when you play a creature card and it enters the battlefield, that creature cannot attack the very same turn it comes down. It has to wait one full turn before it can swing at anyone — as if the creature just got yanked from another plane of existence and is still dizzy. Cards with the 'haste' ability are the exception. What is this waiting rule called?
context: Garfield introduced the rule to prevent first-turn one-shot kills and to give the opponent a chance to respond before a new creature swings.

question: In Magic: the Gathering, when you use a card's power you rotate it 90 degrees sideways on the table so you know you already used it this turn. A land you rotate this way produces one mana for casting spells; a creature you rotate this way is 'used up' from attacking. You straighten the cards back at the start of your next turn. What is this sideways-turning action called?
context: Tapped cards are turned 90 degrees to show they have been used. They straighten back up — untap — during the controller's next untap step.

question: In the 1980s an American professional wrestler grew a bushy blonde mustache, tore off yellow tank tops, and wore a red bandanna. He called his huge biceps his '24-inch pythons.' In the WWF (World Wrestling Federation) ring he cupped his ear to hear the crowd roar, dropped his 'atomic leg drop' on giants, and beat the Iron Sheik in 1984 to win the WWF title. Kids all over America wore his T-shirts. Who was he?
context: Hogan's real name is Terry Bollea. He won his first WWF title from the Iron Sheik on January 23, 1984, at Madison Square Garden.

question: At WrestleMania III in 1987 at the Silverdome in Michigan, Hulk Hogan wrestled a seven-foot-four French giant who weighed over 500 pounds. Hogan body-slammed him in front of 93,000 fans — one of the most famous moments in pro wrestling history. That same giant also acted in the 1987 movie The Princess Bride, playing the gentle, poetry-loving strongman Fezzik. What was the giant's ring name?
context: Andre's huge size came from acromegaly. Hogan body-slammed him at WrestleMania III in front of a Pontiac Silverdome crowd announced as 93,173.

question: One 1980s pro wrestler wore neon sunglasses, feathered cowboy hats, and shouted 'Ooh yeah!' in a raspy voice. His manager was the graceful Miss Elizabeth, who walked him to the ring. Fans called him 'Macho Man' and cheered as he leapt off the top rope with flying elbow drops. In TV commercials he ripped open Slim Jim meat sticks and yelled 'Snap into a Slim Jim!' What was his real ring name?
context: Randy Savage's real name was Randy Poffo. He held the Intercontinental Championship in 1986-87, with a classic match against Ricky Steamboat at WrestleMania III.

question: In late-1990s WWF (World Wrestling Federation), a bald, black-vest-wearing Texan wrestler named Steve Austin ended almost every match with one signature finishing move. He would stagger to his feet, grab his opponent by the head, kick him in the gut so he doubled over, then drop straight down to his knees and slam the opponent's jaw hard across the top of his own shoulder. Fans lost their minds every time it hit. What was this finishing move called?
context: Austin would kick the opponent in the gut, drop to a seated position, and bring the opponent's jaw down across his shoulder. The move was almost impossible to make look fake.

question: In the late 1990s a third-generation pro wrestler — his father and grandfather had both wrestled in WWF (World Wrestling Federation) — became one of the top stars in the company. He raised one eyebrow like nobody else could, called himself 'the People's Champion,' pounded his big elbow into fallen foes, and roared a catchphrase asking fans if they could smell what he was cookin'. He later became a huge Hollywood action-movie star. Who is he?
context: The Rock's real name is Dwayne Johnson. His father was 'Soulman' Rocky Johnson; his grandfather was High Chief Peter Maivia. He debuted in 1996 as Rocky Maivia.

question: One WWF (World Wrestling Federation) wrestler stood almost seven feet tall and wore all black — a long duster coat, a wide brimmed black hat, and black gloves. He walked to the ring in near-total darkness while a slow funeral bell tolled overhead. Fans called him 'the Deadman.' For over twenty years he won every single match he wrestled at WrestleMania, building the longest unbeaten streak in the sport. Who is he?
context: The Undertaker debuted at Survivor Series in November 1990. His WrestleMania streak began at WrestleMania VII in 1991 and ran to 21-0 before Brock Lesnar broke it at WrestleMania XXX.

question: Every spring since 1985, the WWE (World Wrestling Entertainment) company has held its biggest wrestling event of the year — a super-show that fans watch on pay-per-view worldwide. Hulk Hogan body-slammed the giant Andre at the third one; the Undertaker built his famous unbeaten streak at it; Hollywood stars like Mr. T and singer Cyndi Lauper have joined the ring. What is this yearly super-event called?
context: WrestleMania I took place March 31, 1985, at Madison Square Garden. Mr. T tag-teamed with Hulk Hogan in the main event.

question: One fan-favorite WWF (World Wrestling Federation) wrestler came from a huge wrestling family in Calgary, Canada — the Hart family, trained by their father Stu Hart in a brutal basement gym called the Dungeon. In the ring he wore pink and black tights with pink sunglasses, and boasted he was 'the best there is, the best there was, and the best there ever will be.' Fans nicknamed him 'the Hitman.' Who was he?
context: Bret Hart was part of the wrestling Hart family from Calgary. He held the WWF Championship five times. His pink-and-black gear became iconic merch.

question: In 1988 the billionaire cable-TV owner Ted Turner bought a Georgia pro wrestling company and grew it into a national rival to WWF (World Wrestling Federation). From 1995 to 2001, his company's Monday Nitro show fought WWF's Monday Night Raw head-to-head every week on cable TV — a fight fans still call 'the Monday Night Wars.' Turner's company signed Hulk Hogan away and led the ratings for 83 straight weeks. What was it called?
context: World Championship Wrestling launched Monday Nitro in September 1995 to compete directly with WWF Raw. Vince McMahon purchased WCW in March 2001 when it folded.

question: Pro wrestler Mick Foley was famous in WWF (World Wrestling Federation) for playing three totally different characters. One was Dude Love, a smooth-talking 1970s lover-boy in tie-dye; another was Cactus Jack, a wild bearded bruiser from the hardcore deathmatch scene. The third one wore a torn brown leather mask, drooled, spoke to a puppet-sock on his hand called Mr. Socko, and lived down in a boiler room. What was that third masked character called?
context: Mick Foley's leather-mask Mankind persona debuted in 1996. He won the WWF Championship for the first time on Raw, January 4, 1999. His memoir 'Have a Nice Day' was a 2000 bestseller.

question: In 1996 at a WWF (World Wrestling Federation) tournament called King of the Ring, the bald Texan wrestler Stone Cold Steve Austin won the final by beating a Bible-preaching wrestler named Jake 'the Snake' Roberts. In his victory speech Austin mocked a famous Bible verse Roberts liked to quote — and stole the exact chapter-and-verse reference to coin his own new catchphrase. The reference then went on millions of black T-shirts sold worldwide. What was the reference?
context: Stone Cold coined 'Austin 3:16' at King of the Ring 1996 after beating Bible-thumping Jake Roberts in the tournament final. The line: 'Austin 3:16 says I just whipped your ass.'

question: In WWF (World Wrestling Federation) in the mid-1990s, one wrestler was nicknamed 'the Heartbreak Kid.' He led a rowdy, rule-breaking group called D-Generation X alongside Triple H. At WrestleMania 12 in 1996, he beat Bret Hart in a 60-minute non-stop 'Iron Man Match' for the world heavyweight title. His signature move was a jumping super-kick to the jaw he called Sweet Chin Music. What was his real ring name?
context: Shawn Michaels — real name Michael Hickenbottom — won his first WWF title from Bret Hart at WrestleMania XII in March 1996. He founded D-Generation X in 1997 with Triple H.

question: In the American city of Seattle, the National Football League (NFL) has a team that plays inside a big stadium called Lumen Field. The team wears blue, green, and silver jerseys, and their fans are so loud the crowd once set a world record for stadium noise. What is this Seattle NFL team called?
context: The Seahawks joined the NFL as an expansion team in 1976. They played at the Kingdome from 1976 to 1999, briefly at Husky Stadium, then at Seahawks Stadium (Qwest/CenturyLink/Lumen) from 2002.

question: In the early 2010s, one bruising running back for the Seattle Seahawks in the National Football League (NFL) earned the nickname 'Beast Mode' because he ran through defenders like a wrecking ball. He was famous for munching Skittles candy on the sideline between plays. Who was this Seahawks running back?
context: Marshawn Lynch came to Seattle in 2010. His 'Beast Quake' 67-yard touchdown against the Saints on January 8, 2011, registered on a real seismograph at the University of Washington.

question: In February 2014, one young Seattle Seahawks quarterback led his team to crush the Denver Broncos 43-8 in Super Bowl XLVIII, the National Football League (NFL) championship. He kept starting for Seattle for years, then in 2022 the Seahawks traded him away to those same Denver Broncos. Who was this Seahawks quarterback?
context: Russell Wilson was a third-round pick out of Wisconsin in 2012. He became the Seahawks' starter immediately and led them to two straight Super Bowls.

question: In the early 2010s, four defensive backs of the Seattle Seahawks in the National Football League (NFL) hit ball-carriers so hard that fans gave the group a scary nickname. The group was cornerback Richard Sherman, safety Earl Thomas, hard-hitting safety Kam Chancellor, and cornerback Brandon Browner. What was the nickname?
context: The Legion of Boom shut down the Denver Broncos 43-8 in Super Bowl XLVIII on February 2, 2014. Brandon Browner is credited with coining the nickname.

question: In 2010, the Seattle Seahawks hired a new head coach from the University of Southern California (USC) college football team. He was famous for his huge grin, boundless energy, and always chewing gum on the sideline. He would coach Seattle for more than a decade and win a Super Bowl. Who was this Seahawks head coach?
context: Pete Carroll took over after a successful run at USC. He won Super Bowl XLVIII in his fourth season and reached Super Bowl XLIX the next year.

question: In 1997, one left-handed Seattle Mariners outfielder crushed 56 home runs in a single Major League Baseball season — one of the greatest power years ever. He was so cool that he posed with his baseball cap on backward for the cover of Sports Illustrated magazine. Who was this superstar Mariners slugger?
context: Junior was drafted first overall by the Mariners in 1987. He debuted in April 1989 at age 19. His sweet swing made him the face of baseball in the 1990s.

question: In 2001, a Japanese baseball star crossed the Pacific to play right field for the Seattle Mariners in Major League Baseball. In his very first American season he collected 242 hits and won both Rookie of the Year and Most Valuable Player (MVP) — a feat almost nobody in history had pulled off. Who was this Japanese Mariners outfielder?
context: Ichiro had been a superstar for the Orix Blue Wave in Japan. He came to Seattle in 2001 and had 242 hits, the most by a rookie since 1911.

question: One Seattle Mariners hitter was so beloved by the city that Seattle officially renamed a street next to the ballpark in his honor. Over his career he batted .312, was famous for driving in runs in clutch spots, and in 2019 the Baseball Hall of Fame voted him in. Who was this Mariners hitter?
context: Edgar Martinez played his entire career in Seattle from 1987 to 2004. The best-DH-of-the-year award was renamed the Edgar Martinez Award in his honor.

question: One left-handed Seattle Mariners pitcher stood a towering 6 feet 10 inches tall, and his fastball terrified every batter who stepped in. Fans nicknamed him 'The Big Unit' for his enormous size. In 1990 he threw a no-hitter against Detroit, meaning not a single batter got a hit off him the whole game. Who was he?
context: Randy Johnson came to the Mariners from Montreal in 1989. His no-hitter against the Tigers was the first in Mariners history. He won four straight Cy Young Awards after Seattle traded him.

question: One Seattle Mariners pitcher from Venezuela was so dominant that fans nicknamed him 'King Felix' and packed a bleacher section called the King's Court in yellow shirts to cheer his starts. In 2012 he pitched a perfect game against the Tampa Bay Rays, retiring all 27 batters in a row. Who was he?
context: Felix Hernandez retired all 27 batters that day at Safeco Field, striking out 12. It was Major League Baseball's 23rd perfect game. He won the 2010 AL Cy Young Award.

question: In 1993 the American mathematician Richard Garfield designed a new kind of card game called Magic: The Gathering (MtG), in which players cast spells and summon creatures from personal decks they built themselves. Wizards of the Coast printed the very first two runs, called Alpha and Beta, with bold thick black card borders. Later that same year Wizards rushed a third run into shops to keep up with demand. It was called Unlimited. How did Unlimited look different from Alpha and Beta?
answer: It used white borders instead of black
choices: It used white borders instead of black
It included 20 brand-new cards not in Alpha
It dropped all rare cards from the print run
It used a metallic foil finish on every card
context: Unlimited was meant to make the game more available; Wizards underprinted Alpha (about 2.6 million cards) and Beta. White borders distinguished a reprint from a first printing.

question: After Magic: The Gathering (MtG) exploded onto game-shop shelves in 1993, its inventor Richard Garfield rushed the very first expansion set to print in December of that year. He borrowed its whole flavor from the old Middle Eastern folktales of Scheherazade — genies, camels, sultans, and desert cities — printing cards like Juzam Djinn, Library of Alexandria, and Erhnam Djinn that became instant collector prizes. What was this first-ever MtG expansion set called?
context: Arabian Nights was designed by Richard Garfield as a tribute to the 1001 Nights. Library of Alexandria became one of the strongest lands ever printed.

question: In March 1994 Wizards of the Coast printed the second Magic: The Gathering (MtG) expansion, an artifact-heavy set that told the story of a legendary war between two brothers in the ancient land of Terisiare. One brother was a brilliant tinkerer who built weapons from careful engineering; the other seized raw artifact power without truly understanding it. Their war eventually shattered the world and cooled the whole planet into an Ice Age. What were the two brothers named?
context: Antiquities introduced the Brothers' War storyline, which would dominate MtG flavor lore for years. Mishra fell to Phyrexian corruption; Urza survived as a planeswalker.

question: In June 1994 Wizards of the Coast released a huge Magic: The Gathering (MtG) expansion of 310 cards, the largest set the game had ever printed. It introduced a brand-new card type called legendary creatures — unique named heroes and villains like Nicol Bolas and Sivitri Scarzam that players could only run one copy of per deck. It also brought in the game's first multicolored cards and an odd combat rule called banding. What was the set called?
context: Legends had 310 cards designed by Steve Conard, Robert Gutschera, and others. It introduced characters like Kei Takahashi, Sol'kanar the Swamp King, and Nicol Bolas the elder dragon legend.

question: In the trading card game Magic: The Gathering (MtG), the most valuable early cards are called the Power Nine. Four of them are 'moxen' — small artifact stones that let you tap them to add one mana of a specific color to cast spells. One is named Mox Pearl. Which color of mana does Mox Pearl produce?
context: The five moxen — Pearl, Sapphire, Jet, Ruby, Emerald — each tap for one mana of white, blue, black, red, and green respectively. Mox Emerald is the green one.

question: In the trading card game Magic: The Gathering (MtG), one iconic white flying creature has been printed since the very first set (called Alpha) in 1993. She is an angel with 4 power and 4 toughness for five mana, and she has both flying and vigilance so she can attack without tapping. What is this famous white angel called?
context: Serra Angel appears on the box art of multiple MtG sets. The artist Douglas Schuler illustrated the iconic Alpha version. The card became a banner image for the white color identity.

question: In the trading card game Magic: The Gathering (MtG), one of the most famous blue spells cancels an opponent's spell before it can even happen. It costs one blue mana plus one generic mana, and it has appeared in nearly every set since the original Alpha printing in 1993. What is this classic blue spell called?
context: Counterspell was printed in Alpha at common at UU casting cost. Its simplicity made it the gold standard for blue control. Later sets have made the spell more expensive or conditional.

question: In Magic: The Gathering (MtG), one tiny green mana-creature has been reprinted in edition after edition since the game's 1993 debut, making it one of the most-printed cards in MtG history. It costs a single green mana to cast, has the flying ability so nothing on the ground can block it, and taps to add one mana of any color you like — perfect for jump-starting a five-color deck. What is this iconic green flyer called?
context: Birds of Paradise is a 0/1 flier from Alpha. The Mark Poole artwork showed a colorful tropical bird perched on a branch. Birds is the iconic green mana fixer.

question: On January 23, 1984, at Madison Square Garden in New York City, the muscular blond hero Hulk Hogan beat the villainous Iranian wrestler the Iron Sheik and won his first World Wrestling Federation (WWF) championship. Hogan used one signature two-move combination to finish the Sheik. What were those two moves?
answer: The leg drop, after a big boot
choices: The leg drop, after a big boot
The piledriver, after a body slam
The pedigree, after a knee strike
The sleeper hold, after a clothesline
context: Hogan's act was simple: take a beating, 'Hulk up' as the audience cheered, then big boot and leg drop for the win. He held the title until February 1988.

question: On March 29, 1987, WrestleMania III drew 93,173 fans to the Pontiac Silverdome in Michigan. In the main event, Hulk Hogan bodyslammed Andre the Giant. In the semi-main, Randy 'Macho Man' Savage defended his Intercontinental (IC) Championship against 'The Dragon' Ricky Steamboat in a fifteen-minute classic. How did the IC title match end?
answer: Steamboat won the IC title from Savage
choices: Steamboat won the IC title from Savage
Savage retained with help from Miss Elizabeth
Roddy Piper lost his retirement match
British Bulldog won the tag-team titles
context: Steamboat-Savage at WrestleMania III is widely considered one of the best wrestling matches of all time. The two had rehearsed every spot in advance and called nothing on the fly.

question: At the Survivor Series in Montreal on November 9, 1997, Bret Hart was scheduled to drop the WWF Championship to Shawn Michaels. Instead, in the middle of the match, Vince McMahon told the referee to ring the bell on a hold Bret hadn't tapped out of. What was that hold?
answer: The Sharpshooter, Bret's own signature submission
choices: The Sharpshooter, Bret's own signature submission
The figure-four leg lock, applied to the wrong leg
The sleeper hold, held until Bret went limp
The crossface, with Shawn pulling Bret's chin back
context: The Montreal Screwjob is wrestling's most infamous double-cross. McMahon's behind-the-scenes role created the heel character 'Mr. McMahon' that helped fuel the Attitude Era.

question: At the King of the Ring 1996 wrestling pay-per-view, 'Stone Cold' Steve Austin won a one-night tournament by beating Jake 'The Snake' Roberts — a wrestler known for quoting the Bible — in the final. In his post-match speech, Austin mocked Jake's Scripture style and coined a two-word catchphrase that became a wrestling icon. What was the phrase?
context: Austin's exact line: 'You talk about your Psalms, you talk about John 3:16 — Austin 3:16 says I just whipped your ass!' The phrase put Austin's character over.

question: On June 28, 1998, at the King of the Ring pay-per-view in Pittsburgh, Mick Foley (wrestling as Mankind) climbed a sixteen-foot Hell in a Cell steel cage that covered the whole ring to fight The Undertaker. Undertaker first threw him off the side onto the announce table below. Foley climbed back up. Undertaker chokeslammed him again. What did Foley crash through next?
answer: The top of the cage, falling through to the ring
choices: The top of the cage, falling through to the ring
A stack of tables placed at ringside
A pile of steel folding chairs by the ring post
context: Foley was first thrown 16 feet off the top of the cell through the Spanish announce table. Later, he was chokeslammed THROUGH the top of the cell to the mat below. Both falls happened in the same match.

question: On May 19, 1996, at Madison Square Garden in New York City, the WWF (World Wrestling Federation) hosted a live event called In Your House: Beware of Dog. At the end of the night, a group of real-life best friends who worked for the company broke wrestling's oldest rule — never let fans see the good guys and bad guys hanging out — and hugged each other on stage in front of the whole arena. The moment became known as the Curtain Call, and the group of friends was called The Kliq. Who were the five men?
answer: Shawn Michaels, Razor Ramon, Diesel and Hunter Hearst Helmsley, who is Triple H
choices: Shawn Michaels, Razor Ramon, Diesel and Hunter Hearst Helmsley, who is Triple H
Bret Hart, Owen Hart, British Bulldog, Jim Neidhart, and Pillman
Hulk Hogan, Macho Man, Ultimate Warrior, Roddy Piper, and Mr. T
Stone Cold, The Rock, Mankind, Big Show, and Undertaker
context: Triple H was Hunter Hearst Helmsley at the time. The MSG curtain call broke kayfabe — heels and faces hugged. Vince McMahon was furious and punished Triple H by holding back his push.

question: On the night of July 7, 1996, at World Championship Wrestling (WCW)'s Bash at the Beach pay-per-view, Hulk Hogan shocked wrestling forever. For 13 years the biggest baby-face hero in the business, Hogan walked to the ring, dropped a leg on his own good-guy teammate, and joined heels Scott Hall and Kevin Nash as the mysterious 'third man'. What was their new faction called?
answer: The New World Order, or nWo
choices: The New World Order, or nWo
context: Hogan's heel turn — 'You can stick it, brother' — was one of the most iconic moments in wrestling. Fans threw garbage in the ring. The nWo dominated WCW programming for years.

question: On March 29, 1998, at WrestleMania XIV in Boston, boxing heavyweight champion Mike Tyson took a shocking guest role for the World Wrestling Federation (WWF). In the weeks before, he had been running a television storyline with the rebellious wrestling faction D-Generation X (DX). What was his official on-screen job at the main event that night?
answer: Special outside enforcer of the WWF Championship main event
choices: Special outside enforcer of the WWF Championship main event
Guest referee for the Undertaker vs Kane match
Special timekeeper at ringside during the main event
Special interviewer for the Raw post-show
context: Tyson's appearance was a major mainstream-attention coup. He counted the pin after Stone Cold's Stunner on Shawn Michaels — apparently switching loyalties from DX to Austin in the closing seconds. The Tyson-Austin angle reportedly drew the most media attention since Andre vs Hogan WM III.

question: From 1993 to 2001 a wild indie wrestling promotion based out of a small bingo hall in South Philadelphia, Pennsylvania became famous for barbed-wire matches, table-and-ladder brawls, and blood-soaked hardcore fights. Its booking mastermind was the New York manager Paul Heyman, and its rowdy stars included the mysterious high-flyer Sabu, the fan-favorite hometown hero Tommy Dreamer, and the shoot-fighter Taz. What was this Philadelphia promotion called?
context: ECW pioneered hardcore wrestling in the United States. Paul Heyman's edgy, indie-feel programming pressured WWF and WCW to push their content envelope. ECW folded in early 2001.

question: Triple H, whose real name is Paul Levesque, is one of professional wrestling's biggest stars — and later became WWE (World Wrestling Entertainment)'s head of talent. His signature finishing move is a face-down setup: he hooks both of his opponent's arms behind their back, tucks their head between his knees, and falls forward, driving the opponent's face into the mat. What is the move called?
context: Triple H started using the Pedigree in 1995. He started as Hunter Hearst Helmsley, a snobby New England aristocrat character, before D-Generation X turned him into a tough heel.

question: On April 1, 2001, at WrestleMania X-Seven in the Houston Astrodome in Texas, the hero Stone Cold Steve Austin fought The Rock for the World Wrestling Federation (WWF) title in the main event. Late in the match, a shocking figure jumped into the ring and helped Austin win, flipping Austin from good guy to bad guy. Who was that surprise helper?
answer: Vince McMahon, marking Austin's heel turn
choices: Vince McMahon, marking Austin's heel turn
Shane McMahon, after he ran in from the entranceway
Triple H, who had been Austin's longtime ally
Kurt Angle, mid-feud with both wrestlers
context: Austin's heel turn shocked fans. McMahon handed Austin chairs and helped him beat down The Rock. The booking was hotly criticized; Austin's heel run is widely seen as a major creative misstep.

question: On March 17, 2002, at WrestleMania X8 in Toronto's SkyDome, Hulk Hogan returned to the World Wrestling Federation (WWF, now WWE) after its purchase of World Championship Wrestling (WCW). Booked as the villain, he faced the current top hero The Rock in an 'Icon vs. Icon' match. The Toronto crowd surprised the bookers completely. What did they do?
answer: Cheering Hogan as the face and booing The Rock
choices: Cheering Hogan as the face and booing The Rock
Booing both men equally throughout the match
Chanting for Stone Cold Steve Austin to come out
Sitting in silence during the entire entrance
context: Hogan was scripted as the heel; the Toronto crowd ignored the script and treated him like the legend he was. Hogan turned face on the spot; The Rock embraced it.

question: The Seattle Seahawks joined the National Football League (NFL) as an expansion team in 1976. One of their first draft picks was a small-and-slow wide receiver from Tulsa nobody wanted. He played his entire 14-year career in Seattle, retired in 1989 with then-NFL records in catches and yards, and later served in the US Congress. Who was he?
context: Largent was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1995. He later served as a US Representative for Oklahoma from 1994 to 2002. The Seahawks number 80 is retired in his honor.

question: On January 19, 2014, the Seattle Seahawks hosted the San Francisco 49ers in the National Football Conference (NFC) championship game — winner going to the Super Bowl. In the final minute, with Seattle leading 23-17, 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick lofted a fade pass to the corner of the end zone. Seahawks cornerback Richard Sherman leaped up and tipped the ball away — a Seattle teammate caught the deflection and the Seahawks were headed to Super Bowl 48. Which 49ers receiver was Kaepernick throwing to when Sherman got the tip?
context: Sherman tipped the pass to teammate Malcolm Smith for the interception. The Erin Andrews postgame interview where Sherman shouted that he was the best corner in the game became instantly iconic.

question: Super Bowl 49 (XLIX) was played on February 1, 2015, in Glendale, Arizona, between the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots. With 26 seconds left and Seattle trailing 28-24, Seahawks quarterback Russell Wilson stood one yard from the winning touchdown. He threw a quick slant toward the goal line — but an unknown rookie Patriots cornerback stepped in front of the receiver, caught the ball, and ended the game right there. Who was the rookie who made the game-saving interception?
context: Butler was an undrafted rookie out of West Alabama. The Seahawks' decision to pass instead of handing the ball to Marshawn Lynch became one of the most second-guessed calls in football history.

question: On January 8, 2011, the Seattle Seahawks running back Marshawn Lynch took a handoff late in a wild-card playoff game against the New Orleans Saints. He broke nine tackles on a single 67-yard touchdown run, stiff-arming defenders and stomping the ball across the goal line. So many Seahawks fans jumped and screamed at once inside Qwest Field that a University of Washington seismograph a block away actually registered the tremor. What did the play get nicknamed?
context: The run helped the Seahawks upset the defending Super Bowl champion Saints 41-36. The University of Washington's Pacific Northwest Seismic Network confirmed the seismic signature.

question: In the 2005 NFL (National Football League) season, one Seattle Seahawks running back had the greatest year of his career. He rushed for 1,880 yards and scored 28 touchdowns, both leading the league, and the sportswriters named him NFL Most Valuable Player (MVP). Then his Seahawks were beaten in Super Bowl 40 by the Pittsburgh Steelers 21-10 in a title game full of controversial referee calls. Who was this MVP running back?
context: Alexander played at Alabama before being drafted by Seattle in 2000. He set the then-NFL single-season touchdown record with 28 in 2005. Super Bowl XL was decided 21-10 with several controversial officiating calls against Seattle.

question: In October 1995 the Seattle Mariners and New York Yankees played the deciding Game 5 of the American League Division Series inside the Kingdome. In the bottom of the 11th inning, tied 4-4, Mariners hitter Edgar Martinez lined a sharp double down the left-field line. Joey Cora scored easily from third, and a young Ken Griffey Jr. came flying around from first, sliding home headfirst with the winning run. Which Yankees pitcher had thrown that fateful pitch to Edgar?
context: Edgar's Double saved baseball in Seattle. The 1995 'Refuse to Lose' campaign and that hit are credited with securing public funding for what became Safeco Field.

question: In a 1996 episode of the NBC comedy Seinfeld, cranky Frank Costanza — the father of George Costanza — shouts a legendary rant right at New York Yankees owner George Steinbrenner: 'How could you trade Jay Buhner?!' Buhner really was a Seattle Mariners outfielder, and the Yankees really had traded him away in 1988 for another player. Who was the player the Yankees got back in that real-life trade?
context: The Yankees traded Buhner to Seattle in July 1988 for the aging Ken Phelps. Buhner hit 310 home runs for Seattle. The Seinfeld scene immortalized the trade as a Yankees blunder.

question: In 2001 the Seattle Mariners went on a historic tear, winning 116 regular-season games — the most in a single Major League Baseball season by any team of the modern era. That win total tied a record that had stood untouched since 1906, when one turn-of-the-century National League club also won 116 games in a single season. Which team originally set the 1906 record?
context: The 1906 Cubs won 116 games in a 152-game season; the 2001 Mariners won 116 in 162. Both teams failed to win the World Series — the Mariners lost the ALCS to the Yankees 4-1.

question: During the 2004 Major League Baseball season, Seattle Mariners right fielder Ichiro Suzuki chased a record that had stood since 1920 — most hits in a single season. All summer he sprayed singles, choppers, and bunts across American ballparks, finally passing George Sisler's mark of 257. How many total hits did Ichiro end that record-breaking season with?
context: Sisler's record of 257 had stood since 1920 — 84 years. Ichiro broke it on October 1, 2004. His 2004 batting average was .372. He hit 262 in 161 games.

question: On September 30, 2022, the Seattle Mariners hosted the Oakland Athletics with a chance to end the longest active playoff drought in North American major pro sports — twenty-one years without postseason baseball, going all the way back to 2001. In the bottom of the ninth, tied at 1-1, the Mariners' switch-hitting rookie catcher stepped in as pinch-hitter and drove a walk-off home run into right field. The dugout emptied at the plate. Who hit the wild-card-clinching homer?
context: The 2022 Mariners snapped a 21-year postseason drought — the longest active drought in the four major North American sports. They beat the Blue Jays in the AL Wild Card series.

question: American game designer Richard Garfield invented the trading card game Magic: The Gathering (MtG) in 1993. That same year he finished his doctorate (PhD) in mathematics from the University of Pennsylvania. The particular branch of math he studied is all about counting arrangements and analyzing games, and it directly helped him design MtG with balanced odds. What branch of mathematics was it?
answer: Combinatorial mathematics, specifically combinatorial game theory
choices: Combinatorial mathematics, specifically combinatorial game theory
Differential geometry, the mathematics of curved surfaces
Number theory, especially prime distribution and factorization
Topology, the mathematics of connectedness and continuity
context: Garfield was teaching at Whitman College when MtG took off. He had already designed RoboRally as a personal project. The mathematical rigor he brought to deckbuilding probabilities is part of why MtG balances so well even today.

question: Peter Adkison founded Wizards of the Coast in 1990 in a garage in Renton, Washington. He met Richard Garfield through a mutual acquaintance and saw a prototype of Magic in 1991. Adkison initially wanted to publish a different game by Garfield first. What was that other game?
choices: Cosmic Encounter, a sci-fi negotiation game
Talisman, a fantasy quest board game
context: Adkison loved RoboRally but the production cost was too high for the tiny Wizards startup. Garfield then designed Magic as something cheap to print. RoboRally finally published in 1994 after Magic's runaway success bankrolled WotC.

question: Magic: the Gathering's first World Championship was held at Gen Con in Milwaukee from August 18-21, 1994. Sixteen-year-old player Zak Dolan defeated Bertrand Lestree in the finals using a deck centered on a single artifact-type monster card. What was Dolan's win condition?
answer: Su-Chi, a powerful Antiquities artifact creature
choices: Su-Chi, a powerful Antiquities artifact creature
Sengir Vampire, the iconic Alpha vampire
Serra Angel, the white flying finisher
Lord of Atlantis, the blue merfolk lord
context: Dolan's deck used dual lands plus Power Nine acceleration into Su-Chi for fast clock pressure. The win earned him a $1,000 prize and his name etched in the Magic record books as the first World Champion.

question: In April 1996 Wizards of the Coast created a Magic: The Gathering (MtG) list of cards they officially promised never to reprint again, called the Reserved List. It was born from a huge fan revolt one year earlier: in July 1995 Wizards had released a compilation set that reprinted a big chunk of the most famous cards from earlier expansions like Antiquities and Legends, which crashed the collector market and made longtime players furious. What was the 1995 reprint set called?
choices: Revised, the third edition of the base set
context: Chronicles reprinted cards from Arabian Nights, Antiquities, Legends, and The Dark in cheap white-bordered form. Collectors who had paid premium prices saw values drop overnight. The Reserved List, including the Power Nine, was the calmer-down promise.

question: In June 1994 the Magic: The Gathering (MtG) expansion Legends introduced dozens of huge new legendary creatures. One card was a five-headed dragon-goddess borrowed straight from Dungeons and Dragons: Tiamat, queen of evil dragons. Another was a mighty red seven-power ancient wyrm — a scheming, primordial reptile who would become the game's most famous recurring villain across the next thirty years of storylines. Who was this blue-black-red 7/7 legendary creature?
answer: Nicol Bolas, the elder dragon legend
choices: Nicol Bolas, the elder dragon legend
context: The Legends Elder Dragons were Nicol Bolas, Arcades Sabboth, Chromium, Palladia-Mors, and Vaevictis Asmadi. They were among the first multicolor cards ever printed. Bolas became a central villain in lore.

question: In 1993 the trading card game Magic: The Gathering (MtG) shipped its first print run — a set fans now call Alpha, of only about 2.6 million cards. The very next print run, called Beta, and every printing after used the same designs. Even so, experienced collectors can tell an Alpha card from a Beta by one physical difference in the card itself. What tells them a card is Alpha?
answer: Rounder corners than Beta and all later printings
choices: Rounder corners than Beta and all later printings
Thicker cardstock than any later printing
Glossy front coating not used in later sets
Smaller text font on the rules box
context: Alpha cards have a noticeably larger corner radius than Beta cards. Beta sharpened the corners to standard playing-card dimensions. The Alpha rounded corners are the easiest visual tell of a 1993 first-run card.

question: MtG's Color Pie organizes the five colors along a circle: white is opposite black, blue is opposite red, green is opposite black. Each color has two 'enemy' colors and two 'allied' colors. White's allied colors are blue and green. What are white's two enemy colors?
context: The Color Pie matters mechanically — allied colors share more themes (white-blue control, blue-black graveyard, white-green lifegain) while enemy colors are designed in opposition. White's law-and-order conflicts with black's selfishness and red's freedom.

question: The trading card game Magic: The Gathering (MtG) held its very first Pro Tour at the Park Central Hotel in New York City in February 1996. The game's maker, Wizards of the Coast, invited 128 of the world's top players to compete for a $100,000 prize pool — an unheard-of purse for a card game at that time. The winner played a fast, aggressive strategy called White Weenie, using cheap little white creatures to swarm his opponents. Who won that first Pro Tour?
context: Loconto beat Bertrand Lestree in the finals using a white aggressive creature deck — a strategy not yet popular. The Pro Tour established competitive MtG as a serious sport with cash prizes. Loconto won $12,000.

question: From May 1963 to January 1971, the Italian-American strongman Bruno Sammartino held the World Wide Wrestling Federation (WWWF) championship without losing it once — a run of nearly eight years, still the longest single title reign in pro wrestling history. On the night his reign finally ended at Madison Square Garden in New York, one heel wrestler pinned him and took the belt. Who beat Sammartino that night?
choices: Pedro Morales, the Puerto Rican grappler
Superstar Billy Graham, the muscle-bound icon
context: Koloff pinned Sammartino on January 18, 1971, ending a 2,803-day reign. The MSG crowd was silent in shock. Koloff held the belt just 21 days before dropping it to Pedro Morales.

question: On March 31, 1985, at the very first WrestleMania inside Madison Square Garden in New York City, the muscular hero Hulk Hogan teamed with a hugely famous celebrity from film and TV to fight in the main event. Together they beat the villain team of Rowdy Roddy Piper and 'Mr. Wonderful' Paul Orndorff. Who was Hogan's celebrity tag team partner that historic night?
answer: Mr. T, fresh off Rocky III and The A-Team
choices: Mr. T, fresh off Rocky III and The A-Team
Cyndi Lauper, the pop star manager
context: Mr. T's involvement linked wrestling to mainstream Hollywood. Cyndi Lauper was at ringside; Muhammad Ali was the special outside enforcer; Liberace was the timekeeper. The whole night was a celebrity spectacular that legitimized the event.

question: Andre the Giant's iconic confrontation with Hulk Hogan at WrestleMania III took years to build. The two had been on-screen friends until February 7, 1987, when Andre publicly turned on Hogan on the Piper's Pit talk segment. What did Andre famously rip off Hogan's neck?
answer: Hogan's crucifix necklace, leaving a cut on his chest
choices: Hogan's crucifix necklace, leaving a cut on his chest
Hogan's iconic yellow bandanna with the red H
The WWF Championship belt itself, in a shocking grab
A handful of Hogan's signature yellow beard
context: Andre, prompted by his new manager Bobby 'The Brain' Heenan, tore Hogan's crucifix off in a violent flourish. The on-camera blood from the chain digging in was reportedly real. The angle launched a year of buildup to WrestleMania III.

question: On April 1, 1990, at WrestleMania VI inside the SkyDome in Toronto, Canada, the face-painted, tassel-wearing powerhouse the Ultimate Warrior beat Hulk Hogan in a rare champion-versus-champion match. Each wrestler had walked to the ring wearing a different championship belt. After the match, only one belt remained — the two titles had been unified. Which two belts got merged that night?
choices: WWF Championship and World Tag Team Championship
WWF Championship and World Television Championship
WWF Championship and King of the Ring crown
context: Warrior was the IC champion; Hogan held the WWF title. The Warrior won and held both belts for the first time in WWF history. He held the WWF title until SummerSlam 1990, when he lost it to Sgt. Slaughter.

question: On August 29, 1992, the World Wrestling Federation (WWF) held its SummerSlam pay-per-view at Wembley Stadium in London — the biggest match card ever staged outside North America. In the main match, Canadian star Bret 'The Hitman' Hart defended his Intercontinental Championship in front of more than 80,000 British fans, most of them cheering not for Bret but for his real-life brother-in-law, an English wrestler challenging him. The Brit won the belt that night. Who was Bret's opponent?
answer: Davey Boy Smith, the British Bulldog
choices: Davey Boy Smith, the British Bulldog
Jim Neidhart, his Hart Foundation tag partner
Mr. Perfect, his then-rival Curt Hennig
context: Davey Boy Smith was married to Bret's sister Diana. The Wembley match was a 26-minute classic. Bret carried Smith, who later admitted he had blanked on much of the choreography and that Bret called every spot in real time.

question: On January 4, 1999, the World Wrestling Federation (WWF) show Monday Night Raw aired a taped episode showing Mick Foley — wrestling under the strange sack-masked character Mankind — winning the WWF Championship for the very first time. That same night, rival wrestling company World Championship Wrestling (WCW) was airing its live show Monday Nitro directly against Raw. Knowing the taped WWF result had leaked, someone at WCW's announce table read the spoiler on the air, hoping viewers would change the channel. Who delivered the spoiler?
choices: Eric Bischoff, the head of WCW
Ric Flair, the Four Horsemen leader
Mean Gene Okerlund, the WCW interviewer
context: Schiavone said 'Mick Foley is gonna win the WWF Championship — that's gonna put a lot of butts in seats.' Roughly 600,000 viewers reportedly flipped from Nitro to Raw. Schiavone has expressed lasting regret over the announcement.

question: Stone Cold Steve Austin's first WWF Championship win came at WrestleMania XIV on March 29, 1998, in Boston. He beat Shawn Michaels in Shawn's last match for over four years — Michaels had been suffering from a serious injury. What injury caused Shawn's hiatus?
answer: A serious back injury, including a herniated disc
choices: A serious back injury, including a herniated disc
A torn rotator cuff that required reconstructive surgery
A career-ending concussion from a casket match
A torn ACL from a leap off the Hell in a Cell
context: Shawn had originally hurt his back at Royal Rumble 1998 during a casket match with the Undertaker. He held on to the title for WrestleMania despite barely being able to walk. He did not wrestle again until 2002.

question: In the late 1990s the WWF (World Wrestling Federation) superstar Dwayne 'The Rock' Johnson turned the sneering insult 'jabroni' into a household word, using it to call out wrestlers he considered nobodies. The term came from old traveling-carnival wrestling slang. It named a wrestler whose only job was to lose on purpose so that the top star would look strong. What was that traditional losing-role called inside the wrestling business?
answer: A job or jobber, hence jabroni
choices: A job or jobber, hence jabroni
A heel or henchman in the locker room
A bumper, the rookie who took practice falls
context: A 'jobber' is someone who does the job — loses to make the star over. The Rock anglicized 'jabroni' from the Italian/carny mispronunciation. The term entered the cultural lexicon largely because of him.

question: Kane debuted at the In Your House: Bad Blood pay-per-view on October 5, 1997, interrupting an Undertaker vs Shawn Michaels Hell in a Cell match. The first-ever Hell in a Cell match itself ran 30 minutes, after which the lights went out. Who arrived in a red-and-black costume to attack the Undertaker?
choices: The Big Boss Man, freshly heel
context: Kane was Glenn Jacobs, who had played multiple gimmicks (Isaac Yankem DDS, the fake Diesel). The Undertaker-Kane brother feud became one of WWF's longest-running stories, going all the way to a 2010 WrestleMania match.

question: On August 9, 1999, during the World Wrestling Federation (WWF) television show Monday Night Raw, a mystery 30-second countdown clock ticked down while The Rock was cutting a promo in the ring. When it hit zero, the arena went into flashing lights, the crowd exploded, and a cocky new wrestler strolled out to cut The Rock off mid-sentence. What was this brand-new character called?
choices: Tazz, the WWF debut from ECW
context: Y2J — short for Year Two-Thousand Jericho — referenced the Y2K bug. Jericho had been WCW's star and chose to jump ship for a bigger role. He went on to become the first Undisputed Champion in WWF history in December 2001.

question: In the early 2000s the beloved Mexican-American WWE (World Wrestling Entertainment) wrestler Eddie Guerrero played a heel — the bad guy — who openly cheated to win. He'd hide brass knuckles in the ring, hit the referee behind their back, then grin at the camera. Instead of denying it, Eddie leaned all the way in with a three-word catchphrase he'd holler to the crowd, and fans loved him so much they chanted it back at him. What was Eddie's three-word phrase?
context: Eddie Guerrero made the heel turn an art form: hit referees from the blind side, then plead innocence, then act offended. His tragic death in November 2005 — at age 38 — devastated the wrestling world.

question: American wrestler Kurt Angle signed with the World Wrestling Federation (WWF) in late 1999 with a credential no other WWF wrestler could match — a real Olympic gold medal from the 1996 Summer Games in Atlanta, Georgia. Fans mocked him with 'You suck!' chants, but he really was an Olympic champion. In what specific sport and weight class did Angle win his 1996 gold medal?
context: Angle won gold despite a broken neck — he wrestled with two cracked vertebrae. His credentials helped him transition into wrestling instantly. His three I's were Intensity, Integrity, and Intelligence.

question: In 1989, Seattle Seahawks wide receiver Steve Largent retired from the National Football League (NFL) holding every major career record for pass catchers — most receptions, most yards, most touchdowns. Five years later, in 1994, he ran for the U.S. House of Representatives as a Republican and won his very first campaign. Which state's congressional district did Congressman Largent go on to represent?
context: Largent was a four-term congressman until 2002, when he made an unsuccessful run for Oklahoma governor. He had been the all-time leader in catches (819), receiving yards (13,089), and TD catches (100) when he retired.

question: For twelve straight seasons from 1997 to 2008, the Seattle Seahawks' offensive line was anchored by one enormous Alabama-born left tackle drafted sixth overall out of Florida State. He made nine Pro Bowls, protected quarterbacks like Matt Hasselbeck, and paved running lanes for MVPs like Shaun Alexander. He never played for another team and was elected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2014. What was his name?
context: Walter Jones was inducted to the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2014. He famously held out three times as the franchise tagged him in consecutive years — and never missed a game from those holdouts. He blocked for Shaun Alexander's MVP season.

question: Russell Wilson was a third-round pick (75th overall) in the 2012 NFL Draft. He had transferred for his final college season from one school to another after being passed over as the starter at his original school. Which two schools did he attend in football?
answer: NC State, then Wisconsin for his senior year
choices: NC State, then Wisconsin for his senior year
Virginia Tech, then Florida State for graduate transfer
Boise State, then Oregon for a transfer year
Stanford, then North Carolina for a transfer year
context: Wilson played quarterback and baseball at NC State. When Mike Glennon was named starting QB for 2011, Wilson used the graduate transfer rule to go to Wisconsin. He led the Badgers to the Rose Bowl that season.

question: The National Football League championship game XLVIII was played on February 2, 2014, at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey between the Denver Broncos and the Seattle Seahawks. The Broncos, led by veteran quarterback Peyton Manning, were the favorites. On the very first play from scrimmage, Manning was still reading the defense at the line when the center hiked the ball — it sailed straight over Manning's head into the end zone, where a Broncos lineman jumped on it. What did that opening play score for Seattle?
answer: A safety, the fastest in Super Bowl history at 12 seconds
choices: A safety, the fastest in Super Bowl history at 12 seconds
A touchdown after Lynch recovered the fumble
A field goal after Hauschka kicked from the 5-yard line
A turnover on downs after Manning failed to recover
context: Center Manny Ramirez snapped the ball before Manning was ready. The ball flew through the end zone for a safety. The 12-second score was the fastest in Super Bowl history. The Broncos never recovered.

question: Cortez Kennedy was a huge defensive tackle who played eleven seasons in the National Football League (NFL) for the Seattle Seahawks. In 1992 his team had a terrible season and finished with only two wins and fourteen losses. Even on a losing team, Kennedy was a wrecking ball on the defensive line, and the league honors its top defender each year. Kennedy took home that award. What was it called?
answer: NFL Defensive Player of the Year
choices: NFL Defensive Player of the Year
Walter Payton Man of the Year Award
NFL Comeback Player of the Year
context: Cortez Kennedy was virtually impossible to single-block. He recorded 14 sacks from defensive tackle in 1992. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2012. He died unexpectedly in May 2017 at age 48.

question: Ken Griffey Jr. was the Seattle Mariners' star center fielder in the 1990s — a slugger with a gorgeous swing and a highlight-reel glove. In 1995 he tied a Major League Baseball record by hitting home runs in eight consecutive games, matching Don Mattingly and Dale Long. Earlier that same season, though, Junior made a full-speed catch running toward the outfield wall of the Mariners' indoor stadium, the Kingdome, and paid a huge price for the play — he missed months of the season. What was the injury?
answer: He broke his left wrist crashing into the Kingdome wall making a catch
choices: He broke his left wrist crashing into the Kingdome wall making a catch
He tore his hamstring legging out an infield single
He suffered a season-ending concussion from a beanball
He shattered his ankle stealing third base
context: Griffey crashed into the wall on May 26, 1995 making a spectacular catch. He returned in August. The injury cost Seattle his presence for half a season, but his return helped fuel the 'Refuse to Lose' playoff push.

question: Ken Griffey Jr's father, Ken Griffey Sr., joined the Mariners for the 1990 season, allowing father and son to play together in the same outfield. On September 14, 1990, they did something no other father-son duo had ever done in a Major League game. What was it?
answer: Hit back-to-back home runs in the same inning
choices: Hit back-to-back home runs in the same inning
Started a triple play together in the outfield
Each hit two home runs in the same game
context: Griffey Sr. and Jr. hit back-to-back homers off Kirk McCaskill of the Angels at Anaheim Stadium. Junior was 20; Sr. was 40. They had played together since August 31, 1990. No father-son duo has ever done it since.

question: In 2001 the Japanese hitter Ichiro Suzuki joined the Seattle Mariners as a rookie. He collected 242 hits, batted .350, and won both the American League Rookie of the Year and the Most Valuable Player awards. On top of those, his outfield defense and his batting stroke each earned another famous honor that season. Which two awards did he add?
answer: Gold Glove and Silver Slugger in right field
choices: Gold Glove and Silver Slugger in right field
Roberto Clemente Award and Cy Young Award
Hank Aaron Award and Babe Ruth Award
Comeback Player of the Year and All-Star MVP
context: Ichiro's 2001 was unprecedented for a rookie. He won 10 consecutive Gold Gloves and 10 consecutive Silver Sluggers. He stole 56 bases, then a Mariners record for a single season.

question: One legendary Seattle Mariners hitter, born in New York in 1963 and raised in Puerto Rico, spent most of his career as a designated hitter (DH), rarely playing in the field. He hit .312 lifetime, made seven All-Star teams, and was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 2019. Major League Baseball had long given out a yearly award to the best DH in the game — and after his greatness redefined the position, the league renamed that trophy after someone. Who is the DH-of-the-year prize named for?
context: MLB renamed the Outstanding DH Award the Edgar Martinez Award in 2004, the year he retired. He won it five times during his career, before they renamed it for him.

question: The 2001 Mariners won 116 games but lost the American League Championship Series (ALCS) to the New York Yankees 4 games to 1. The Mariners had reached the ALCS once before, in 1995. Which team eliminated the Mariners from the 2000 ALCS?
choices: The Red Sox, in a 4-1 series
context: The 2000 Mariners were the team Alex Rodriguez left after — he signed with Texas for $252M. They made the ALCS that year and lost to the Yankees. The 2001 team set a record and lost to the Yankees again.

question: Magic: the Gathering's Power Nine is the most coveted set of cards in the game's history. Eight of the nine were printed only in Alpha, Beta, and Unlimited (1993). The ninth was reprinted in subsequent base sets through 1995 before joining the Reserved List. Which card had that broader print history?
answer: Time Vault, which appeared in Beta, Unlimited, Revised, and Fourth Edition
choices: Time Vault, which appeared in Beta, Unlimited, Revised, and Fourth Edition
Mox Pearl, the one mox printed in all white-border base sets
Black Lotus, reprinted in International Edition only
Ancestral Recall, reprinted in Chronicles 1995 by accident
context: Time Vault — an artifact that taps for two extra turns if untapped consecutively — was originally so broken Wizards errata-ed it multiple times. The Power Nine are: Black Lotus, Ancestral Recall, Time Walk, Timetwister, and the five Moxes. Time Vault is sometimes called the 'tenth' Power but more often grouped with the nine.

question: In 1993, mathematician Richard Garfield invented Magic: The Gathering (MtG), a trading card game where each player builds a unique deck and duels using spells and creatures. Garfield built the game around one guiding rule: any three cards drawn together should combine into some kind of workable plan. He borrowed that combo-first idea from another game he had loved for years — a science-fiction board game where every player controlled an alien species with one game-breaking special power. Which game inspired him?
answer: Cosmic Encounter, a science-fiction negotiation game from 1977
choices: Cosmic Encounter, a science-fiction negotiation game from 1977
Diplomacy, the World War I negotiation board game
Settlers of Catan, the resource-trading board game
context: Cosmic Encounter gives each player a unique alien race with a different rule-breaking power. The constant exception-creation taught Garfield how interesting it is when every card breaks at least one base rule. Garfield was a longtime board-gamer who eventually designed Roborally, King of Tokyo, and others.

question: Magic: the Gathering's first World Championship in August 1994 at Gen Con in Milwaukee was won by 16-year-old Zak Dolan. The runner-up, Bertrand Lestree from France, was famous for a single deck that has since become legendary in MtG circles. What kind of strategy was Lestree's deck?
answer: A green creature-stomp deck featuring Erhnam Djinn and forest mana acceleration
choices: A green creature-stomp deck featuring Erhnam Djinn and forest mana acceleration
A white-blue control deck featuring the Power Nine and counters
A black-red burn deck featuring Hypnotic Specter and Lightning Bolt
A mono-blue prison deck featuring Time Walk and Howling Mine
context: Lestree's green stompy deck became iconic; his use of Land Tax and big green creatures inspired later 'Erhnamgeddon' (Ernham Djinn + Armageddon) decks. Garfield himself credited Lestree's deck as one of the first to show MtG could be played at a tournament-tactics level.

question: MtG's June 1994 Legends expansion was the largest set ever printed up to that point — 310 cards. Legends introduced multicolor cards, the legendary supertype, and the 'banding' mechanic. It also introduced a card that became infamous for an unusual restriction on how many copies you can have in your deck — a single card. What card was that?
answer: Karakas, a legendary land restricted because it could bounce any legendary creature
choices: Karakas, a legendary land restricted because it could bounce any legendary creature
Mana Crypt, an artifact that dealt damage to its controller
The Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale, a legendary land taxing creatures
Mana Drain, a counterspell that produced bonus mana
context: Karakas was eventually restricted to one copy in Vintage and banned in Legacy because it counters powerful legendary creatures. The Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale, another iconic Legends land, was not restricted but became infamously expensive. Mana Drain was restricted in Vintage for being a one-cost counterspell that effectively generated free mana.

question: On August 5, 1993, the first sets of the trading card game Magic: The Gathering (MtG) rolled off the presses, timed to reach the huge Gen Con gaming convention in Milwaukee. The game's tiny maker, Wizards of the Coast, was down to its last dollars — founder Peter Adkison could not even wait for delivery. He got in a car, drove all the way to the print shop himself, and loaded the first boxes of cards straight into his trunk. In what town was the print shop?
answer: From Carthage, Tennessee, where the printing plant was located
choices: From Carthage, Tennessee, where the printing plant was located
From Cincinnati, Ohio, the nearest Hasbro production hub
From Toronto, Canada, where the cards were printed for export
From Mexico City, where the cardstock was sourced
context: The Carthage TN plant — a Cartamundi/USPCC facility — printed the original Alpha sheet. Adkison rented a U-Haul and personally drove cards to Gen Con. The story of those first sales is recounted in 'Generation Decks' and in interviews Adkison gave in the 2010s.

question: MtG's 1994 Legends set introduced the Elder Dragons: five legendary three-color dragons that each cost 8 mana. One of them became the game's most enduring villain, returning across storylines for the next thirty years. Which Elder Dragon, in blue-black-red, is that recurring villain?
context: Nicol Bolas is depicted with horns and golden eyes; the original Legends artwork by Mark Tedin became iconic. The Elder Dragon Highlander format (later renamed Commander) took its name from this cycle. Bolas became a planeswalker in lore, then de-sparked, then returned multiple times.

question: The Black Lotus card from MtG Alpha has become a symbol of trading-card value. In 2021, a single Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) Gem Mint 10 Alpha Black Lotus signed by Christopher Rush, the original illustrator, sold at auction for a record-breaking sum. What was the approximate price?
context: The card was sold by PWCC Marketplace in January 2021. Christopher Rush, who illustrated Black Lotus and other iconic Alpha cards, died in March 2016. Signed Rush Lotuses are especially prized. A 2023 sale of another PSA 10 Alpha Lotus reportedly exceeded $540,000 privately.

question: Magic: the Gathering's first banned-and-restricted list for tournament play in 1994 named several cards. One Alpha sorcery, when combined with Fireball, could kill an opponent on turn one by trading a huge chunk of the caster's own health for a burst of colorless mana. The card was eventually restricted to one per deck rather than banned outright. What was the sorcery?
answer: Channel, the Alpha green sorcery converting life into mana
choices: Channel, the Alpha green sorcery converting life into mana
Mishra's Workshop, the Antiquities artifact land producing colorless mana
Strip Mine, the original land-destruction land from Antiquities
Bazaar of Baghdad, the Arabian Nights draw engine of choice
context: Channel-Fireball was a notorious combo for first-turn kills. The combination was named so widely that the gaming retailer Channel Fireball (founded by Jon Finkel and Luis Scott-Vargas) took its name from the play. Channel itself remains restricted in Vintage to this day.

question: In 1991, Texas wrestler Steve Austin — later famous worldwide as 'Stone Cold' Steve Austin in the World Wrestling Federation (WWF) — joined the rival wrestling company World Championship Wrestling (WCW) as a good-looking villain called 'Stunning' Steve Austin. He won two WCW titles in four years there. But in 1995 the head of WCW, Eric Bischoff, decided to cut him — while Austin was at home recovering from a torn triceps surgery. Bischoff did not call. He did not visit. How did the firing reach Austin?
answer: A FedEx envelope delivered to Austin while he was injured
choices: A FedEx envelope delivered to Austin while he was injured
A phone call during Austin's recovery from triceps surgery
An in-person meeting at the WCW offices in Atlanta
A handwritten letter mailed to Austin's Texas home
context: Austin had torn his triceps tendon while wrestling in Japan. WCW released him because Bischoff said Austin couldn't draw. Austin used the firing as fuel — the bitter chip on his shoulder created the 'Stone Cold' character. He went to ECW briefly before debuting in the WWF in early 1996.

question: Mick Foley's 1999 autobiography 'Have a Nice Day: A Tale of Blood and Sweatsocks' was a New York Times bestseller. Foley wrote the entire book longhand in spiral notebooks. The hand-written manuscript was unusual in another way that became part of the book's mythology. What was unique about how Foley wrote it?
answer: He wrote the whole 500+ page book in pencil while flying coach between WWF house shows
choices: He wrote the whole 500+ page book in pencil while flying coach between WWF house shows
He dictated it to his wife, who transcribed it on a typewriter
He composed it in a hotel office during a year-long retirement
He emailed chapters to ghostwriter J.R. Moehringer for editing
context: Foley wrote in spiral notebooks during his constant travel. Editor Michael Wright assembled the chapters from Foley's handwritten pages. The book sold over 1 million copies. Foley dedicated it to his daughter Noelle. Three follow-up memoirs followed — Foley Is Good, The Hardcore Diaries, and Countdown to Lockdown.

question: The Montreal Screwjob on November 9, 1997, at the Molson Centre, came at the Survivor Series in Bret Hart's home country of Canada. After referee Earl Hebner called for the bell on a hold Bret had not submitted to, Shawn Michaels won the WWF Championship. What did Bret Hart do to Vince McMahon after the show?
answer: Punched McMahon in the locker room, breaking his ankle in the resulting fall
choices: Punched McMahon in the locker room, breaking his ankle in the resulting fall
Filed a lawsuit for breach of contract that took two years to settle
Sent McMahon a hand-written resignation letter the next morning
Spit in McMahon's face during a press conference in Toronto
context: Bret punched McMahon backstage; Vince sprained his ankle when he fell. The incident is captured in the 1998 documentary 'Wrestling with Shadows.' Bret left for WCW and didn't return to WWE until 2010. McMahon developed his on-screen 'Mr. McMahon' heel character largely as a response to the Montreal aftermath.

question: D-Generation X's signature catchphrase was a question and answer, delivered with crotch-chopping flourishes that became merch gold. Shawn Michaels and Triple H would shout the question; the crowd would shout the answer. What was the call-and-response?
answer: Are you ready? — followed by 'two words: SUCK IT'
choices: Are you ready? — followed by 'two words: SUCK IT'
Whatcha gonna do? — followed by 'Hulkamania runs wild'
Can I get a hell yeah? — followed by Stone Cold's whoop
Who's the man? — followed by 'The Rock is the man'
context: DX formed in 1997 with Shawn Michaels, Triple H, Chyna, and Rick Rude. After Shawn's back injury in 1998, Triple H led the second iteration including X-Pac and the New Age Outlaws. Their crotch-chops and 'SUCK IT' became defining Attitude Era moments.

question: The Rock's first WWF Championship reign began at Survivor Series on November 15, 1998. The Rock pinned Mankind in the finals of a 14-man tournament for the vacant WWF title. What controversial development from the match created a key Attitude-Era heel turn?
answer: Vince McMahon switched alignment and helped The Rock cheat to win, forming the Corporation
choices: Vince McMahon switched alignment and helped The Rock cheat to win, forming the Corporation
The Rock low-blowed Mankind without a referee seeing it
Mankind tapped out to a fake submission for a cash payoff
Shawn Michaels returned to interfere on The Rock's behalf
context: The Rock had been a babyface; his joining the Corporation heel faction with McMahon was a major character pivot. McMahon called The Rock 'The Corporate Champion.' This set up the year-long Rock-Mankind-Austin triangle that defined late 1998 and 1999.

question: Goldberg's undefeated streak in World Championship Wrestling (WCW) began in September 1997 and eventually reached a claimed 173 wins with zero losses, according to WCW's on-air announcers. Then he finally lost at Starrcade on December 27, 1998. Who beat him that night?
answer: Kevin Nash, with help from Scott Hall using a stun gun
choices: Kevin Nash, with help from Scott Hall using a stun gun
Hulk Hogan, in a one-on-one match without interference
Sting, with a Scorpion Death Lock submission
Bret Hart, after a Sharpshooter that Goldberg verbally submitted to
context: Scott Hall ran in disguised as a security guard and hit Goldberg with a taser disguised as a cattle prod. Kevin Nash then pinned him with a Jackknife Powerbomb. Goldberg's real win-loss record in WCW was much lower than 173-0, but the kayfabe number is the famous one.

question: In the mid-1990s, star wrestler Sting was one of the biggest faces of World Championship Wrestling (WCW). For years he had been the company's smiling face-painted good-guy hero — bright colors, blond flat-top haircut, huge arena energy. In 1996 he changed everything. He grew silent, switched to black leather and white face paint, and started appearing high in the arena rafters holding a black baseball bat. His new look was copied directly from a 1994 movie about a rock musician who returns from the dead. Which movie?
choices: Phantom of the Opera, the Broadway revival
context: Sting hid in the rafters of WCW arenas for months in 1996-97, watching events without intervening. He finally returned at Starrcade 1997 to face Hollywood Hogan for the WCW World title. The Crow-inspired character became Sting's most iconic look.

question: Mike Tyson appeared at WrestleMania 14 as the special enforcer in the main event between Stone Cold Steve Austin and Shawn Michaels. His booking was a massive publicity win for the WWF. Roughly what did the WWF reportedly pay Tyson for that appearance?
answer: Around $3 million for his WrestleMania involvement and lead-up TV appearances
choices: Around $3 million for his WrestleMania involvement and lead-up TV appearances
About $1.5 million flat fee for the night
Approximately $500,000 with no TV appearance bonus
context: Tyson appeared on multiple Raw episodes leading up to WrestleMania XIV. He clashed with Austin on Raw in January 1998, with Austin shoving him; the whole angle drew massive buzz. The Tyson buy-in is credited with reviving WWF's mainstream attention right before Austin took over as champion.

question: On September 4, 1995, World Championship Wrestling (WCW) launched Monday Nitro on Turner Network Television, kicking off a head-to-head Monday-night broadcast war against WWF Raw. Lex Luger's surprise appearance drew the opening cheers, but the biggest shock arrived at the end of the show. What happened in Hulk Hogan's main-event match?
answer: Sting, his ally, attacked him after his match with Big Bubba Rogers
choices: Sting, his ally, attacked him after his match with Big Bubba Rogers
He lost the WCW Championship to Vader in a clean pin
He was attacked by Ric Flair and the Four Horsemen on his way out
He was injured by a chair shot from a returning Randy Savage
context: Sting's heel-turn attack on Hogan was a shocking debut-night moment. Lex Luger had just appeared, also stunning the WWF — he was supposedly under contract there. The night signaled the start of the Monday Night Wars, which ran until 2001.

question: Vince McMahon Jr. inherited control of Capitol Wrestling Corporation from his father in 1982. Under his ownership it became WWF and then WWE. Vince made an aggressive move that altered the wrestling business permanently — he ignored the unwritten rule that promoters didn't poach other territories' top talent. The first major star he poached, kicking off the national expansion, was who?
answer: Hulk Hogan, who had been working for Verne Gagne's AWA
choices: Hulk Hogan, who had been working for Verne Gagne's AWA
Andre the Giant, who had been a Vince Sr loyalist
Bob Backlund, who was already WWWF champion
Roddy Piper, from Stampede Wrestling in Calgary
context: Hogan had been working for Verne Gagne's AWA and had developed Hulkamania there. Vince Jr signed him in December 1983 and immediately put the WWF title on him in January 1984. The territorial system collapsed within a few years; Vince had bought the country.

question: Chyna, billed as the Ninth Wonder of the World (Andre the Giant having been the Eighth), broke major gender barriers in the WWF. In 1999, she became the first woman to enter the Royal Rumble, and later that year became the first to win the Intercontinental Championship (IC). Who did she defeat for that IC belt at the No Mercy 1999 pay-per-view?
answer: Jeff Jarrett, in a 'Good Housekeeping' gimmick match
choices: Jeff Jarrett, in a 'Good Housekeeping' gimmick match
Chris Jericho, in a singles match with no time limit
Triple H, in a stipulation match on Raw
X-Pac, in a no-disqualification gimmick match
context: Jarrett had been champion. The Good Housekeeping match involved household objects (irons, vacuum cleaners, frying pans) as weapons. Chyna's real name was Joan Laurer. She passed away in April 2016.

question: The Guerrero family became one of the most famous names in pro wrestling. Eddie Guerrero later became a World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) champion, but the family tree went much deeper -- his father, known in the ring simply as Gory, was a lucha libre legend who trained sons and grandsons and ran his own regional wrestling promotion for decades starting in the 1940s. That promotion was based in one particular city on the U.S.-Mexico border. Where did Gory run his shows?
answer: El Paso, Texas — Gory Guerrero ran a promotion there from the 1940s
choices: El Paso, Texas — Gory Guerrero ran a promotion there from the 1940s
Mexico City — the Guerreros co-founded CMLL
San Antonio — the Guerrero brothers ran a Texas territory
Los Angeles — Eddie's family ran the LA Coliseum circuit
context: Gory Guerrero, Eddie's father, was a luchador legend who ran his own promotion. Eddie's brothers Hector, Chavo Sr, and Mando all wrestled professionally. Eddie debuted in lucha libre at AAA before going to ECW, then WCW, then WWE.

question: Super Bowl XL on February 5, 2006, in Detroit ended in a 21-10 loss for the Seahawks to the Pittsburgh Steelers. The game was marred by officiating controversies. Late in the third quarter, Seattle thought it had taken the lead on a Jerramy Stevens catch ruled in-bounds; head referee Bill Leavy reversed it. Years later, what did Leavy publicly admit about his officiating in that game?
answer: He had 'kicked' two specific calls and the controversy haunted him
choices: He had 'kicked' two specific calls and the controversy haunted him
He had been bribed by a Pittsburgh booster prior to the game
His crew had been improperly trained on the rules in effect
He believed the league had pressured him to favor Pittsburgh
context: Leavy made his public apology at Seahawks training camp in 2010. He acknowledged the Darrell Jackson offensive pass interference (waving off a TD) and a holding call on Sean Locklear were both wrong calls. Mike Holmgren said the team felt they had to beat 'two opponents' in the game.

question: Marshawn Lynch was the Seattle Seahawks' bruising running back, nicknamed 'Beast Mode' after a phrase he had picked up as an undergraduate at Cal-Berkeley. Lynch famously hated the required Super Bowl-week media sessions. In the days before Super Bowl 49 in early 2015, he arrived at the podium — and to avoid a heavy National Football League (NFL) fine for skipping media day, he answered every single reporter's question with one identical repeated sentence. What was the sentence?
answer: I'm just here so I won't get fined
choices: I'm just here so I won't get fined
Beast Mode, that's all I got
context: Lynch had been fined repeatedly by the NFL for refusing to speak to media. At Super Bowl XLIX media day, he attended for less than five minutes and used the line as his only response. The NFL eventually changed media-availability rules after the Lynch saga.

question: The Seahawks-Patriots Super Bowl XLIX (49) ended with one of the most famous play calls in football history. With one yard to go and 26 seconds left, on second down, offensive coordinator Darrell Bevell called a slant pass to Ricardo Lockette instead of a Lynch run. Why did Bevell later say the team didn't run the ball there?
answer: To save time and avoid a third-down clock issue
choices: To save time and avoid a third-down clock issue
Wilson had audibled out of the planned run call
The Patriots had only one timeout left and Seattle panicked
Lynch was injured and needed a play to catch his breath
context: Bevell took heat from fans for the call. Pete Carroll defended it as the best decision given the Patriots' goal-line stack expected a run. Malcolm Butler had been studying that exact play on film all week. The play call is one of the most second-guessed in NFL history.

question: On January 8, 2011, Seattle Seahawks running back Marshawn Lynch made a legendary 67-yard touchdown run against the visiting New Orleans Saints in a National Football League (NFL) playoff game.
