question: A blue-haired teenage girl from the city arrives on her motorbike where the wild boy Goku lives alone in the mountains. She carries a strange invention, the Dragon Radar, which pings whenever it detects one of seven magic orbs. Goku and the girl team up to hunt them. What is her name?
context: Bulma is the daughter of Dr. Brief, founder of Capsule Corp (Japan's most innovative inventor). Her name comes from the Japanese pronunciation of 'bloomers' (underwear); Toriyama named all the Briefs family after underwear. She eventually marries Vegeta.

question: In the Pokemon anime, ten-year-old Ash Ketchum starts his journey from Pallet Town with his stubborn partner Pikachu. On Route 1, the very first path outside town, he catches his first wild Pokemon — a small green bug that will later evolve twice into the Butterfree he tearfully sets free in a famous Season 1 goodbye episode. What kind of Pokemon did he first catch?
context: Episode 3 ('Ash Catches a Pokemon') has Ash threading a Poke Ball through Pidgeotto's wings to capture the Caterpie below. The Butterfree-release episode ('Bye Bye Butterfree,' Episode 21) traumatized a generation of late-90s kids.

question: In Kohei Horikoshi's manga My Hero Academia, the number-one hero All Might passes his inherited superpower — his Quirk — down to shy middle-schooler Izuku Midoriya. But the Quirk didn't begin with All Might. In the earliest days of Quirks, two brothers with matching powers fought each other bitterly. One brother could steal other people's Quirks and hoard them; the other could pass a single Quirk down across generations. Their rivalry became the show's central conflict. What are the two rival powers called?
answer: One For All and All For One
choices: One For All and All For One
context: All For One can steal quirks; his idealistic younger brother received One For All as a quirk-stockpiling counter. Each successor adds new strength to the next, and the brother's spirit was unwittingly attached — which is why Deku can communicate with past holders.

question: In Hajime no Ippo, Ippo's most personal title fight, held in 2000, is against a boxer from Osaka nicknamed the Naniwa Tiger. His signature Smash hook once knocked Ippo down in an earlier match, and the two grow to respect each other. Who is Ippo's title-fight opponent?
context: Sendo first appeared as a heel character mocking Ippo before their first fight. He becomes the OPBF Japanese Featherweight Champion. His finishing blow, 'Smash,' is a hook from a crouched stance. Morikawa modeled Sendo loosely on real Japanese boxer Takenori Hosaka.

question: Demon Slayer's nine Hashira each master a unique Breathing Style. The Stone Hashira is a tall, blind, prayer-bead-wearing warrior universally considered the strongest among the active pillars. Tanjiro trains under him during the Hashira Training Arc. Name him.
context: Gyomei was nearly executed in his civilian life after killing demons that attacked the orphanage he tended; the law refused to believe demons existed. Stone Breathing has five forms. He fights with a flail-and-axe weapon connected by a chain, used together with bead-prayers.

question: Naruto Shippuden opens two-and-a-half years after the first Naruto series, with the ninja hero Naruto Uzumaki now a teenager. It introduces the Akatsuki, a group of nine rogue ninja in black cloaks patterned with red clouds. Their opening move is to kidnap the young ruler of the desert Village Hidden in the Sand — a red-haired former enemy who has since become one of Naruto's dearest friends. Who do they take?
context: Gaara carries the One-Tailed beast, Shukaku, sealed inside him, which is why the Akatsuki, who hunt the tailed beasts, come for him. His kidnapping launches the rescue mission that opens Shippuden.

question: In Eiichiro Oda's manga One Piece, the young Monkey D. Luffy grows up in Windmill Village worshipping a crew of pirates who drink at the local bar. Before they sail away, their red-haired captain hands the boy his own treasured straw hat, on one condition: Luffy must become a great pirate someday and bring it back to him. Who gave Luffy the hat?
context: Shanks gives Luffy his straw hat before leaving Windmill Village, on the condition that Luffy becomes a great pirate and returns it. The same chapter has Shanks lose his left arm saving the boy from a Sea King, a monstrous sea beast.

question: Hajime Isayama showed his early pages of Attack on Titan, the story of humans huddled behind stone walls, to the editors of the most famous boys' weekly in Japan. They told him to change his style to suit their magazine. He refused, walked away and took the story to Kodansha instead. Which magazine did he walk away from?
context: Isayama first took the story to Shueisha's Weekly Shonen Jump in 2006, and its editors asked him to rework his style to fit the magazine. He declined and went to Kodansha, which launched Attack on Titan in its monthly Bessatsu Shonen Magazine in September 2009.

question: In the manga Death Note, the Japanese high schooler Light Yagami finds a supernatural notebook that kills anyone whose name is written in it. He decides to secretly murder criminals worldwide from behind his school desk, hoping to become the god of a new clean world. To keep his identity hidden, he picks a nickname that sounds like the English word 'killer' spoken in a Japanese accent. What do the detective L and the news channels end up calling him?
context: 'Kira' is a romanization of the English word 'killer' transliterated through Japanese phonetics. Light adopts it as the persona under which he claims to be God of the new world. The Kira name becomes shorthand among investigators and a cult-following emerges in-universe.

question: The Elric brothers try to bring their mother back with human transmutation, alchemy's ultimate taboo. The rebound costs Edward an arm and a leg and takes his brother's whole body. At the moment of failure they meet something that shows the source of alchemy. What do they meet?
answer: The Gate of Truth, with the entity called Truth at its threshold
choices: The Gate of Truth, with the entity called Truth at its threshold
The Philosopher's Stone, dissolved in their mother's blood
The shadow of their father Hohenheim, watching silently
The homunculus Envy, in his serpent form, taunting them
context: Truth is a faceless white figure who personally collects the 'toll' for human-transmutation attempts. The Gate of Truth contains all knowledge of alchemy and the universe's structure. Each alchemist who sees the Gate is taking a piece of forbidden knowledge with terrible cost.

question: In Yoshihiro Togashi's manga Hunter x Hunter, the twelve-year-old friends Gon Freecss and Killua Zoldyck finish the Hunter Exam and head for a towering martial-arts stadium where fighters climb the floors one bout at a time. There a soft-spoken master named Wing teaches them Nen, the life-energy behind every fight in the series. What is that tower called?
context: Gon and Killua travel to Heavens Arena, a towering martial-arts arena, where they climb its floors and train under Wing, the master who teaches them Nen. The arc runs from chapter 44 to chapter 63 of the manga.

question: In JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 3, the Japanese high schooler Jotaro Kujo and his globe-trotting grandfather Joseph Joestar race from Tokyo to Egypt in fifty days to save Jotaro's mother. Jotaro is cool, laconic and hard to impress, and both his signature finger-pointing pose and his grumbled catchphrase, yare yare daze, or good grief, come from Hirohiko Araki's favourite screen tough guy. Which actor did Araki model Jotaro on?
context: Araki modelled Jotaro on Clint Eastwood, poses and catchphrases included: the pointing pose comes from Eastwood holding a .44 Magnum, and yare yare daze imitates the kind of lines Eastwood said in his films.

question: In Yoshihiro Togashi's manga Yu Yu Hakusho, the delinquent Yusuke Urameshi comes back from the dead as a Spirit Detective and learns one signature move. He points his index finger like a pistol, gathers his spirit energy into the tip, and fires it as a single crackling blast. What is the move called?
context: The Spirit Gun, or Rei Gun, is a shot of spirit energy that Yusuke fires from his index finger, and it is his signature technique. He develops it with guidance from Botan, the ferry girl of the Spirit World.

question: Shuichi Shigeno's Initial D began in 1995 and ended in 2013. Takumi drives a Toyota Trueno AE86 that was already ten years old and discontinued when the series started. Fans gave the panda-colored AE86 a popular slang nickname. What is that nickname?
context: AE86 is the chassis code. The panda color scheme — white top, black bottom — became one of car culture's most-recognized liveries. Toyota's GT86 / Subaru BRZ revival in 2012 was directly inspired by Initial D's continuing popularity. Takumi's father Bunta drove the original.

question: In the Pokemon anime, a pink, balloon-round Jigglypuff keeps following Ash and his friends from town to town, desperate for someone to sing to. The trouble is its lullaby: everyone who hears it falls fast asleep before the song is over, and Jigglypuff takes this as a terrible insult every single time. What does it do to the sleeping audience?
answer: It scribbles on their faces with its marker
choices: It scribbles on their faces with its marker
It steals the food from their backpacks
It sticks flower petals in their hair
It rolls over them like a beach ball
context: Jigglypuff's song puts everyone who hears it to sleep, and when it notices, it angrily uses its marker, which doubles as its microphone, to draw on their faces.

question: Dr. Gero builds the android Cell as the ultimate weapon in Dragon Ball Z, assembling him from the cells of all the Z Fighters and beyond. To achieve his perfect form, Cell must absorb two earlier-model androids. Which two does he hunt and absorb?
context: Androids 17 and 18 are originally human siblings (Lapis and Lazuli) who were kidnapped by Dr. Gero and converted. Cell's Perfect Form, achieved by absorbing them both, makes him sleeker, more confident, and proportionally more powerful — the arc's iconic design moment.

question: Majin Buu, the strange pink demon sealed away centuries earlier by the old Supreme Kais, proves too strong for adult Goku's normal punches and energy beams in Dragon Ball Z. Goku's ultimate weapon is a giant blue ball of energy, charged by asking all living beings on Earth to raise their hands and pour their life energy into one attack. What is that signature attack called?
choices: The Big Bang Attack (Bigu Ban Atakku)
context: Goku first learns the Spirit Bomb from King Kai during the Saiyan arc. It uses borrowed energy and requires the donor's consent. In the Buu arc, Vegeta and others must convince Earth's population to raise their hands — a famously emotional moment as Hercule (Mr. Satan) leads the request.

question: Demon Slayer's 2020 anime film Mugen Train adapts chapters 53 through 69 of Koyoharu Gotouge's manga directly. The story climax comes when a member of the demon world's twelve strongest fighters, called an Upper Moon, fights and kills one of the nine top demon-slayers — the Flame Hashira. Watching him die traumatizes young hero Tanjiro and the other survivors on the train. Which Upper Moon demon murders the Flame Hashira?
context: Akaza was once a martial artist named Hakuji whose family was poisoned by yakuza. He was turned into a demon by Muzan and lost most of his human memories. Rengoku's death in the manga came as a shock to readers; Akaza later seeks rematches with strong human martial artists.

question: In My Hero Academia, the main villain organization is led by a young man with dry, cracked skin whose touch causes objects to crumble. His mentor, the original holder of the show's ur-quirk, is sealed inside a high-tech prison. What is the leader's name?
context: Tomura is the grandson of Nana Shimura, the seventh One For All wielder before All Might. He was raised by All For One after his quirk Decay manifested and killed his abusive family. The character body horror — five severed-hand prosthetics covering his face — became one of MHA's most-merchandised images.

question: In George Morikawa's Japanese boxing manga Hajime no Ippo, Coach Genji Kamogawa is a gruff, retired professional boxer who runs the Kamogawa Boxing Gym where the shy hero Ippo Makunouchi trains. A long flashback reveals that as a young Japanese boxer in the late 1940s, Kamogawa shared a fierce rivalry with an American soldier he met and fought during the postwar American occupation of Japan. What is that American soldier's name?
context: Ralph Anderson is the arrogant American officer of the post-war flashback. He leaves Kamogawa's friend Ginpachi Nekota with permanent brain damage through an illegal rabbit punch, and Kamogawa answers him with his fearsome but self-destructive Tekken, the Iron Fist.

question: In the manga Demon Slayer, human sword fighters use combat styles called Breathing Techniques — Water Breathing, Flame Breathing, Thunder Breathing, and so on — each modeled on an element or an animal's movement. All of these styles branched off from one single original style long ago. That first style was mastered by the greatest demon slayer who ever lived, a Sengoku-era warrior named Yoriichi Tsugikuni. What is that first, original Breathing style called?
context: Yoriichi Tsugikuni, the original swordsman, invented Sun Breathing and was the only person ever to develop the Demon Slayer Mark naturally. Tanjiro's family preserved the original Sun Breathing as a religious dance called Hinokami Kagura, taught from father to son in secret.

question: Goku looks up at a full moon in Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball, and his furry tail sets off a wild rampaging change he cannot control, big enough to crush houses. Toriyama loosely based the kid hero on Sun Wukong of the classic Chinese novel Journey to the West, tail included. What does Goku turn into?
answer: A giant ape called the Oozaru, hundreds of feet tall
choices: A giant ape called the Oozaru, hundreds of feet tall
A giant flame-breathing tiger called the Konjishi
A dragon-headed warrior called the Ryusenjin
context: Saiyans transform into Oozaru under any moon's reflected sunlight, increasing their power roughly tenfold but losing most rational control. Vegeta's tail is also cut off; eventually almost all Saiyans on Earth lose their tails. The Great Ape transformation appears one last time in DBZ Cell arc through Cell Junior.

question: Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun is a Japanese manga about a haunted school and its Seven Mysteries, ghost stories that turned out to be real spirits. The third mystery, called Misaki Stairs, is a hidden rear stairwell in the school where climbing to the top can swap two people's souls between their bodies. What sad event from the school's past created this ghost mystery?
answer: A schoolgirl named Misaki was bullied to suicide on the back staircase decades ago
choices: A schoolgirl named Misaki was bullied to suicide on the back staircase decades ago
A teacher named Misaki was murdered by students during the war years
A young art teacher named Misaki disappeared mid-class and was never found
A student named Misaki accidentally died in a chemistry-lab fire
context: The first three mysteries are introduced relatively quickly in the manga. Misaki Stairs becomes important in a body-swap arc involving Nene and a classmate. Each of the Seven Mysteries has a specific 'territory' on the school grounds that bounds its power.

question: In Masashi Kishimoto's ninja manga Naruto, the loud orange-clad hero Naruto Uzumaki ends sentence after sentence with the same childish verbal tic, dattebayo, a sound with no real dictionary meaning that just makes him sound like a brat demanding attention. The English dub of the early anime had to put something in its place. What phrase did it use?
context: Kishimoto wanted a childlike catchphrase for Naruto, and dattebayo came to mind. The first episodes of the English dub replaced it with Believe it!, and later episodes swapped that for You know?

question: Ichigo and his friends invade the Soul Society in the third and longest of the four major arcs of Tite Kubo's Bleach. They mean to rescue a captured comrade before her execution, and they storm the prison that holds her. What is that place called?
answer: Senzaikyu, the Tower of Penitence atop Sokyoku Hill
choices: Senzaikyu, the Tower of Penitence atop Sokyoku Hill
Seireitei Citadel and the Sealed Inner Vault
The Kuchiki Manor and Captain's Senate Hall
The Royal Realm of the Soul King's Palace
context: The Soul Society arc spans about 60 chapters and more than 40 anime episodes. Senzaikyu, the Tower of Penitence, stands atop Sokyoku Hill, and the race to reach the condemned prisoner before her execution ends on one of Bleach's most-discussed cliffhangers.

question: One Piece is a Japanese manga about a straw-hatted pirate boy named Monkey D. Luffy sailing the world in search of a legendary treasure. Some pirates in the story eat cursed fruits called Devil Fruits, which give strange powers but cost the eater the ability to swim forever. Devil Fruits come in three groups — Paramecia (weird body powers, like Luffy's rubber-stretch), Zoan (turning into animals), and one third group that is the rarest and strongest. What is it called?
context: Logia users can transform their bodies into and control an element — fire (Ace), magma (Akainu), light (Kizaru), darkness (Blackbeard). They're functionally immune to most physical attacks unless the opponent has Armament Haki or Sea-Prism Stone. Only a few dozen are known by the series' early arcs.

question: In Death Note, the character L is known for his crouched sitting posture and endless sugar habit, and he solves major cases under several aliases. Only a handful of people know his real name, because any Death Note holder could kill him by using it. What is his real name?
context: L is the world's top three detectives all rolled into one anonymous identity. Watari (Quillsh Wammy) is his handler and the founder of Wammy's House orphanage that produces his successor candidates. Light learns L's real name in the manga only at the very moment L is dying.

question: Hiromu Arakawa drew the Elric brothers' homeland to look like early-1900s Germany, with alchemy in place of gunpowder and state alchemists serving as soldiers. What is that country named?
context: The seven homunculi are each made from Father's own discarded sins. Father plans to absorb God (the entity called Truth) using Amestris's population as living sacrifices. The bordering nations Aerugo, Drachma, Creta, and the eastern Xing form the surrounding political landscape.

question: Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun is a 2020 anime from studio Lerche, based on Aida Iro's manga about ghost stories haunting a Japanese high school. The show is famous for its chalk-on-blackboard art and soft watercolor scenes. Its opening theme song was such a fan hit that people rushed out to buy the single. What was that opening theme called?
choices: Mizu no Yume by Bump of Chicken
context: The Jibaku Shounen Band is a fictional in-universe band assembled for the anime's marketing campaign with voice actors as members. The 'No.7' title references Hanako as the seventh mystery. The anime aired in early 2020 and was animated by Lerche.

question: Goku willingly holds his brother Raditz still at the start of Dragon Ball Z's Saiyan arc while a rival fires a beam through both of them. The rival is a longtime enemy of Goku turned reluctant ally, and the blast ends Goku's life along with his brother's. Who fires the beam?
context: Piccolo's Special Beam Cannon (Makankosappo) is the only technique strong enough to pierce Raditz's armor in that scene. Both Goku and Raditz die. Piccolo's redemption arc — from Demon King's son to mentor of Goku's son Gohan — is one of DBZ's most beloved character developments.

question: In My Hero Academia, the Sports Festival in Season 2 ends with a final tournament that crowns one of Class 1-A as the top first-year combatant of U.A. High. The festival's iconic final fight between two ice-and-fire-quirked students became the franchise's first 'classic' battle. Who won the tournament?
answer: Katsuki Bakugo, who was strapped to a pillar for the medal ceremony
choices: Katsuki Bakugo, who was strapped to a pillar for the medal ceremony
Shoto Todoroki, who refused to use his fire side until the final
Izuku Midoriya, who broke both his arms beating Shinso
Tenya Iida, who used his engine-quirk Recipro Burst to clinch it
context: The festival ran from chapters 23 to 44 of the manga. Bakugo's refusal to accept his championship gracefully — he wanted to fight Todoroki at full power — became one of the series' character-defining beats. The medal-podium pillar gag became fan meme material.

question: In Kohei Horikoshi's manga My Hero Academia, the underground hero Eraserhead can cancel other people's Quirks — the superpowers people are born with — just by staring at them. He is the strict homeroom teacher of Class 1-A, where the hero Izuku Midoriya trains. Eraserhead's civilian name is a hidden Japanese-word pun that points directly to what he does in a fight. What everyday object does the pun in his name point to?
answer: His given name Shota is written with the kanji for 'erase'
choices: His given name Shota is written with the kanji for 'erase'
His name Shoto Aizawa intentionally rhymes with his Boku no Hero predecessor
His name Shota Aizawa was a pre-existing villain from My Hero Academia: Vigilantes
His name Shota Aizawa shares kanji with 'eraser-headed Buddhist saint'
context: Eraserhead's quirk, Erasure, only works while he keeps eye contact and doesn't blink. The signature scarf he wears is a special capture weapon made of stiffened steel-wire-and-cloth. His pessimistic line 'You'd better all be ready to take this seriously' became one of MHA's most-quoted moments.

question: Hajime no Ippo is George Morikawa's long-running boxing manga about a shy Japanese teen named Makunouchi Ippo. His grizzled trainer, Coach Kamogawa, takes Ippo and his gym-mate Takamura Mamoru to a quiet beach town for brutal off-season training. Takamura, the strongest boxer in the Kamogawa gym, has to drag one huge piece of gear across the sand for hours to build his legs. What did Kamogawa make him drag?
answer: A horsedrawn carriage tire used for sled-pull resistance training
choices: A horsedrawn carriage tire used for sled-pull resistance training
A boulder strapped to his back called the Iwa-no-Kokuhaku stone
A pair of fishing nets weighed down by lead sinkers in each hand
A pull-cart of cement bags totaling 80 kilograms across the beach
context: Takamura's beach training is one of Hajime no Ippo's most-replicated sequences in shonen sports manga. The visual of him sprinting up sand dunes with the massive tire became an anime staple. Coach Kamogawa's actual training methods were partly modeled on the brutal Toko Boxing Gym regimen in 1950s Tokyo.

question: Koyoharu Gotouge's Demon Slayer manga concluded in May 2020 with a final battle against Muzan that stretched over 80 chapters. As Muzan died, he bit Tanjiro, briefly transforming him into the most powerful demon in history. One of Tanjiro's closest friends then breaks through his tearful shouted plea and reaches him in time. Who reaches him in time to save him?
answer: His sister Nezuko, who reverses his demon transformation through her own restored humanity
choices: His sister Nezuko, who reverses his demon transformation through her own restored humanity
His mentor Giyu Tomioka, with Lady Tamayo's antidote arrow shot through the demon mark
His friend Zenitsu, with the Seventh Form of Thunder Breathing newly mastered
His master Sakonji Urokodaki, who returns from retirement for the final battle
context: The Tanjiro-as-demon sequence is one of the manga's most-debated reveals. Nezuko's restored humanity (achieved earlier through the Lady Tamayo medicine and her own willpower) is what gives her the spiritual force to reach her brother. Gotouge gave the manga a 23-chapter epilogue set in modern-day Tokyo with reincarnated descendants of the cast.

question: Masashi Kishimoto drew Naruto for Weekly Shonen Jump from 1999 to 2014. Readers who picked up a demon-fighting manga called 666 Satan, published in English as O-Parts Hunter, were struck by how much its art looked like Naruto's, and some accused one artist of copying the other. The explanation was simple: its creator had been drawing manga at Masashi's side since early childhood. Who is he?
context: Seishi Kishimoto, the creator of 666 Satan, is Masashi's identical twin brother. The two have drawn manga together since early childhood, and Seishi has said the similarities are not intentional but come from sharing so many of the same influences.

question: One Piece's power system, called Haki, treats willpower as a kind of aura energy that dominates late-series combat. Three types are confirmed: defensive Armament, perceptive Observation, and a rare third type usable by only one in a million people. What is the third rare type called?
answer: Conqueror's Haki (Haoshoku Haki / Color of the King)
choices: Conqueror's Haki (Haoshoku Haki / Color of the King)
Emperor's Haki (Yonkō Haki / Color of the Throne)
Pirate-King's Haki (Kaizoku Ō Haki / Color of the Crown)
Dragon's Haki (Ryūou Haki / Color of the World)
context: Conqueror's Haki is innate — it cannot be trained, only awakened. Holders can knock out weaker beings just by exerting it. Notable users: Luffy, Shanks, Whitebeard, Roger, Big Mom, Kaido. The Wano arc revealed Conqueror's can be coated on weapons or strikes at the most advanced levels.

question: Levi, the short, scowling Survey Corps captain of Attack on Titan, owes his compact build to a masked vigilante Hajime Isayama saw in the 2009 film of Alan Moore's graphic novel Watchmen, by Isayama's own account. Isayama made Levi spotless, as a contrast to that character's grubbiness. Which Watchmen character was it?
context: Isayama modelled Levi on Rorschach from Watchmen after watching the film adaptation, giving him a similar build but making him obsessed with cleanliness as a contrast to Rorschach's grubbiness. Levi leads an elite squad within the Survey Corps.

question: In Death Note, L meets Light face to face for the first time at a university entrance ceremony, where both are named the top scorer. They introduce themselves under fake names, kicking off the show's cat-and-mouse rivalry. Which university hosts that meeting?
answer: To-Oh University, fictional Tokyo Imperial-style elite institution
choices: To-Oh University, fictional Tokyo Imperial-style elite institution
Tokyo University (Todai), the real-world institution Light secretly attends
Kanto Hogan University, the elite criminology-program school
Daikoku University, the fictional analogue to Kyoto Imperial
context: Light entered To-Oh under his own name; L appeared as the alias 'Hideki Ryuga' (sharing a name with a real Japanese pop star, a deliberate Ohba joke). The entrance ceremony scene where L whispers 'I am L' to Light became one of the manga's most-iconic two-page spreads.

question: Father, the villain of Hiromu Arakawa's manga, sets up a country's wars in advance for a plan of his own. One top military leader runs that plan from the inside. Who is that leader?
answer: King Bradley, the Fuhrer, who is the homunculus Wrath
choices: King Bradley, the Fuhrer, who is the homunculus Wrath
General Hakuro, the Briggs Mountain commander
General Grumman, Roy Mustang's secret backer
General Olivier Armstrong, the Briggs Northern Front
context: Bradley was Father's homunculus seventh sin, Pride — an experiment that began with a human body rather than alchemical creation. His Ultimate Eye lets him predict any opponent's moves. The reveal that Amestris's entire history was a multi-century setup orchestrated by Father is the manga's largest single plot twist.

question: Yoshihiro Togashi, the creator of Yu Yu Hakusho, began Hunter x Hunter in Weekly Shonen Jump in 1998. While the first volume was being finished, a fellow manga artist pitched in on the grey shading, laying screentone on its single-color pages, and early in 1999 she married Togashi. She was already famous in her own right for a magical-girl series about a clumsy schoolgirl who fights evil in a sailor-suit uniform. Which series did she create?
context: Naoko Takeuchi, the creator of Sailor Moon, helped apply screentone to the single-color pages of Hunter x Hunter's first volume. She married Togashi on 6 January 1999.

question: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 4, Diamond Is Unbreakable, ran from 1992 to 1995 and traded the world tour of Part 3 for one quiet seaside town, Morioh, where the high schooler Josuke Higashikata and his friends keep stumbling on strange Stand users among the neighbours. Hirohiko Araki modelled Morioh on a real place: the city where he himself grew up. Which city?
context: Morioh is modelled on a part of Sendai in Miyagi Prefecture, Araki's hometown, and in 2012 a big JoJo exhibition opened there. Part 4 ran in Weekly Shonen Jump from May 1992 to December 1995.

question: Yoshihiro Togashi's Yu Yu Hakusho, the story of a delinquent struck by a car while saving a child and sent back as a Spirit Detective, became a hit TV anime from Studio Pierrot in 1992. Its opening theme, a bouncy pop single by the singer-songwriter Matsuko Mawatari released in November 1992, carries a title that translates as Smile Bomb. What is the song's Japanese title?
context: Hohoemi no Bakudan, Japanese for Smile Bomb, is a 1992 single by Matsuko Mawatari that became the opening theme of the Yu Yu Hakusho anime. Studio Pierrot made the series with Fuji Television and Yomiko Advertising, and Togashi ended the manga in 1994, exhausted by the weekly schedule.

question: Shuichi Shigeno's Initial D ended in July 2013 after about 18 years of serial runs. Takumi's final race is against a rival driver named Shinji Inui, who drives an AE86 of his own. The finish is famously bittersweet, not a clean win. Where is the final race held?
answer: Mt. Akagi, in Project D's hometown-circuit conclusion
choices: Mt. Akagi, in Project D's hometown-circuit conclusion
Mt. Akina, the original training mountain returning for the finale
Mt. Haruna, the local touge of the Real Akina geography
Mt. Tsumagoi, an unfamiliar northern course neutral to both teams
context: Project D is the third-generation racing team Takumi and Keisuke Takahashi join in the manga's later arcs. Shinji is the AE86's rival driver — younger, naturally talented, and clearly modeled as a 'mirror' Takumi figure. The MF Ghost manga (2017-) continues the Initial D universe with a new protagonist and Takumi as a senior figure.

question: Studio Ghibli's Princess Mononoke (1997) had a famously huge production, with over 144,000 hand-drawn frames. Miyazaki himself retouched about 80,000 of them. The English dub cast Claire Danes as San, Billy Crudup as Ashitaka, and a famous American actor as the cursed boar god in the opening. Who voices that boar god?
answer: Keith David, the actor known for his deep growling voice work
choices: Keith David, the actor known for his deep growling voice work
Liam Neeson, fresh off his Schindler's List performance
Patrick Stewart, in a brief opening-narration cameo
Gillian Anderson, also voicing Moro the wolf goddess
context: Neil Gaiman wrote the English dub script, working closely with Miyazaki's exacting standards. Studio Ghibli's Miramax distribution deal famously required a 'no cuts' clause — Harvey Weinstein wanted to trim Mononoke; Miyazaki sent him a katana with 'No Cuts' inscribed on it. Gillian Anderson did voice the wolf goddess Moro.

question: In Aida Iro's Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun, Hanako and his twin brother Tsukasa both died at age thirteen. Hanako, then named Amane Yugi, murdered his own twin before being killed himself, one of the manga's most debated backstories. The violin-playing twins grew up in what kind of neighborhood?
answer: A traditional middle-class working-family neighborhood with their seamstress mother absent often
choices: A traditional middle-class working-family neighborhood with their seamstress mother absent often
A wealthy uptown district where their politician father had been promoted recently
An impoverished urban ward where their orphaned grandmother raised them alone
A rural farming village where their elderly grandfather served as the local priest
context: The Amane-and-Tsukasa backstory is revealed across multiple flashback arcs in the manga. The 'why did Amane kill his twin' mystery is central to the deeper plot. Aida Iro's clear, painterly art style and gentle horror aesthetic earned the series significant adult readership beyond the typical shonen demographic.

question: Goku fights the space tyrant Frieza on Planet Namek in a showdown that Akira Toriyama's manga says lasts five minutes. The anime was running faster than Toriyama could draw new chapters, so the animators stretched the fight with filler: energy-charging, scowling and repeated flashbacks. About how many weekly TV episodes did they spread those five minutes over?
answer: Roughly 19 episodes, spread across about half a year of weekly broadcast
choices: Roughly 19 episodes, spread across about half a year of weekly broadcast
Roughly 12 episodes, the standard 'major-arc' length of late-80s anime
Roughly 30 episodes, the most-padded fight in DBZ history
Roughly 7 episodes, surprisingly faithful to the manga's pace
context: The 'five minutes that lasted half a year' became a meme even at the time. The reason: Namek's planet-destruction countdown was set at five minutes of real time, which the anime stretched to allow Toriyama to keep up with his manga pace. The actual planet-destruction shockwave was eventually filmed to dramatic effect.

question: The anime team behind Dragon Ball GT (Grand Tour) invented material of their own when the show began airing in Japan in 1996, with no manga left to follow after Akira Toriyama's original had ended. They gave Goku a fresh transformation covered in red fur from head to toe, with his Saiyan tail grown back and his hair once again jet black. What is that new form called?
context: Super Saiyan 4 was designed by Tadayoshi Yamamuro, Dragon Ball's chief animation director. The form bypasses the gold-haired SSJ aesthetic for red fur and a Mohawk-style mane, returning to the Saiyans' Great Ape-tied roots. The form is non-canonical to Toriyama's later Dragon Ball Super continuity but remains beloved.

question: Tite Kubo first armed his Soul Reapers with guns, not the named blades called zanpakuto that they carry in Bleach. The project carried a gun-flavoured working title that was still in use when the series was first announced, until the guns became swords late in development. What was that working title?
context: Kubo's early Soul Reapers used guns, so the project was first called Snipe; he switched to swords late in development and later weighed titles such as Black and White before settling on Bleach. Jump rejected the first proposal, and Akira Toriyama, the creator of Dragon Ball, later wrote Kubo a letter of encouragement after reviewing the concept.

question: Eiichiro Oda's One Piece is the bestselling manga ever printed, and Oda says his love of pirates goes back to a cartoon he watched as a small boy: a German-Japanese animated series about a clever little Viking boy who gets his father's crew of burly Northmen out of trouble with brains instead of muscle. Watching it, Oda realised that Vikings are a kind of pirate. Which series got him hooked?
context: Oda has said his interest in pirates was probably sparked by the anime Vicky the Viking, which taught him that Vikings are a type of pirate. Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball was his biggest influence as an artist.

question: Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun is a 2020 supernatural anime from studio Lerche, adapted from Aida Iro's manga about ghosts haunting a Japanese high school called Kamome Academy. Even though the story is full of spirits and dark mysteries, the anime's colors never feel scary. The art team picked an unusual look for the whole series that made the ghosts feel gentle and dreamy. What color style did they choose?
answer: Soft pastel watercolors with chalk-blackboard accents
choices: Soft pastel watercolors with chalk-blackboard accents
Stark monochrome with neon-light highlight accents
Bright saturation with high-contrast comic-book inks
context: The series' distinctive look — chalk transitions, watercolor backgrounds, paper-cutout intro — set it apart from typical 2020s anime aesthetics. The opening sequence inspired countless TikTok and AMV recreations. Aida Iro's original manga art style is even more delicate; the anime adapted it with admirable fidelity.

question: Before Naruto began its weekly run in 1999, Masashi Kishimoto tried the idea out as a single one-shot story in the summer 1997 issue of Akamaru Jump. That first Naruto was not yet an orphan ninja with a demon sealed inside him: Kishimoto built the one-shot around a different idea of who, or what, the boy really was. What was the hero of the 1997 one-shot?
answer: A young fox spirit posing as a human boy
choices: A young fox spirit posing as a human boy
A boy raised by wolves in a mountain shrine
A runaway samurai's son hiding in a temple
A toad summoner's apprentice in the hills
context: Kishimoto's one-shot in the summer 1997 issue of Akamaru Jump starred a young fox spirit who passes himself off as a human boy named Naruto. An even earlier idea, never printed, would have made Naruto a chef.

question: In Hirohiko Araki's manga JoJo's Bizarre Adventure, characters fight with 'Stands' — invisible spirit fighters that only other Stand users can see. Araki, a lifelong rock fan, named nearly every Stand after a song, band, or album. That's a nightmare for the anime studio David Production, which has to rename or blur them for streaming rights. Part 3 is the exception, and it includes the vampire Dio Brando's time-stopping Stand, 'The World'. What are the Part 3 Stands named after?
answer: The tarot Major Arcana, one card to each Stand
choices: The tarot Major Arcana, one card to each Stand
The 1976 Frankie Valli single 'My Eyes Adored You' (renamed for licensing)
The 1981 song 'In the Air Tonight' by Phil Collins (similar musical motif)
The 1969 Beatles album cut 'Across the Universe' (extended track name)
context: Araki's musical references include over 300 character and Stand names taken from rock and metal artists. The David Production anime adaptation occasionally renamed Stands for international broadcast — 'Strawberry' became 'Wagon Wheel' in some markets, 'Sex Pistols' became 'Six Bullets,' etc. The original Japanese broadcasts kept the names intact.

question: In Yoshihiro Togashi's manga Hunter x Hunter, twelve-year-old Killua Zoldyck runs away from home to become a Hunter. His family are the world's most feared assassins, and they live on a private mountain estate called Kukuroo Mountain, protected by high walls and traps. The very first obstacle at the outer gates is a huge, monstrous creature chained there. Only trained family members can walk past without being torn apart. What is at the gates?
answer: Mike, a massive guard hound trained to identify family bloodlines
choices: Mike, a massive guard hound trained to identify family bloodlines
Spike, an albino tiger captured from the Dark Continent
Zilch, a former Hunter Mafia chimera bound by a Manipulation Stand-equivalent
Click, a centuries-old phoenix trained by Zeno's grandfather
context: Mike's full name in the manga is 'Mike,' deliberately mundane against the elaborate Zoldyck family. He's the size of a small house and has eaten dozens of intruders. The Testing Gate at the entrance has six tonnage-weighted doors; Killua opens the third by default, the heaviest only opened by the patriarch Silva.

question: The Pokemon anime reached American television on September 7, 1998, with the episode Pokemon, I Choose You!, and it opened on a power-rock theme song whose shouted promise, Gotta catch 'em all, a generation of kids learned by heart. John Siegler and John Loeffler wrote it, and David Rolfe played the guitar. Which singer belted out the vocals?
context: Jason Paige sang the Pokemon Theme, written by John Siegler and John Loeffler, with David Rolfe on guitar. It premiered with the first English episode, Pokemon, I Choose You!, on September 7, 1998, and was the theme of the Indigo League season.

question: Goku shocks everyone in the final fight of the Cell Games by stepping aside and pushing his son Gohan forward. Cell hosts the tournament in Dragon Ball Z to show off his perfect form, and father and son have trained together in the Hyperbolic Time Chamber. Why does Goku step aside?
answer: Goku has determined Gohan has greater untapped potential and a hidden form Cell hasn't seen
choices: Goku has determined Gohan has greater untapped potential and a hidden form Cell hasn't seen
Goku has secretly absorbed a fatal disease and saves his strength for the wish-revival
Goku has decided to die in the tournament to let Gohan inherit the family role of Earth's defender
Goku has been Saiyan-cursed by Vegeta's secret bargain and cannot win the fight
context: Gohan goes Super Saiyan 2 for the first time in the Cell Games after Cell crushes Android 16's last words. The transformation, animated by Mitsuo Hashimoto, became one of DBZ's most iconic moments. Gohan's Cell-decimating Kamehameha was set up by Goku from the other side; the father-son combo move is one of the franchise's most emotional sequences.

question: Studio Ghibli's Howl's Moving Castle came out in 2004, directed by Hayao Miyazaki and based on Diana Wynne Jones' fantasy novel. When Disney produced the English dub, it hired a big Hollywood cast. Calcifer, the wisecracking fire demon who keeps Howl's magical castle walking around, was voiced by a famous American stand-up comedian who improvised much of the demon's dialogue. Which comedian was it?
answer: Billy Crystal, who improvised much of Calcifer's English-dub dialogue
choices: Billy Crystal, who improvised much of Calcifer's English-dub dialogue
Robin Williams, who voiced Howl's grandfather in the early scenes
Eddie Murphy, who provided the Witch of the Waste's voice
Dan Aykroyd, who took the King Sulliman role for the dub
context: The English dub also included Christian Bale (Howl), Emily Mortimer (young Sophie), Jean Simmons (old Sophie), and Lauren Bacall (Witch of the Waste). Calcifer is the fire-demon that powers Howl's moving castle through a contract that's secretly bound to Howl's heart. Disney distributed the dub through Miramax until that contract ended.

question: Goku and Gohan train in the Hyperbolic Time Chamber, a pocket world inside Kami's Lookout, the palace above Korin Tower, where one Earth day equals a full year of training. Only two trainees can enter at once, and each person has a lifetime cap. What is that lifetime entry limit?
answer: Two cumulative days (two years of training) total per person across their lifetime
choices: Two cumulative days (two years of training) total per person across their lifetime
One cumulative day (one year of training) total per person across a lifetime
Three cumulative days (three years of training) total per person across their lifetime
One year of training maximum per individual entrance, no lifetime cap
context: The two-day lifetime rule is established early but interpreted loosely later in the series. The chamber's environment — 50x Earth gravity, harsh temperature extremes, no horizon — makes survival difficult. The chamber was destroyed by Super Buu in the Buu arc, eliminating the franchise's deus-ex-machina training tool for later arcs.

question: Masashi Kishimoto's hero Naruto Uzumaki cannot get enough of the noodles at Ichiraku Ramen, his favourite stall in the Hidden Leaf Village. Fittingly, the boy is named after a ramen topping: a slice of white fish cake with a pink spiral running through it, often laid on top of the noodles. What is that topping called?
context: Naruto's name derives from narutomaki, the swirled fish cake used as a ramen topping, which suits a boy who lives on Ichiraku's noodles. His family name, Uzumaki, is the Japanese word for a spiral or whirlpool.

question: Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata's Death Note has an iconic chapter where Light realizes L is in the same room as him for the first time. The two have been monitoring each other's behavior for weeks. The scene that confirms their suspicions involves Light, L, and a specific clandestine activity at L's hotel suite. What is the activity?
answer: A televised tennis match Light watches while L watches him watching
choices: A televised tennis match Light watches while L watches him watching
An informal chess game between Light and Soichiro Yagami at L's invitation
A car ride from To-Oh to Light's home with Watari at the wheel
A surveillance-camera review with Light helping L with the case
context: The tennis sequence is famously voiced in inner monologue, with both Light and L providing first-person commentary on what they're observing about the other. Obata's drawing style on this sequence — close-ups of eyes, the ball, the racket — became defining for the manga's psychological-thriller register. The eventual face-to-face came at the To-Oh entrance ceremony.

question: Eiichiro Oda began One Piece in Weekly Shonen Jump in July 1997, but he learned the trade as an assistant to other manga artists. At nineteen he joined the team behind a hit samurai manga about a wandering swordsman who carries a reverse-blade sword and has sworn never to kill again, and its creator, Nobuhiro Watsuki, credits Oda with helping create one of its characters. Which manga was it?
context: Oda assisted on Shinobu Kaitani's Suizan Police Gang and Masaya Tokuhiro's Jungle King Tar-chan before joining Rurouni Kenshin at nineteen. Nobuhiro Watsuki credits him with helping create the character Honjo Kamatari.

question: My Hero Academia is Kohei Horikoshi's superhero manga set in a world where most people are born with powers called Quirks. Shoto Todoroki, son of the top hero Endeavor, has half-ice and half-fire abilities. He refused to use the fire half for years because his cruel father had forced it on him through abusive training. During his first year at hero school, one moment finally broke through and he lit up his left side. What changed his mind?
answer: Deku's heart-to-heart with him during their Sports Festival fight
choices: Deku's heart-to-heart with him during their Sports Festival fight
His mother Rei's hospital recovery and explicit forgiveness offered
Endeavor's near-death battle against the high-end Nomu years later
Iida's brother Tensei being assaulted by Stain in a related arc
context: The Sports Festival arc semi-final fight between Deku and Todoroki is one of MHA's defining episodes. Deku — bleeding, broken, and using One For All at minimum percent — convinced Todoroki that his fire was 'his own, not his father's.' The scene cemented Horikoshi's reputation for combining shonen fights with character development. Todoroki's reconciliation with his family unfolds over the manga's last 100 chapters.

question: My Hero Academia is Kohei Horikoshi's superhero manga where most people have powers called Quirks. Shota Aizawa is the sleepy homeroom teacher of Class 1-A and the pro hero known as Eraser Head. His Quirk lets him shut off foes' powers just by staring at them without blinking. He also carries a signature weapon looped around his neck that lets him bind and restrain enemies at a distance. What is that weapon?
answer: His capture weapon — a binding scarf of steel-wire-cored cloth
choices: His capture weapon — a binding scarf of steel-wire-cored cloth
A pair of armored gauntlets — with retractable wire-launchers in each palm
A monofilament whip — coiled around his belt and weighted at the tip
A modified bullwhip — braided from carbon-aramid fiber with handle grips
context: Aizawa's quirk Erasure cancels other quirks while he keeps eye contact, and his dry eyes force him to blink — limiting how long he can use it. His capture weapon (officially called sōki bōgu / 'binding equipment' in the manga, often translated as 'capture weapon' or 'binding scarf') gives him a physical fighter's option during the seconds between quirk-cancels. The scarf trails from his neck like a scarf at rest, then articulates under his control during combat.

question: George Morikawa started his boxing manga Hajime no Ippo, 'The First Step,' in Weekly Shonen Magazine in 1989 and has drawn it ever since, well past a hundred volumes, about a bullied fisherman's son who learns he can hit. Morikawa did his research ringside, watching live fights at venues such as Tokyo's Korakuen Hall, and he did not stop at drawing gyms. He owns a real boxing gym in Tokyo where professional fighters train. What is it called?
context: Morikawa owns JB Sports Gym, a working boxing gym in Tokyo, and he studied the sport by attending live matches at venues such as Korakuen Hall. Early in his career he briefly employed a teenage Kentaro Miura, later the creator of Berserk, as an assistant.

question: Demon Slayer is a hit anime adaptation of Koyoharu Gotouge's manga, animated by the Tokyo studio Ufotable. Each demon slayer fights with a Breathing Style that has its own colors and look on screen. When the young hero Tanjiro Kamado unleashes his Water Breathing attacks, the animation makes them actually flow like real rippling water pouring off the blade. Fans praised the visual technique the studio invented for those water scenes. What did Ufotable use?
answer: A custom CGI-and-2D blend called digital chiaroscuro shading, with hand-painted Japanese-watercolor overlays
choices: A custom CGI-and-2D blend called digital chiaroscuro shading, with hand-painted Japanese-watercolor overlays
Pure 2D animation done frame-by-frame, with no CGI assistance whatsoever
Toon-shaded CGI exclusively, with no traditional cels at any production stage
Stop-motion-style sequencing combined with photographed live-action water elements
context: Ufotable's animation pipeline became industry-influential after Demon Slayer's success. The studio combines hand-painted backgrounds and character cels with carefully-calibrated CGI for the dynamic-effect sequences. The Mugen Train film's effect-animation work won multiple Japanese animation awards. The 'digital chiaroscuro' technique was originally developed for the studio's Fate/Zero adaptation in 2011.

question: In Masashi Kishimoto's manga Naruto, the Fourth Hokage performs the Dragon Sealing Method — a forbidden jutsu that binds the demonic Nine-Tailed Fox spirit inside the newborn Naruto Uzumaki. The seal's ink patterns, dragon imagery, and chanted mantras weren't invented from scratch — Kishimoto based them on a real esoteric Japanese talisman tradition that blends Shinto rites with mountain-Buddhist warding. Which Japanese religious complex is that tradition tied to?
answer: Mount Koya's esoteric Buddhist-Shinto syncretic tradition, with mountain-ascetic Shugendo influences
choices: Mount Koya's esoteric Buddhist-Shinto syncretic tradition, with mountain-ascetic Shugendo influences
Ise Grand Shrine's purely Shinto purification-rite documentation
Nikko Toshogu's elaborate Tokugawa-era warding talisman archive
context: Kishimoto did extensive Buddhist-Shinto research during Naruto's serialization. The Sealing Jutsu vocabulary borrows from Mikkyo (esoteric Buddhism) ritual language. The 'Five Element' chakra system (Fire, Water, Earth, Wind, Lightning) corresponds to the Godai cosmology shared between Shinto and Buddhist traditions. The Jinchuriki concept — humans imprisoning gods — has loose parallels to real-world Inari fox-spirit lore.

question: One Piece is Eiichiro Oda's pirate manga in Weekly Shonen Jump, which has now sold over 500 million copies worldwide. Oda first pitched the story to his editor in 1997, when he was still a young rookie mangaka. He drew up a rough outline of the pirate adventure and told the editor how long he thought the series would run. Roughly how many chapters did the young Oda say the manga would last?
answer: About five years' worth — Oda originally planned roughly 250 chapters total
choices: About five years' worth — Oda originally planned roughly 250 chapters total
About ten years' worth — Oda planned roughly 500 chapters total
About fifteen years' worth — Oda planned roughly 750 chapters total
About twenty years' worth — Oda planned roughly 1,000 chapters total
context: Oda is famously documented as believing he would finish the series quickly. As of 2026, One Piece has crossed 1,100 chapters and is in its final saga. Oda's continued recommitment to the original ending — 'I'll never deviate from what I planned' — has become a fan running joke. The series has been the best-selling manga of every single year from 2008 through the present.

question: Fans crowdfunded bronze statues of Eren, Mikasa and Armin as children, gazing up at a towering concrete dam that stands in for Wall Maria from Attack on Titan. The statues stand in the small mountain-ringed basin in Kyushu where Hajime Isayama grew up, and he has said many times that its scenery inspired his manga. Which town is it?
context: Isayama was born in Oyama, now part of Hita City in Oita Prefecture, and Hita made him its tourism ambassador in 2014. The statues stand in front of Oyama Dam; Isayama advised on them, and his handprint and signature sit near the base.

question: Death Note is a 2003 Weekly Shonen Jump manga written by Tsugumi Ohba and drawn by Takeshi Obata. The story centers on a black leather notebook with English writing across the cover that kills anyone whose name is written on its pages. Obata drew the cover several times before locking in the final design. He worked from a real object that his publisher supplied him as a physical reference. What real notebook did Obata use as his model?
answer: A Moleskine-style notebook with custom hand-cut leather cover provided by Shueisha's production team
choices: A Moleskine-style notebook with custom hand-cut leather cover provided by Shueisha's production team
A Hong Kong-import calligraphy notebook with traditional Chinese binding
A vintage 1940s Italian notebook from the publisher's reference archives
A standard Japanese school-supply composition book modified by the author
context: Obata reportedly had Shueisha's production team prepare a hand-tooled leather notebook as the visual reference. The cover's grain texture, the binding stitch, and the page-edging were all carefully reproduced in Obata's panels. The English-language 'Death Note' lettering on the cover became one of the manga's most iconic visual elements. The 2017 Netflix adaptation's prop notebook was also custom-made to Obata's design.

question: Edward Elric claps his hands to transmute, a faster trick than drawing a circle on the ground or having one tattooed on the palms. He came by it after the forbidden ritual that took his arm and leg, and it is uncommon among alchemists. What gave Edward the ability to skip the formal circle?
answer: He had seen the Gate of Truth and 'paid the toll' for human transmutation knowledge
choices: He had seen the Gate of Truth and 'paid the toll' for human transmutation knowledge
His father Hohenheim's Philosopher's-Stone-blood lineage gave him innate transmutation access
His mentor Izumi Curtis taught him a secret hand-clap technique she'd kept private
His prosthetic automail arm contained a built-in transmutation array invented by Winry
context: The 'paid the toll' framework is FMA's central magic-system principle: every alchemist who exceeds normal rules has seen the Gate. Other circle-less alchemists include Alphonse (also paid the toll for the failed transmutation), Izumi Curtis (paid for losing her ability to bear children), and the homunculus Father (who is essentially a transmutation circle made flesh). The 'hand-clap' technique became one of the manga's most-imitated visual signatures.

question: Yoshihiro Togashi's Hunter x Hunter has often paused because of his back pain. The longest single break ran from 2018 to 2022. During that time, Togashi posted slow updates on Twitter about his page count. About how many pages did he finish in the four-year break before the manga came back?
answer: About 95 pages — released as 10 chapters in October 2022
choices: About 95 pages — released as 10 chapters in October 2022
About 30 pages — released as 4 chapters in mid-2022
About 200 pages — saved for a full-volume publication
About 60 pages — held for an as-yet-unreleased volume 38
context: Togashi's October 2022 return chapter was the manga's first new content since November 2018. The 10-chapter burst was Volume 37, focused on the Dark Continent expedition arc. Togashi's published explanations cite a herniated disc and chronic lower-back problems that prevent him from drawing at a manga-rate page schedule. His wife Naoko Takeuchi (creator of Sailor Moon) has reportedly assisted with some assistance-tasks during his recovery.

question: Hirohiko Araki's JoJo's Bizarre Adventure has run for 38 years across nine Parts. Araki's art style — huge muscles, dramatic poses, fashion looks — has changed a lot. He has said two things shaped it most: Italian Renaissance paintings, and what kind of Western fashion magazine?
answer: Italian high-fashion photography of the 1960s through 1980s, especially Versace campaigns
choices: Italian high-fashion photography of the 1960s through 1980s, especially Versace campaigns
French haute-couture sketches of the 1950s, especially Dior and Balmain runway documentation
American Vogue editorial spreads of the 1970s, especially Diana Vreeland-era cover work
British rock-magazine cover photography of the 1980s, especially NME and Smash Hits
context: Araki studied Michelangelo's Renaissance sculpture for his muscular anatomy and poses, and his designs borrow from Italian high fashion, including Versace and Gucci; in 2011 he even drew for a Gucci collaboration. In 2009 the Louvre invited him to its exhibition of comics set in the museum.

question: Yoshihiro Togashi's manga Yu Yu Hakusho, about a teenage delinquent turned Spirit Detective, ran in Weekly Shonen Jump from 1990 to 1994. A lifelong fan of the occult and horror films, Togashi showed his editors rough drafts under the working title How to be a Ghost. Once the series was approved he proposed a different title, but a manga with a similar-sounding name, Chin-Yu-Ki, had already begun, so he swapped in Hakusho, meaning report, the first word that came to mind. What was the title he gave up?
context: Togashi first proposed YuYu-Ki, roughly Poltergeist Chronicles, but Chin-Yu-Ki was already in print, so he chose Hakusho, Report, instead, giving YuYu Hakusho, the Poltergeist Report. His working title for the rough drafts had been How to be a Ghost.

question: Shuichi Shigeno's street-racing manga Initial D turned Japan's mountain-pass drifting into a cultural phenomenon, and the anime turned Eurobeat — a fast, driving Italian dance genre — into its signature sound. The Japanese label Avex Trax licensed the tracks and pushed one particular Italian musician as the reigning king of Eurobeat, giving him more song placements than anyone else across the show's early episodes. What was that musician's stage name?
answer: Dave Rodgers, whose tracks like 'Deja Vu' and 'Speedy Speed Boy' became Initial D staples
choices: Dave Rodgers, whose tracks like 'Deja Vu' and 'Speedy Speed Boy' became Initial D staples
Max Coveri, whose tracks like 'Running in the 90s' became Initial D staples
Manuel Tognella, whose tracks like 'Driving Spirit' became Initial D staples
Mickey B, whose tracks like the wartime-coded title cut became Initial D staples
context: Dave Rodgers (born Giancarlo Pasquini in Italy, 1963) is widely credited as the Eurobeat genre's most iconic figure. His tracks were licensed extensively by Avex Trax for Initial D's soundtrack across the 1990s and early 2000s. 'Deja Vu' specifically — the iconic 'Akina Downhill' theme — became one of the most-recognized anime music tracks of all time, with billions of YouTube plays.

question: Studio Ghibli's 1997 fantasy film Princess Mononoke, directed by Hayao Miyazaki, opens on a rural Japanese village suddenly attacked by a rampaging demon-boar named Nago. Writhing black tentacles of corruption cover Nago's body — and those tentacles were Ghibli's first major experiment mixing computer graphics with hand-drawn animation. The rest of the film stayed almost entirely hand-drawn. About what share of the finished film's shots used any computer graphics?
answer: About 10 percent of total shots, mostly in the demon-corruption and forest-spirit sequences
choices: About 10 percent of total shots, mostly in the demon-corruption and forest-spirit sequences
About 30 percent of total shots, throughout the film for textures and crowd scenes
About 1 percent of total shots, restricted to a single establishing-shot sky
About 50 percent of total shots, in an unprecedented CGI integration for Ghibli
context: Ghibli's CGI use grew gradually from Princess Mononoke through the 2000s. Spirited Away's bathhouse sequences used CGI for set extension and crowd work. Howl's Moving Castle used CGI for the castle's mechanical animations. Miyazaki's approach has consistently been to use CGI only where traditional cel animation would be impractical or impossible. The Princess Mononoke demon-corruption tentacles set the studio's CGI-aesthetic standard.

question: Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun is Aida Iro's manga about ghosts haunting Kamome Academy, a Japanese high school. Seven spirits called the Seven Mysteries rule the halls. Between them scurry the tiny mochi-shaped fox spirits called the Mokke, who use a special little candy as spirit money to trade between the Mysteries. Fans of the series say the candy is also said to grant small wishes. What sweet do the Mokke trade?
answer: Konpeito, traditional Japanese sugar-candy-stars, traded as spiritual currency
choices: Konpeito, traditional Japanese sugar-candy-stars, traded as spiritual currency
Mochi-rice cakes, blessed by the Mokke clan's matriarch
Ningyo-yaki, traditional doll-shaped pancakes filled with bean paste
Wagashi, traditional seasonal sweets made for tea ceremony
context: Konpeito (also spelled konpeitō) is the small star-shaped sugar candy of Japanese tradition, originally brought to Japan by 16th-century Portuguese traders. Aida Iro uses the candy as Hanako-kun's currency-of-the-supernatural with deliberate cultural-resonance. Konpeito are central to several arcs in the manga, including the resolution of the Mirror Mystery storyline. The Mokke themselves are tiny, mostly-cute creatures who serve as the manga's comic relief.

question: Death Note, by writer Tsugumi Ohba and artist Takeshi Obata, pits high schooler Light Yagami — the notebook-wielding killer known as Kira — against the world's greatest detective, L. In chapter 58 of the manga, Light figures out that L has him under close surveillance. As he thinks through his options, his internal narration walks the reader through six lettered contingency plans, A through F. Which of those plans did Light actually execute?
answer: Plan B, the contingency that involved a specific date-marked notebook-page
choices: Plan B, the contingency that involved a specific date-marked notebook-page
Plan A, the primary intended approach with no contingency
Plan E, the doomsday option with a Watari-targeting clause
Plan F, the only one Light actually rehearsed in advance
context: Chapter 58 of the manga is widely cited as one of Death Note's tightest-written sequences. Light's internal monologue — listing six lettered plans, executing the contingency, and silently saying 'just as planned' — was animated by Madhouse in the 2006 anime with iconic effect. The 'just as planned' moment became one of anime's most-quoted phrases, alongside 'I'll take a potato chip... AND EAT IT.'

question: Trunks, a teenager from the future, travels back in Dragon Ball Z to warn the Z Fighters. In his timeline Goku has died of a heart virus and androids have killed all the Z Fighters. Trunks hands Goku something to take when the same virus strikes. What is it?
answer: A specific anti-heart-virus pharmaceutical from the future, in a Capsule Corp medicine bottle
choices: A specific anti-heart-virus pharmaceutical from the future, in a Capsule Corp medicine bottle
A sample of Dr. Gero's android-engineering blueprints in microfilm format
A Saiyan-bloodline immunity injection developed by Bulma's lab in the future
A serum from a senzu-bean cross-bred with synthetic immune-system tissue
context: The future-Trunks visit kicks off the Cell Saga; Trunks is the son of Bulma and Vegeta in a future where Goku died and the Z fighters were destroyed. Toriyama's careful work to keep both timelines coherent (the future Trunks's birth, the present-day Trunks's birth, the medicine plot point) became a model for shonen time-travel structures. Trunks's red Capsule Corp jacket and his sword (passed down from Tapion in the films) became iconic franchise looks.

question: Toshiro Hitsugaya speaks the command 'Souten ni Zase, Hyorinmaru!' in Tite Kubo's Bleach, loosely 'Reign over the frozen heavens, Hyorinmaru!', and his sealed sword turns into a long-bladed ice-dragon-themed weapon. Every Soul Reaper's sealed sword has a release phrase of its own. Hitsugaya is the captain of which squad?
context: Hitsugaya, the youngest captain in the Gotei 13, leads Squad 10, with Rangiku Matsumoto as his lieutenant. The Stealth Force, or Onmitsukido, belongs to Squad 2, whose captain Soi Fon is its commander in chief.

question: In Eiichiro Oda's One Piece, the Wano arc confirmed the 'Joy Boy' legend from the Void Century. The Void Century is a 100-year gap in history, about 800 years ago, when a lost civilization was wiped out by 19 other kingdoms — the ancestors of today's World Government. What is the erased kingdom called?
answer: The Great Kingdom, the only name the story has given it
choices: The Great Kingdom, the only name the story has given it
The Kingdom of Lulusia, the central island-nation of the One Piece world
The Holy Kingdom of God Valley, where the original Celestial Dragons originated
The Atlantean Crown, the underwater nation Joy Boy's people ruled
context: The Great Kingdom's destruction is the foundational event of One Piece's worldbuilding. The 'Will of D.' inheritance system (Luffy's middle name, Roger's middle name, Blackbeard's middle name) is a remnant of the lost kingdom's bloodline. The Marines and World Government have suppressed all knowledge of the kingdom's name and history for 800 years. The truth of the Void Century is set to be revealed in One Piece's final saga.

question: Demon Slayer, Koyoharu Gotouge's manga about demon-hunting swordsmen in Taisho-era Japan, ended in 2020. Its final chapter jumps roughly a hundred years into the future and shows the whole cast reincarnated as ordinary high schoolers in modern Tokyo. One of those reborn characters is drawn sitting alone at a cafe, reading a book. Which reincarnated hero is it?
answer: Kanao Tsuyuri's reincarnation, reading a romance novel at a Tokyo cafe
choices: Kanao Tsuyuri's reincarnation, reading a romance novel at a Tokyo cafe
Tanjiro's reincarnation, reading a children's storybook on a train
Kanroji Mitsuri's reincarnation, reading a Greek mythology textbook
Zenitsu's reincarnation, reading a music magazine in the school library
context: The modern-Tokyo epilogue runs from chapters 200 to 205 of the manga. The reincarnations are mostly cousins or descendants of the original cast, with a few exceptions (Kanao herself appears slightly older). The manga's final beat is a quiet, peaceful Tokyo scene contrasting against the demon-fighting violence of the main story. Gotouge was clear in interviews that this 100-years-later setting was intentional.

question: Masashi Kishimoto, the creator of Naruto, grew up idolising the creator of Dragon Ball, but in his early teens he lost interest in drawing manga. What pulled him back was a promotional image for a 1980s Japanese animated film, whose art struck him so hard that he studied its creator's drawings and tried to imitate the style. Which film was it?
context: A promotional image for the 1988 film Akira reignited Kishimoto's passion for drawing, and he studied Katsuhiro Otomo's artwork and tried to imitate it. As a boy he had idolised Akira Toriyama, and Goku's personality helped shape Naruto.

question: Hajime Isayama told fans in interviews that he based the Survey Corps badge in Attack on Titan on a real-world military unit he had researched. The soldiers scout beyond the walls to fight giant titans, and their green uniforms carry crossed wings, one white over one blue, nicknamed the Wings of Freedom. Which real squadron did he copy?
answer: The British Royal Air Force's Pathfinder squadron of WWII
choices: The British Royal Air Force's Pathfinder squadron of WWII
The Imperial Japanese Army's Tokkotai (Special Attack Unit) of WWII
The German Luftwaffe's Schnellbomber squadron of the early Battle of Britain
The Soviet Union's Yak-9 aerial-superiority wing of the Eastern Front
context: Isayama studied multiple Western military traditions for AOT's visual design. The Survey Corps's crossed-wings emblem, the boot-and-trouser uniform style, and the cavalry-rank organization all draw from real WWII-era European militaries. The German-language naming convention for characters (Eren, Mikasa, Armin, etc.) similarly draws from Isayama's research. The Pathfinder squadron's role — finding enemy territory in the dark — fits the Survey Corps's narrative function.

question: In Hirohiko Araki's manga JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 5, Golden Wind, the story moves to Naples in 2001 and follows Giorno Giovanna, a fifteen-year-old who sets out to rise through the city's mafia. His Stand's fists pour life into whatever they strike, turning stones and scraps into plants and animals. From Part 4 on, Araki named Stands after music, and this one shares its name with a 1995 album by an American pop star. Which musician?
context: Giorno's Stand, Gold Experience, can give life to anything its fists touch, turning lifeless objects into plants or animals. Its name matches The Gold Experience, the album Prince released in September 1995, a few months before Golden Wind began.

question: Death Note by Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata ran in Weekly Shonen Jump from 2003 to 2006. Partway through the manga, the world's greatest detective L is killed, and he is replaced by a young albino boy named Nate River, whom his handlers call Near. Near plays with toys and dice on the floor while cracking cases. Every time he sits down to think, he does one signature nervous habit. What does Near always do while he thinks?
answer: He twists a single lock of his white hair around his index finger
choices: He twists a single lock of his white hair around his index finger
He arranges a chess match between miniature figures on a desk
He cracks his knuckles in a specific six-finger pattern
He counts dice and arranges them in pyramidal stacks on the floor
context: Near's hair-twisting habit is one of the manga's most-replicated character tics. Obata's drawings show the gesture frequently — close-ups of the finger in the curl of white hair became standard Near framing. The character is meant to be even more reclusive than L, with anxieties about social contact. Near's eventual confrontation with Light, ending the manga's main arc, is structured as a deliberate parallel-mirror to L's earlier confrontation.

question: Studio Bones went back to Hiromu Arakawa's manga in 2009 with a second anime, Brotherhood, and stuck to it faithfully all the way to the end. The 2003 anime had run out of manga and invented its own ending, and fans complained for years. The new show's very first opening song was a fast rock number. Which act performed it?
answer: Yui (a solo artist, not a band), whose 'Again' opens Brotherhood's first arc
choices: Yui (a solo artist, not a band), whose 'Again' opens Brotherhood's first arc
Asian Kung-Fu Generation, whose 'Rewrite' opened the 2003 series instead
The High Wide and Handsome, an indie group used for opening rotations
L'Arc-en-Ciel, whose 'My Heart Draws a Dream' was used for Episode 50
context: Yui's 'Again' became one of the most-recognized anime opening themes of the late 2000s. Her solo work was characterized by acoustic guitar-driven J-rock with strong vocal melodies. The Brotherhood adaptation by Studio Bones is widely considered the better adaptation of the manga, with five different opening themes across its run. Asian Kung-Fu Generation's 'Rewrite' is iconic but belongs to the 2003 series.

question: Akira Toriyama took a new idea to his editor at the time, Kazuhiko Torishima, for the Frieza fight in Dragon Ball: a Saiyan who hits a breaking point of rage and transforms, with gold hair. How did Torishima react when Toriyama pitched it?
answer: Torishima loved it and reportedly told Toriyama 'this is the breakthrough'
choices: Torishima loved it and reportedly told Toriyama 'this is the breakthrough'
Torishima resisted, calling the idea derivative of Berserk's behavior shift
Torishima requested major design changes including different hair color
Torishima initially rejected the idea, suggesting a power-up sword instead
context: Toriyama and Torishima had a famously productive working relationship. The Super Saiyan design — gold hair, teal eyes, glowing aura — emerged from Toriyama's own preference for high-contrast color palettes and was approved with minimal editorial intervention. The transformation became one of anime's most-imitated tropes, with countless other shonen series featuring similar 'breakthrough power-up' sequences. The Saiyan-rage trigger remained part of the franchise's core canon through Dragon Ball Super.

question: Hercule, a loud, muscle-bound tournament champion called Mr. Satan in the Japanese version, struts around Dragon Ball Z's Buu Saga claiming he defeated the villain Cell, when it was really the teenage hero Gohan. Later he redeems himself by shouting Earth's people into raising their arms and pouring their life energy into Goku's massive attack. What kind of real-world figure was Akira Toriyama parodying with Hercule?
answer: A bombastic Western pro wrestler, with a name riffing on Hulk Hogan
choices: A bombastic Western pro wrestler, with a name riffing on Hulk Hogan
A Japanese sumo grand champion (yokozuna), of late-1980s celebrity status
A 1980s American bodybuilding magazine cover star, in the Lou Ferrigno mold
An Italian motorcycle daredevil of the Evel Knievel tradition
context: The Hercule / Mr. Satan name choice was a deliberate Toriyama joke. The character's hairstyle, his boastful interview style, his merchandising-heavy fame — all reference the pro-wrestling celebrity culture of the late 1980s. Hercule's redemption arc in the Buu Saga — convincing humanity to save Goku, befriending Majin Buu — turned what was a comic-relief satire into one of the franchise's most-loved characters. The dub's name 'Hercule' was a licensing-driven change from his Japanese 'Mr. Satan.'

question: Eiichiro Oda's One Piece introduced the Pirate King concept in chapter one with the words of the executed Pirate King Gol D. Roger: 'My treasure? If you want it, it's yours. I left everything I had in One Piece.' These were the public final words spoken by Roger on the execution platform at Loguetown. The execution started 22 years before Luffy's chapter-one departure. Roger's final words and their public broadcast kicked off what's referred to in the franchise as what era?
choices: The Golden Age of the Sea
context: The Great Pirate Era is the World Government's name for the twenty-two years of piracy that followed Roger's public execution, when his last words sent crowds of would-be pirates to sea. Luffy's goal, to find the One Piece and become King of the Pirates, takes up Roger's challenge.

question: Yoshihiro Togashi's manga Hunter x Hunter opens with the Hunter Exam — a brutal multi-stage test that turns ordinary applicants into licensed Hunters, elite roving agents with world-class privileges. The stages include a marathon run through poison-swamp, cooking a bizarre wild animal to a fussy chef-judge, and a survival tournament aboard an airship. The whole exam is run by a tiny, wizened old master who chairs the licensing guild itself. Who chairs the first-arc exam?
answer: Netero, the chairman of the Hunter Association
choices: Netero, the chairman of the Hunter Association
Hisoka, the freelance examiner who'd taken the test years prior
Bisuke (Biscuit Krueger), in disguise as a child examiner
Kurapika, who's actually a fellow applicant taking it for the first time
context: Netero himself organized and oversaw the year-one Hunter Exam in which Gon, Killua, Kurapika, and Leorio participated. His chairmanship would later become important in the Chimera Ant arc when he personally challenges Meruem. The Hunter Exam is a recurring narrative device in the franchise; it's been remade in five different forms across Togashi's various story arcs. The Hunter Association's secret 'Zodiacs' inner circle is one of HxH's most-imitated worldbuilding elements.

question: When the Pokemon anime launched in Japan in April 1997, ten-year-old Ash Ketchum oversleeps on his big day, finds the three Red-and-Blue starters already taken, and ends up with a stubborn electric mouse named Pikachu. The choice was deliberate. Masakazu Kubo of the anime's development team said Pikachu passed a checklist: a warm design, a non-threatening color, a face that could show feeling, a cry kids could say. Why did the team pass over all three starters?
answer: Picking one would open a gap with every child who had chosen a different starter
choices: Picking one would open a gap with every child who had chosen a different starter
Nintendo had promised the starters' likenesses to a rival toy company
Satoshi Tajiri wanted the starters saved for the first Pokemon feature film
The three starters' designs were too detailed to animate on a weekly budget
context: The anime team chose Pikachu partly because using a starter would have created a gap with children who had picked a different one, and partly because Pikachu was popular with schoolchildren and appealed to boys and girls alike. Masakazu Kubo said a checklist guided the choice: a warm design, a non-threatening color, an expressive face, a cry children could pronounce, and a cute look.

question: Hirohiko Araki's JoJo's Bizarre Adventure is famous for poses that twist like Renaissance statues. In 2009 the Louvre in Paris chose Araki as one of five artists to make new comics set inside the museum for an exhibition. For his story he sent a character from Part 4: a prickly young manga artist whose Stand, Heaven's Door, turns people into books he can read. Who stars in it?
context: Araki was one of five artists invited to the Louvre's 2009 exhibition The Louvre Invites Comic-Strip Art, and his story, Rohan at the Louvre, stars Rohan Kishibe, the manga artist from Part 4. It was published in France the following year.

question: In Rob Reiner's 1987 fantasy film The Princess Bride, a poor farm boy named Westley works for a beautiful farm girl named Buttercup on her family's little country farm.
