Whenever she asks him for anything at all, whether to fetch a bucket, pass a pitcher, or chase down a stray sheep, he answers with the exact same three-word reply, said quietly with a small smile. Buttercup slowly figures out those three words really mean 'I love you.' What are the three words?
context: Westley's catchphrase is revealed to mean 'I love you.' Cary Elwes played Westley; Robin Wright played Buttercup. William Goldman wrote both the 1973 novel and screenplay.

question: In Rob Reiner's 1987 fantasy film The Princess Bride, a short, bald, loudmouth Sicilian mastermind named Vizzini leads a trio of kidnappers up the sheer Cliffs of Insanity with the kidnapped Princess Buttercup. Every time one of his plans goes wrong, or the mysterious black-masked Man in Black keeps climbing after them no matter what, Vizzini shouts one big fancy word (the same word every time) as if repeating it will bend reality back into shape. What is that word?
context: Inigo Montoya finally responds: 'You keep using that word. I do not think it means what you think it means.' The line became one of the most-quoted in 80s film history.

question: In Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim graphic novels and Edgar Wright's 2010 film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, a scrawny Toronto slacker bass-player named Scott Pilgrim falls in love with a pink-haired American delivery girl named Ramona Flowers. Before Ramona will date him for real, Scott must fight and defeat each and every one of her former partners, one by one, in over-the-top video-game-style duels. How many evil exes must Scott defeat in total?
context: The League of Evil Exes is led by Gideon Graves, the seventh and final boss. Bryan Lee O'Malley's six graphic novels (2004-2010) inspired Edgar Wright's 2010 film and the 2023 Netflix anime.

question: Bowser, voiced by Jack Black, sits down at the grand piano in his flying fortress in The Super Mario Bros. Movie and pours out a love ballad to Princess Peach. The song became a chart hit outside the film. What is it called?
context: Jack Black voiced Bowser and performed the song, which became a viral hit and was Oscar-shortlisted. The Illumination film was directed by Aaron Horvath and Michael Jelenic.

question: Doc Brown wires his flux capacitor into a stainless-steel 1980s sports car in Back to the Future. Its gullwing doors lift like wings, and it must reach 88 miles per hour to jump through time. What kind of car is it?
context: Director Robert Zemeckis chose the DeLorean for its iconic gull-wing doors that would look like a UFO when people first saw it. Christopher Lloyd played Doc Emmett Brown; Michael J. Fox replaced Eric Stoltz as Marty after several weeks of filming.

question: Ray Stantz and the other Ghostbusters climb a Manhattan skyscraper in the 1984 comedy to trap a Sumerian demon-god named Gozer, who commands them to choose the form of their destructor. Ray pictures the mascot from a marshmallow bag, and a hundred-foot version in a sailor hat stomps down Fifth Avenue. What is the monster called?
context: Ray Stantz (Dan Aykroyd) accidentally chose the form by thinking of 'the most harmless thing.' Ivan Reitman directed; the screenplay was by Aykroyd and Harold Ramis.

question: Doc Brown clutches his frizzy white hair and yells the same old-fashioned two-word exclamation at every huge shock in the Back to the Future trilogy, in 1985, in 1955, in the future of 2015 and in the Old West of 1885. What is his catchphrase?
context: Christopher Lloyd ad-libbed the phrasing on set; it appears repeatedly in all three films (1985, 1989, 1990). The 'Doc Brown' character was inspired by physicist Jack Parsons and conductor Leopold Stokowski.

question: In the 1984 film The Karate Kid, Daniel LaRusso, hurt in one leg at the tournament final, spreads his arms like a bird's wings and kicks from his good leg. What is this signature move called?
context: Daniel learned the crane stance by watching Mr. Miyagi (Pat Morita) practise it on a beach. John G. Avildsen directed, and Ralph Macchio played Daniel.

question: In Tony Scott's 1986 action film Top Gun, a cocky young U.S. Naval aviator named Pete Mitchell reports to the elite fighter-pilot school in Miramar, California, where he flies F-14 Tomcat jets and plays shirtless volleyball on the beach. Every Navy pilot has a nickname (called a call sign) that other pilots radio each other by. Pete's call sign fits his reckless, rule-breaking, hot-shot flying style. What is Pete Mitchell's call sign?
context: Tom Cruise played Maverick. Director Tony Scott was Ridley Scott's brother. The Navy got a recruitment boom from the film and reportedly opened recruiting stations near theaters.

question: In Richard Donner's 1985 adventure film The Goonies, a gang of Oregon kids follow a pirate treasure map into a network of underground caves under their coastal town. Deep in the basement of the criminal Fratelli family's hideout they find a huge, gentle, deformed man chained to a wall by his own cruel mother and brothers. Once the kids free him, he shares a Baby Ruth candy bar and quickly bonds with the plump kid nicknamed Chunk. What is the deformed prisoner's own nickname?
context: John Matuszak played Sloth, the deformed brother of the Fratelli crime family. Director Richard Donner and producer Steven Spielberg developed the story together. Sean Astin played Mikey.

question: Steven Spielberg's E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial strands an alien in a California suburb, and a lonely boy named Elliott finds him hiding in the backyard tool shed. To coax him upstairs, Elliott lays a trail of orange-and-brown candy across the lawn and up to his bedroom. What brand of candy does Elliott use?
context: Mars Inc. famously turned down product placement for M&Ms; Hershey paid $1 million for Reese's Pieces. Sales tripled within two weeks of the film's release. Steven Spielberg directed.

question: Steven Spielberg's Raiders of the Lost Ark sends Indiana Jones racing the Nazis for a gilded chest that held the tablets of the Ten Commandments. Hitler believes it will make his armies unstoppable. What is it called?
context: Steven Spielberg directed and George Lucas produced. Harrison Ford was cast as Indy after Tom Selleck dropped out because of his commitment to Magnum, P.I. In the Bible, the Ark held the tablets of the Ten Commandments and travelled with the Israelites through the desert. The Nazis come back as the villains of the third film, Last Crusade (1989); Temple of Doom (1984) used the Thuggee cult instead. Spielberg famously called the Nazis 'the bad guys nobody minds seeing punched.'

question: In the 1984 movie The Terminator, Arnold Schwarzenegger plays a killer cyborg sent back from the future. He goes to a Los Angeles police station hunting his target, Sarah Connor. A desk clerk tells him he cannot come in. Arnold says one short line and walks out. Minutes later he crashes a car right through the front doors. What did he say to the clerk?
context: James Cameron wrote and directed. Schwarzenegger originally objected to the line, suggesting 'I will be back,' but Cameron insisted. The phrase became Arnold's signature.

question: Harrison Ford's Indiana Jones teaches archaeology on campus, but he hunts lost treasure in the same outfit every time: a brown leather jacket, a bullwhip on his belt, and one particular hat pulled low over his eyes. What kind of hat is it?
context: The hat became so iconic that the production team had a strict 'never lose the hat' rule on set. Harrison Ford wore it across all four films from 1981 to 2008. Originally inspired by old serial-adventure heroes.

question: In the 1987 movie Predator, Arnold Schwarzenegger plays Major Dutch Schaefer, the leader of a special-forces team trapped in a Central American jungle. An invisible alien hunter is picking them off one by one. When a rescue helicopter finally lifts through the trees, Dutch turns and shouts at his surviving team to run for it. What does he yell?
context: John McTiernan directed. Arnold's character Major Dutch Schaefer leads a special forces team hunting an extraterrestrial big-game hunter. Jesse Ventura plays a teammate; he later became Governor of Minnesota.

question: In James Cameron's 1991 movie Terminator 2: Judgment Day, a shape-shifting cyborg is sent back in time from the future to kill young John Connor, the boy who will one day lead humanity's war against the machines. This new cyborg is made of liquid metal — it can flow through bars and form its arms into blades. What is this new model of Terminator called?
context: Robert Patrick played the T-1000. The liquid-metal effects by ILM cost the film much of its $102 million budget — the most expensive film made up to that point. James Cameron returned to direct.

question: The 1982 movie Conan the Barbarian stars Arnold Schwarzenegger as the young warrior Conan. A snake-cult wizard named Thulsa Doom murders Conan's parents, and grown-up Conan spends the film hunting him down for revenge. Thulsa Doom is played by the deep-voiced American actor who also voiced Darth Vader in the Star Wars films. Who plays Thulsa Doom?
context: John Milius directed; Arnold Schwarzenegger played Conan. The film opens with Conan's father teaching him the 'riddle of steel.' Carlos Palomino played Thulsa Doom with James Earl Jones providing the voice.

question: In George Lucas's 1977 movie Star Wars, Princess Leia of the Rebel Alliance has stolen the Empire's most guarded military secret. Right before Darth Vader captures her ship, she hides the stolen files inside a little astromech droid named R2-D2 and jettisons him down to a nearby desert planet. Luke Skywalker and Han Solo then risk their lives to get those files to the Rebels. What has Leia hidden inside R2-D2?
context: The technical readout of the Death Star — stolen by Rebel spies on Toprawa in events later expanded by Rogue One (2016) — is hidden in R2's memory along with Leia's hologram message: 'Help me, Obi-Wan Kenobi. You're my only hope.' R2 escapes the captured Tantive IV, lands on Tatooine, and the rest is the plot of A New Hope. The Death Star plans reveal the vulnerable exhaust port Luke later exploits.

question: In Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim comics and Edgar Wright's 2010 film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, Scott is a broke 23-year-old in Toronto who plays bass in a garage-rock band with his friends Stephen Stills and Kim Pine. To date the American delivery girl Ramona Flowers, he has to defeat her seven evil exes in video-game-style fights. What is the name of Scott's band?
context: Sex Bob-omb is named after Mario's Bob-omb enemy. The band's songs for the 2010 film were written by Beck. Bandmates are Stephen Stills 'the talent' and drummer Kim Pine.

question: Princess Peach rules the Mushroom Kingdom in The Super Mario Bros. Movie and is raising an army to stop Bowser. First she runs Mario through an obstacle course of spinning saws and fireballs to see if he is tough enough. Who voices Peach?
context: Chris Pratt voiced Mario, Charlie Day voiced Luigi, Jack Black voiced Bowser, Seth Rogen voiced Donkey Kong, and Keegan-Michael Key voiced Toad. The film grossed over $1.36 billion worldwide.

question: Rick Deckard, Harrison Ford's burnt-out detective in Ridley Scott's 1982 film Blade Runner, hunts artificial humans through a rainy, neon-lit future Los Angeles. The Tyrell Corporation builds them for hard labor in off-world colonies, and four have escaped back to Earth. What are they called?
context: Ridley Scott directed. Harrison Ford played Deckard. Based on Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel 'Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?' The Tyrell Corporation manufactures the replicants.

question: The Princess Bride is Rob Reiner's 1987 fantasy movie, based on William Goldman's novel. In one scene, the hero Westley and his love Buttercup run through the Fire Swamp. They face three hazards there: patches of lightning sand, sudden flame spurts, and packs of rodents of unusual size. What short acronym do fans use for those giant rats?
context: Westley famously denies their existence — 'Rodents of Unusual Size? I don't think they exist' — right before being attacked by one. The practical-effect ROUSes were stuntmen in rat suits set on fire (carefully).

question: The Last Crusade pairs Indiana Jones with his father, a grumpy medieval historian who has hunted the Holy Grail all his life. Steven Spielberg had modelled Indy on James Bond, so he gave him Bond for a dad: the actor who played 007 through the 1960s, twelve years older than Harrison Ford. Who is he?
context: Connery (born 1930) was only 12 years older than Harrison Ford (born 1942). Spielberg's own explanation: 'I always thought of James Bond as the inspiration for Indiana Jones, so why not have James Bond actually be Indy's father?' Connery had played Bond in six films from 1962 to 1971, and again in 1983's Never Say Never Again. Steven Spielberg directed; the film's MacGuffin was the Holy Grail.

question: In the 1993 Western Tombstone, Kurt Russell plays the lawman Wyatt Earp and Val Kilmer plays his tuberculosis-ridden friend Doc Holliday. The movie is set in the Arizona silver-mining town of Tombstone in 1881. Early on, the Earp brothers and Doc face off against a gang of red-sashed outlaws called the Cowboys in a thirty-second shootout in a narrow lot behind a livery stable — the most famous gunfight in the American Old West. What is this real gunfight called?
answer: The Gunfight at the O.K. Corral
choices: The Gunfight at the O.K. Corral
context: The historical gunfight happened on October 26, 1881, in Tombstone, Arizona Territory. Kurt Russell played Wyatt Earp; Val Kilmer played Doc Holliday. Wyatt Earp lived until 1929 in Los Angeles.

question: Scott Pilgrim vs. the World is Edgar Wright's 2010 movie, based on Bryan Lee O'Malley's comic. Scott Pilgrim is a broke 23-year-old bass player living in Toronto. He can't afford his own apartment, so he crashes with a roommate who is openly gay, gives him snarky advice, and even shares his bed. What is that roommate's name?
context: Kieran Culkin played Wallace in the 2010 film. Wallace is consistently the smartest character in the room and gets the best deadpan lines. Bryan Lee O'Malley confirmed Wallace based on real friends in Toronto's queer arts scene.

question: The Super Mario Bros. Movie opens on Mario and Luigi, two Italian-American brothers who have just started their own plumbing business in New York City and share an apartment with their loud extended family. Which borough is their home?
context: The film opens with the Mario Brothers as struggling plumbers in their Brooklyn apartment. The 'Super Mario Bros. Plumbing' commercial was directly recreated for the film. The brothers fall down a warp pipe under the city.

question: In George Lucas's 1977 movie Star Wars: A New Hope, we first meet Luke Skywalker on a hot, dry world with two suns hanging in the sky. Luke lives with his Uncle Owen and Aunt Beru on a moisture farm, doing chores and staring at the horizon, dreaming of leaving to fight for the Rebellion. Sand people and scavenging Jawas roam the wastes. What is the name of this desert planet?
context: Tatooine scenes were filmed in Tunisia. Owen and Beru Lars raise Luke on the moisture farm. The name was inspired by Tataouine, an actual town in southern Tunisia.

question: James Cameron's Aliens wakes a warrant officer from decades of frozen sleep and sends her back to LV-426 beside a squad of Colonial Marines. She straps into a yellow power loader, a walking forklift, to square off against the alien queen. What is her name?
context: Sigourney Weaver played Ripley across four Alien films (1979, 1986, 1992, 1997). Her power-loader vs. xenomorph queen fight is one of cinema's most-imitated practical-effect sequences. Cameron also wrote the screenplay.

question: In Rob Reiner's 1987 film The Princess Bride, the swordsman Inigo Montoya and the giant Fezzik carry their friend Westley — who is only mostly dead — to a witch doctor named Miracle Max, played by Billy Crystal. Max sells them a magic chocolate-coated pill that revives Westley enough to storm Prince Humperdinck's castle and rescue Princess Buttercup. As the three set out, Max's wife Valerie (played by Carol Kane) cheerfully shouts a farewell after them. What does she shout?
choices: Try not to die out there!
context: Billy Crystal played Miracle Max; Carol Kane played Valerie. The pair were married only seven days of shooting but their improvised banter became some of the film's most-quoted material.

question: Rob Reiner's beloved 1987 film The Princess Bride, starring Cary Elwes and Robin Wright, is based on a 1973 fantasy novel of the same name. Very unusually, the same American writer wrote both the original novel and the movie's screenplay himself. He was also famous in Hollywood for the line 'Nobody knows anything' — his blunt summary of how the movie business really worked. Who was this writer?
context: Goldman also wrote Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969) and All the President's Men (1976), winning two Oscars for screenwriting. He framed The Princess Bride as a faux-abridgement of a fictional 'S. Morgenstern' classic.

question: The friendly giant Fezzik in Rob Reiner's 1987 fantasy film The Princess Bride was played by the French wrestler Andre the Giant, who stood 7 feet 4 inches tall. His enormous size wasn't natural — it was caused by a rare medical condition that made his body keep pumping out growth hormone long after childhood. The same condition wore out his heart and killed him in 1993 at just 46. What was the condition called?
context: Acromegaly is a pituitary disorder causing excess growth hormone in adulthood. Andre's real name was Andre Roussimoff. He won WrestleMania III against Hulk Hogan in 1987 and feuded with Hogan in the WWF for years.

question: Edgar Wright's 2010 film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World is a video-game-flavored comedy based on six graphic novels by Canadian cartoonist Bryan Lee O'Malley (2004-2010). Michael Cera stars as awkward Toronto bassist Scott Pilgrim, who has to defeat the seven evil ex-boyfriends of his mysterious purple-haired dream girl Ramona Flowers to earn the right to date her. Which actress played Ramona Flowers in the film?
context: Winstead (American, from Rocky Mount NC) had previously starred in Final Destination 3 (2006). Anna Kendrick played Scott's sister Stacey; Aubrey Plaza played the foul-mouthed Julie Powers.

question: The Super Mario Bros. Movie puts Mario on Rainbow Road in a kart chase straight out of the Mario Kart games. Just as he pulls into the lead, the series' most infamous item streaks in, homing on whoever is in first place, and knocks him clean off the track. What is the item called?
context: The Blue Shell debuted in Mario Kart 64 (1996) and is famous for homing in on the first-place racer. Donkey Kong (Seth Rogen) drives in the same race; the sequence ends with the Rainbow Road bridge collapsing.

question: A Canadian television sitcom star stepped into Robert Zemeckis's 1985 comedy Back to the Future after weeks of filming with a serious young actor as the teen hero Marty McFly. Zemeckis had decided the first actor was too dramatic, so he reshot almost every Marty scene from scratch. Which actor took over the role?
context: Stoltz was reportedly too dramatic for the comedy. Fox was committed to Family Ties and shot the film at night and on weekends, sleeping in his car between sets. Steven Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment produced.

question: A widowed field mouse desperately seeks help for her sick child before a farmer's plow destroys her home. This dark fantasy of 1982 is the first feature from the studio Don Bluth set up after he quit Walt Disney Animation in September 1979. What is the film called?
context: Based on Robert C. O'Brien's 1971 novel Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH. Bluth's defection took 17 Disney animators with him, leaving the studio scrambling on The Fox and the Hound. NIMH stands for National Institute of Mental Health.

question: Dirk the Daring, the knight of a 1983 Cinematronics arcade game, picks his way through a dragon's castle in hand-drawn cartoon footage from Don Bluth and his team, all to rescue a princess. What is her name?
context: Dragon's Lair was so popular at $0.50 per play (double the standard quarter) that machines had to be reset constantly. The game won several industry awards in 1983 and inspired the Space Ace follow-up in 1984.

question: Ivan Reitman's 1984 comedy Ghostbusters sends Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd and Harold Ramis chasing ghosts through New York City as the parapsychology professors Peter Venkman, Ray Stantz and Egon Spengler. The team hires a fourth member later on, an ordinary guy named Winston Zeddemore. Which actor plays Winston?
context: The role was originally written for Eddie Murphy. Hudson was paid significantly less than Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, and Harold Ramis. He reprised the role in Ghostbusters II (1989) and the 2021 Afterlife sequel.

question: Philip K. Dick wrote a 1968 novel about a bounty hunter named Rick Deckard who tracks down fugitives on a bleak future Earth. Ridley Scott turned the book into the 1982 film Blade Runner, starring Harrison Ford. What was the novel called?
answer: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
choices: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch
context: Dick died in March 1982, three months before Blade Runner's June 25 release. The novel features Mercer-ism, mood organs, and the empathy box — most cut from the film. Hampton Fancher wrote the original screenplay; David Peoples did rewrites.

question: Vangelis, a Greek musician who had just won an Oscar for the Chariots of Fire theme, scored the 1982 film Blade Runner. He built most of its dreamy electronic sound on a single giant polyphonic synthesizer, a rare Japanese keyboard weighing around 200 pounds. Which synthesizer did he mostly use?
context: Vangelis (Evangelos Papathanassiou) used the CS-80 for nearly every iconic Blade Runner cue. The synthesizer cost around $7,000 in 1982 dollars and had a polyphonic keyboard with ribbon-controlled pitch bend.

question: John Milius's 1982 fantasy film Conan the Barbarian, starring Arnold Schwarzenegger as the Cimmerian warrior Conan, opens with a thundering choral piece called 'Anvil of Crom' — pounding drums, chanting horns, blaring brass, and cracking whips. The Greek-American composer behind that score also wrote music for The Hunt for Red October and RoboCop. Who was he?
context: Poledouris's score is widely considered one of the greatest in fantasy-film history. He also scored RoboCop (1987) and Starship Troopers (1997). Director John Milius wanted the score 'as though Wagner had written it from a Mongol's perspective.'

question: For his 1977 movie Star Wars, George Lucas wanted a big, old-fashioned symphonic score instead of the electronic synthesizer music that was fashionable in the 1970s. He hired the American composer John Williams, who wrote the blaring brass-fanfare main theme every kid can hum. Williams recorded the score not in Hollywood but in England, with one of the world's most famous orchestras. Which orchestra played the Star Wars soundtrack?
context: Williams recorded the score at Anvil Studios in Denham, England across two weeks in March 1977. The Star Wars score won the Oscar that year. Williams used Wagnerian leitmotifs — assigning specific themes to specific characters (Vader, the Force, Princess Leia).

question: Sean Astin, who would later play Samwise Gamgee in the Lord of the Rings movies, first became famous as the asthmatic kid hero Mikey in Richard Donner's 1985 adventure The Goonies. Sean's real-life mother was also a Hollywood star — she had won an Oscar at age 16 for playing the young Helen Keller in The Miracle Worker back in 1962, and later had her own hit TV sitcom. Who was Sean's actress mother?
context: Sean later starred in Rudy (1993) and as Sam Gamgee in The Lord of the Rings (2001-2003). His Goonies co-star Josh Brolin was 17 during filming and went on to play Thanos in the MCU.

question: The Goonies was a 1985 kid-adventure movie about a gang of friends hunting pirate treasure to save their neighborhood from being bulldozed. Its theme song 'Good Enough' was written and sung by American pop star Cyndi Lauper. Two years earlier, in 1983, Lauper had exploded onto the music scene with her first solo album — packed with hits like 'Girls Just Want to Have Fun' and 'Time After Time.' What was that breakout album called?
choices: Girls Just Want to Have Fun
context: She's So Unusual sold over 6 million copies and produced four top-5 singles including 'Time After Time' and 'Girls Just Want to Have Fun.' Lauper's 'The Goonies 'R' Good Enough' music video featured cameos from WWF wrestlers including The Iron Sheik.

question: The 1990 action movie Total Recall stars Arnold Schwarzenegger as Douglas Quaid, an ordinary construction worker who starts to suspect his memories are all fake — that he is really a secret agent on Mars whose mind was wiped clean. The film was adapted from a 1966 short story by American science fiction writer Philip K. Dick. What was Dick's original story called?
answer: We Can Remember It for You Wholesale
choices: We Can Remember It for You Wholesale
The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch
The Man in the High Castle of Time
Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said
context: Dick's 1966 story is much shorter than the film and lacks the Mars setting. Verhoeven had directed RoboCop three years earlier. The famous three-breasted Martian mutant appears in both the 1990 original and 2012 remake.

question: In the 1987 sci-fi action film Predator, Arnold Schwarzenegger leads a squad of commandos through a Central American jungle where an invisible alien hunter picks them off one by one. The towering alien was played by a 7-foot-2 American actor whose face was hidden under the mask. That same year, the very same tall performer suited up in a different costume to play the friendly Bigfoot named Harry, in the family comedy Harry and the Hendersons. Who was this actor?
context: Hall played the Predator in both 1987 and 1990. He also played Harry in Harry and the Hendersons (1987). Hall died in 1991 at age 35 from AIDS-related complications. Jean-Claude Van Damme was originally cast as the Predator but was replaced after just two days of filming.

question: The British director Tony Scott — younger brother of Ridley Scott — made the 1986 fighter-pilot blockbuster Top Gun starring Tom Cruise. Nine years later, in 1995, Scott directed a tense underwater thriller in which Gene Hackman and Denzel Washington play a nuclear-submarine captain and his executive officer who violently disagree over whether to launch their missiles at Russia. What was that submarine movie called?
context: Crimson Tide starred Denzel Washington and Gene Hackman. Tony Scott also directed True Romance (1993), Enemy of the State (1998), and Man on Fire (2004). He was Ridley Scott's younger brother.

question: In Richard Donner's 1985 film The Goonies, a group of kids from Astoria, Oregon go looking for buried pirate treasure to save their neighborhood from being demolished. In the abandoned seaside restaurant above the treasure caves, a hideout is being used by a rough Italian-American crime family — Mama, her sons Jake and Francis, and their monstrous-looking brother Sloth. What is this criminal family's last name?
context: Anne Ramsey played Mama Fratelli; Robert Davi played Jake; Joe Pantoliano played Francis. Sloth was their imprisoned brother (John Matuszak). The setting was Astoria, Oregon — also the filming location.

question: Burt Reynolds voices Charlie B. Barkin, a German Shepherd gangster in 1930s New Orleans, in a hand-drawn animated musical the former Disney artist Don Bluth made in 1989. What is the movie called?
context: The film opened the same day as The Little Mermaid (November 17, 1989) and was crushed at the box office by Disney's hit. Dom DeLuise voiced Charlie's friend Itchy. Bluth's NIMH was 1982; American Tail 1986; Land Before Time 1988.

question: In 2010, British director Edgar Wright released Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, a movie about a 23-year-old bass player who must defeat his new girlfriend Ramona's seven evil exes in video-game-style fights. It was based on a graphic novel series by Canadian cartoonist Bryan Lee O'Malley, and both the books and the film are set in the same snowy Canadian city where O'Malley wrote them. Which city is that?
context: The film features Toronto landmarks: the Honest Ed's discount store (now demolished), Casa Loma castle, the St. Lawrence Market, and the Bathurst Street subway station. O'Malley grew up in London, Ontario but set the story in Toronto where he lived in his 20s.

question: Scott Pilgrim vs. the World is a 2010 movie and graphic novel series about a Canadian rock bassist named Scott who lives in Toronto. Before he meets his real love Ramona Flowers, Scott is dating a starry-eyed 17-year-old Catholic high-school girl — she comes to all his band's concerts, thinks he is the coolest guy alive, and is brutally heartbroken when he dumps her for Ramona. What is this high-school girlfriend's name?
context: Ellen Wong played Knives in the 2010 film. She's introduced as 'Knives Chau, 17 years old.' Knives's story arc — discovering Scott's douchebaggery and finding her own strength — is one of the comic's most-loved subplots.

question: The Super Mario Bros. Movie made over a billion dollars in 2023, and Jack Black's lovesick piano ballad for Bowser became its best-known song. The rest of the score, built from Nintendo's classic game tunes, was written by an American composer. Who wrote it?
context: Tyler also composed for the Fast and Furious franchise. The score arranges classic Mario themes by Koji Kondo (the original Nintendo composer) throughout. Kondo received a 'thematic material by' credit on the film.

question: The 1993 Western Tombstone dramatizes real events in 1881 Arizona, where Kurt Russell's Wyatt Earp and his brothers clashed with a gang of cattle rustlers known as the Cowboys, who wore red sashes to signal each other. The gang's brutal ringleader in the film shoots the town's marshal Fred White in an opium daze near the start. This character is based on a real historical outlaw. Who was the leader of the Cowboys?
context: Curly Bill was historically the unofficial leader of the Cowboys, though Johnny Ringo (Michael Biehn in the film) was also iconic. Powers Boothe played Curly Bill. After Morgan Earp's murder, Wyatt led a vendetta ride that hunted the Cowboys across the Arizona Territory.

question: American director Rob Reiner is best known for the 1987 fairytale comedy The Princess Bride, with its famous sword fights and 'inconceivable' line. Three years earlier, in 1984, Reiner made his first film — a mock-documentary (a movie that pretends to be a real documentary but is actually a comedy) about a fictional British heavy metal band on a disastrous American tour. Fans still quote it, and its amps famously 'go up to eleven.' What was that earlier film called?
context: Reiner co-wrote Spinal Tap with Christopher Guest, Michael McKean, and Harry Shearer (who all starred). Reiner also played the director Marty DiBergi. His other 80s hits: Stand By Me (1986), Princess Bride (1987), When Harry Met Sally (1989), Misery (1990).

question: Temple of Doom, the darker 1984 prequel, gives Indiana Jones a young sidekick, Short Round, a Shanghai street kid who drives the getaway car. The Saigon-born boy who played him left acting for decades to work on stunts behind the camera, then came back to win an Oscar in 2023. What is his name?
context: Ke Huy Quan also played Data in The Goonies (1985). He stepped away from acting in the 1990s and worked as a stunt coordinator. He made a major comeback as Waymond Wang in Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022), winning the Oscar.

question: In the early 1980s, Canadian filmmaker James Cameron wrote a science-fiction script called The Terminator — about a killer robot sent back in time to murder a young waitress named Sarah Connor. The producers loved the script but wanted a more experienced director. Cameron refused to give up the job. He agreed to sell them the entire script for one tiny fee, on the condition that he got to direct it himself. What did he take for the whole script?
context: Cameron sold the script to Hemdale Pictures for $1 in exchange for the director's chair. The Terminator made $78M on a $6.4M budget and launched both Cameron's and Arnold Schwarzenegger's A-list careers.

question: Ridley Scott spotted the airbrushed art book Necronomicon and hired the Swiss surrealist painter behind it for his 1979 space-horror film Alien, advertised with the tagline 'In space no one can hear you scream.' The nightmare stalking the towing ship Nostromo was a skeletal black beast with a second inner mouth. Who designed the alien?
context: Giger was a Swiss surrealist whose 1977 art book Necronomicon (no relation to Lovecraft) caught Scott's eye. The 'biomechanical' aesthetic — fusion of skeletal and machine forms — defined the franchise. Giger won the Oscar for Visual Effects.

question: Raiders of the Lost Ark opens with Indiana Jones creeping through a booby-trapped Peruvian temple toward a small gold idol on a stone pedestal. He knows the pedestal is weight-triggered, so he has brought something to set down on it the instant the idol comes away. What does he swap onto the pedestal?
context: Indy underestimates the weight; the trap triggers anyway. The giant rolling boulder sequence followed. The opening was inspired by old Republic Pictures Saturday-morning serials Lucas and Spielberg loved as kids.

question: Rutger Hauer reportedly cut Roy Batty's monologue in Ridley Scott's 1982 Blade Runner down to its iconic length, ending on 'All those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain.' Most of those famous lines were not in David Peoples's shooting script. When did Hauer write his version?
answer: The night before shooting, in his hotel room
choices: The night before shooting, in his hotel room
During the table read three weeks before filming
On set between takes with Scott approving each line
Two months after wrap, for the redubbed director's cut
context: Hauer cut Peoples's longer speech down and added the 'tears in rain' image. The film crew reportedly applauded after the take. Roy Batty had been hunting Deckard but spares him at the moment of his own death — one of cinema's most-studied scenes.

question: The opening of Rob Reiner's 1987 The Princess Bride shows young Fred Savage in bed playing a baseball video game on a Commodore Amiga computer while his grandfather (Peter Falk) arrives. Savage was already cast in another show that would start the following January and run six seasons. What was the show?
context: The Wonder Years premiered on ABC in January 1988 (filmed late 1987). Savage played Kevin Arnold with Daniel Stern's voiceover as the adult narrator. He was 11 during The Princess Bride filming.

question: Andre the Giant (Andre Roussimoff) played Fezzik in The Princess Bride. The 7-foot-4 wrestler famously could not properly read the script due to dyslexia, so co-star Mandy Patinkin would help him memorize lines. Andre had also worked with another famous filmmaker a few years earlier. In what earlier film did Andre appear besides Princess Bride?
context: Andre had played a 'Bigfoot' character in The Six Million Dollar Man (1976) and the title role in a Hulk Hogan Saturday-morning cartoon. He died January 27, 1993 in Paris from congestive heart failure at age 46. His pre-Princess Bride wrestling fame had peaked with WrestleMania III (1987) vs. Hulk Hogan.

question: In Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim graphic novels, published as six volumes between 2004 and 2010, Ramona Flowers is the American delivery girl Scott Pilgrim falls for. A running visual joke is that Ramona dyes her hair a new color for each book — readers can tell which volume they are in just by looking at her head. Across volumes 1, 2, and 3, what order do her hair colors go in?
context: O'Malley said the hair-color changes signal Ramona's emotional state and the relationship's phases. In the 2010 film, Mary Elizabeth Winstead wore wigs to match. The 2023 Netflix anime brought back the color sequence more closely than the film could.

question: Edgar Wright's 2010 film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World climaxes with a rock-concert battle inside a Toronto music club modeled on the real-life venue Lee's Palace on Bloor Street. In the six-volume comic that the film adapts, cartoonist Bryan Lee O'Malley gives the venue a different, more villainous name — it's the private concert hall of Ramona's seventh and worst evil ex, the record-label mogul Gideon Graves. What does the comic call the venue?
context: Gideon Graves is Ramona's seventh evil ex and the leader of the League. Jason Schwartzman played him in the 2010 film. The Chaos Theatre fight features the famous 'Power of Love' sword vs. the 'Power of Self-Respect' sword sequence.

question: Mrs. Brisby, a field mouse, discovers a colony of super-intelligent rats in the farmer's rosebush in Don Bluth's first independent film. The rats have escaped from a real government mental-health laboratory that experimented on them. The film follows a 1971 children's novel that won the Newbery Medal. Who wrote the book?
context: O'Brien (pen name for Robert Leslie Conly) died in 1973 before seeing the film. The novel was titled 'Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH.' Bluth changed Frisby to 'Brisby' to avoid trademark conflict with the Wham-O flying disc.

question: Don Bluth's knight Dirk the Daring pulled huge crowds in 1983 at 50 cents a play, double the normal quarter. Every frame of the cartoon sat on a laserdisc inside the arcade cabinet. Yet arcade owners still ended up losing money on the cabinets. Why?
answer: The laserdiscs wore out after roughly 10,000 plays and machines required constant repair
choices: The laserdiscs wore out after roughly 10,000 plays and machines required constant repair
Players completed the game in ten minutes so cabinets couldn't generate enough revenue
Nintendo's Donkey Kong released the same month and dominated arcade floor space
The cabinets weighed 600 pounds, requiring two-person installation in most arcades
context: The Pioneer laserdisc players were never designed for the constant-load arcade environment. Cinematronics replaced thousands of laserdiscs and players. Dragon's Lair sequels (Space Ace 1984, Dragon's Lair II: Time Warp 1991) attempted to recapture the magic. The original was the first video game in the Smithsonian.

question: Stuntman Bill Bryan climbed into a suit for the giant mascot monster of 1984's Ghostbusters and walked through a tabletop New York, filmed at miniature scale to look a hundred feet tall. That one sequence cost more than all the film's other effects combined. A Hollywood special-effects veteran directed the work, and his other 1980s credits included Return of the Jedi and Poltergeist. Who was that veteran?
answer: Richard Edlund and his Boss Film Studios
choices: Richard Edlund and his Boss Film Studios
Stan Winston and his creature shop in Van Nuys
Phil Tippett and his stop-motion animation team
Rob Bottin and his The Thing prosthetics company
context: Stay-Puft was a suit worn by stuntman Bill Bryan, filmed at miniature scale to make him look 100 feet tall against tabletop New York buildings. Edlund had been ILM's visual-effects supervisor on the Star Wars OT before founding Boss Film. The Stay-Puft sequence cost more than the rest of the film's effects combined.

question: In 1981, the AT-AT (All Terrain Armored Transport) walkers in The Empire Strikes Back's Hoth sequence were filmed using stop-motion animation. The lead animator who pioneered the 'go-motion' blur technique on those scenes (and on E.T. the same year) went on to design the iconic alien dinosaurs in Jurassic Park. Who is he?
context: Tippett's go-motion technique used motion-controlled rods to slightly blur each frame, eliminating the jerky look of pure stop-motion. He was set to do Jurassic Park's dinosaurs in stop-motion until Spielberg switched to CGI. Tippett's quote: 'I think I'm extinct.' He got 'Dinosaur Supervisor' credit instead.

question: Tony Scott's 1986 blockbuster Top Gun stars Tom Cruise as the hotshot Navy pilot Maverick at the elite Miramar fighter-weapons school in California. Because the film needed real F-14 Tomcats, the Navy had a say over the script, and it asked for changes. One concerned Maverick's love interest, Charlie: the early script made her an enlisted member of the Navy, which ran straight into the military's ban on officers dating enlisted personnel. What was she rewritten as?
answer: A civilian contractor working with the Navy
choices: A civilian contractor working with the Navy
A fellow officer on the Top Gun staff
A British exchange pilot at Miramar
context: The Navy's script approval changed several things: the opening dogfight moved from Cuba to international waters, the language was toned down, a crash on a carrier deck was cut, and Charlie went from an enlisted woman to a civilian contractor because the military forbids fraternization between officers and enlisted personnel. In the film she is a civilian astrophysicist who instructs at the school.

question: The Ghostbusters find a sentient river of pink slime flowing beneath Manhattan in the 1989 sequel Ghostbusters II. To fight it, the team uses the Statue of Liberty as a giant ghost-busting weapon. What animates the statue?
answer: The team plays 'Higher and Higher' by Jackie Wilson to charge the slime with positive emotions
choices: The team plays 'Higher and Higher' by Jackie Wilson to charge the slime with positive emotions
Egon's modified proton pack uses neutron-charged ectoplasm to walk the statue
The Statue of Liberty's flame ignites the slime through chemical pyrokinesis
Peter Venkman's slimer pet drags the statue via psychokinetic ectoplasmic feedback
context: Ghostbusters II features Janosz Poha (Peter MacNicol), the Carpathian art restorer being manipulated by the 16th-century painted villain Vigo the Carpathian. The film grossed $215M worldwide. Bobby Brown's 'On Our Own' was the theme song.

question: Marty McFly reaches 1955 in Robert Zemeckis's Back to the Future wearing a bright red down-filled puffer vest, a design the townsfolk have never seen. They mistake it for a completely different kind of garment. Seeing his underwear label later, they even start calling him Calvin Klein. What do the locals think the vest is?
answer: A life preserver (they think he's a sailor who fell off a boat)
choices: A life preserver (they think he's a sailor who fell off a boat)
A fireman's life vest from the local volunteer station
A Russian air-force flight survival vest from the Eisenhower era
A cowboy-inspired buoyancy aid worn by 1955 rodeo participants
context: The famous Calvin Klein joke wasn't accidental — Calvin Klein launched his eponymous brand in 1968 and had become a household name by the 1985 production. Robert Zemeckis specifically wrote the gag to land with 1985 audiences. The puffer vest itself was a then-current style.

question: In 1985's The Goonies, the film's iconic 'truffle shuffle' scene features Chunk (Jeff Cohen) lifting his shirt and shaking his belly to gain entry to Mikey's house. Cohen was famously typecast by the role. He grew up to be a successful Hollywood professional in what field — not acting?
answer: Entertainment law (he became a major-studio attorney)
choices: Entertainment law (he became a major-studio attorney)
Film direction (he directed three indie thrillers in the 2010s)
Restaurant ownership (he opened a Beverly Hills steakhouse)
Real-estate development (he built a luxury hotel chain)
context: Jeff Cohen graduated from UCLA Law School and became founding partner of Cohen Gardner LLP, representing major Hollywood talent and studios. He stopped acting in his teens, calling the experience formative but unsustainable. He maintains friendly relationships with co-stars Sean Astin and Corey Feldman.

question: Released in 1982, John Milius's Conan the Barbarian opens with Conan's father teaching him the riddle of steel before being killed by Thulsa Doom. The opening text-on-screen quote is genuine Nietzsche rather than a line from Robert E. Howard. What's the quote and source?
answer: 'That which does not kill us makes us stronger' — Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols 1888
choices: 'That which does not kill us makes us stronger' — Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols 1888
'In steel a man's soul finds its purest test' — fictional, written by John Milius himself
'The sword is mightier than the kingdom' — from Robert E. Howard's Conan stories
'Crom counts the slain, not the conquests' — from L. Sprague de Camp's pastiches
context: The Nietzsche quote is genuine — from Twilight of the Idols (1888), aphorism 8 of Maxims and Arrows. Milius was a self-confessed Nietzschean. The riddle of steel — 'what is steel compared to the hand that wields it' — is Milius's own invention for the film, not from Howard.

question: In 1983, George Lucas released Return of the Jedi, the third Star Wars film. The Ewoks were furry, teddy-bear-like forest warriors who lived on the moon of Endor and helped the Rebels beat the Empire. A young British actor named Warwick Davis played Wicket W. Warrick, the little Ewok scout who befriends Princess Leia in the woods. Standing only two feet eleven inches tall, Davis was cast for his height in what was his very first movie role. How old was Warwick Davis when he took on the part of Wicket?
context: Davis later starred in Willow (1988), Leprechaun (1993), and Harry Potter (as Professor Flitwick + Griphook the goblin). He was originally cast as a different Ewok and only got the Wicket role when Kenny Baker fell ill. His daughter Annabelle has the same condition (spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita).

question: In the 1987 fairytale film The Princess Bride, actors Cary Elwes and Mandy Patinkin fight a long, witty sword duel on the edge of a cliff — and they performed most of the swordplay themselves. Their teacher was Bob Anderson, a former British Olympic fencer who spent decades secretly choreographing movie duels around the world. Anderson also helped train the sword-fighting cast of another huge film franchise. Which series did he work on?
answer: Star Wars (he was Darth Vader's swordsman in the OT)
choices: Star Wars (he was Darth Vader's swordsman in the OT)
Indiana Jones (he choreographed the Petra sword fight in Last Crusade)
James Bond (he taught Roger Moore the For Your Eyes Only sequences)
The Three Musketeers (the 1973 Richard Lester version)
context: Anderson was an Olympic fencer (1952 GBR) who became Hollywood's go-to sword choreographer. He wore the Darth Vader costume in the lightsaber duels of Empire and Jedi (with David Prowse acting elsewhere and James Earl Jones voicing). He also choreographed the 1973 Three Musketeers.

question: The Horned King raises an undead army of skeleton warriors in Disney's animated fantasy from Lloyd Alexander's Prydain Chronicles, much scarier material than the studio's usual princess tales. Those frightening scenes break a decades-long streak, making the film the first Disney animated feature rated above G. Don Bluth often gets the blame for it, though he had no part in it. Which film is it?
choices: The Hunchback of Notre Dame, in 1996
context: The Black Cauldron was Disney's most-expensive animated feature at the time ($44M) and bombed. The Horned King's army of cauldron-born undead earned the PG. Don Bluth was NOT involved despite often being credited — he had defected six years earlier.

question: Steven Spielberg's studio Amblin backed Don Bluth on The Land Before Time, the story of a young dinosaur named Littlefoot on a dangerous journey to find safety. Bluth and Amblin had teamed up two years earlier on another beloved animated film. Which film was it?
answer: An American Tail (1986), about Russian-Jewish mice immigrating to America
choices: An American Tail (1986), about Russian-Jewish mice immigrating to America
Anastasia (1997), about the orphaned Russian princess
Rock-a-Doodle (1991), about a rooster who can stop the sun
All Dogs Go to Heaven (1989), about a Louisiana gambler dog
context: American Tail's Fievel character was inspired by Spielberg's grandfather. Spielberg never produced Anastasia (Fox Animation) or All Dogs (Goldcrest Films) — those were post-Spielberg Bluth projects. Land Before Time was meant to be a quiet meditative film; the eventual 14 direct-to-video sequels were not Bluth's work.

question: In 1993's Tombstone, the climactic gunfight at the O.K. Corral is historically inaccurate — the real 1881 gunfight lasted approximately 30 seconds and was actually in a narrow vacant lot near, but not in, the O.K. Corral. The real fight killed three of the Cowboys faction. Who was NOT among the dead?
answer: Ike Clanton (he fled the fight unarmed)
choices: Ike Clanton (he fled the fight unarmed)
Tom McLaury (shot by Doc Holliday's shotgun)
context: Ike Clanton had instigated the fight by drunkenly threatening the Earps the night before but ran when shooting started. Tom McLaury, Frank McLaury, and Billy Clanton were killed. Virgil and Morgan Earp were wounded. Wyatt was untouched. Doc Holliday took a graze. The real fight is now reenacted in Tombstone, Arizona for tourists.

question: In Edgar Wright's 2010 Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, the climactic battle with Gideon Graves uses a 'Power of Love' sword Scott earns from defeating Todd Ingram, the third evil ex. What special-ability tag does the Power of Love sword have in the game's UI (user interface) text on screen?
context: The sword appears with a Final Fantasy-style item-acquisition screen showing the stats. Scott also earns a Power of Self-Respect sword when fighting his Nega-Scott self. Both swords appear in the climactic Chaos Theatre battle against Gideon Graves.

question: In Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim graphic novels, Scott's third evil ex Todd Ingram has vegan powers. When he violates his vegan diet, the Vegan Police arrive to strip him of his abilities. What two specific items does Todd eat to trigger the Vegan Police visit in the film?
answer: Half-and-half in his coffee, then chicken parmigiana
choices: Half-and-half in his coffee, then chicken parmigiana
Milk in cereal, then a hamburger from Wimpy's
Cheese on a pizza, then ice cream at Honest Ed's
Butter on toast, then beef chow mein takeout
context: Brandon Routh played Todd in the 2010 film. The Vegan Police agents are played by Thomas Jane and Clifton Collins Jr. Todd's powers include super-strength, telekinesis, and bowl-cut hair. After being de-veganed, he's reduced to a regular bassist who Scott easily defeats.

question: In Edgar Wright's Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, the band Sex Bob-omb performs throughout the film. The film's music was overseen by Nigel Godrich (Radiohead's producer), with original songs written by which musician known for his 1990s solo career?
choices: Jack White of The White Stripes
context: Beck wrote 'Garbage Truck' and 'We Are Sex Bob-omb' for the film. Broken Social Scene's Brendan Canning and Kevin Drew also contributed. The Clash at Demonhead's songs (Envy Adams's band) were written by Metric's Emily Haines.

question: Donkey Kong's grumpy old father in The Super Mario Bros. Movie is Cranky Kong, who rules Kong Island from his throne. He is older than the film: he goes back to 1981 and Nintendo's first barrel-throwing coin-op, where Mario, then called Jumpman, climbed girders to rescue a woman named Pauline. Who was Cranky in that first cabinet?
answer: The original Donkey Kong from the 1981 arcade game
choices: The original Donkey Kong from the 1981 arcade game
King Kong from a separate Universal Studios franchise
Diddy Kong's grandfather from the SNES Donkey Kong Country games
An entirely new character invented for Donkey Kong 64
context: Cranky's identity as the original DK was established in Donkey Kong Country (1994). The film's Donkey Kong is technically Donkey Kong Jr., who appeared in the 1982 arcade game. The Donkey Kong Country reference in the movie includes a brief snippet of the iconic 1994 banana theme.

question: Littlefoot, the young dinosaur of Don Bluth's 1988 film The Land Before Time, journeys on with his friends after his mother's death. No movie star plays him: an ordinary American boy speaks every one of his lines. Who voices Littlefoot?
choices: Pat Hingle, the famous voice of the original Bluto
Brian Doyle-Murray, brother of Bill Murray
Macaulay Culkin, before his Home Alone breakout
context: Damon's other notable credit was Newsies (1992). The Land Before Time spawned 13 direct-to-video sequels (1994-2016) without Bluth's involvement. The original is widely considered the only one worth watching by fans.

question: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade ends its hunt in a chamber lined with dozens of cups, one of them the Holy Grail, and an immortal knight stands guard over them. The greedy financier Donovan, played by Julian Glover, seizes the gaudiest goblet and drinks from it. It is the wrong one. What does the knight say?
choices: He picked the cup of pride
context: Robert Eddison played the immortal Grail Knight. The drinking-from-the-wrong-cup effect (Donovan rapidly ages and disintegrates) was Industrial Light & Magic's most-complex prosthetic-and-puppet sequence to that point. The line is a near-perfect mirror of 'he chose wisely' moments later.

question: The 1984 movie The Karate Kid tells the story of Daniel LaRusso, a bullied New Jersey teenager who moves to California and secretly trains in karate under his apartment building's handyman, Mr. Miyagi. It was directed by American filmmaker John G. Avildsen, who had already won the Academy Award for Best Director for another underdog sports film, this one about a poor Philadelphia boxer given one shot at the heavyweight title. Which film was that?
context: Rocky won Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Film Editing in 1977. Karate Kid's emotional structure mirrors Rocky's — the unlikely mentor, the romantic subplot, the climactic tournament. Pat Morita's performance as Mr. Miyagi earned a Best Supporting Actor nomination.

question: John McTiernan's 1987 action-horror film Predator drops Arnold Schwarzenegger's commando squad into the Central American jungle to be picked off one by one by an invisible alien hunter — later fans learn the species is called the Yautja. The Predator hunts by heat rather than by sight, and to show what the alien sees on screen, the filmmakers refused to fake the effect in post-production. They shot with a real, then-cutting-edge machine that turned heat into false-color video. What was it?
answer: A real Inframetrics 525 thermal imaging camera, normally used for industrial inspection
choices: A real Inframetrics 525 thermal imaging camera, normally used for industrial inspection
Stop-motion overlays composited frame-by-frame in post-production
False-color time-lapse photography exposed through dichroic filters
A custom video feedback loop with chromatic separation lenses
context: The Inframetrics 525 cost approximately $80,000 in 1986. The Predator's thermal POV had to be filmed separately and then matted in. The technology had previously been used to identify roof leaks and electrical equipment failures.

question: The 1990 action film Total Recall stars Arnold Schwarzenegger as a construction worker who may — or may not — really be a spy on Mars with fake memories. Dutch filmmaker Paul Verhoeven directed the finished movie, full of exploding heads and Martian mutants. But years before Verhoeven took the job, a completely different director had been attached to the project. He worked on it for a while before quitting over big creative arguments with the producers. Who was that first director?
answer: David Cronenberg, who left over creative differences with the producers
choices: David Cronenberg, who left over creative differences with the producers
Bruce Beresford, who was attached for two years in pre-production
Patrick Duncan, who wrote an early draft but never directed
Russell Mulcahy, who was set to direct after Highlander's success
context: Cronenberg's vision was reportedly much closer to Philip K. Dick's original short story — psychological-horror-focused rather than action-blockbuster. He left in 1985. The project then went through many directors before Carolco Pictures hired Verhoeven post-RoboCop.

question: Colonial Marines reach a lost human colony in James Cameron's 1986 sequel Aliens and find every colonist dead or missing, except one terrified little girl hiding alone in the air ducts. Sigourney Weaver's warrant officer has come with them, after 57 years of hibernation drifting in space. What is that girl's name?
context: Carrie Henn played Newt; this was her only film role. Newt's family had named her Rebecca but her brother called her Newt because she could 'fit into all the small places.' In Alien 3 (1992), Newt dies in the opening sequence — a creative decision that infuriated Cameron, who had final-cut authority on Aliens but not Alien 3.

question: In 1984, director James Cameron was casting his sci-fi thriller The Terminator. He almost gave the muscular Austrian actor Arnold Schwarzenegger the role of the hero Kyle Reese, not the killer cyborg. Then Cameron and Schwarzenegger met for lunch, and by the end of that meal Cameron had switched him over to the villain — the unstoppable Terminator itself. What meal supposedly changed Cameron's mind?
answer: There was no specific dish; Cameron just realized Arnold's bulk and accent fit the Terminator better
choices: There was no specific dish; Cameron just realized Arnold's bulk and accent fit the Terminator better
Arnold ordered steak rare and ate aggressively, suggesting the cold cyborg
Arnold's hostess insisted on Italian, which Cameron found revealingly mild
The lunch was at Schatzi's, Arnold's Austrian-themed Santa Monica restaurant
context: The screenplay had originally Arnold as Reese (the human soldier sent back to protect Sarah Connor). Cameron later said Arnold's physical presence and the Austrian accent made him ideal for the unstoppable cyborg. Lance Henriksen had been considered for the T-800 and got the role of Detective Vukovich instead.

question: Andre the Giant played the friendly giant Fezzik in 1987's The Princess Bride. The 7-foot-4 wrestler was at the peak of his fame after his April 1987 WrestleMania III match against Hulk Hogan at the Pontiac Silverdome — a match that drew 93,173 fans and ended with Hogan body-slamming the 520-pound Andre. By 1987, Andre's acromegaly was advancing rapidly. During Princess Bride production, Rob Reiner had to accommodate which specific medical issue?
answer: Andre's back was failing; many of his scenes required hidden rigs to support his weight during lifts
choices: Andre's back was failing; many of his scenes required hidden rigs to support his weight during lifts
Andre's eyesight was deteriorating; he needed his lines read aloud right before each take
Andre needed dialysis treatment three times during production at a Surrey hospital
Andre's hands were so swollen he couldn't grip Westley's leg in the cliff-climbing scene
context: Andre had back surgery just before Princess Bride filming. The famous 'rhyming' scene where Fezzik recites poetry with Vizzini reportedly took multiple takes because Andre would lose his place. Reiner has said working with Andre was one of his life's great honors. The wrestler died January 27, 1993 in Paris.

question: From 2004 to 2010, Canadian cartoonist Bryan Lee O'Malley wrote and drew the Scott Pilgrim graphic novels. They were small, black-and-white paperbacks that looked and read like Japanese manga. British director Edgar Wright — the guy who had just made Shaun of the Dead — snapped up the film rights in 2005, before book two had even hit shelves. What was that second book called?
choices: Scott Pilgrim and the Infinite Sadness
context: The six volumes: Precious Little Life (2004), vs. the World (2005), and the Infinite Sadness (2006), Gets It Together (2007), vs. the Universe (2009), Finest Hour (2010). Wright's film took the title of volume 2 and adapted plot beats from all six. O'Malley drew the final volume's color art in part because the Netflix anime announcement had created industry curiosity.

question: The Super Mario Bros. Movie opens on the brothers' own television advert for their plumbing business, made to look like a worn home-video tape. The advert is a near shot-for-shot copy of a real piece of Nintendo advertising. From what era does the original come?
answer: 1989, when Nintendo had Mario and Luigi appear in a Super Mario Bros. 2-era promotional cassette tape
choices: 1989, when Nintendo had Mario and Luigi appear in a Super Mario Bros. 2-era promotional cassette tape
1995, in a Nickelodeon-style cable TV ad introducing Mario 64
1985, in the original Famicom-era Japanese commercials for Super Mario Bros.
2003, in the GameCube launch advertising campaign for Mario Sunshine
context: The 'Plumbing Service' commercial was hand-animated to match late-80s home-video tape quality. Easter eggs in the Brooklyn opening include the Punch-Out!! gym sign, the Mario Movie 2 logo on the Plumbing van rear, and references to the Wrecking Crew. The commercial's website (supermariobrosplumbing.com) was actually registered as a real domain by Universal Studios.

question: Steven Spielberg named a cartoon mouse after his own grandfather, a real man he had loved as a boy. The mouse was Fievel, a young Russian-Jewish immigrant who got separated from his family sailing to America, in the 1986 film Spielberg made with Don Bluth. What was that grandfather's last name?
context: Phillip 'Fievel' Posner emigrated from Ukraine to America in the early 20th century. The film's central song 'Somewhere Out There' (sung by Linda Ronstadt and James Ingram) was a top-5 hit. American Tail spawned a sequel (Fievel Goes West, 1991) and a TV series. Bluth left the franchise after the first film.

question: Robert Zemeckis filmed for four to five weeks with a different actor as Marty McFly in Back to the Future, then replaced him. The Amblin team realized the chemistry wasn't working, paid out the original actor and refilmed everything with a new lead. Who was the original Marty?
context: Eric Stoltz had just come off the Oscar-buzzy Mask (1985, where he played a young man with cranial dysplasia). The BTTF team felt he was too dramatic for the comedic tone the film needed. Michael J. Fox was the original first choice but had been unavailable due to his Family Ties shooting schedule. After the swap, Family Ties producer Gary David Goldberg let Fox shoot BTTF during Family Ties production gaps — Fox filmed late nights and weekends for months. Stoltz was paid in full for his weeks of work and went on to a strong indie-film career.

question: Don Bluth left Walt Disney Animation in 1979, and about a dozen animators followed him. He had been at Disney since 1955, when he worked on Sleeping Beauty as a 17-year-old in-betweener, and he had been lead animator on The Rescuers (1977). What had frustrated him at the studio?
answer: Disney was using xerography to cheapen the animation process and cutting fluid hand-drawn detail
choices: Disney was using xerography to cheapen the animation process and cutting fluid hand-drawn detail
Disney was outsourcing in-between animation work to a studio in Tokyo
Disney was about to license its characters to a kids' meal partnership at McDonald's
Disney was reorganizing its Burbank studio to share space with the theme parks
context: Bluth specifically named the loss of inking-by-hand and the elimination of multi-plane camera shots. Xerography (the photocopy-style process pioneered on 101 Dalmatians in 1961) gave a rougher line quality. Bluth's later films restored multi-plane and hand-inking. The Disney Renaissance starting with The Little Mermaid (1989) partly addressed his original grievances.

question: Don Bluth went back to the laserdisc in 1984 for a follow-up to his first arcade cartoon, this time released by Sega, with a science-fiction theme. The first game's cabinet had sold for $4,300, roughly double a standard cabinet's price, and players had paid 50 cents a play, double the standard quarter. What was the 1984 follow-up called?
context: Space Ace starred Dexter, the lasso-wielding space hero who transforms via the 'Infanto Ray.' Both Dragon's Lair and Space Ace ran on Pioneer LD-V1000 laserdisc players and used digital frame addressing for gameplay branching. American Laser Games later attempted live-action laserdisc games (Mad Dog McCree, 1990) that flopped.

question: Test crowds in Denver and Dallas turned hostile toward Blade Runner's pacing and lack of narration in May 1982. Warner Bros. forced Ridley Scott to add a Harrison Ford voiceover before the June 25 release, and Ford reportedly delivered it badly on purpose, hoping it would be cut. What was added besides the voiceover?
answer: A 'happy ending' featuring outtake footage from Stanley Kubrick's The Shining
choices: A 'happy ending' featuring outtake footage from Stanley Kubrick's The Shining
An opening expository newsreel explaining the off-world colonies
A new scene where Deckard explicitly states he's a replicant himself
A live-action prologue with Edward James Olmos's Gaff explaining the case
context: The aerial footage flying over forests was originally shot by Kubrick for The Shining's opening but unused. Scott borrowed the footage for the 1982 theatrical 'happy ending.' The 1992 Director's Cut and 2007 Final Cut removed both the voiceover and the happy ending, restored the unicorn dream sequence, and clarified Deckard's possible replicant identity.

question: The 1982 movie Conan the Barbarian starred Arnold Schwarzenegger. Basil Poledouris wrote the score in Rome. Director John Milius told him to make it sound like Wagner mixed with a Mongol horseman. What sound anchors the famous 'Anvil of Crom' opening?
answer: A choir over hammer-on-anvil percussion with timpani and brass underneath
choices: A choir over hammer-on-anvil percussion with timpani and brass underneath
Solo cello over a string section playing the main theme in counterpoint
A brass-and-bone-flute fanfare over taiko drums
A Hungarian zither over a string ensemble in minor pentatonic
context: Poledouris hired blacksmiths to physically pound anvils on the studio floor for the percussion track. The choir sang in Latin (specifically: 'Doom upon all things, doom and woe' translated). The score became one of the most-licensed fantasy themes for film trailers in the next 40 years. Poledouris died in 2006 at age 61.

question: In 1993's Tombstone, Val Kilmer's Doc Holliday was widely considered the film's standout performance, eclipsing star Kurt Russell. Kilmer reportedly stayed in character with consumptive coughing for months. The film's original director was George P. Cosmatos, but Russell has long claimed he was the uncredited true director. The original director who was fired three weeks into shooting was the screenwriter himself. Who?
answer: Kevin Jarre, who also wrote Glory (1989) and the Tombstone screenplay itself
choices: Kevin Jarre, who also wrote Glory (1989) and the Tombstone screenplay itself
John Carpenter, who left over budget disputes with Disney's Hollywood Pictures
Andy Garcia, in his first attempted directorial debut after a delayed Godfather Part III
Steve Beck, the visual-effects supervisor who had directed second-unit work
context: Jarre was fired three weeks into shooting because the production was running behind. He had written a much longer epic screenplay; Cosmatos cut it considerably. Russell has said publicly that he 'ghost-directed' the film with Cosmatos as a paper-only credit. Jarre's screenplay credit remained intact. He died in 2011 at age 56.

question: Edgar Wright's 2010 Scott Pilgrim vs. the World was a financial disappointment on release ($47M on a $90M production+marketing budget) but became a cult favorite on home video. The film features Brandon Routh as Todd Ingram, Chris Evans as Lucas Lee, and Brie Larson as Envy Adams. Two of those cast members have also played other comic-book heroes in the following decade. Which roles?
answer: Routh played Superman (Returns, 2006, pre-Scott Pilgrim) and Evans played Captain America (First Avenger, 2011)
choices: Routh played Superman (Returns, 2006, pre-Scott Pilgrim) and Evans played Captain America (First Avenger, 2011)
Larson played Captain Marvel (2019) and Routh played Atom on CW's Legends of Tomorrow
Evans played the Human Torch (Fantastic Four, 2005) and Routh played the Atom on CW
Larson played Squirrel Girl on a Marvel pilot and Evans played Captain America
context: All four answers are partially true. Routh played Superman in 2006 and the Atom on CW Arrowverse shows. Evans had played the Human Torch in 2005's Fantastic Four before becoming Cap in 2011. Larson played Captain Marvel starting in 2019. The Scott Pilgrim casting was prescient about which young actors would dominate the next decade.

question: Released in 1985, Steven Spielberg's The Goonies was directed by Richard Donner, who had earlier made The Omen (1976) and Superman (1978). The film's plot involves the kids finding the treasure map of a 17th-century pirate named One-Eyed Willy. What real-world pirate was Willy loosely based on?
answer: No single specific pirate; the character was original to writer Chris Columbus
choices: No single specific pirate; the character was original to writer Chris Columbus
Blackbeard (Edward Teach), with the eye-patch motif transposed from another period
Henry Morgan, the Welsh privateer turned governor of Jamaica
Anne Bonny's husband Calico Jack Rackham, executed in Jamaica in 1720
context: Chris Columbus wrote the screenplay based on Spielberg's story outline. Columbus later directed Home Alone (1990) and the first two Harry Potter films (2001, 2002). One-Eyed Willy's ship 'The Inferno' was a full-scale practical-effect ship constructed for the climax — Donner refused to destroy it after filming, and crew members have said it sat in a warehouse for years.

question: James Cameron made Aliens in 1986, turning Ridley Scott's 1979 horror film into an action-heavy war picture, and earned Sigourney Weaver an Oscar nomination for Best Actress. The sequel became one of the most celebrated in cinema, and fans expected him to jump straight into a third. What did Cameron do next?
answer: Cameron's next film was The Abyss (1989), not an Aliens sequel
choices: Cameron's next film was The Abyss (1989), not an Aliens sequel
Cameron immediately directed Alien 3 (1992) before The Abyss
Cameron directed Aliens 4 in 1995 before True Lies
Cameron made a Working Title Aliens 2.5 between Aliens and T2
context: Alien 3 (1992) was directed by David Fincher (his directorial debut, an experience he has called a 'horror story'). The Abyss followed Aliens for Cameron. Cameron and Sigourney Weaver were both deeply disappointed by Alien 3's killing of Newt and Hicks. Weaver's involvement in Alien 3 was strange — she was a producer.

question: Director John McTiernan had one of the greatest three-year runs in action-movie history. In 1987 he directed Predator, starring Arnold Schwarzenegger as a commando hunted through the jungle by an alien. Then, back-to-back, he made two more iconic action films before 1990 was out — one starring Bruce Willis, the other starring Sean Connery. What were those two films?
answer: Die Hard (1988) and The Hunt for Red October (1990)
choices: Die Hard (1988) and The Hunt for Red October (1990)
Die Hard (1988) and Last Action Hero (1993)
Lethal Weapon (1987) and The Russia House (1990)
RoboCop (1987) and Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989)
context: McTiernan's Die Hard-Predator-Hunt for Red October trio is one of the great action-director runs in cinema. He later went to prison briefly in 2013 for lying to the FBI about a wiretapping incident involving a private investigator. His daughter Annaliesa Henrik McTiernan is also a filmmaker.

question: In the 1990 science-fiction film Total Recall, Dutch director Paul Verhoeven built a rowdy Martian bar full of strange mutants. One of the movie's costliest special-effects scenes featured a mutant dancer named Mary — a red-dressed woman with three breasts. The American actress who played Mary later left acting entirely and became a working newspaper and magazine journalist, covering serious real-world stories. What is her name?
answer: Lycia Naff, who later played the Three-Breasted Whore (her IMDB credit) and went on to journalism
choices: Lycia Naff, who later played the Three-Breasted Whore (her IMDB credit) and went on to journalism
Sharon Stone, who had a similar bit role here before Basic Instinct (1992)
Roxann Dawson, who played B'Elanna Torres on Star Trek Voyager (1995-2001)
Mel Johnson Jr., the cabbie character actor's daughter playing a mutant niece
context: Lycia Naff appeared in three scenes total in the film. The three-breasted effect was a practical prosthetic, not CGI. Verhoeven famously delights in inserting transgressive imagery in commercial films (RoboCop's ED-209 boardroom shooting, Starship Troopers's flesh-eating brain bug). Naff later worked as an entertainment journalist for the National Enquirer.

question: In 1986, Tony Scott directed Top Gun on a $15M budget, which was high for a non-effects-driven film at the time. The Navy provided the F-14 Tomcats but required script approval. Tom Cruise nearly drowned during one stunt scene that was eventually cut from the final film. What was the cut sequence?
answer: An underwater ejection-seat training drill at the NAS Miramar pool
choices: An underwater ejection-seat training drill at the NAS Miramar pool
A high-altitude bailout sequence over the Mojave Desert salt flats
A submarine-deck landing simulation in the Pacific off San Diego
A water-survival exercise in San Francisco Bay near Alcatraz
context: Cruise was reportedly fine but the producers cut the sequence due to liability concerns. Cruise's later fame for doing his own stunts (notably the helicopter sequence in Mission: Impossible — Fallout) descends partly from his Top Gun experience. The 2022 sequel Top Gun: Maverick brought back the underwater stunt theme with Cruise actually performing G-force flight in real Navy aircraft.

question: In 1986's Top Gun, the famous beach volleyball scene was added at the last minute by producer Don Simpson. The scene's homoerotic subtext has been widely discussed by film critics. Tony Scott reportedly resisted including it. What real-life element of Cruise's career did the scene contribute to?
answer: It established Cruise's shirtless-action-star image that would dominate the next decade of his filmography
choices: It established Cruise's shirtless-action-star image that would dominate the next decade of his filmography
It introduced his Scientology recruiting pitch to younger actors in early on-set rehearsals
It started his publicly known feud with co-star Val Kilmer (Iceman) over creative direction
It led to his marriage to Nicole Kidman, whom he met at a Top Gun production party
context: The volleyball scene was added by producer Don Simpson against Scott's wishes. Simpson and Jerry Bruckheimer were known for adding 'beefcake' shots to their films. Cruise's subsequent shirtless scenes in The Color of Money (1986), Cocktail (1988), and Mission: Impossible (1996) reinforced the look. He met Nicole Kidman on Days of Thunder (1990), not Top Gun.

question: Dan Aykroyd first wrote Ghostbusters for himself and three friends: John Belushi, Eddie Murphy and John Candy. Belushi died of a drug overdose in 1982, before filming ever started, so Bill Murray took over his part, the wisecracking parapsychologist Peter Venkman. Aykroyd later said Venkman's whole loose, mischievous vibe was a direct tribute to Belushi. Which earlier Belushi roles did Aykroyd mean?
answer: Animal House (1978) and The Blues Brothers (1980) — Belushi's Bluto/Jake energy translated into Venkman
choices: Animal House (1978) and The Blues Brothers (1980) — Belushi's Bluto/Jake energy translated into Venkman
Continental Divide (1981) and Neighbors (1981) — Belushi's late-career romantic-lead attempts
1941 (1979) and Goin' South (1978) — Spielberg/Nicholson-era serious roles
Saturday Night Live's Samurai sketches (1976-1979) — the deadpan-anarchist character type
context: Belushi died of a drug overdose on March 5, 1982 in Hollywood's Chateau Marmont. Aykroyd had developed the Ghostbusters concept partly as a Belushi vehicle. Eddie Murphy declined because of Beverly Hills Cop conflict; the role became Winston Zeddemore (Ernie Hudson). Aykroyd's brother Peter Aykroyd had inspired the idea via the family's interest in spiritualism.

question: In 1985, director Ron Howard — the redheaded kid who had grown up playing Opie on The Andy Griffith Show — made the sci-fi drama Cocoon. In it, a group of retirement-home men swim in a pool full of glowing alien pods and suddenly feel young and strong again. Don Ameche won the Best Supporting Actor Oscar for it. What Disney movie, released the year before Cocoon, had Howard directed too?
answer: Splash (1984), with Tom Hanks and Daryl Hannah as the mermaid
choices: Splash (1984), with Tom Hanks and Daryl Hannah as the mermaid
Night Shift (1982), with Henry Winkler and Michael Keaton
Gung Ho (1986), with Michael Keaton at the Japanese auto plant
Willow (1988), with Warwick Davis and Val Kilmer in the lead roles
context: Splash was Touchstone Pictures' first release — Disney's adult-oriented label. Howard's career took off after Splash. He had been Opie on The Andy Griffith Show and Richie on Happy Days before transitioning to directing in the late 1970s. His next big hit was Backdraft (1991).

question: In Princess Bride, William Goldman's 1973 novel famously frames itself as the abridgement of a fictional classic by 'S. Morgenstern.' Many readers wrote to Goldman asking for the 'unabridged' version. Goldman's introduction included a real publisher offer that became famous. What did he promise readers who wrote in?
answer: He'd send them the unabridged 'reunion scene' between Westley and Buttercup, but the publisher legally couldn't reproduce it
choices: He'd send them the unabridged 'reunion scene' between Westley and Buttercup, but the publisher legally couldn't reproduce it
He'd send them a corrected manuscript page from S. Morgenstern's original text
He'd send them a Florinese-language certificate of completion from the abridgement
He'd send them his personal copy of the original Morgenstern hardback for inspection
context: Goldman's gag was elaborate — readers who wrote to the publisher (Harcourt Brace) received an apologetic form letter explaining that 'the Morgenstern estate had refused permission' for the reunion scene to be reproduced. The book has a real publisher's-introduction-style apparatus throughout. Goldman never wrote a real Morgenstern manuscript; the joke continues.

question: Don Bluth's team spent seven months on a 1983 Cinematronics laserdisc game in which the dragon Singe holds a princess. The game ran 22 minutes, yet it contained more individual hand-drawn animation than most full feature films. How many cels did the team draw?
answer: Approximately 50,000 cels — three times the count of a typical 80-minute Disney feature
