choices: Approximately 50,000 cels — three times the count of a typical 80-minute Disney feature
Approximately 12,000 cels — comparable to a single Looney Tunes short
Approximately 250,000 cels — comparable to The Lion King (1994)
Approximately 8,000 cels — heavily reusing animation across branches
context: Bluth's team worked for 7 months on the project. The non-linear branching structure meant scenes that the player might or might not see depending on choices. The original arcade laserdiscs are now considered collectible artifacts of arcade history. Don Bluth himself estimated the cel count in interviews.

question: Vigo the Carpathian, a 16th-century tyrant, waits with his spirit trapped in a self-portrait at a Manhattan art museum in the 1989 sequel Ghostbusters II. A towering former heavyweight boxer plays him. What is that actor's name?
answer: Wilhelm von Homburg (real name Norbert Grupe)
choices: Wilhelm von Homburg (real name Norbert Grupe)
Bill Bixby (best known as the original TV Hulk's Bruce Banner)
Ernie Reyes Sr. (the martial-arts coach who choreographed the Karate Kid)
Tor Johnson (the Plan 9 from Outer Space wrestler who died in 1971)
context: Homburg's German accent was so thick that director Ivan Reitman dubbed all his lines using Max von Sydow. Homburg had been a pro wrestler before becoming an actor. He died in 2004 at age 63. His one-time girlfriend was actress Romy Schneider.

question: Back to the Future stages the DeLorean's first time jump at Twin Pines Mall, and the name sets up a small pine-tree gag. Robert Zemeckis shot the scene at a real Southern California shopping center that went by another name. Which real location was it?
answer: Puente Hills Mall in Industry, California (despite often being misidentified as Burbank)
choices: Puente Hills Mall in Industry, California (despite often being misidentified as Burbank)
Hollywood Mall, a since-demolished shopping center on Sunset Boulevard
Northridge Fashion Center, the locations team's alternate-day backup
Universal CityWalk, before its later 1990s development
context: Puente Hills Mall has hosted multiple BTTF reunions. The Twin Pines / Lone Pine joke is one of the film's many small payoffs from Marty's brief 1955 actions affecting 1985. The mall's actual location is in the city of Industry, southeast of Los Angeles. Universal-themed Marty's Cafe operated at the mall for years.

question: In 1984, director John G. Avildsen, who had already won a Best Director Oscar for Rocky, made The Karate Kid, about a bullied teenager named Daniel LaRusso learning karate from an elderly Japanese-American handyman, Mr. Miyagi. The studio could not simply use the title. A comic-book publisher already owned a superhero called Karate Kid, a martial-arts member of the Legion of Super-Heroes since 1966, so the filmmakers needed its permission. Which publisher?
context: DC Comics owns Karate Kid, a member of the Legion of Super-Heroes created in 1966, and in 1984 the filmmakers received DC's permission to use the title for the film and its sequels.

question: The 1987 sci-fi film Predator, starring Arnold Schwarzenegger, needed a terrifying alien hunter to menace his commando squad in the Central American jungle. The first Predator suit looked like a skinny insect with a long red neck, and it was worn on set by a young Jean-Claude Van Damme. Schwarzenegger and director John McTiernan both hated the design and demanded a full redo. The redesign was handed to a legendary special-effects sculptor who had also built the creatures for Aliens and The Thing. Who was he?
context: Stan Winston Studio became the go-to creature-effects shop in the 1980s and 90s — also doing Terminator (1984), Aliens (1986), Predator (1987), Jurassic Park (1993), and Edward Scissorhands (1990). Winston died of multiple myeloma in 2008 at age 62. Jean-Claude Van Damme had originally been cast as the Predator but quit after one day.

question: In 1991's T2, James Cameron pushed CGI (computer-generated imagery) to new heights with the liquid-metal T-1000. Industrial Light & Magic (ILM) spent months developing the morphing software, dramatically expanding what was possible in film effects. The breakthrough was made possible by a custom 'morph' program written by an ILM engineer. What was that engineer's name?
answer: Doug Smythe, who later won an Academy Award for the morphing technology
choices: Doug Smythe, who later won an Academy Award for the morphing technology
John Knoll, the inventor of Photoshop while at ILM
Dennis Muren, the special-effects supervisor on the OT Star Wars films
Phil Tippett, fresh from his go-motion T-Rex work at the time
context: Doug Smythe led the morphing-software team at ILM. The T-1000's effects took several minutes of screen time to render per second. The technology was reused on Death Becomes Her (1992) and helped enable Jurassic Park (1993). The morph effect became so culturally iconic that Michael Jackson's Black or White music video (1991) immediately copied it.

question: Stan Winston's crew built James Cameron's Alien Queen as a real costume for the 1986 film Aliens. Sigourney Weaver drove the yellow power loader herself after a few rehearsals, and four trained cats took turns as Jonesy the cat. How tall was the Queen costume, and how was it worked?
answer: Fourteen feet, operated by two puppeteers inside and a crane for movement
choices: Fourteen feet, operated by two puppeteers inside and a crane for movement
Twelve feet, with rod puppeteers controlling only the upper body
Eighteen feet, with hydraulics controlled by joystick offstage
Sixteen feet, with three suit performers stacked vertically inside the costume
context: The Queen costume was designed by Stan Winston and operated by 14-16 people total when the rod-and-puppet team was counted. Sigourney Weaver insisted on doing her own Power Loader stunts after a few rehearsals. The cat Jonesy was played by four trained cats.

question: The 1993 Western film Tombstone tells the story of legendary lawman Wyatt Earp and his friends facing down outlaws in the 1880s Arizona town of Tombstone. American actor Val Kilmer plays Doc Holliday, a tubercular gambler and gunfighter who coughs blood and drinks whiskey between duels. In one tense scene, Doc stares down his rival Johnny Ringo and mutters an old Latin proverb: 'in vino veritas.' What does that Latin phrase mean in English?
context: Doc Holliday was historically a Georgia dentist who turned to gunfighting after his tuberculosis diagnosis. He died at age 36 in Glenwood Springs, Colorado in 1887. Val Kilmer's performance is widely considered one of the greatest portrayals of the historical character. The film also features Bill Paxton as Morgan Earp.

question: The 1990 gangster film Goodfellas was directed by American filmmaker Martin Scorsese and stars Ray Liotta as Henry Hill — a real New York mobster who spent decades inside the Lucchese crime family before turning informant for the FBI. The screenplay was adapted from a 1985 non-fiction book by American journalist Nicholas Pileggi, drawn from hundreds of taped interviews Pileggi had done with the real Hill himself. What was Pileggi's book called?
answer: Wiseguy: Life in a Mafia Family
choices: Wiseguy: Life in a Mafia Family
The Goodfella's Tale: Henry Hill's Story
The Mob: A Made Man's Memoir
context: Pileggi co-wrote the screenplay with Scorsese. The title 'Goodfellas' was changed because of an unrelated TV series called Wiseguy (1987-90). Henry Hill, the real-life informant subject, died in 2012. The film's improvised dinner scenes (especially Joe Pesci's 'Funny how?' bit) became iconic.

question: Marty McFly tries to order a soft drink in a 1955 diner in Robert Zemeckis's Back to the Future, the film that earned $381M worldwide on a $19M budget. Both names he gives the soda clerk mean nothing to the man, which is the famous gag. Which two drinks does Marty try to order?
answer: Tab and Pepsi Free, neither of which existed in 1955
choices: Tab and Pepsi Free, neither of which existed in 1955
Diet Coke and Sprite Zero, Coca-Cola products from later decades
Mountain Dew and Sunkist, brands that hadn't yet been launched
Coca-Cola Classic and New Coke, distinguishing the 1985 confusion
context: Marty asks for a Tab — the soda clerk responds 'I can't give you a tab unless you order something.' Marty then asks for a Pepsi Free — the clerk says 'You want a Pepsi, pal, you're gonna pay for it.' Tab and Pepsi Free were both real Pepsi/Coca-Cola products in 1985 (diet variants). The gag plays on 1955 versus 1985 vocabulary differences.

question: In 1987 the American comedy director Mel Brooks released Spaceballs, a movie that spoofed Star Wars. The hero Lone Starr piloted a Winnebago spaceship across the galaxy with his best friend Barf, a big lovable half-man, half-dog creature Brooks called a Mawg. Barf had floppy ears, a wagging tail, and a huge appetite. He was played by a warm-hearted, heavyset Canadian comedy actor famous for movies like Uncle Buck and Planes, Trains and Automobiles. Who played Barf the Mawg in Spaceballs?
context: Candy died in 1994 at age 43 from a heart attack. Rick Moranis played Dark Helmet (the Vader parody). Bill Pullman played Lone Starr (the Han Solo parody). Spaceballs took Star Wars to task for marketing itself through merchandise — the 'Spaceballs the Lunchbox' running gag was prescient.

question: The 1987 movie The Princess Bride opens with a boy playing a baseball video game on a Commodore Amiga. His grandpa comes to read him a story. The game shown was published by Accolade in 1985. Many fans got it wrong and thought it was a 1989 sequel. What was the real title?
answer: Hardball! (the 1985 original, not Hardball II from 1989)
choices: Hardball! (the 1985 original, not Hardball II from 1989)
World Series Baseball by Atari Ages
context: Hardball was Accolade's first hit, programmed by Bob Whitehead. The Amiga prop in the film was a Commodore Amiga 1000 (released 1985). Fred Savage was 11 during filming and was already cast in The Wonder Years pilot that same year. Norman Reynolds had production-designed Star Wars (1977) and Empire Strikes Back (1980) before Princess Bride. The video-game prop is one of the most-Googled details of any 80s film opening.

question: In Canadian cartoonist Bryan Lee O'Malley's six-volume Scott Pilgrim graphic novel series, hero Scott must defeat the seven evil exes of his girlfriend Ramona Flowers one by one to keep dating her. Ramona's fourth evil ex is the only female fighter Scott has to face — a katana-wielding young woman Ramona briefly dated during college. What is this fourth ex's name?
context: Roxie Richter is Ramona's fourth evil ex and only female ex. Mae Whitman played her in the 2010 Edgar Wright film. The 'L-word' chapter title alludes to Ramona's revelation of her 'little bi-furious phase in college.' Whitman is also famous as Katara's voice in Avatar: The Last Airbender. Envy Adams (Brie Larson) is Scott's heartbreaking ex-girlfriend. Knives Chau is Scott's then-current 17-year-old high school girlfriend. Kim Pine is Sex Bob-omb's drummer.

question: The original 1985 NES Super Mario Bros. famously contains a glitch in World 1-2 that lets players warp into a 'Minus World' (World -1) — actually a corrupted underwater Water Level 7 that loops with no exit. The Japanese Famicom Disk System version had a DIFFERENT result for the same glitch sequence. What happens on the Famicom Disk version?
answer: The Minus World is three different glitch-worlds depending on Mario's exact clip position, and one is even completable
choices: The Minus World is three different glitch-worlds depending on Mario's exact clip position, and one is even completable
The Minus World plays back the title screen in distorted color, freezing the console
The Minus World becomes World 0, an inverted version of 1-1 with reversed gravity
The Minus World contains the developer Easter egg crediting Shigeru Miyamoto by name
context: The cartridge ROM version's Minus World loops because the corrupted tile is read as Water Level 7's start. The Famicom Disk version stores level data slightly differently in RAM, so the result varies. SMB's Minus World is one of the most-studied glitches in video-game history. The 1-2 warp pipe was intended to send Mario to Worlds 2-4; the glitch hijacks the warp routine.

question: Khary Payton, who voiced Cyborg on Teen Titans for years, plays the Penguin King in The Super Mario Bros. Movie, defending his Snow Kingdom against Bowser. The kingdom's hut and its long, winding toboggan run are lifted from a world in Super Mario 64, the 1996 game. Which world?
answer: Cool, Cool Mountain — the snowy peak with the cabin and the slide level
choices: Cool, Cool Mountain — the snowy peak with the cabin and the slide level
Snowman's Land — the wider Mario 64 ice level with the big snowman
Sherbet Land — from Mario Kart 64, not Super Mario 64
Freezeflame Galaxy — actually from Super Mario Galaxy (2007), post-N64
context: Cool, Cool Mountain features a baby penguin lost on the slope that Mario can rescue. The level appeared in Super Mario 64 (Nintendo 64, 1996), one of the most-celebrated 3D platformers ever. The 2023 film's Snow Kingdom design directly evokes the Cool, Cool Mountain cabin and slide aesthetic. The Khary Payton casting for the Penguin King is itself a deep cut — he voiced Cyborg on Teen Titans for years.

question: Christopher Lloyd's Doc Brown swings out on a cable in the clock-tower climax of Back to the Future, filmed at the courthouse on the Universal Studios backlot, the same set used for To Kill a Mockingbird (1962). What was unusual about the setup that allowed for this famously dangerous-looking shot?
answer: The cable was attached to Lloyd's stunt double via a hidden harness, and a pulley counterweight system did most of the swing motion
choices: The cable was attached to Lloyd's stunt double via a hidden harness, and a pulley counterweight system did most of the swing motion
Lloyd performed the stunt himself with no harness, and ILM digitally added the cable in post-production
The clock tower was a half-scale forced-perspective miniature, and the stunt was filmed sideways
The scene was filmed using bluescreen, with the cable swing entirely added via matte painting
context: The Universal Studios courthouse was actually built for To Kill a Mockingbird in 1962. The clock face was added for BTTF and remained a Universal Studios tour stop for years. The original Back to the Future Part II (1989) revisited the scene from a different angle. Zemeckis's commitment to practical effects on the trilogy gave it a tactile quality CGI sequels often lack.

question: Mars Inc. famously passed on putting M&Ms in Steven Spielberg's 1982 film E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, and Hershey signed a $1 million deal with Universal instead, for another candy to lure the alien. Within weeks of release, sales of that candy jumped dramatically. By what factor did sales rise in the months after the film's release?
answer: Sales tripled, making it one of the most successful product placements in film history
choices: Sales tripled, making it one of the most successful product placements in film history
Sales doubled, restoring Hershey's market share against M&Ms briefly
Sales quadrupled in the first month, then settled to a 50% lift
Sales increased tenfold, leading Hershey to triple production capacity
context: The Mars Inc. rejection of M&Ms is one of the most-cited examples of poor marketing decision-making. Hershey's $1M deal was modest by today's standards but groundbreaking in 1982. E.T. grossed $359M domestically, holding the all-time record until 1997's Titanic. Spielberg's son Mikaela was born around the time of the film's production, partly influencing its child-centric perspective.

question: John Williams's 1977 score for Star Wars: A New Hope was performed by the London Symphony Orchestra at Anvil Studios in Denham, England. Williams used Wagnerian leitmotifs — assigning specific themes to specific characters. The famous 'Imperial March' (Darth Vader's theme) does NOT actually appear in the original 1977 film. When did it debut?
answer: The Empire Strikes Back (1980), where Williams introduced it as Vader's leitmotif
choices: The Empire Strikes Back (1980), where Williams introduced it as Vader's leitmotif
Return of the Jedi (1983), where it premiered in the throne-room confrontation
The original 1977 film, in a slower, less-recognizable form during the Death Star scenes
The 1997 Special Edition rerelease, which added the Imperial March to several Vader scenes
context: The Imperial March (technically 'The Imperial March/Darth Vader's Theme') premiered in The Empire Strikes Back (1980). The original 1977 Star Wars used the Main Title theme for Vader's appearances. Williams composed the leitmotif specifically for the Empire score. The London Symphony Orchestra has now recorded Williams's Star Wars scores for every theatrically released film through the entire saga.

question: Burt Reynolds reportedly had a specific personal reason for voicing Charlie B. Barkin in Don Bluth's 1989 musical. Disney's The Little Mermaid came out the same day, November 17, and crushed the film at the box office. Why did Reynolds reportedly take the role?
answer: His pet Doberman 'Bruno' had recently died, and the part connected him to processing the loss
choices: His pet Doberman 'Bruno' had recently died, and the part connected him to processing the loss
His agent forced the role to fulfill a three-picture deal with United Artists
He needed quick income while waiting for the Cannonball Run III project to greenlight
He wanted to learn animation voice-work for a planned cartoon based on his career
context: Reynolds was at the peak of his Hollywood power in the late 1980s but had begun the steep decline that defined his 1990s. All Dogs Go to Heaven was his only major animated voice role. He died in 2018 at age 82. Bluth has spoken in interviews about Reynolds being deeply committed to the part despite the film's box-office disappointment.

question: Released in 1982, John Carpenter's The Thing was a financial disappointment at $19.6M against an $11M budget — partly because it opened against E.T. (June 25, 1982 Carpenter; June 11, 1982 E.T.). The film's practical effects by Rob Bottin pioneered creature transformation imagery. The most-iconic transformation sequence involves a character's head detaching and growing spider legs. The shot has a specific cultural nickname. What's it called?
answer: The Norris head-spider, named after the character (Charles Hallahan) whose head transforms
choices: The Norris head-spider, named after the character (Charles Hallahan) whose head transforms
The Bennings split, named for the first character to obviously transform in the film
The Blair monster, the basement creature's first reveal moment
The Palmer transformation, the most-quoted body-horror scene in the kennel
context: The Norris head-spider scene features the head growing spider legs and walking across the floor. The famous line: 'You've gotta be fucking kidding.' Rob Bottin was 22 when he supervised the effects. Stan Winston also contributed (the dog-thing transformation). The Thing has been reassessed as one of the greatest horror films ever made, its initial commercial failure attributed to E.T.'s family-friendly competition.

question: Ray Parker Jr. wrote the theme song for the 1984 comedy Ghostbusters, and it became one of the year's biggest hits, three weeks at number one on the Billboard chart. It immediately triggered a famous copyright-infringement lawsuit as well. Who sued Parker for plagiarism, and what was the disputed song?
answer: Huey Lewis sued for similarity to 'I Want a New Drug' (1984); the case settled out of court
choices: Huey Lewis sued for similarity to 'I Want a New Drug' (1984); the case settled out of court
Lionel Richie sued for similarity to 'All Night Long' (1983); won damages on appeal
Tina Turner sued for similarity to 'What's Love Got to Do With It' (1984); was dismissed
Prince sued for similarity to 'When Doves Cry' (1984); settled for publishing royalties
context: The settlement included a non-disclosure clause. Lewis later spoke about it in interviews, costing him a confidentiality-violation lawsuit from Parker. The Ghostbusters theme spent three weeks at #1 on Billboard Hot 100 in September 1984. Ray Parker Jr. was also a respected session guitarist who had played on records by Stevie Wonder and Barry White.

question: Released in 1987, Predator was filmed in the jungles around Mismaloya and Palenque in Mexico. The brutal production conditions — heat, humidity, dysentery — led to multiple cast members losing significant weight. Arnold Schwarzenegger was reportedly the only major cast member who didn't get sick. The film's iconic 'tribal chief' final-act scene features Schwarzenegger covered in mud to mask his heat signature from the Predator's thermal vision. The mud sequence had a specific real-world inspiration. What?
answer: Vietnam War-era veterans had reportedly used mud to evade NVA night-vision optics, inspiring the script choice
choices: Vietnam War-era veterans had reportedly used mud to evade NVA night-vision optics, inspiring the script choice
African elephant-hunting tribes had used mud to mask their scent from elephants, per anthropologist consultants
Camo-pattern mudding was a then-current US Army Ranger field training technique
Schwarzenegger improvised the mud move during a take, and McTiernan kept it in
context: John McTiernan had researched military jungle-warfare tactics for the film. The mud-covering scene became Predator's most-iconic visual. Carl Weathers (Apollo Creed from Rocky) played Dillon, the CIA contact. Bill Duke and Jesse Ventura played other commandos. Ventura's catchphrase 'I ain't got time to bleed' was reportedly ad-libbed by him on set.

question: James Cameron clashed extensively with the British crew at Pinewood Studios while shooting his 1986 film Aliens, over American versus British filmmaking practices. The story still told from that set has him firing the entire crew on the first day. What did he really do?
answer: Cameron actually held his ground until the crew, expecting to be fired, came back, and the film was made
choices: Cameron actually held his ground until the crew, expecting to be fired, came back, and the film was made
He brought in his own American crew from The Terminator after the British crew walked out
He hired Stanley Kubrick's longtime first AD to manage the British team
He made a deal with the union to let Sigourney Weaver be technically a producer to satisfy quotas
context: Cameron's reputation for being demanding came partly from Aliens. He has said in interviews that the crew was unaccustomed to working at the pace he wanted. Sigourney Weaver was famously paid $1M for Aliens (a then-record for a female lead in an action film). The film's $18M budget was modest by 1980s standards. Aliens received seven Oscar nominations and won two.

question: The 1985 science-fiction film Cocoon is about a group of Florida retirees who sneak into a neighbor's swimming pool and discover alien pods that make them feel young again. American actor Don Ameche plays retiree Art Selwyn and won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for the role. In one show-stopping scene, seventy-seven-year-old Ameche crashes a nightclub dance floor and pulls off a real breakdance move — spinning on his shoulder blades while his legs point straight at the ceiling. Which breakdance move did Ameche perform?
answer: A backspin (the move where the body rotates on the upper back/shoulders)
choices: A backspin (the move where the body rotates on the upper back/shoulders)
A windmill (the legs swing in a vertical circle while the back stays on the floor)
The moonwalk (Michael Jackson had popularized it in March 1983)
context: Ameche was 77 when he won the Oscar — at the time the second-oldest recipient of the Best Supporting Actor category. He had been a major film star in the 1930s and 40s and Cocoon revitalized his career. The breakdancing scene was performed by a stunt double for the actual spinning moves, but Ameche performed all the dance footwork himself. The 1988 sequel Cocoon: The Return reunited most of the original cast.

question: Universal Studios and the producers Steven Spielberg and George Lucas reportedly forced significant cuts on Don Bluth's Land Before Time after test audiences with children expressed distress. It was going to be a much darker film, and the release version of 1988 is 69 minutes long. How much footage was reportedly cut from Bluth's original?
answer: Approximately 12 minutes, including a more graphic Sharptooth (T-Rex) attack and a longer death sequence for Littlefoot's mother
choices: Approximately 12 minutes, including a more graphic Sharptooth (T-Rex) attack and a longer death sequence for Littlefoot's mother
Approximately 3 minutes, mostly Bluth-favorite dialogue between Cera and Littlefoot
Approximately 18 minutes, including an entire subplot about Petrie's missing father
Approximately 6 minutes, focusing on Ducky's separation from her family early in the film
context: Bluth has been ambivalent about the cuts in subsequent interviews. The death of Littlefoot's mother was reportedly so traumatic in the original cut that test-screening parents complained Universal had screened a horror film. The cuts gave the film a tighter pace at the cost of much of its emotional depth. Bluth left the franchise after the original; the 13 direct-to-video sequels are widely considered inferior.

question: Fievel's sister Tanya sings 'Somewhere Out There' with him from the far end of the New York night sky, the two of them longing to find each other, in Don Bluth's 1986 cartoon. The duet is a top-5 hit on Billboard, and a specific technique gives the sequence its visual depth. Which technique is it?
answer: A multi-plane camera, the same technology Bluth had championed at Disney before his 1979 defection
choices: A multi-plane camera, the same technology Bluth had championed at Disney before his 1979 defection
Rotoscoping over live-action performers in costume for the song's choreography
Computer-assisted 'tweening' on a Cray supercomputer that ILM had loaned to Bluth
Inverse-kinematic limb animation, an early version of the modern 3D rigging technique
context: Multi-plane camera (invented by Disney's Iwerks in 1937) involved multiple glass planes of artwork being filmed through a camera that focused on each at different depths. Bluth's commitment to the technique was central to his break from Disney. The 'Somewhere Out There' sequence in An American Tail features at least 5 planes of moving artwork. Linda Ronstadt and James Ingram's recording of the song reached #2 on Billboard.

question: Released in 1990, Paul Verhoeven's Total Recall featured a transgressive approach to violence that was typical of Verhoeven's RoboCop-era Hollywood work. The film's Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) rating fight was famous. Verhoeven and the studio submitted the film a total of 8 times before getting an R rating. What was the specific scene that gave the MPAA the most trouble?
answer: Schwarzenegger using a human body as a shield in the subway shootout
choices: Schwarzenegger using a human body as a shield in the subway shootout
The three-breasted Martian mutant Mary's brief topless scene
Sharon Stone's character being shot in the head and the explicit aftermath
Quaid's eye-popping scene as the Mars atmosphere reaches him
context: The subway scene shows Schwarzenegger holding a dead body in front of him as bullets riddle it. The MPAA initially gave it an X rating. Verhoeven darkened the lighting and slightly trimmed the frame count to get the R. Total Recall earned $261M worldwide. Verhoeven's career trajectory continued with Basic Instinct (1992), Showgirls (1995), and Starship Troopers (1997) before he returned to European cinema.

question: Released in 1984, the original Karate Kid earned Pat Morita a Best Supporting Actor nomination for his Mr. Miyagi, a gentle Japanese-American handyman who carries painful memories of the Second World War. Morita knew that era first-hand: as a child during World War II (WWII) he and his family were held in American internment camps. Where was the real Pat Morita interned?
answer: Gila River, Arizona (then transferred to Tule Lake, California for security reclassification)
choices: Gila River, Arizona (then transferred to Tule Lake, California for security reclassification)
Manzanar, California (the best-known camp of the war)
Heart Mountain, Wyoming (the highest-altitude camp in the system)
Topaz, Utah (where Morita's family had owned a Sacramento Valley restaurant)
context: Morita was born in Isleton, California in 1932 to immigrant parents. He had spinal tuberculosis as a child and spent nine years in a Sacramento hospital. After the war, his family ran restaurants. He moved into stand-up comedy in the 1960s as 'The Hip Nip' and broke into TV with Happy Days. The Karate Kid (1984) was his career-defining role. He died in 2005 at age 73.

question: Released in 1993, Tombstone went through a famously chaotic production. Director Kevin Jarre was fired three weeks into shooting. George P. Cosmatos was hired as a paper replacement — the film's lead actor has long claimed that he himself did most of the actual directing, with Cosmatos a credit-only figurehead. Cosmatos's son Panos confirmed his father's role on a 2018 podcast. What did Panos confirm?
answer: His father George had been a paid 'frontman' director; Kurt Russell did most of the directorial work
choices: His father George had been a paid 'frontman' director; Kurt Russell did most of the directorial work
His father had a longer cut that was never released by Hollywood Pictures
Val Kilmer had directed all his own consumption-coughing scenes via improvisation
Wyatt Earp's grand-niece had been a behind-the-scenes consultant for historical accuracy
context: Panos Cosmatos directed Mandy (2018) and Beyond the Black Rainbow (2010). His confirmation matched what Kurt Russell had publicly claimed since 2006. George P. Cosmatos directed Rambo: First Blood Part II (1985) and Cobra (1986) for Sylvester Stallone, who had similar paper-director arrangements. Tombstone went on to become a Western canon classic despite the production chaos.

question: Temple of Doom opens in a glittering Shanghai nightclub in 1935, with a song-and-dance number, a poisoned drink and a diamond deal gone wrong. Raiders had already hidden George Lucas's droids on a tomb wall, C-3PO and R2-D2 carved among the hieroglyphs. This film slips in another Star Wars nod: the name of the club. What is it called?
context: In a nod to Star Wars, the Shanghai nightclub where Temple of Doom begins is called Club Obi-Wan. Raiders of the Lost Ark had already hidden R2-D2 and C-3PO among the hieroglyphs in the Well of Souls.

question: Released in 1985, Steven Spielberg's The Goonies was directed by Richard Donner. Donner had directed The Omen (1976) and Superman (1978). The Goonies featured a young Sean Astin (Mikey), Josh Brolin (Brand), Corey Feldman (Mouth), Jonathan Ke Quan (Data), Jeff Cohen (Chunk), and Martha Plimpton (Stef). The film's emotional climax has the kids discovering One-Eyed Willy's pirate ship. The ship was built as a full-scale practical effect. What happened to the ship after filming?
answer: Donner refused to destroy it; it sat in a warehouse for years before being scrapped in the early 2000s
choices: Donner refused to destroy it; it sat in a warehouse for years before being scrapped in the early 2000s
It was sold to Universal Studios theme park and became part of the Earthquake ride decoration
It was donated to the Astoria Maritime Museum in Astoria, Oregon (the filming location)
It was burned for the Goonies' 20th-anniversary 2005 ceremony with Donner's blessing
context: Donner reportedly hated destroying built sets. The Goonies' ship 'The Inferno' was constructed at a major budget cost. Donner has said in interviews that the ship was scrapped reluctantly years later. The Astoria, Oregon film locations have become a tourist attraction; the Goon Docks (Mikey's house) was vandalized so frequently that the city eventually moved the original mailbox to City Hall.

question: In 1986, Tony Scott shot Top Gun's carrier scenes aboard real Navy ships, filming F-14 Tomcats in exactly the light he wanted. During one sequence the carrier's commanding officer changed course, and the light Scott was shooting in shifted with the ship. Scott asked to go back to the old course and was told what it cost to turn the carrier. So he wrote the captain a check on the spot. How much was it for?
context: When Scott asked the carrier to keep its earlier course, he was told it cost $25,000 to turn the ship, so he wrote the captain a check and kept filming. The carrier sequences were shot aboard the Enterprise and the Ranger, and the film's enemy MiG-28s were really Northrop F-5s.

question: The 1991 action film Terminator 2: Judgment Day was directed by James Cameron and starred Arnold Schwarzenegger as a reprogrammed protector robot. Its villain, the shape-shifting liquid-metal T-1000, was one of the first big Hollywood uses of computer-generated imagery (CGI). The film's rebellious teenage hero John Connor was played by a total unknown named Edward Furlong, cast at the very last minute. How was Furlong first discovered by the film?
answer: Casting director Mali Finn spotted him at a Pasadena YMCA, where he was 13 years old and hanging out with friends
choices: Casting director Mali Finn spotted him at a Pasadena YMCA, where he was 13 years old and hanging out with friends
He was a child model who had appeared in Sears catalogs and was already on Cameron's shortlist
His mother sent his school photo to the production office along with thousands of others
His uncle was a stunt coordinator at Stan Winston Studios who recommended him
context: Mali Finn had been the casting director for Cameron's The Abyss (1989). Furlong had no prior acting experience. T2 was Furlong's debut. He won the MTV Movie Award for Best Breakthrough Performance. His personal life later deteriorated severely; he has struggled with addiction since the late 1990s. Robert Patrick (the T-1000) was a relatively obscure character actor who broke through with T2.

question: Edgar Wright's 2010 Scott Pilgrim vs. the World features a famous '8 dollars' joke when Scott pays at the cinema box office. The scene caused some misinterpretation among American audiences who didn't realize the price reflected a specific real-world fact about the source material. What's the joke about?
answer: Toronto movie ticket prices in 2010 were genuinely around $8, anchoring the story in a specific Canadian setting
choices: Toronto movie ticket prices in 2010 were genuinely around $8, anchoring the story in a specific Canadian setting
American movie tickets in 2010 were genuinely $8 in suburbs, matching Scott's apparent class status
The Canadian dollar in 2010 was at near-parity with USD, making the price internationally legible
The Honest Ed's discount theater near Lee's Palace charged exactly $8 for second-run shows
context: Scott Pilgrim is intensely rooted in Toronto-as-portrayed-by-Bryan-Lee-O'Malley. The price detail is the kind of granular accuracy that makes the comic feel like a memoir. Honest Ed's was a real discount store at Bloor and Bathurst, demolished in 2017 to make way for apartments. Lee's Palace (the inspiration for the Chaos Theatre) is still operating. The Scott Pilgrim Universe (a sketch series) and the 2023 Netflix anime expanded on the same Toronto.

question: In Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim graphic novels, the climactic battle features Scott earning the 'Power of Love' sword by defeating Todd Ingram. The +1 sword that ends the same chapter is used against Gideon Graves. The final reveal — that Scott actually defeats Gideon using a 'Power of Self-Respect' sword — comes from a specific encounter with his Nega-Scott. What does Nega-Scott represent?
answer: Scott's repressed memories of being a terrible boyfriend, especially to Knives Chau and Envy Adams
choices: Scott's repressed memories of being a terrible boyfriend, especially to Knives Chau and Envy Adams
Scott's college-era addiction to alcohol that he'd been hiding from Ramona
Scott's subconscious Canadian guilt complex inherited from his immigrant Scottish parents
Scott's actual brother Lawrence whom Scott had repressed memories of from childhood
context: Nega-Scott is the personification of Scott's flaws he hasn't acknowledged. In the 2010 film, the encounter is brief and played for laughs ('We have a lot in common, actually'). In the graphic novels, the Nega-Scott confrontation is treated more seriously, with Scott finally taking responsibility for his past. The 2023 Netflix anime adapted both versions in different episodes.

question: Bowser storms the peaceful Snow Kingdom in The Super Mario Bros. Movie by bowling giant snowballs across the ice at its penguin defenders. Nintendo fans spotted the move at once as a callback to a boss fight in Super Mario 64, the game where Mario first ran around a full three-dimensional world. Which boss and stage?
answer: Chief Chilly's snowball attack in Snowman's Land, where the boss rolls snowballs at Mario
choices: Chief Chilly's snowball attack in Snowman's Land, where the boss rolls snowballs at Mario
Mr. Blizzard's whirling-snowball spawn in Cool Cool Mountain
Big Boo's Haunt ice-room reflection puzzle from the third star
The Bob-omb Battlefield's giant cannonball physics test from the first stage
context: Chief Chilly is the boss of Snowman's Land in Super Mario 64. The fight involves a giant snowman shooting smaller snowballs that Mario must navigate. The 2023 film's Penguin King is voiced by Khary Payton, and the Snow Kingdom sequence directly references multiple Mario games. Director Aaron Horvath and Michael Jelenic are reportedly huge Mario fans and overloaded the film with Easter eggs.

question: Released in 1991, James Cameron's Terminator 2 sent a new killer after young John Connor: the T-1000, a liquid-metal cyborg that pours through bars and turns its arms into blades. Robert Patrick, a lean, little-known actor then living in his car, won the part with his intense presence. But Cameron's first choice had been a sneering, spiky-haired British rock singer, until a motorcycle crash badly injured the singer's leg. Who was he?
context: Billy Idol was originally cast as the T-1000 before a motorcycle crash seriously injured his leg; Cameron later said he probably would not have cast him in hindsight. Casting director Mali Finn felt Robert Patrick had the intense presence the part needed.

question: Robert Zemeckis and Bob Gale sent Marty McFly and Doc Brown to October 21, 2015 in the 1989 film Back to the Future Part II, and filled that fictional 2015 with silly guesses: hoverboards floating over sidewalks, Nikes that laced themselves up, a nineteenth Jaws sequel. Only one guess about the real world came true, and it stunned Gale years later. Which one?
answer: The Cubs winning the World Series in 2016 (just one year late from the film's October 21, 2015 prediction)
choices: The Cubs winning the World Series in 2016 (just one year late from the film's October 21, 2015 prediction)
Hoverboards becoming an actual consumer product (the 2015 self-balancing scooter)
Video calls with multi-channel interfaces (similar to Marty's TV-call scene)
Movies running 19+ sequels (the Jaws 19 joke poster in the film)
context: The Chicago Cubs hadn't won a World Series since 1908. Their 2016 victory broke the longest drought in major American sports. Bob Gale's screenplay had positioned the joke as the most-impossible thing about 2015. Other predictions in BTTF Part II have come partially true — video calls (FaceTime), self-tying shoes (Nike's 2016 release), Pepsi Perfect (released as Pepsi Perfect for the 2015 anniversary).

question: The Grail temple in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade has a real rose-red front: a tomb face carved into a cliff at Petra, in Jordan, by Nabataean masons two thousand years ago. Local Bedouins believed a pharaoh had hidden riches in the stone urn at its top and fired rifles at it to crack it open; the bullet scars still show. What does the tomb's Arabic name, Al-Khazneh, mean?
context: Al-Khazneh means the Treasury in Arabic, a name the area's Bedouins gave it in the early nineteenth century from a legend that riches lay in its urn, which is solid sandstone. The film used the façade as the entrance to the Grail temple and shot the interior at Elstree Studios in England.

question: Fievel and his family board a ship leaving Russia in the 1986 cartoon Don Bluth made with Steven Spielberg, a story based on Spielberg's family history of Russian-Jewish immigration. Their flight is historical. What real event forces this wave of Jews to flee?
answer: The Russian pogroms of the 1881-1884 period, which displaced over 2 million Eastern European Jews
choices: The Russian pogroms of the 1881-1884 period, which displaced over 2 million Eastern European Jews
The Russo-Japanese War of 1904-1905, with Jewish refugees fleeing both conflicts
The Bolshevik Revolution of 1917, when many Jewish families chose Bolshevik or anti-Bolshevik sides
The Russian Civil War of 1918-1922, fleeing the Red Army's anti-Jewish campaigns
context: The American Tail era is specifically the 1880s-1890s Russian pogroms. Spielberg's grandfather Phillip Posner emigrated around this period. The film's reference is subtle — the Mousekewitz family's flight from a wave of cats with bandanas evokes the pogroms without explicit historical detail. Fievel's separation from his family on the boat to America happens during a storm. The film's release in November 1986 was timed for the holiday season.

question: In the 1987 Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles cartoon, four teenage mutant turtles named after Renaissance artists lived in the New York City sewers and fought crime for their giant rat sensei Splinter. Each turtle wore a different colored mask and used a different weapon. One turtle wore an orange mask and swung two wooden sticks joined by a chain, called nunchucks. He was the goofy, fun-loving one who yelled 'Cowabunga' whenever he did something cool. Which turtle is this?
context: The four turtles are named after Italian Renaissance masters: Leonardo (blue, katanas), Raphael (red, sai), Donatello (purple, bo staff), Michelangelo (orange, nunchucks). 'Cowabunga' became Mikey's signature exclamation through the cartoon.

question: In the 1985 cartoon ThunderCats, a group of cat-like warriors fled their dying home planet of Thundera and crash-landed on a strange world called Third Earth. Their young leader was still growing into his job, and he carried a magical weapon called the Sword of Omens that let him see far-off dangers when he shouted, 'Sword of Omens, give me sight beyond sight.' The lion-maned hero raised the sword and cried 'Thundercats, ho!' to summon his teammates. Who is this young leader?
context: Lion-O leads the Thundercats on Third Earth after fleeing the dying planet Thundera. Other team members include Panthro (panther engineer), Cheetara (cheetah speedster), Tygra (tiger), and the twin cubs WilyKit and WilyKat.

question: In the 1984 cartoon The Transformers, giant living robots from the planet Cybertron came to Earth. They could disguise themselves as regular vehicles. The good robots, called Autobots, protected humans and searched for energy. The bad robots, called Decepticons, tried to steal that same energy. The Autobot leader was a wise, brave commander who transformed into a red-and-blue Freightliner semi truck and led his team with the battle cry 'Autobots, roll out.' Who is this Autobot leader?
context: The Transformers cartoon launched in September 1984 alongside the Hasbro toy line. Optimus Prime leads the Autobots; Megatron leads the Decepticons. The tagline 'More than meets the eye' became cultural shorthand.

question: In the 1985 cartoon G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero, an elite team of American soldiers battled the evil terrorist group Cobra around the world. The Joes had famous members like the ninja Snake Eyes, the sharpshooter Duke, and the pilot Ace. Every time the team charged into action — leaping from jets or racing tanks into battle — every soldier shouted the same short two-word rallying cry together. What is the G.I. Joe team's battle cry?
context: G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero ran 1985-1987 with 95 episodes. Cobra Commander led the terrorist organization Cobra alongside Destro and the Baroness. Each episode famously closed with a PSA — 'Knowing is half the battle.'

question: In the 1983 cartoon Inspector Gadget, a bumbling cyborg detective solved crimes in Metro City with the help of his clever niece Penny and his loyal dog Brain. Behind every scheme was a mysterious criminal mastermind whom viewers never fully saw. The camera showed only his big leather chair and his black-gloved hand petting his mean, growling cat named Mad Cat. Who is this hidden villain who ran the crime ring?
context: Inspector Gadget's niece Penny and dog Brain solve most of the cases while Gadget bumbles around with his cybernetic gadgets. Dr. Claw's face was never shown — viewers only saw his armored gauntlet and his white cat. The line 'I'll get you next time, Gadget — NEXT TIME' closed many episodes.

question: In 1987 Disney launched a new afternoon cartoon called DuckTales, starring the rich old duck Scrooge McDuck and his three young nephews Huey, Dewey, and Louie having adventures around the world in search of gold and treasure. The show is famous for its catchy theme song. Right after the singers sing the word 'DuckTales,' the whole chorus cheers a short, punchy two-syllable sound. What is that little cheer that opens the DuckTales theme?
context: DuckTales followed Scrooge McDuck, his nephews Huey, Dewey, and Louie, and a cast including Webby and pilot Launchpad McQuack. The theme song's 'DuckTales — Woo-oo!' hook lodged in a generation's heads. Scrooge's vault of gold coins, where he swam in money, was iconic.

question: In 1992 the Fox Kids channel started a Saturday-morning X-Men cartoon based on the Marvel Comics team. The X-Men are mutants — humans born with special powers like laser eyes, weather control, and claws. They lived at a big mansion in New York that was really a secret school for gifted young mutants. The school's founder was a kind, bald man in a wheelchair who could read minds and speak into other people's thoughts. Who is this X-Men leader?
context: X-Men: The Animated Series ran 1992-1997 with 76 episodes. The lineup included Cyclops, Wolverine, Storm, Rogue, Gambit, Jubilee, Beast, and Jean Grey. The opening theme by Ron Wasserman became one of the most-remembered cartoon themes ever.

question: In 1993 Warner Bros. and the film director Steven Spielberg launched an animated cartoon called Animaniacs. It followed three wacky black-and-white cartoon siblings — two brothers and a little sister — who had been locked away in a vault in the 1930s and now lived on top of the Warner Bros. water tower in Burbank, California. Their three names all rhymed and were shouted together in the theme song. What are the three Warner siblings' names?
context: Animaniacs was produced by Steven Spielberg for Warner Bros. and Amblin Entertainment. The Warner siblings shared the show with recurring segments like Pinky and the Brain (two lab mice plotting to take over the world). Dot's full name was Princess Angelina Contessa Louisa Francesca Banana Fanna Bo Besca III.

question: In 1907 a baby boy was born in Iowa and named Marion Robert Morrison. He grew up big, tall, and rugged, and eventually moved to Hollywood. Studio bosses decided 'Marion' would never do as a name for the tough cowboy heroes he was going to play. Under a new manly stage name, he became the most famous cowboy actor in American movie history, starring in classic Westerns like The Searchers in 1956 and True Grit in 1969. What stage name did Marion Morrison use in the movies?
context: Marion Robert Morrison was given the stage name John Wayne in 1930 for the film The Big Trail. He won his only Best Actor Oscar for True Grit in 1969, playing the one-eyed Rooster Cogburn. His friends called him 'Duke,' a nickname from a childhood dog.

question: In the 1960s the Italian director Sergio Leone made three Western films — A Fistful of Dollars, For a Few Dollars More, and The Good, the Bad and the Ugly — shot mostly in Spain and Italy. Fans nicknamed these movies the Spaghetti Westerns. All three starred the same tall, squint-eyed American actor as a mysterious gunslinger in a poncho who chewed on a small cigar and was known only as the Man with No Name. Who was that American actor?
context: Eastwood played the Man with No Name in A Fistful of Dollars (1964), For a Few Dollars More (1965), and The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (1966). Sergio Leone directed all three. Ennio Morricone composed the scores. Eastwood went on to direct his own Westerns including Unforgiven (1992), for which he won Best Director.

question: On October 26, 1881, in the silver-mining town of Tombstone, Arizona, the lawman Wyatt Earp joined his brothers Virgil and Morgan and their tubercular dentist friend Doc Holliday to face a gang of outlaw cowboys led by the Clanton and McLaury brothers. In roughly thirty seconds of pistol fire in a narrow lot near a livery stable and photography studio, three of the outlaws were shot dead. It became the most famous gunfight in the American Old West. What is this legendary shootout called?
answer: The Gunfight at the OK Corral
choices: The Gunfight at the OK Corral
context: The gunfight on October 26, 1881 actually took place in a vacant lot near the rear of the OK Corral, not inside it. The Earp side (Wyatt, Virgil, Morgan, and Doc Holliday) faced the Clantons and McLaurys. Thirty seconds, thirty shots — three of the cowboys were killed.

question: In the 1965 TV special A Charlie Brown Christmas, based on Charles Schulz's Peanuts comic strip, sad-sack kid Charlie Brown is put in charge of picking a Christmas tree for his school's play. He walks past all the big fancy fake aluminum trees on the lot and comes home instead with the smallest, saddest little real tree he can find. His friends laugh at his pick. What kind of tree did Charlie Brown choose?
choices: A perfect tall fir from the lot
A blue spruce decorated with tinsel
context: A Charlie Brown Christmas (1965) was the first Peanuts TV special and aired on CBS December 9, 1965. Vince Guaraldi composed the iconic jazz score including 'Linus and Lucy.' Linus's recitation of Luke 2:8-14 — 'And there were in the same country shepherds...' — became the most-remembered scene.

question: In December 1964, American families sat down for a new stop-motion TV special called Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer. Puppets acted out the story of Santa's misfit reindeer with the glowing red nose. The little studio that made it went on to produce Frosty the Snowman, The Year Without a Santa Claus, and many other Christmas classics. What was that studio called?
context: Arthur Rankin Jr. and Jules Bass formed Rankin/Bass Productions in 1960. Their stop-motion 'Animagic' technique was actually animated by Tadahito Mochinaga's studio MOM in Tokyo. Burl Ives narrated Rudolph as Sam the Snowman. Other Rankin/Bass classics: Frosty the Snowman (1969), Santa Claus is Comin' to Town (1970), The Year Without a Santa Claus (1974).

question: In 1985 an animated TV special aired on American television starring a fat orange tabby cat who hates Mondays and eats whole pans of lasagna in one sitting. In this special, he and his goofy dog friend Odie dress up as pirates and land on a haunted tropical island. The cat is based on Jim Davis's newspaper comic strip that has run in papers since 1978. What is his name?
context: Garfield's Halloween Adventure aired on CBS October 30, 1985 and won a Primetime Emmy. Lorenzo Music voiced Garfield. The special's spooky pirate-ghost sequence features one of TV's eeriest narrated monologues, delivered by an unseen old man on the haunted island.

question: In 1990 the Christmas comedy Home Alone came out, directed by Chris Columbus and written by John Hughes. The film shows a big McCallister family in a Chicago suburb rushing to catch a plane to Paris for Christmas vacation. In the panic, they forget one of their sons at home. The clever eight-year-old boy, played by the child actor Macaulay Culkin, then defends his house from two bumbling burglars using paint cans, sticky glue, and a whole army of booby traps. What is the boy's name?
context: Home Alone was directed by Chris Columbus, written by John Hughes, and starred Macaulay Culkin as Kevin. The two bumbling burglars Harry (Joe Pesci) and Marv (Daniel Stern) called themselves the 'Wet Bandits.' The film was the highest-grossing live-action comedy in history until 2011.

question: In the 1983 cartoon Inspector Gadget, the bumbling cyborg detective Inspector Gadget lived in Metro City with his young niece and his big dog Brain. Gadget always messed up his missions and never noticed, but his niece secretly did the real detective work. She carried a wristwatch that was really a two-way radio and a Computer Book that could unlock doors and hack machines. She solved almost every case for her clueless uncle. What is the smart niece's name?
context: Penny works with the dog Brain to solve the cases Inspector Gadget gets credit for. Her computer book contained a video phone, a printer, encyclopedic data, and other gadgets. Don Adams (Get Smart's Maxwell Smart) voiced Inspector Gadget; Cree Summer Francks voiced Penny in the first season.

question: In 1990 the cartoon Tiny Toon Adventures debuted on television, showing younger student versions of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, and other Warner Bros. characters attending a school called Acme Looniversity. The show was executive produced by a very famous American film director — the same man who had already made the alien-and-a-boy movie E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial in 1982 and would soon direct the dinosaur blockbuster Jurassic Park in 1993. Who is this famous director?
context: Tiny Toon Adventures (1990-1992) featured Buster Bunny, Babs Bunny, Plucky Duck, Hamton J. Pig, and Elmyra Duff. Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment co-produced with Warner Bros. Animation. The success of Tiny Toons led directly to Spielberg producing Animaniacs (1993) and the Pinky and the Brain spinoff.

question: In the 1987 Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles cartoon, four teenage turtles named Leonardo, Donatello, Raphael, and Michelangelo lived in the New York City sewers and were trained in the ninja arts by their giant rat sensei Splinter. Between missions the turtles were obsessed with one specific junk food and ordered it by the whole box from delivery drivers up above the manhole cover. What is the food the Ninja Turtles love above all others?
context: The pizza obsession was invented for the 1987 cartoon — Eastman and Laird's 1984 black-and-white comic had no special pizza fixation. The cartoon used it for kid-friendly humor and toy merchandise (the Turtle Van featured a Pizza Thrower weapon).

question: In the 1983 cartoon He-Man and the Masters of the Universe, brave Prince Adam of the planet Eternia is secretly the mightiest warrior in the universe. To become his hero form, Adam raises his glowing Sword of Power to the sky and shouts a magic phrase. Then lightning strikes him and he transforms into He-Man. What does he shout?
context: Filmation produced the Masters of the Universe cartoon as a syndicated half-hour show tied to the Mattel toy line. Prince Adam transforms in Castle Grayskull, the source of mystical power on the planet Eternia. His arch-foe is the blue-skinned Skeletor.

question: In a 1984 American cartoon, five brave young space pilots each flew a huge robotic vehicle shaped like a lion — the black lion, red lion, blue lion, green lion, and yellow lion. When their enemies attacked planet Arus, the five lions would leap into the sky and combine together into one giant humanoid robot with glowing eyes and a flaming blazing sword. What is this giant combined robot, the Defender of the Universe, called?
context: Voltron: Defender of the Universe was assembled from the Japanese anime Beast King GoLion. The five lion pilots are Keith (black / head), Lance (red), Pidge (green), Hunk (yellow), and Allura (blue). The opening narration declared Voltron defender of the universe.

question: In the 1983 comedy A Christmas Story, a boy named Ralphie Parker lives in a 1940s Indiana town and wants only one gift for Christmas. Every adult he tells — his mother, his teacher, even a department-store Santa — warns him he'll shoot his eye out. He asks for it anyway. What gift did Ralphie want?
context: A Christmas Story (1983) was directed by Bob Clark and based on Jean Shepherd's stories. Shepherd narrates as adult Ralphie. The full description is 'An official Red Ryder carbine-action 200-shot range model air rifle with a compass in the stock and this thing that tells time.'

question: In 1957 an American children's author published a rhyming picture book called How the Grinch Stole Christmas!, about a grumpy green creature who tries to steal the holiday from the cheerful Whos of Whoville. In 1966 the story became a half-hour animated TV special narrated by the deep-voiced horror star Boris Karloff. What pen name did the book's author use?
context: The book and TV special were by Theodor Seuss Geisel. The 1966 special was directed by Chuck Jones of Looney Tunes fame. Boris Karloff narrated and voiced the Grinch. 'You're a Mean One, Mr. Grinch' was performed by Thurl Ravenscroft, who also voiced Tony the Tiger.

question: In the 1990 cartoon Captain Planet and the Planeteers, the spirit of Earth, called Gaia, gave five kids from different countries five magic rings. When trouble was too big to solve alone, the kids raised their rings together and combined their powers to summon Captain Planet, a green-mulleted, blue-skinned superhero who cleaned up polluters. Each of the five rings carried one specific power. What are the five ring powers?
context: Captain Planet was created by Ted Turner and ran 1990-1996. The five Planeteers were Kwame (Earth), Wheeler (Fire), Linka (Wind), Gi (Water), and Ma-Ti (Heart). They were summoned by Gaia (Whoopi Goldberg). Captain Planet's catchphrase was 'The power is yours!'

question: For decades, the Warner Bros. Looney Tunes cartoons — starring Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Wile E. Coyote, and Elmer Fudd — ended the same way. A stuttering pink pig named Porky Pig would pop his head through a red-and-orange concentric bullseye at the very end of every cartoon short, tip his hat, and stutter out a little three-word sign-off before the screen closed to black. What did Porky Pig say to close every Looney Tunes cartoon?
context: Porky Pig's iconic stuttered 'Th-th-th-that's all folks!' was used as the end-card for Warner Bros. Looney Tunes shorts from 1937. Mel Blanc voiced Porky and most of the Looney Tunes cast — Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Yosemite Sam, Tweety, Sylvester. Blanc was known as 'the man of a thousand voices.'

question: In 1985 the toy company Mattel and the animation studio Filmation launched a new cartoon, a spin-off of He-Man and the Masters of the Universe whose title promised a Princess of Power. Its hero was the long-lost twin sister of Prince Adam of Eternia — the prince who transforms into He-Man. When she raised her Sword of Protection and shouted 'For the honor of Grayskull,' she transformed into a blonde warrior princess. What name does she go by once she has transformed?
context: She-Ra: Princess of Power launched September 1985 as a sister cartoon to He-Man. Princess Adora was He-Man's twin who had been kidnapped at birth by Hordak and raised on Etheria. She-Ra is Adora's transformed name. Her transformation phrase: 'For the honor of Grayskull — I am She-Ra!'

question: In 1986 the American cartoon studio Rankin/Bass — fresh off the hit series Thundercats — launched a new after-school space adventure. It was set in the year 2839, far out in a deep-space region called Galaxy Limbo. A team of part-human, part-metal heroes with mechanical wings guarded the sector from an intergalactic mob boss named Mon*Star. What was this hero team called?
context: SilverHawks tagline — 'partly metal, partly real' — described the cyborg team led by Quicksilver. Other members included Bluegrass (the country-singing pilot), Steelheart, and Steelwill. Their main antagonist was Mon*Star, designed as the science-fiction equivalent of Thundercats' Mumm-Ra.

question: In the 1984 cartoon The Transformers, the evil Decepticons are led by Megatron, a silver robot from Cybertron who wants the Earth's energy for himself. Every Transformer hides in plain sight as a machine, and the Autobot leader Optimus Prime folds down into a red-and-blue truck. Megatron's disguise in the original toy line and cartoon is far smaller and far more sinister. What does Megatron turn into?
context: In the original 1984 toy line and cartoon, Megatron transformed into a Walther P38 pistol; the American toy came with a scope and a silencer. Later toy-safety laws pushed Hasbro to give him a different alternate mode.

question: In 1989, an American animation studio put out a Saturday-morning cartoon called Captain N: The Game Master to celebrate everything Nintendo. In it, an ordinary teenage boy is playing his NES (Nintendo Entertainment System) console one night when the screen flickers and drags him bodily into Videoland, a magical realm where every classic Nintendo character is real. Videoland's Princess Lana needs a champion to defeat the evil Mother Brain from the game Metroid. What is the boy hero's name?
context: Captain N teamed Kevin with Mega Man, Simon Belmont, Kid Icarus's Pit, and Princess Lana. Villains included Mother Brain (from Metroid), King Hippo, and Eggplant Wizard. The show ran only three seasons because Nintendo's licensing terms got restrictive. Notably, the show's Mega Man was voiced as a green-skinned creature, not the blue robot.

question: In 1992, Warner Bros. launched Batman: The Animated Series on Fox Kids. Its brooding, shadowy look came from a rule its creators invented: paint every background on black paper first, then add color on top. Producer Bruce Timm ran the show with one other man — a DC Comics writer who would later oversee the whole DC Animated Universe, including Superman, Justice League, and the character Harley Quinn, whom he co-created. Who was he?
context: Batman: The Animated Series ran 1992-1995 on Fox Kids and won four Daytime Emmys. Kevin Conroy's voice became the definitive Batman; Mark Hamill's Joker the definitive animated Joker. Dini also introduced Harley Quinn in episode 22, 'Joker's Favor,' as a one-off henchwoman who became a permanent fixture.

question: Disney's 1994 animated series Gargoyles tells the story of a clan of stone warriors who were cursed to sleep as statues on a Scottish castle for a thousand years. In modern New York City the spell finally breaks and they wake up. By day they are stone; by night they glide the skyline and defend the humans below. Who was their tall purple leader and the city's chief protector?
context: Goliath was voiced by Keith David. The show featured an unusually deep voice cast including many Star Trek: The Next Generation alumni — Marina Sirtis as Demona, Jonathan Frakes as David Xanatos, Brent Spiner, Michael Dorn, and Avery Brooks. The Shakespeare-quoting tone and serialized arcs gave it a reputation as the most adult of the 90s Disney Afternoon cartoons.

question: In 1991 Disney launched a Saturday-morning spinoff of its hit series DuckTales. It starred a self-appointed masked duck hero in a purple cape and a floppy fedora who protected the fictional city of St. Canard from cartoon supervillains. Every episode he would leap out of the shadows and announce himself with the same dramatic catchphrase. What was it?
answer: I am the terror that flaps in the night
choices: I am the terror that flaps in the night
By the power of the duck pond
Avenge me at the lake, brothers
context: Darkwing Duck (1991) starred Drake Mallard, who would dramatically declare 'I am the terror that flaps in the night! I am the Darkwing Duck!' His sidekicks were Launchpad McQuack (from DuckTales) and his adopted daughter Gosalyn. His arch-foes included Negaduck, Megavolt, and the criminal organization F.O.W.L.

question: The American movie star John Wayne headlined dozens of Westerns like Stagecoach and The Searchers across a forty-year career. He was born in 1907 in the small farming town of Winterset, Iowa. Wayne only picked up his famous stage name later in Hollywood — his real birth name has come up in trivia game shows for decades. What was he actually named at birth?
context: Wayne adopted the stage name in 1930 when he was cast in The Big Trail. His Iowa childhood nickname was 'Duke,' after his family's Airedale Terrier. The other names in the choices belong to Rock Hudson (Scherer), Tony Curtis (Schwartz), and Cary Grant (Leach) — all stage names of the same era.

question: In 1956 the American director John Ford — the king of the Hollywood Western — cast John Wayne in a dark, sweeping frontier film. Wayne played Ethan Edwards, a bitter Confederate veteran who spends years riding across the Southwest hunting for his young niece, taken by a Comanche raiding party. Many critics call it the greatest Western ever made. What is this film called?
context: Wayne played Ethan Edwards. The young niece was played by Natalie Wood. The famous closing shot — Wayne framed in a doorway looking out at the desert before walking away — has been homaged in countless later films. Director John Ford and Wayne made fourteen films together over their careers.

question: The 1960 Hollywood Western The Magnificent Seven, starring Yul Brynner and Steve McQueen, follows seven gunslingers hired by a poor Mexican village to defend it from bandits. The movie is actually a remake of a 1954 black-and-white Japanese epic. That Japanese original, directed by Akira Kurosawa, is set in feudal Japan and follows seven masterless samurai hired by farmers to protect their rice harvest from raiders. What was the Kurosawa film called?
context: The Magnificent Seven starred Yul Brynner as Chris Adams, leading a band of gunfighters defending a Mexican village from bandits. The cast included Steve McQueen, Charles Bronson, James Coburn, Robert Vaughn, Brad Dexter, and Horst Buchholz. Elmer Bernstein's score became one of the most recognizable in film history. Sergio Leone's A Fistful of Dollars was a 1964 remake of Kurosawa's Yojimbo.

question: On August 2, 1876, in the muddy frontier boomtown of Deadwood in Dakota Territory, the famous gunfighter James 'Wild Bill' Hickok sat playing five-card draw poker in Nuttal and Mann's Saloon Number 10. A drifter named Jack McCall walked up behind Hickok and shot him in the back of the head. The two-pair poker hand Hickok was holding when he died became famous forever in Old West lore as the 'dead man's hand.' What pair of pairs did he hold?
choices: Two pair, kings and queens — all red
Three sevens — all black, with one off-card
Four-of-a-kind tens — held to the chest
context: James Butler Hickok was sitting with his back to the saloon door when Jack McCall walked in and shot him at the No. 10 saloon. The 'Dead Man's Hand' — two black aces and two black eights — became the most-mythologized poker hand in American history. The unknown fifth card has been debated by historians.

question: In 1992 Clint Eastwood directed and starred in Unforgiven, a grim Western that won Best Picture at the Academy Awards. Eastwood played William Munny, an old widower and reformed killer who takes one last bounty job. The film's villain is a smug, brutal town sheriff nicknamed Little Bill Daggett — a performance that also won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actor. Which actor played Little Bill?
context: Hackman also won Best Supporting Actor for the role. Morgan Freeman played Munny's old partner Ned Logan; Richard Harris played the legendary gunfighter English Bob. Eastwood had held the David Webb Peoples script since the early 80s, waiting until he was old enough to play Munny convincingly. The film's dedication was to Sergio Leone and Don Siegel.

question: The 1993 stop-motion movie The Nightmare Before Christmas is often mistakenly credited to Tim Burton. Burton designed the characters, wrote the story, and produced the film — but he was busy directing Batman Returns and couldn't run the day-to-day stop-motion shoot. The real director spent three grueling years animating every puppet frame by hand. Who was that director?
context: Burton was occupied with Batman Returns and Ed Wood during production. Henry Selick later directed James and the Giant Peach (1996), Coraline (2009), and Wendell & Wild (2022). The film took three years and a team of stop-motion animators producing roughly one minute of footage per week. Danny Elfman wrote the songs and provided Jack Skellington's singing voice.

question: In 1989's National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation, a well-meaning suburban dad named Clark Griswold tries to give his family the perfect old-fashioned holiday. Nothing goes right: a pushy trailer-park cousin shows up, a squirrel bursts out of the tree, the lights won't work, and his Christmas bonus turns out to be a jelly-of-the-month subscription. Which comic actor played Clark Griswold?
context: Chevy Chase had played Clark in two earlier Vacation films (1983 and 1985) before Christmas Vacation. Beverly D'Angelo played his wife Ellen. Randy Quaid as Cousin Eddie was the film's breakout supporting performance. The 'where's the Tylenol' rant after the Christmas Eve disasters has been quoted at family holidays for thirty years.

question: 1990's Home Alone was the highest-grossing live-action comedy of its era. It starred a young Macaulay Culkin as Kevin McCallister, an eight-year-old accidentally left behind when his big family flies to Paris for Christmas. The John Hughes screenplay is unforgettable, but Hughes did not sit in the director's chair — that job went to a filmmaker who later directed the first two Harry Potter movies. Who directed Home Alone?
context: Hughes had originally meant Home Alone for Patrick Read Johnson but Johnson chose to direct Spaced Invaders instead. Columbus went on to direct Mrs. Doubtfire (1993) and the first two Harry Potter films. The Wet Bandits Harry and Marv were played by Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern. John Williams composed the score.

question: The 1965 Peanuts television special A Charlie Brown Christmas was scored not with a big orchestra but with a small jazz piano trio. The composer wrote gentle, thoughtful tunes like Linus and Lucy and Christmas Time Is Here — songs that became inseparable from Charles Schulz's newspaper comic strip for decades afterward. Who was this jazz pianist and composer?
context: Vince Guaraldi was a San Francisco jazz pianist already known for his Grammy-winning 'Cast Your Fate to the Wind.' He scored most of the Peanuts specials until his death in 1976. 'Linus and Lucy' became the de facto Peanuts theme. The famous children's choir on 'Christmas Time Is Here' was recorded with a group of San Francisco schoolchildren.

question: In the 2003 comedy Elf, Will Ferrell plays a cheerful giant of a man named Buddy who grew up at the North Pole believing he was one of Santa's elves. When he learns he is actually human, Buddy travels to New York City in a bright yellow tights-and-hat costume to meet his real father. The film was directed by an actor-turned-filmmaker who later launched Marvel's original Iron Man movie in 2008. Who directed Elf?
context: Favreau cast James Caan as Buddy's father, Walter Hobbs. Bob Newhart played Papa Elf and narrated. Ferrell improvised much of his dialogue including 'Buddy the Elf — what's your favorite color?' Favreau went on to direct 2008's Iron Man, launching the MCU. He also gave himself a small role in Elf as Dr. Leonardo.

question: The 1991 Nickelodeon cartoon Rugrats followed a gang of babies — Tommy Pickles, Chuckie Finster, and the twins Phil and Lil — as they explored a big adult world from a knee-high point of view. The show was made by a small independent Los Angeles animation house, founded in the early 1980s by a husband-and-wife team who would go on to produce The Wild Thornberrys and As Told by Ginger. What was this studio called?
context: Arlene Klasky and Gabor Csupo founded their studio in 1982 and also produced Aaahh!!! Real Monsters and the original Simpsons short for The Tracey Ullman Show. Rugrats ran 1991-2004 on Nickelodeon, becoming the network's longest-running cartoon. Tommy was voiced by E.G. Daily; Chuckie by Christine Cavanaugh, then Nancy Cartwright (also Bart Simpson).

question: In 1991 Nickelodeon launched a wildly gross and surreal cartoon called The Ren & Stimpy Show. It starred a hot-tempered asthmatic chihuahua named Ren Hoek and his dim-witted, big-eyed cat pal Stimpy. In 1992 the network fired the show's Canadian-born creator over blown deadlines and constant fights with executives about the content. Who was he?
context: John K's studio Spumco produced the early seasons before Nickelodeon transferred production to Games Animation after firing him. The cartoon's dense detail, sudden close-ups, and gross-out humor influenced an entire generation of animators including Genndy Tartakovsky and Craig McCracken. Episodes like 'Stimpy's Invention' (which introduced 'Happy Happy Joy Joy') became cultural touchstones.

question: The 1987 syndicated cartoon BraveStarr mixed a classic Western with science fiction. A Native American marshal patrolled the frontier mining planet New Texas, keeping order alongside his talking horse companion. The horse could rear up and stand on two legs, aim and fire a shotgun, and speak fluent English. What was the horse's name?
context: BraveStarr aired in syndication for one 65-episode season. Marshal BraveStarr drew on four animal spirits — Eyes of the Hawk, Ears of the Wolf, Strength of the Bear, Speed of the Puma. Thirty/Thirty was a sentient cyber-horse named after the .30-30 Winchester rifle. The series ended Filmation's run; the studio closed in 1989.

question: In 1984, two young comic-book artists sharing a rented studio in Dover, New Hampshire, self-published a small black-and-white comic on borrowed money. It was meant as a joke — a spoof of the gritty Marvel hero Daredevil and the funny-animal comic Cerebus the Aardvark. Their story followed four turtles trained in ninjutsu by a rat sensei named Splinter. That silly parody exploded, and by the 1987 hit cartoon Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles it was everywhere. Which two creators made the original comic?
context: Eastman and Laird drew the first issue at a kitchen table in Dover, New Hampshire and printed 3,000 copies funded by a tax refund. The book became an instant collector item. The cartoon, the toys, and four feature films all followed. The 1990 live-action film directed by Steve Barron was the highest-grossing independent film of its time.

question: On January 23, 1985, the very first episode of the American cartoon Thundercats aired on television. It opened with the young lord Lion-O and his fellow cat-people warriors — Cheetara, Panthro, Tygra, and the twin cubs — escaping their home planet Thundera as it exploded into fire behind their ship. They crash-landed on a strange new world covered in the ruins of an ancient human civilization. What did they call this new home world?
context: Thundercats was produced by Rankin/Bass (the same Christmas-special studio) with animation by the Japanese studio Pacific Animation Corporation. The series ran 130 episodes through 1989. The opening battle cry 'Thundercats, ho!' was Lion-O's call to action.

question: In the 1983 Filmation cartoon He-Man and the Masters of the Universe, Prince Adam of the planet Eternia raises his magic sword and shouts 'By the power of Grayskull!' to transform into the mightiest man in the universe. He defends the good guys from Castle Grayskull. His blue-skinned skull-faced enemy Skeletor plots against him from a rival dark mountain fortress on the opposite side of Eternia. What is this evil base called?
context: Snake Mountain was Skeletor's headquarters on Eternia, opposite King Randor's Eternos and the heroic Castle Grayskull. The Mattel toy version came with a hidden microphone that distorted the user's voice. The Fright Zone was instead Hordak's base in the She-Ra spinoff.

question: In the 1970 Rankin/Bass stop-motion Christmas special Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town, a young red-haired orphan named Kris Kringle grows up delivering toys to lonely children. He runs into a bumbling, self-important Bavarian-style mayor who rules a joyless gray town called Sombertown. The mayor has outlawed toys entirely and orders them burned in the town square. What was this puffed-up mayor's name?
context: Fred Astaire narrated as the mailman S.D. Kluger. Mickey Rooney voiced the young Kris. The Winter Warlock had been frozen-hearted until Kris brought him a toy, melting his heart in the song 'Put One Foot in Front of the Other.' Heat Miser and Snow Miser were in a different Rankin/Bass special, The Year Without a Santa Claus (1974).

question: In Disney's 1990 syndicated cartoon TaleSpin, the animal characters from The Jungle Book were reimagined as 1930s cargo pilots working out of a bustling coastal city called Cape Suzette. The star of the show was the same laid-back brown bear who once sang The Bare Necessities in Disney's 1967 animated film — now retooled as a scruffy freelance pilot with a yellow shirt and a battered leather cap. Who was this bear?
context: Baloo flew the Sea Duck and worked for Higher for Hire under the no-nonsense Rebecca Cunningham. His co-pilot was the young orphan navigator Kit Cloudkicker. The sky-pirate villain Don Karnage led the Air Pirates. Shere Khan was reimagined as a polite but ruthless industrialist. The show was part of Disney Afternoon alongside DuckTales, Rescue Rangers, and Darkwing Duck.

question: In the 1985 Thundercats cartoon, the villain dwells in a black pyramid on Third Earth. Most of the time he's a shrivelled mummy. When he calls on the Ancient Spirits of Evil, he transforms into a hulking blue-skinned demigod with the catchphrase 'Ancient Spirits of Evil, transform this decayed form into…' WHAT?
context: Mumm-Ra's pyramid lair on Third Earth held statues of four 'Ancient Spirits of Evil' — designed as parodies of real Egyptian and Mesoamerican deities. His powers waned the longer he stayed in his transformed body, forcing him to retreat to his sarcophagus. Mumm-Ra's signature appearance was based on the 1932 Boris Karloff film The Mummy.

question: The 1984 Transformers toys sold by Hasbro in America were not new inventions. They came from two existing Japanese toy lines made by the company Takara — one called Diaclone (transforming vehicles piloted by tiny drivers) and one called Microman (small transforming spy figures). Hasbro simply picked the coolest molds and gave them new American names. Which Diaclone truck toy became the heroic Autobot leader Optimus Prime?
context: In Takara's Diaclone line, the Optimus Prime mold was called Battle Convoy — still 'Convoy' is Optimus Prime's name in Japan today.
