question: In 1996, Sony's PlayStation needed a mascot to fight Nintendo's Mario and Sega's Sonic. A small California studio called Naughty Dog created a spinning orange creature in blue jeans and giant sneakers, who dashes through tropical islands smashing wooden crates and battling the mad scientist Dr Neo Cortex. Name him.
context: Created by Naughty Dog's Jason Rubin and Andy Gavin. Sony used him as the unofficial mascot to challenge Mario and Sonic during the 32-bit era. He never spoke a real language — just yelled 'WOAH!'.

question: In 1996, the British studio Core Design and its publisher Eidos released Tomb Raider, one of the first great 3D adventure games. The hero is a wealthy British archaeologist who explores ancient tombs armed with twin pistols. She wears a long brown braid and short khaki shorts, and her body is famously blocky because 1996 polygon graphics were angular. Name her.
context: Designed by Toby Gard at Core Design in Derby, England. Angelina Jolie played her in the 2001 film. The original PS1 model had only 540 polygons — most of them on Lara herself.

question: In 1997 the British studio Rare released a Nintendo 64 (N64) shooter based on the James Bond film GoldenEye. Its multiplayer mode split the TV screen into quarters so four friends could hunt each other through levels from the movie. The most-hated character pick was the short bowler-hatted henchman from the earlier Bond film Goldfinger, because his tiny hitbox made him almost impossible to shoot. Name him.
context: Oddjob's shorter stature meant bullets often passed over his head — friends made house rules banning him. The split-screen four-player mode was added late in development and became the killer feature.

question: The 2001 launch game for Microsoft's brand-new Xbox console was Halo: Combat Evolved, a first-person shooter made by the Seattle studio Bungie. It stars a hulking human super-soldier in polished green metal armor, fighting alien invaders called the Covenant on a giant ring-shaped world. A blue holographic AI named Cortana lives inside his helmet and guides him. What is the soldier called?
context: Master Chief's full designation is Spartan-117 — but he's only called by it once in the original game. His face is never shown in the trilogy. Voice actor Steve Downes recorded his lines while standing because he felt it sounded more authoritative.

question: In 1986 Nintendo released a game called Metroid for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The player controlled a lone bounty hunter in a bright orange power suit, blasting through the winding caves of the alien planet Zebes to hunt a space pirate boss. If you finished the game fast enough, the ending revealed a huge secret about the hunter under the helmet. What was the twist?
context: Metroid director Yoshio Sakamoto and designer Gunpei Yokoi kept Samus's identity hidden from the marketing and manual. Faster endings revealed more — the under-three-hour ending famously showed her in a bikini, an early-arcade tradition.

question: A beaten fighter stands staggering with almost no health left in Midway's bloody 1992 arcade game Mortal Kombat. The deep-voiced announcer yells two famous words. What does the announcer yell?
context: The 'FINISH HIM!' prompt gave the player about five seconds to input the Fatality button-sequence specific to each character. Scorpion's Fatality — ripping off his mask and breathing fire — was the most replicated on schoolyards.

question: In 1989 Sega released its 16-bit home console in North America, a sleek black machine that would launch Sonic the Hedgehog in 1991 and famously run Mortal Kombat with the uncensored blood code that its Nintendo rival banned. In Japan and Europe the same console was called the Mega Drive. What was it called in North America?
context: Known as the Mega Drive in Japan and Europe. Sega's 'Genesis does what Nintendon't' campaign was a generation-defining piece of console-war marketing. The system was discontinued in 1997.

question: Nintendo's grey 1985 console saved the American video-game business after the 1983 arcade crash that had killed off Atari. It came bundled with a Super Mario Bros and Duck Hunt cartridge and a plastic light gun called the Zapper. Its logo carries three big letters: NES. What do those letters stand for?
context: Nintendo designed the front-loading cartridge slot to look like a VCR so retailers — burned by the 1983 crash — would shelve it next to home video instead of in the toy aisle.

question: Namco's 1980 arcade game Pac-Man sends its round hero through a blue maze to eat every pellet on the screen. Ghosts with different personalities hunt him: some chase directly, some cut him off, some wander. In the classic game, how many ghosts chase him?
context: Blinky (red, direct chase), Pinky (pink, ambush ahead of Pac-Man), Inky (cyan, uses Blinky's position in a complex calc), and Clyde (orange, wanders randomly). Each ghost's personality was deliberate.

question: Nintendo's Super Mario Bros series stars a mustached Italian plumber named Mario who runs, jumps, and stomps his way through the pipe-lined Mushroom Kingdom. In most of the games he has to rescue the kingdom's kind pink-dressed Princess Peach from a huge spike-shelled turtle-dragon king who breathes fire, roars, and leads an army of little turtle Koopas. Name the king.
context: Known in Japan as Koopa. The princess he kidnaps was named Princess Toadstool in the US until Super Mario 64 (1996) renamed her Peach. The Bowser-Peach kidnapping plot is the franchise's running joke.

question: Don Bluth, a former Disney animator, drew a 1983 arcade game by hand, and the machine played his cartoon back off a laserdisc. A player flicked the joystick or hit the sword button in time to steer a bumbling knight, Dirk the Daring, past spike traps and collapsing floors. What was the game called?
context: Animated by former Disney legend Don Bluth (The Secret of NIMH, An American Tail). The game ran off a laserdisc — the first arcade title to do so. Stranger Things' Dustin Henderson loves it.

question: In 2000, the Japanese company Sony released the follow-up to its wildly popular original PlayStation console. The new black block-shaped machine was the first game console that could also play movie discs, which turned it into many families' first movie player. It sold over 155 million units worldwide, becoming the best-selling home console ever. What was it called?
context: The PS2's DVD playback was a major selling point — DVD players still cost $300+ in 2000 and the PS2 played them at $299 plus games. Launch lineup included SSX, Tekken Tag, and Madden 2001.

question: Capcom's 1991 arcade hit Street Fighter II gives the fighting genre its first playable woman, an Interpol detective among eight world warriors. She wears a blue cheongsam dress with white boots, spiked bracelets and ox-horn hair buns, and her signature move is a rapid-fire kick. Who is she?
context: Designer Akira Yasuda based her costume on Chinese opera. Her signature move is the Hyakuretsukyaku — Hundred Rending Legs — a rapid kick performed by mashing the kick button. Her flip kick (Spinning Bird Kick) is iconic.

question: Heihachi, the cruel grandfather of the wealthy Mishima clan, feuds with his estranged son Kazuya and grandson Jin in Namco's 1994 3D arcade fighter, from the same studio as Pac-Man. Wild guest fighters like the samurai-ghost Yoshimitsu join the family feud. What is the series called?
context: Tekken means 'iron fist' in Japanese. Sega's Virtua Fighter (1993) actually beat it to the 3D fighter market, but Tekken's PS1 port made the home transition smoother. The Mishima family feud has been the series' through-line since the original.

question: Seth Gordon's 2007 documentary follows Steve Wiebe, a mild-mannered Washington science teacher, as he goes after the Donkey Kong world record held by the hot-sauce tycoon Billy Mitchell. What is the film called?
context: Full title: The King of Kong: A Fistful of Quarters. The film became a cult hit and made household names of obscure arcade-scene figures Walter Day (Twin Galaxies founder), Billy Mitchell (the pizza-parlor owner), and Steve Wiebe (the high-school teacher).

question: In 2006 Nintendo released a small white home console that came with a slim wand-shaped controller. Sensors on top of the TV read the wand's motion, so players swung it in the air to hit tennis balls, bowl strikes, and throw punches in the pack-in game Wii Sports. Grandparents and little kids picked it up as easily as teenage gamers, and the machine sold out worldwide for months. Name the system.
context: Nintendo intentionally chose 'Wii' — pronounced 'we' — to signal a console for everyone, not just gamers. The blue-ocean strategy worked: Wii sold 101 million units, outselling the technologically superior 360 and PS3.

question: Konami invented a famous cheat code in the 1980s, dreamed up by developer Kazuhisa Hashimoto. Players typed it into games like the run-and-gun shooter Contra on the NES (Nintendo Entertainment System) to unlock extra lives and hidden power-ups. The code is a specific button sequence: some Up presses, some Down presses, then Left, Right, Left, Right, and finally B, A, and Start. How many Up presses does the code start with?
context: The full code: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A. In Contra it gave 30 lives. The code was originally created by Konami developer Kazuhisa Hashimoto for the 1986 game Gradius because he found his own game too hard.

question: In 1996 Nintendo released Super Mario 64 for its new Nintendo 64 console — Mario's very first game in full 3D. Mario runs into Princess Peach's castle to find that she has been captured by the dragon-turtle king Bowser. Instead of ordinary doors, the castle walls have magic paintings that suck Mario into hidden worlds, where he must collect glowing Power Stars. How many Power Stars can Mario grab in all across the entire castle?
context: Only 70 Stars are required to face Bowser in the final battle, but completionists collect all 120 to unlock Yoshi on the roof of the castle. SM64 launched the N64 in June 1996 and redefined 3D platforming.

question: A Namco designer lifted a slice out of a pizza one lunchtime, by his own later account, and looked at the wedge missing from the pie. That, he said, gave him the round shape of Pac-Man, the hero of the company's 1980 arcade game. Who was the Namco designer?
context: Iwatani also designed the ghost AI: Blinky chases directly, Pinky tries to ambush, Inky uses a complex calc involving Blinky's position, and Clyde wanders randomly. Pac-Man became the first widely-licensed video-game character.

question: Nintendo's 1981 arcade game Donkey Kong called its jumping hero Jumpman and sent him up steel girders to rescue a woman from a big angry ape. By the time the sequel Donkey Kong Jr. arrived in 1982, he had the proper name Nintendo still uses for him today. What was he renamed?
context: Mario was named after Mario Segale, Nintendo of America's warehouse landlord in Tukwila WA, who reportedly stormed into a staff meeting demanding overdue rent. Miyamoto designed Mario's red hat and mustache to work around NES sprite limitations.

question: A co-founder of a young California game company oversaw the first commercial video-game success in 1972, the arcade hit that launched the whole industry. A few years later he started a family pizza-and-arcade restaurant chain built around an animatronic mouse mascot called Chuck E. Cheese. Who was he?
context: Bushnell tasked engineer Allan Alcorn with building Pong as a training exercise. Alcorn made it too good and it became Atari's first hit. Bushnell sold Atari to Warner in 1976 for $28M and later founded Chuck E. Cheese as a way to put arcade machines in front of kids.

question: Tomohiro Nishikado released a shooting game called Space Invaders in 1978. Row after row of aliens marched down the screen while the player fired a laser cannon to blast them. In arcades across Japan, kids and grown-ups lined up to play. What did people say the whole country ran out of?
context: Designer Tomohiro Nishikado. The story of the 100-yen shortage is partly folklore — coin production did rise in 1978 — but Space Invaders genuinely earned over $2 billion by 1982, making it one of the highest-grossing entertainment products in history.

question: One of the few women working on arcade games co-designed Centipede in 1981, a rare programmer who wanted a game her friends would enjoy playing. A rolling trackball steers a bug-shooter through a field of mushrooms, blasting a wiggling centipede that splits into smaller pieces every time it is hit. What was her name?
context: Bailey came to Atari from General Motors, where she had written 6502 assembly for embedded car systems. She designed Centipede with Ed Logg, intending the bright pastel colors and arcing screen movement to appeal to a broader audience than the prevailing shoot-em-up boys.

question: A designer at the American arcade company Williams built Defender in 1981, sending the player's ship sideways across an alien planet to rescue tiny humans, with a control panel famous for being hard. He went on to make another classic in 1982, a shooter with two joysticks. Who was he?
context: Jarvis designed Defender to be intentionally hard — the player flies a spacecraft over a horizontal landscape, rescuing humanoids from alien abductors while juggling thrust, fire, and smart bombs. Robotron 2084 (1982) was the dual-stick blueprint that Geometry Wars later popularized.

question: A bouncing smiley face named Evil Otto comes after any player who dawdles in Stern Electronics' 1980 maze-shooter, and he cannot be killed. The player runs through glowing rooms blasting boxy robots while a scratchy synthesized voice, one of the first in arcades, barks 'Got the humanoid! Got the intruder!' What was the game called?
context: Designed by Alan McNeil. Berzerk's electronic-voice chip set the player against robots Otto and lookalikes. In 1981, a 19-year-old player at a Calumet City IL arcade died of a heart attack after posting a high score — leading to a parental-panic episode and the 'Berzerk killed a man' urban legend.

question: A 1979 black-and-white arcade game drawn in glowing line vectors puts a small wedge-shaped ship among drifting boulders. Its pilot rotates to aim and fires, and each boulder, when hit, breaks into smaller ones. Little flying saucers pop in from the edges to shoot back. What is the game called?
context: Designed by Ed Logg and Lyle Rains. Players quickly discovered the 'lurking' exploit: clearing all but one small asteroid, then hiding while waiting for UFOs to shoot for high points. Atari later patched it by ramping UFO frequency.

question: Shigeru Miyamoto, Nintendo's young designer, wanted his first big arcade game in 1981 to star a licensed American comic-strip trio: a hero, his tall girlfriend and a huge bully. The licensing deal fell through, so he invented his own cast: a carpenter, the carpenter's girlfriend and a giant ape. Which comic strip had he wanted?
context: The Popeye license eventually came through and Nintendo released a Popeye arcade in 1982 — but by then DK was already an enormous hit. Designer Miyamoto's first game was DK; he was 28 years old.

question: Konami's 1981 arcade game sends a little frog hopping from the bottom of the screen to the top. It crosses a busy highway of cars and trucks, then a river, no swimming allowed, leaping between drifting logs and diving turtles to reach a lily pad. What is the game called?
context: Frogger was distributed in the US by Sega/Gremlin. Its eight-direction joystick (no diagonals) and one-life-at-a-time-on-a-lily-pad design influenced decades of crossing-style games. A Seinfeld 1998 episode 'The Frogger' was built around George trying to move an arcade cabinet across a street.

question: Q*bert, a little orange creature with a long tubular nose, hops from cube to cube across a pyramid in Gottlieb's 1982 arcade game, changing each cube's color as he lands. When he loses a life to a snake or a falling bad guy, a speech bubble pops up above his head. What does it show?
choices: A sad face with rolling tears
A red exclamation point in a triangle
context: Designed by Warren Davis and Jeff Lee. The @!#?@! grawlix cloud became a Q*bert signature. Lee also created the iconic sound chip noise Q*bert makes — generated by a coil-spring impact sensor mounted in the cabinet.

question: Namco's 1981 arcade shooter Galaga sends bug-like aliens swooping down the screen, and a boss ship can grab the player's fighter with a tractor beam. A rescued fighter doubles the firepower. Galaga was the sequel to an older Namco game from 1979 that started the swooping-formation style. What was that older game called?
context: Galaxian (1979) introduced the dive-bombing enemy pattern. Galaga added the dual-fighter recovery — letting the captured ship fly alongside the rescued one for double firepower. Galaga famously cameos in Joss Whedon's 2012 Avengers when a SHIELD employee on the helicarrier is caught playing it.

question: Two players take to a fantasy sky above lava pits in Williams Electronics' 1982 brawler, one on a white ostrich, the other on a blue-gray stork. Each mashes a flap button to gain altitude and tries to be the higher when they collide. What is the game called?
context: Designed by John Newcomer. Co-op two-player Joust was the killer two-player arcade experience of the era. Newcomer chose ostriches because the design needed an animal that visually communicated mid-air flapping while still looking heroic.

question: A little man in a white space suit tunnels through colored dirt in Namco's 1982 arcade game, chased by round red Pookas and fire-breathing green Fygars. His only weapon is a pump: he jams it into a monster and pumps until the creature bloats up and pops like a balloon. What is the game called?
context: Designed by Masahisa Ikegami. The protagonist's real name was Taizo Hori — a Japanese pun on 'horitai zo' meaning 'I want to dig.' Dig Dug's hero went on to become the father of Mr. Driller (1999), a Namco mid-sized franchise of its own.

question: Williams Electronics' brutal 1982 shooter hands its lone hero two joysticks instead of a stick and a fire button: the left stick moves him, the right aims and fires in eight directions. Endless waves of chunky enemies pour in to kill him and the last human family. What is the game called?
context: Jarvis designed Robotron's twin-stick controls after breaking his hand in a car accident — the simpler-than-keyboard scheme was easier for his recovering hand. The control scheme later defined Smash TV (1990), Geometry Wars (2003), and countless indie shooters.

question: The red ghost in Namco's 1980 arcade game Pac-Man heads straight for the hero along the shortest path in the maze grid, closing the distance every frame. Each ghost has its own color and its own personality coded into its behavior, and the red one's is the most aggressive. What is the red ghost's name?
context: Iwatani designed each ghost with a distinct AI: Blinky (red) — direct chase; Pinky (pink) — ambush ahead of Pac-Man's facing direction; Inky (cyan) — flanks using a vector from Blinky; Clyde (orange) — wanders randomly when close to Pac-Man. The personalities have been preserved across every port.

question: A Sega designer sat the player in a red Ferrari convertible with a blonde girl in the passenger seat for the 1986 arcade racer OutRun. The player chose a radio station and drove across European countryside, and at each checkpoint the road forked. The same designer later made Virtua Fighter and Shenmue. Who was he?
context: Suzuki had also designed Hang-On (1985) and would later design After Burner (1987), Virtua Fighter (1993), Shenmue (1999), and the Virtua series. OutRun's three songs — Magical Sound Shower, Splash Wave, and Passing Breeze — by Hiroshi Kawaguchi defined arcade-driving music.

question: Nintendo dropped the blood from its home version of Midway's bloody arcade fighter Mortal Kombat in 1993, but Sega kept it on the Genesis, hidden behind a secret code entered on the title screen. What was the code?
context: The Genesis ABACABB code is a tribute to Genesis (the band) and their 1981 album of the same name. The SNES port lacked blood entirely until Mortal Kombat II (1994). The Genesis port outsold the SNES version, partly because of the code.

question: In 1985, Nintendo brought its home game console to America and called it the Nintendo Entertainment System, or NES. It came bundled with one game that showed families exactly what the machine could do — smooth side-scrolling levels, catchy chiptune music, and secret pipes that warped between worlds. Millions of American kids first met a mustachioed plumber named Mario in this pack-in cartridge. What was the game?
context: SMB's World 1-1 has been studied as a masterclass in tutorial design — within 30 seconds the player learns that Goombas hurt you, mushrooms power you up, jumping on enemies is the attack, and that question-blocks dispense items. Designed by Miyamoto with Takashi Tezuka.

question: In Nintendo's 1985 game Super Mario Bros. on the Nintendo Entertainment System, World 1-2 hides a famous secret. If Mario times his jumps right, he can run along the top of the pipes and out over the ceiling of the underground level. There, three green warp pipes are lined up, each firing Mario to a much later world in the game. Which three worlds do those pipes lead to?
context: The other Warp Zone is in World 4-2 and leads to Worlds 5, 6, and 7. The 'minus world' glitch (W -1) is reached by clipping past the warp-zone wall instead of entering it normally — a frame-perfect jump as Mario emerges from a pipe.

question: In 1991, Sega launched a new mascot on its Genesis console — a blue hedgehog named Sonic who could curl into a ball and blast through loop-de-loops at high speed. The lead programmer behind the game had one goal: make Sonic run faster than any video-game hero before him. He wrote the physics code that let Sonic roll down hills and rocket back up the other side. Who was the programmer?
context: Designer Naoto Ohshima created Sonic's visual look; programmer Yuji Naka built the rolling-physics engine that made Sonic feel uniquely fast. Sega Technical Institute team (later including Mark Cerny, future PlayStation architect) produced Sonic 2 in 1992.

question: In 1986 Nintendo's designer Shigeru Miyamoto shipped a hit for the Famicom (the Japanese Nintendo Entertainment System). It was the first Famicom game with a battery inside the cartridge to save your progress between play sessions — a huge deal in an era when you usually lost everything at power-off. Players controlled a green-tunic elf-boy hero named Link, roaming a top-down overworld and clearing nine hidden dungeons full of monsters. Name the game.
context: Miyamoto credited his childhood exploration of caves and forests near Sonobe, Kyoto, as the inspiration. The gold-colored cartridge of the US release was a Nintendo of America marketing decision to make the box stand out on shelves.

question: In 1998 Nintendo released a Legend of Zelda game for the Nintendo 64 (N64). It was co-directed by Eiji Aonuma and Shigeru Miyamoto with a soaring orchestral score by Koji Kondo, and reviewers at the time called it the best video game ever made. In the story, the boy hero Link pulls a legendary sword from its stone pedestal and wakes up seven years later as a grown man wielding the Master Sword against the dark king Ganondorf. Name the game.
context: Ocarina of Time's Z-targeting (named for the N64's Z trigger) revolutionized 3D-game camera and combat design. The Water Temple — designed by Yoichi Yamada — became the most-cursed dungeon in series history for its iron boots inventory-swapping.

question: In 1997, Squaresoft released Final Fantasy VII on Sony's new PlayStation console. It was a huge role-playing game with pre-rendered movie scenes and 3D battles — so much data that Squaresoft could not fit it on one game disc. Players who were used to Nintendo cartridges holding a whole game on one chip were stunned. Final Fantasy VII shipped as a boxed set of compact discs. How many discs came in the box?
context: FF7's full data — pre-rendered backgrounds, FMV cutscenes, voice-light audio — wouldn't fit on a 64MB Nintendo 64 cartridge, which is why Square moved to Sony's PlayStation. The move broke the Nintendo-Square partnership and made FF a PlayStation flagship for two decades.

question: In 1995, Squaresoft released a Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) role-playing game about a boy who accidentally opens a time portal at a medieval fair. It became a legend called Chrono Trigger. Two giants wrote it: Hironobu Sakaguchi of Final Fantasy and Yuji Horii of Dragon Quest. For the character art they hired a manga star famous for drawing Dragon Ball. Who was he?
context: Chrono Trigger's 'Dream Team' was Hironobu Sakaguchi (Final Fantasy), Yuji Horii (Dragon Quest), and Toriyama (Dragon Ball). Director Takashi Tokita and music by Yasunori Mitsuda (his breakthrough work; he was hospitalized from overwork during the score).

question: In 1997, the British studio Rare released GoldenEye 007 for the Nintendo 64. Its four-player split-screen mode became a legend in dorm rooms across the world. One weapon players loved to sneak into the map let you stick an explosive on a wall or floor. When any enemy walked too close, it went off. What was this weapon called?
context: Designed by Martin Hollis's team at Rare, GoldenEye's multiplayer was added late in development as an experiment. The proximity-mine-only mode — players laying mines and waiting — was a Friday-night campus staple from 1997 through 2001.

question: In 1996, the Japanese company Capcom released the horror game Resident Evil on the Sony PlayStation. The player controlled an elite police officer trapped in Spencer Mansion, a spooky estate full of shuffling zombies, giant snakes, and a room-sized carnivorous plant with a long whipping tongue. The Capcom director behind the game invented a new genre and called it 'survival horror.' Who was he?
context: Mikami also directed Resident Evil 4 (2005), which fundamentally redefined third-person shooter cinematography with its over-the-shoulder camera. The original RE was famous for its prerendered backgrounds, fixed camera angles, and infamously stilted voice-acting ('Jill sandwich').

question: In 1998, Konami released Metal Gear Solid on the Sony PlayStation. The player controlled a soldier codenamed Solid Snake who sneaked into a snowy nuclear base in Alaska to stop a giant walking tank called Metal Gear. The game had full voice acting, cinematic camera cuts, and an orchestral soundtrack — it played more like a Hollywood movie than a video game. Who directed it?
context: Kojima had directed Metal Gear (1987) and Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake (1990) for the MSX2 home computer in Japan. MGS1's Psycho Mantis boss famously required the player to physically unplug the controller and re-plug it into Port 2 to defeat his mind-reading.

question: Pokemon Red and Green came out in Japan in 1996, and Red and Blue reached the US in 1998. The founder of the studio Game Freak designed them. As a boy in Tokyo, he loved catching beetles and dragonflies in the creeks near his home. He built Pokemon so kids could feel that same hunt through their Game Boy. Name him.
context: Tajiri pitched the idea to Nintendo around 1990, and it took six years to ship. Ken Sugimori drew the original creatures, and Junichi Masuda composed the music.

question: In 1999, the American game company Wizards of the Coast printed the first English-language Pokemon trading cards. Kids traded them at recess, and booster packs cost about three dollars. Out of that first 'Base Set,' one holographic 'shiny' rare became the most-wanted card of all — collectors have paid tens of thousands of dollars for a mint copy of it. Which Pokemon is on that card?
context: The Base Set Charizard holo, especially in 'Shadowless' or '1st Edition' subprints, regularly sells for thousands of dollars. The original print run distinguished by a thin shadow border on the right side of the card frame. A PSA 10 1st Edition Shadowless Charizard has sold for over $400,000.

question: In 1984, a young programmer at the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow built a puzzle game on a boxy computer called the Elektronika 60. Colored blocks in four-square shapes fell from the top of the screen, and the player rotated and slid them to fill each row without gaps. He named the game Tetris, from the Greek word for four. Because he made it on a state computer, the Soviet government owned the rights for years. What was his name?
context: Pajitnov developed it on an Elektronika 60 — a Soviet-built PDP-11 clone. The game escaped Soviet borders through ELORG (Electronorgtechnica), which licensed it via a labyrinth of disputes resolved by Henk Rogers and Nintendo in 1989, bundling it with the Game Boy.

question: Atari reportedly sent dump trucks to a New Mexico landfill with millions of unsold cartridges of its E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial game and buried them under concrete. The tale passed for an urban legend until diggers really did find the buried games, decades later. In what New Mexico city was the landfill?
context: The story was treated as urban legend until April 26, 2014, when a documentary team led by Zak Penn (writer of Ready Player One) excavated the Alamogordo city landfill and confirmed it — finding thousands of Atari cartridges, console parts, and crushed Atari paperwork.

question: In 1999, the Japanese company Sega launched its very last home video-game console in America, the Dreamcast. Sega picked the release date to be unforgettable — every digit lined up in a row of nines. Ads across the country counted down to the launch, Sega fans lined up outside stores overnight holding empty controllers, and the marketing slogan told everyone the date over and over. What was the Dreamcast's launch date?
context: Sega's 9/9/99 marketing campaign was a huge launch hit — the Dreamcast set first-day-sales records. It launched with NFL 2K, Sonic Adventure, and Soulcalibur. Sega discontinued the console in March 2001 after PS2 dominance crushed it.

question: Nintendo's signature composer of the 1980s wrote two of the most famous tunes in games. He composed the bouncy underground theme of Super Mario Bros. in 1985 and the heroic overworld theme of The Legend of Zelda in 1986. He has stayed with Nintendo for over forty years. Name him.
context: Kondo joined Nintendo in 1984 as the company's first dedicated music composer. The SMB overworld theme is the most-recognized piece of video-game music ever written. Kondo also scored Star Fox 64, Super Mario 64, and most Zelda main themes.

question: Billy Mitchell, a Florida teenager whose family ran a restaurant, sat down at the Donkey Kong cabinet in the family arcade on 4 July 1982. Over one long session he set the world-record score, a number that stood for years and made him an arcade celebrity. What was his score?
context: The 874,300 score was the first Mitchell achieved that gained widespread recognition through Twin Galaxies' verified scoreboard. He didn't break a million points until a later effort, eventually claiming 1,047,200 in 1982-83 (later disputed). The first verified million-point Donkey Kong score on a genuine arcade board was Steve Sanders, on July 9, 1982 at the Twin Galaxies arcade in Ottumwa, Iowa — five days after Mitchell's 874,300. Mitchell would later claim back the record with even higher scores, but the 1982 disputes (resolved in 2018 when Twin Galaxies removed Mitchell's scores after determining his tapes used MAME emulator software, not arcade hardware) make the period a complicated story.

question: Namco's Pac-Man sends its hero into a wrecked maze on the so-called 'kill screen'. At the level where the bonus-fruit table overflows, the right half turns into a garbled mess of letters, numbers and tile-bits that stops the hero from finishing the dot field. What level is the kill screen?
context: 256 is the 8-bit unsigned integer overflow — the level counter wraps around. Billy Mitchell achieved the first publicly verified perfect Pac-Man game in 1999 — every dot, every fruit, every ghost, on every level through 255, ending with a planned death on 256. Score: 3,333,360.

question: High-score chasers on Nintendo's 1981 Donkey Kong hit a strange bug: the bonus timer started far too low. The carpenter hero could barely climb a single rivet before the timer expired and killed him, so the chasers named the spot the 'kill screen'. What level is it?
context: DK has 117 distinct screens cycling across stages and levels — the kill screen is on the 117th screen, technically the first screen of level 22. The bonus timer is calculated as 0x10 * (level + 1) but with a sign-bit bug at level 22 yielding effectively 0 seconds.

question: Boston students at General Computer Corporation built an unauthorized hack of Pac-Man, and Midway licensed and rebadged it as Ms. Pac-Man, released in 1982. It became one of the highest-grossing arcade games in US history. What was the hack called before Midway rebadged it?
context: GCC's Doug Macrae and Kevin Curran built Crazy Otto as a maze game with leg-having characters. Midway approached them and licensed it as the official Pac-Man sequel, much to Namco's annoyance — Namco hadn't authorized any sequel and only later embraced Ms. Pac-Man as canon in 2002.

question: Walter Day opened an arcade in 1981 in a small Iowa town, where his family had a hotel, and began keeping a book of the top scores players hit on his machines. From that pastime grew Twin Galaxies, for decades the official keeper of arcade high scores. Which town was it?
context: Day chose Ottumwa because his family owned a hotel there. Twin Galaxies the arcade opened November 1981. Day became a sort of arcade-scene Mr. Rogers, eventually nicknamed 'the referee' for his constant scorebook updates. The 2007 King of Kong documentary made him a household name.

question: Arcade legend says men in dark suits showed up at a few arcades in Portland, Oregon, in 1981, unplugged a strange black cabinet and hauled it away. Players who tried it had reported headaches, memory loss and even seizures. Nobody has ever proven the story is real. What was that supposed cabinet called?
context: Polybius first appeared on coinop.org in 1998 as a speculative listing. No evidence supports its existence. The legend is widely treated as the foundational creepypasta of arcade culture, parodied in The Simpsons (S25 'Married to the Blob') with a black cabinet labeled 'PROPERTY OF U.S. GOV'T'.

question: Atari gave a single in-house programmer only about five weeks in 1982 to design and code a game of Steven Spielberg's hit movie E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, in time for the Christmas shopping season. The game sold poorly, unsold cartridges were later buried in a New Mexico landfill, and historians blame it as a major cause of the 1983 video-game crash. Which lone programmer got the rushed job?
context: Warshaw had also designed Atari's hit Yars' Revenge (1982). Atari paid $20-25 million for the E.T. license and ordered five million cartridges; only 1.5 million sold. Warshaw still defends the design publicly — it's a complex pit-falling collection game, not 'the worst game ever,' but the rush job and the public memory have stuck.

question: Nintendo launched the Famicom, its first home game console, in Japan on July 15, 1983, over two years before the Nintendo Entertainment System reached the US. The launch lineup was just three games, all home ports of Nintendo arcade hits. Which three games were they?
answer: Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr., and Popeye
choices: Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr., and Popeye
Mario Bros., Super Mario Bros., and Mario Tennis
Excitebike, Ice Climber, and Balloon Fight
context: The Famicom (Family Computer) was designed by Masayuki Uemura and released for ¥14,800 — about $66 in 1983 USD. The 'NES' redesign for the US was a deliberate VCR-look to avoid the 'toy' aisle still poisoned by the 1983 crash.

question: A California company launched a home game console in 1977 that plugged into the family television, and kids popped in cartridges of Combat, Space Invaders and later Pac-Man. Its maker first called the machine by a three-letter name, the initials of what the console technically was. When the bigger 5200 model arrived in 1982, the old machine was renamed the 2600. What was the three-letter name?
context: Atari renamed the VCS to 2600 in 1982 after launching the more advanced 5200. The 2600's joystick had a single button and eight-direction stick. Combat was the pack-in game. Activision was founded in 1979 by Atari programmers angry that Warner Atari wouldn't credit them on cartridges.

question: Super Mario Bros. 2 in North America (1988) was actually a different game from the Japanese sequel. Nintendo of America thought the real SMB2 (later called The Lost Levels) was too hard and reskinned a different Japanese Famicom game for the US market. What was the original game?
context: Doki Doki Panic was a 1987 Famicom Disk System game with mascots from a Fuji TV festival. Nintendo redrew the player-characters as Mario, Luigi, Toad, and Princess Peach. The true Japanese SMB2 finally reached the West in Super Mario All-Stars on SNES (1993) as 'The Lost Levels.'

question: In 1989, Mattel released a strange new accessory for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) that let players control games by moving their hand through the air. Infrared sensors around the TV read the wearer's finger bends and translated them into button presses. The 1989 Nintendo-promoting movie The Wizard put the accessory on its snide teen villain, who sneers that the glove is 'so bad.' What did Mattel name the accessory?
context: The Power Glove worked terribly — only two games used it (Super Glove Ball and Bad Street Brawler), and even those required arduous button-code memorization. Its place in pop-culture is far larger than its actual gaming utility, thanks to The Wizard and reverence in Spielberg's Ready Player One.

question: In 1983, Nintendo released a home game console in Japan called the Famicom, short for Family Computer. Both of its controllers were wired directly into the console — the player could not unplug them. Controller 1 had a D-pad, two action buttons, plus Select and Start. Controller 2 was different. It had no Select or Start buttons at all, but it had one extra part that Controller 1 did not — you could speak into it, and some Famicom games listened. What was it?
context: The Famicom Controller 2 microphone was used in only a few games — most famously The Legend of Zelda, where shouting into the mic killed the Pol's Voice enemy in the eighth dungeon. Western Zelda players had no idea why the enemy was undefeatable — the US NES controller had no mic.

question: By 1987, Hironobu Sakaguchi's company Square was almost out of money. He designed one last role-playing game for the Famicom and named it Final Fantasy because he thought it truly would be his final one. If the game flopped, he planned to quit games and go back to college. Which university had he chosen, and for what degree?
answer: Yokohama National University, for an engineering degree
choices: Yokohama National University, for an engineering degree
Tokyo University, for a literature degree
Kyoto University, for a music degree
Waseda University, for a business degree
context: Sakaguchi was a Yokohama National University engineering student before joining Square. Final Fantasy sold 400,000 copies in Japan, saving the company. Sakaguchi went on to direct Final Fantasy through VI, executive-produce VII-IX, and create Chrono Trigger with Yuji Horii and Akira Toriyama.

question: In 1998, Sega launched the Dreamcast in Japan. The star of its lineup was the first fully 3D Sonic the Hedgehog game, Sonic Adventure, made by the Sonic Team studio inside Sega. Two team leads directed it together. One of them had already directed the dream-world platformer Nights into Dreams. Who were the two directors?
context: Sonic Adventure introduced new characters Big the Cat (fishing), Tails (mech), Knuckles (treasure-hunting), Amy Rose (escape), and E-102 Gamma (shooter) — each with a distinct gameplay style. The 'Crush 40' rock-vocal tracks by Jun Senoue became signature Sonic-3D-era music. Sonic Team's Takashi Iizuka also co-directed.

question: In 1997, the British studio Rare released GoldenEye 007 for the Nintendo 64, a shooter based on the James Bond movie of the same name. Its multiplayer mode became a legend, and every player wanted one weapon above all others. It killed any opponent in a single shot but held only a few bullets at a time. What was this weapon called?
context: Based on the Scaramanga golden pistol from the 1974 Bond film. Holds one bullet; one-shot kills anything. Spawned in random multiplayer locations, leading to mad scrambles. Many multiplayer house-rules tournaments forbid camping the Golden Gun spawn — and forbid Oddjob entirely.

question: In Metal Gear Solid, the 1998 Sony PlayStation stealth game directed by Hideo Kojima, players sneak the soldier Solid Snake through an Alaskan military base. One boss, a telepathic villain named Psycho Mantis, seems to read the player's mind — dodging every attack as if he sees each button press before it happens. Veteran players cracked the fight not by pressing new buttons but by doing something odd to the PlayStation hardware itself. What did they have to do?
answer: Move the controller from Port 1 to Port 2
choices: Move the controller from Port 1 to Port 2
Hold the dualshock motion sensors face-down
Insert a memory card into Slot 2 mid-fight
Press Start while the disc tray was open
context: Psycho Mantis 'read your mind' by reading controller inputs from Port 1 — switching ports cut him off. Earlier in the fight, he also reads the player's memory card and comments on other Konami games saved there ('I see you also like Castlevania!'). Kojima's fourth-wall-breaking signature.

question: The real Japanese sequel to Super Mario Bros. was a brutally hard game called The Lost Levels. It never came to the US on its own. In 1993, Nintendo finally brought it over on a Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) cartridge that also included 16-bit remakes of Super Mario Bros., Super Mario Bros. 2, and Super Mario Bros. 3. What was that cartridge called?
context: All-Stars rebuilt all four NES games with 16-bit graphics by Nintendo R&D4. The Lost Levels added poison mushrooms, wind, and brutal difficulty. The cartridge also came in a Mario World pack-in version. The 1996 Super Mario All-Stars + Super Mario World combined edition is one of the rarest SNES carts.

question: In late 1998, Sega launched its Dreamcast console. Its controller had a slot on top where a tiny memory card slid in. This memory card was unusual — it had its own small liquid crystal display (LCD) screen, a D-pad, and buttons of its own. Players could pop the card out of the controller entirely and play it as a standalone handheld, feeding a virtual pet Tamagotchi-style on the school bus. What did Sega call this memory card?
context: The VMU had 200 blocks of memory and a 48x32 LCD. Sonic Adventure's 'Chao Garden' could be loaded onto the VMU and raised standalone. Sony's PlayStation 1 PocketStation (1999, Japan-only) had a similar concept. The Sega VMU defines a forgotten era of console-peripheral creativity.

question: On August 23, 1991, Nintendo launched the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, or SNES, in North America. It was Nintendo's follow-up to the NES, with sharper 16-bit graphics, a Mode-7 rotating background trick, and a stereo sound chip. The console came bundled with a single pack-in cartridge — a colorful side-scrolling adventure that introduced a green dinosaur named Yoshi and let Mario glide by using a spinning cape. What was the launch title?
context: Super Mario World was developed by Miyamoto's team alongside the SNES hardware itself, debuting Yoshi the dinosaur. The launch lineup also included F-Zero, Pilotwings, SimCity, and Gradius III. Nintendo had been beaten to 16-bit in the US by Sega Genesis (1989), but the SNES caught up by 1993.

question: Chrono Trigger's 1995 SNES score was composed by a then-23-year-old Squaresoft programmer who was so determined to compose a score that he threatened to quit if not given the chance. He was hospitalized from overwork during the composition. Name him.
context: Nobuo Uematsu — Square's main composer — stepped in to write 10 of the game's 65 tracks when Mitsuda fell ill. Mitsuda went on to score Xenogears (1998) and Chrono Cross (1999). His 'Corridors of Time' and 'Schala's Theme' are considered among the best JRPG compositions ever.

question: Sega released two Genesis cartridges in 1994 — a mainline Sonic sequel plus a spin-off starring the red echidna Knuckles. The spin-off cart had a passthrough slot on top, allowing players to plug the mainline sequel in and play them together as one combined game. What was the combined experience called?
context: Plugging Sonic 2 into the S&K cartridge let the player play as Knuckles in Sonic 2 (no extra story). Plugging Sonic 1 or any non-Sonic cart yielded the 'No Way' or 'Blue Sphere' randomly generated minigame. The lock-on cartridge tech was an engineering one-off — Sega never used it again.

question: A secret green ninja waits on the Pit stage of the original 1992 Mortal Kombat arcade game, and only players who meet specific conditions can fight him. Arcade rumour talks of flawless rounds, no blocking and silhouettes crossing the moon. He cannot be selected in the first game, but the sequel makes him playable. What is the green ninja's name?
context: MK1's secret-character lore — silhouettes flying across the moon, double-flawless rounds, no-block challenges — was a closely-guarded arcade rumor. Reptile's combination of Scorpion's spear and Sub-Zero's freeze made him a fan-favorite. MK2 added Smoke, Noob Saibot, and Jade as similar secret-ninja characters.

question: Capcom hid a secret boss inside Super Street Fighter II Turbo in 1994, an update of its famous series of one-on-one duels, and only players who met specific arcade conditions could challenge him. He was a corrupted master of dark energy, the evil brother of the sensei who trained the heroes Ryu and Ken. Who was the hidden boss?
context: Akuma debuted as a secret boss in Super Street Fighter II Turbo (1994) — the only way to fight him was a series of specific arcade conditions (multiple perfect rounds, then a particular character selection). In Japan, the character is called Gouki; the US rename to Akuma was a marketing choice by Capcom USA for a more distinctive Western feel. Akuma is the brother of Ryu and Ken's sensei Gouken; he killed Gouken in a duel before the SF series begins. The character's hair turns white during his Shun Goku Satsu / Raging Demon finisher. The Mike Tyson rumor about the SF2 character renames (Balrog/Vega/M. Bison) is a separate (and correct) bit of trivia — Tyson's name conflict was with the boxer character renamed Balrog in the US, not with Akuma/Gouki.

question: Konami launched Dance Dance Revolution in Japanese arcades in 1998, opening an entirely new genre of rhythm games played on foot-pad controllers. The game belonged to a broader Konami brand that included Beatmania (1997) and Guitar Freaks (1999). What was the brand called?
context: Bemani is short for 'Beat Mania.' DDR reached the US in 1999 and exploded among gym-class fitness programs by the early 2000s. The game's combination of public-arcade visibility, calorie burn, and music-discovery appeal made it the rare rhythm game to cross into mass-culture awareness.

question: In 1994, Sega released a strange add-on for its Genesis console. The device — shaped like a black mushroom cap — plugged straight into the Genesis cartridge slot on top and boosted the whole console up to 32-bit graphics power. Sega rushed it out just as its more powerful Saturn console was about to launch, and the add-on flopped. Sega discontinued it within a year. What was this add-on called?
context: The 32X had its own power supply, AV cables, and required the Genesis to function — a mushroom-tower of plastic. Only 40-ish games were ever released for it, including Doom (with weaker graphics than 3DO), Star Wars Arcade, and Virtua Racing Deluxe. The Sega Saturn launch six months later cannibalized 32X sales.

question: The Nintendo 64 controller (1996) had an unusual three-pronged design — left grip with D-pad, center grip with a new thumb-operated joystick, right grip with face buttons. The player chose two of three grips to hold. What was the central component that defined which two grips?
context: The N64 analog stick was the first analog stick on a major home console — Sony quickly responded with the DualShock (1997). Holding left+center vs left+right depended on what the game needed; Super Mario 64 used center+right, while Mario Party gripped left+right for D-pad-heavy mini-games.

question: In 2001, Bungie's Halo: Combat Evolved launched with the original Xbox. Its hero, the super-soldier Master Chief, is guided through the game by an AI companion named Cortana. Cortana's voice actress is from Seattle. She has kept playing Cortana in every mainline Halo game, all the way through Halo Infinite in 2021. Name her.
context: Jen Taylor is a Seattle-area actress who began voicing Cortana in 2001 and has continued through 30+ years of Halo games. She has also voiced Princess Peach in multiple Mario games (Super Mario Sunshine onward), Daisy, Toad, and Toadette. Outside games, she has theater credits with Seattle's Empty Space Theatre. Jennifer Hale (Commander Shepard, Bastila Shan), Tara Strong (Twilight Sparkle, Bubbles), and Grey DeLisle (Daphne Blake, Azula) are all major game-voice actresses but did not play Cortana.

question: In 1996, Sony's PlayStation got its first blockbuster hero: Crash Bandicoot, an orange marsupial spinning through crates on a jungle island. The studio behind him was Naughty Dog. Naughty Dog had been founded ten years earlier, in 1986, by two University of Michigan classmates who had been coding games together as teenagers. Name the two co-founders.
choices: Mark Cerny and Naughty Dog Anonymous
context: Gavin and Rubin's earlier games included Keef the Thief (1989), Rings of Power (1991), and Way of the Warrior (1994). After Crash, they made Jak and Daxter for PS2, sold Naughty Dog to Sony in 2001, and left in 2004. The studio went on to make Uncharted (Amy Hennig) and The Last of Us (Neil Druckmann).

question: In 2005, Capcom released Resident Evil 4 for the Nintendo GameCube. Older Resident Evil games used fixed haunted-house camera angles that swung around a room. RE4 threw those out and glued a floating over-the-shoulder camera behind the hero, agent Leon Kennedy. That single change reinvented how action video games are filmed. In this new adventure, Leon travels overseas to rescue the U.S. President's daughter. Where does the story take place?
context: Leon S. Kennedy travels to rural Spain to rescue the US President's kidnapped daughter Ashley from a parasite-cult called Los Iluminados. Director Shinji Mikami's over-the-shoulder camera was directly imitated by Gears of War (2006), Uncharted (2007), and Dead Space (2008), defining the post-2005 action-shooter look.

question: An announcer bellows 'He's on fire!' in Midway's 1993 arcade hit NBA Jam when a player sinks three baskets in a row. Two players run a 2-on-2 basketball game full of ten-foot slam dunks and physics-defying jumps that take real NBA stars right off the court, but that voice is the most beloved part. Who voiced NBA Jam?
context: Kitzrow's catchphrases — 'Boomshakalaka!', 'From way downtown!', 'He's heating up!' — were largely improvised in a single Chicago recording session. Kitzrow has voiced almost every Midway and NBA Jam-derivative sports title since. He has no formal sports-broadcast career outside game development.

question: The whole Simpson family fights Springfield's criminals block by block in Konami's 1991 brawler The Simpsons Arcade Game, after Bart accidentally grabs a stolen diamond. Homer swings his fists, Marge whips a vacuum cleaner, Bart rides his skateboard and Lisa cracks a skipping rope. A hidden extra-life donut sits in one exact spot every 90s arcade kid eventually learned. Where does the donut appear?
answer: Behind the bowling alley garbage cans
choices: Behind the bowling alley garbage cans
Inside the Power Plant cooling tower
On top of the Krusty Burger sign
Down a manhole at the courthouse
context: The Simpsons Arcade is a brawler in the X-Men Arcade / TMNT Arcade tradition — Konami's beat-em-up template. The Bonus Round between stages is the bouncing-on-a-trampoline minigame. Homer's nightmare cutscene featuring a giant donut is one of the more surreal arcade interstitials of the era.

question: In 1989, Konami built a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles arcade cabinet with four joysticks side by side so four kids could each play a different turtle. Each turtle wore a different color mask. The one who wore the purple mask was the team's brainy engineer and inventor. Which turtle wore the purple mask?
context: Leonardo (blue) wielded katanas. Donatello (purple) wielded a bo staff. Raphael (red) wielded sai. Michelangelo (orange) wielded nunchaku. The Konami arcade is the second TMNT game (after the 1989 NES original), and is widely considered the definitive beat-em-up of the franchise.

question: Disney's 2012 animated film Wreck-It Ralph fills its arcade machines with cameos from real video-game characters, then seats real bad guys together in one famous group-therapy scene. A Pac-Man enemy sits in the chair and runs the meeting. Which ghost is it?
context: Other real-game cameos: Bowser (Mario), M. Bison and Zangief (Street Fighter), Kano (Mortal Kombat), Doctor Robotnik (Sonic), and Neff (Altered Beast). Sonic himself appears with a 'Public Service Announcement' cameo at Game Central Station. Voice direction by John C. Reilly as Ralph.

question: Dustin Henderson covets the laserdisc cabinet Don Bluth drew, at the Palace Arcade in Hawkins, Indiana, in Season 2 of the Netflix show Stranger Things. He wants to lock in the high score forever, but a mystery player logged as MADMAX quietly beats his record. Who beats Dustin?
context: Max's MADMAX initials on the leaderboard intrigue the boys for episodes before they meet her. Stranger Things' arcade scenes were filmed at a real reproduction arcade in Atlanta, featuring period-accurate cabinets including Pac-Man, Dragon's Lair, Centipede, and Dig Dug.

question: The 1989 Fred Savage movie The Wizard was really one long Nintendo commercial. Kids race across the country to a big Nintendo video-game championship in California. In the final round the movie showed off a brand-new Nintendo game that had not yet reached store shelves in the US, which sent kids everywhere begging their parents for it. Which unreleased game was it?
context: SMB3 wouldn't release in the US until February 1990. The Wizard's climax shows protagonist Jimmy collecting Warp Whistles in World 1 and warping to World 4. The film promoted the Power Glove and Nintendo Power magazine. Universal sued Nintendo over the use of its Hollywood backlot but eventually settled.

question: Steve Wiebe, a Boeing engineer and Washington high-school teacher, finally beat Billy Mitchell's Donkey Kong record in 2003, submitting 1,006,600 from his garage cabinet. Mitchell's old mark had stood on the books of Twin Galaxies for over 20 years. Mitchell responded with a videotape sent by courier. What was his 2007 response score?
context: The 2007 Seth Gordon documentary The King of Kong tracked the rivalry. Wiebe later beat 1,049,100 publicly. In April 2018, Twin Galaxies analyzed Mitchell's pre-2007 tapes and concluded they had been recorded from MAME emulator rather than arcade hardware — disqualifying all of Mitchell's DK records. The disqualification lawsuit continues.

question: Steve Wiebe, a Washington high-school science teacher and recently laid-off Boeing engineer, paid $50 on eBay for a damaged Donkey Kong board in 2003 and built the cabinet in his garage in Redmond. Twin Galaxies referees rejected the first videotape he sent them. What did they question?
answer: The plausibility of his rapid-rivet sequence on the final screen
choices: The plausibility of his rapid-rivet sequence on the final screen
Whether he had used save-state cheats on a board hack
Whether his tape ran over the documented five-hour rules limit
Whether Mitchell had intercepted and substituted the footage
context: In King of Kong, Walter Day sends Twin Galaxies referee Robert Mruczek to inspect Wiebe's cabinet. Mruczek later denied Mitchell or his allies tampered with the inspection; the documentary's villain framing has been disputed by Mitchell's defenders. Wiebe's son Derek and daughter Cannon both appear in the film as kids.

question: A console maker buried piles of unsold cartridges in a New Mexico desert after two of its 1982 games flopped, in the crash of 1983 to 1985 that nearly killed the home console business. One flop was the movie tie-in E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial. The other was a rushed home port of the biggest arcade hit of all time. Which game was that home port?
context: Atari produced 12 million Pac-Man cartridges for a 10-million-installed-base 2600 — they expected to sell to new console buyers. The port's flickering ghosts (a 4-frame palette swap) made it look terrible. Atari sold only 7 million, leaving warehouses full. Combined with E.T., Atari laid off thousands of employees in 1983 and the entire toy aisle stopped stocking games by 1984.

question: Four of Atari's star programmers walked out in 1979 and founded their own studio, Activision. They were angry that Atari, then owned by Warner, refused to put their names on the boxes of the games they had designed. The last straw came from an Atari boss who insulted them at a meeting. What did he say?
answer: That they were no more important to Atari than the assembly-line workers who boxed the cartridges
choices: That they were no more important to Atari than the assembly-line workers who boxed the cartridges
That Bushnell would refuse to honor their stock-option vesting after resignation
That Atari lawyers would sue them for trade-secret breach if they discussed designs
That Kaplan would be fired for putting his name on the title screen of a game
context: Crane and the others split off and immediately released Boxing, Tennis, Skiing, and Dragster. Activision became one of the biggest third-party publishers. Atari sued Activision, but in 1983 settled by allowing third-party publishers — opening the floodgates that contributed to the 1983 crash via low-quality shovelware.

question: Don Bluth and about a dozen colleagues left a feature unfinished when they walked out of Disney Animation Studios and founded Don Bluth Productions. Their new studio later defined the arcade-game-as-cartoon look. What Disney film were they working on at the moment of the walkout?
context: Bluth's 1982 NIMH won the Academy of Science Fiction prize. Steven Spielberg recruited Bluth to direct An American Tail (1986) and The Land Before Time (1988), both major hits. Bluth's 1989 All Dogs Go to Heaven failed against The Little Mermaid (released the same week). The animator's walk-out is widely credited as forcing Disney's late-1980s renaissance under Katzenberg.

question: Sega's CEO Tom Kalinske shocked the industry at E3 May 11, 1995 by announcing the Sega Saturn would launch in North America that same day, earlier than the originally announced September 2 date. The launch backfired badly. Sony immediately countered. What price did Sony announce that day for the PlayStation?
context: Sony's '299' announcement at E3 was the legendary mic-drop moment — Olaf Olafsson of Sony just walked out, said '$299', and left. The Saturn was $399 with only six launch titles. Major retailers KB Toys and Walmart pulled out angrily over being skipped. The Saturn never recovered; Sega exited console hardware after Dreamcast 2001.

question: In the early 1990s, Nintendo and Sony teamed up to build a compact-disc read-only memory (CD-ROM) add-on for the Super Nintendo (SNES) so games could ship on disc instead of cartridge. Sony was already calling its prototype the 'Play Station.' Sony proudly unveiled the design at a 1991 electronics show in Chicago. The very next day, on the same stage, Nintendo publicly shocked Sony by announcing it had dumped Sony for a different CD partner. Who was Nintendo's new partner?
choices: Hitachi, which made the Saturn co-processor
context: Nintendo had grown wary of Sony's contract terms — Sony would have kept all the revenue from CD-based games. Switching to Philips humiliated Sony's CES booth team. Ken Kutaragi convinced Sony chairman Norio Ohga to go ahead with the project as a standalone Sony console — the PlayStation. The Philips CD-i went on to be famously disastrous.

question: Bungie was a small Chicago studio best known for making atmospheric first-person shooters on Apple Macintosh computers in the 1990s. In 2000, Microsoft bought Bungie so its next secret science-fiction shooter — later shipped as Halo: Combat Evolved — could launch Microsoft's brand-new Xbox console. What was Bungie's earlier three-game Mac shooter series that had already made its name in the game industry?
context: Marathon — Marathon 2: Durandal — Marathon Infinity. Halo was originally a Mac-and-PC RTS, then a third-person shooter, then the FPS Xbox launch we know. Bungie left Microsoft in 2007 to make Destiny under Activision. The Marathon trilogy was open-sourced in 2005 by Bungie.

question: Master Chief's John-117 designation refers to him being the 117th Spartan-II inducted into the program — kidnapped as a six-year-old child in 2517 and replaced by a clone. The Spartan-II project was led by a Halsey-named researcher who appears in the games. What was her first name?
choices: Cortana (the AI is a digital copy)
context: Cortana was created from a flash-cloned copy of Halsey's brain — making her effectively Master Chief's surrogate mother in genetic terms. The Spartan-II program took 75 children; 33 survived augmentation. The Halo: First Strike novel by Eric Nylund (2003) is the canonical Halsey/Chief backstory.

question: Super Mario Bros. came out for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) in 1985 and became the best-selling game of the decade. Shigeru Miyamoto led the design, but he had a co-designer. That partner stayed with Miyamoto for the next forty years, working on The Legend of Zelda, more Mario games, and Yoshi's Island. Name Miyamoto's co-designer.
context: Tezuka has co-directed almost every major Mario title (he was the producer on Super Mario Maker and Super Mario Wonder). His and Miyamoto's design philosophy — 'design the player's first 30 seconds perfectly' — defines the SMB World 1-1 tutorial, widely studied in game-design programs.

question: In Super Mario Bros. (1985), the very first stage is called World 1-1. Shigeru Miyamoto carefully placed the first Goomba enemy so it appears in the same instant the player first sees a question-mark block. Miyamoto arranged this on purpose so a kid holding the controller for the first time would learn one specific lesson within seconds. What was the lesson?
answer: That Goombas hurt on touch and die from jumps
choices: That Goombas hurt on touch and die from jumps
That power-up mushrooms grow Mario bigger
That Mario can break bricks from below
That coins are collected by touching them
context: The 30-second sequence — first Goomba, first question-block with a mushroom that the new player likely runs into, first second-level pipes — was deliberately designed as a no-text tutorial. Designer Mark Brown's 'Sequelitis' YouTube video makes the SMB 1-1 case canonical in modern design analysis.

question: Yoshi the green dinosaur first showed up in Super Mario World in on the Super Nintendo. But designer Shigeru Miyamoto had wanted a rideable dinosaur for Mario ever since the very first Super Mario Bros. in 1985 — the older NES just wasn't powerful enough to draw one on screen. On the earliest Nintendo concept sheets, Yoshi had a long, Latin-sounding, dinosaur-style scientific name that also punned on his Mario-world enemies. What was that original name?
context: Yoshi's full name was almost never used in-game. The Mario World manual lists him as 'T. Yoshisaur Munchakoopas' in the US release. Designer Shigefumi Hino. Yoshi has appeared in over 30 Mario titles, has his own series (Yoshi's Island 1995, Yoshi's Story 1997, Yoshi's Crafted World 2019), and is Nintendo's third-most-marketable character behind Mario and Pokemon.

question: Inside Nintendo, the engineering group called Research and Development 1 designed most of Nintendo's hardware from the 1970s into the 1990s. Its lead engineer created the tiny handheld Game & Watch, the cross-shaped D-pad still used on controllers today, the Famicom and Nintendo Entertainment System (NES), and the original Game Boy. Name him.
context: Yokoi's 'lateral thinking with withered technology' philosophy — using mature, cheap components creatively — produced the Game Boy and the entire Game & Watch line. He left Nintendo in 1996 after the Virtual Boy commercial failure and died in a car accident in October 1997, age 56.

question: Final Fantasy VII (1997 PS1) was the franchise's global breakthrough — selling 9.8 million copies and putting Square at the top of the Japanese role-playing game (JRPG) world. The game's protagonist Cloud Strife says he once served in Shinra's elite super-warrior program, whose fighters' eyes glow from the energy pumped into them. What was the program called?
context: SOLDIER is always written in all-caps in-game. SOLDIER 1st Class is the highest rank; Sephiroth was a 1st Class member. Cloud's actual rank history is one of the game's mysteries — explained more fully in Final Fantasy VII Remake (2020-2024) and the Compilation of FFVII (Crisis Core, Advent Children, Dirge of Cerberus).

question: Final Fantasy VII on the PlayStation in 1997 gave players glowing orbs called Materia that plugged into their weapons and armor to grant abilities. The Materia came in different colors, one for each type. Magic spells were green. Command abilities like Steal were yellow. Support Materia was blue. What color were the mighty Summon Materia that called forth Ifrit, Shiva, and Bahamut?
context: Five Materia categories: Green (Magic — Fire, Cure, Bolt), Yellow (Command — Steal, Throw, Sense), Blue (Support — All, Quadra Magic, MP Turbo, slotted as a pair), Purple (Independent — passive stat boost), and Red (Summon — Ifrit, Shiva, Bahamut). The system encouraged build experimentation rare for the era.

question: Nintendo launched the Nintendo 64 in North America in late 1996, more than a year after Sony's PlayStation and Sega's Saturn. Both of those rivals ran on 32-bit chips. Nintendo's marketing hammered on one big technical advantage that the Nintendo 64's very name pointed to. What was the bragging point?
answer: 64-bit CPU processing, twice the bus width of competitors
choices: 64-bit CPU processing, twice the bus width of competitors
CD-quality redbook-audio Game Pak music streams in mono
An on-cart MIDI synthesis chip generating 96 vocal voices
The Z-button trigger as an industry-first analog rear control
context: The N64's 64-bit MIPS R4300i CPU was technically true but marketing-misleading — the actual bus was rarely fully utilized. The launch lineup of two games (Mario 64 and Pilotwings 64) was infamously thin. Nintendo's choice of cartridge over CD-ROM cost it the goodwill of third-party publishers including Square, who took FFVII to PlayStation.

question: Halo: Combat Evolved launched for the Microsoft Xbox in November 2001. It ends in a famously chaotic driving chase. Master Chief, the game's armored super-soldier hero, has to race a Warthog jeep up a long collapsing ramp through corridors packed with Flood parasites as the spaceship Pillar of Autumn blows apart around him. Everyone remembers this level from its ticking countdown music. What is this final level called?
context: The Maw is the tenth and final level. Bungie designer Jaime Griesemer designed the escape sequence in 12 days at the end of development. The Warthog's physics — a four-wheeled jeep that could be driven over corpses, ramps, and walls — defined the open-arena Halo combat. The escape was so popular that Halo 3 ended with a Warthog escape mirroring it.

question: In 1998 the Japanese company Sega released the Dreamcast, a smooth white console with a small memory-card screen built into every controller. It was the first home game console to ship with a modem built right into every unit — a 33.6k or 56k card for dialing up over a phone line. North American Dreamcast owners logged into Sega's own official online service to play games like Phantasy Star Online against people in other cities. What was that service called?
context: SegaNet enabled the first console MMO — Phantasy Star Online (2000), which let players from Japan, US, and Europe play together on shared servers. Dreamarena was the European service. Online play also distinguished NFL 2K1, Quake III Arena Dreamcast, and Chu Chu Rocket. Sega shut down its first-party Dreamcast servers in 2003.

question: In 1999 Wizards of the Coast released the first English printing of the Pokemon Trading Card Game, called the Base Set. Card number 4 was the shiny holographic Charizard, and it became the most-wanted card in every kid's binder. The very first run had two special traits — a small '1st Edition' stamp on the left of the art, and no thin shadow line running down the right side of the card border. Later reprints added that shadow line. Which Base Set Charizard printing sells for the most money at auction today?
context: The Base Set's first print run was 'Shadowless' — no thin shadow border was added until the second print. The 'Edition 1' stamp was on the leftmost cards of the first run. A PSA 10 graded 1st Edition Shadowless Charizard has sold for over $400,000 at auction. WotC's Pokemon TCG printing was managed by Carta Mundi in Belgium.

question: In 1991 Sega released the Genesis side-scrolling brawler Streets of Rage, where three police officers punched and kicked their way through a mob-controlled city. The soundtrack shocked players — pounding house and techno beats built with the Genesis sound chip that sounded like a real club mix. The composer had already scored Revenge of Shinobi in 1989 and the Super Nintendo fantasy game ActRaiser in 1990, and he became one of Japan's most famous game composers. Name him.
context: Koshiro was 24 when he scored Streets of Rage. His Streets of Rage 2 score is widely considered the greatest 16-bit OST. He used a custom Atari ST-based MIDI-tracker tool to push the Genesis FM synthesis hardware further than most thought possible. Koshiro continues composing today — Etrian dungeon-crawlers, 7th Dragon, and modern Streets of Rage 4 (2020).

question: In 1997 the Japanese composer Nobuo Uematsu wrote the final boss theme for Squaresoft's Final Fantasy 7, called 'One-Winged Angel'. It played over the fight against the silver-haired villain Sephiroth. The music mixed rock guitar, orchestra, and a Latin choir chanting the boss's name — Uematsu's first big orchestral video-game piece. He later said the terrifying choral part was inspired by one specific 20th-century classical composer's most famous work. Which composer?
context: The 'estuans interius' Latin chorus directly echoes Carmina Burana. Uematsu also cites Stravinsky and Jimi Hendrix as influences. Uematsu composed over 100 FF songs from 1987-2003, became Square's de-facto musical face, and now leads his own rock band 'The Black Mages,' which performs orchestral-rock arrangements of his game compositions.

question: In 1999, Konami released the horror game Silent Hill on the Sony PlayStation. The player controlled a father searching for his missing daughter in a foggy American town where air-raid sirens signaled that the world would shift into a rusted nightmare version of itself. The soundtrack was not orchestral — it was industrial noise, clanking metal, distorted guitars, and haunting piano. A 30-year-old Konami sound designer composed every track. What was his name?
context: Yamaoka used metal drums, factory machinery, scraping metal, and distorted electronic beats to create the Silent Hill sound. He has scored Silent Hill 1 through Silent Hill: Shattered Memories (2009) and Silent Hill f (2025). The town's foggy, alternate-dimension Otherworld with its rusted iron and bleeding walls was inspired by the films Jacob's Ladder and Eraserhead.

question: GoldenEye 007 (1997, N64) was developed by a small Rare team led by Martin Hollis. The team had no prior FPS experience and developed the multiplayer mode in the final six months of a four-year project. How many people were on the GoldenEye development team?
answer: Nine, including Hollis as project director
choices: Nine, including Hollis as project director
Seventy, the entire Rare studio at the time
context: The nine: Martin Hollis (lead), David Doak (mission designer), Steve Ellis (programmer), Karl Hilton (level artist), Mark Edmonds (programmer), Brett Jones (modeler), Duncan Botwood (level designer), Adrian Smith (modeler), and Graeme Norgate / Grant Kirkhope (music). Multiple team members later founded Free Radical Design and made TimeSplitters (2000).

question: One Sony engineer had earlier designed the SPC700 audio chip that ended up inside Nintendo's Super Nintendo (SNES) — a rare Sony chip living inside a Nintendo box. When the 1991 Nintendo-Sony compact disc (CD) partnership collapsed on stage in Chicago, this engineer was the one who talked Sony's bosses into striking out alone and building their very own gaming console. That console shipped in 1994 as the PlayStation. Name the engineer often called the father of the PlayStation.
context: Kutaragi was widely called 'the father of the PlayStation.' He led hardware development for PS1, PS2, PS3, and the early PSP. Sony forced him into retirement in 2007 after PS3's troubled launch. His Cell Broadband Engine processor in the PS3 was simultaneously a research achievement and a developer pain-point that hurt PS3's third-party support.

question: In 1994, the studio Shiny Entertainment released Earthworm Jim for the Sega Genesis and SNES — a bizarre platformer starring an ordinary earthworm who stumbled into a super-powered robotic space suit and became a hero. The oddball character was designed by a then-young American cartoonist and animator, the same man who would later create the cartoon Catscratch and work on Veggie Tales. Name him.
context: TenNapel sold Earthworm Jim to David Perry's Shiny Entertainment. Perry's team — Nick Bruty, Tom Tanaka, Tommy Tallarico (music) — finished the design. Tallarico's score is considered a high-water mark of Genesis FM synthesis. TenNapel later created Neverhood (1996) on PlayStation, with stop-motion claymation and Terry S Taylor music.

question: Naughty Dog's Crash Bandicoot (1996) was almost called 'Willie the Wombat,' but the team dropped that name to dodge a trademark fight. When artists Charles Zembillas and Joe Pearson drew Crash, which old American cartoon style did they use as a guide?
answer: Looney Tunes (specifically Tex Avery's exaggerated takes)
choices: Looney Tunes (specifically Tex Avery's exaggerated takes)
context: Crash's hyper-exaggerated facial expressions, eyebrow waggles, and head-snap reactions were directly inspired by Avery's wartime cartoons (Red Hot Riding Hood). Pearson and Zembillas had both come from television-cartoon backgrounds. Crash 1's 'Sony Sucks' Bandicoot Mascot Wars marketing campaign was Sony of America's deliberate jab at Sega and Nintendo.

question: The CEO of Twin Galaxies led a technical investigation himself, and in April 2018 the score-keeping organization stripped Billy Mitchell's Donkey Kong records after concluding that the video tapes he had submitted as proof came from an arcade emulator, not a real cabinet. For decades Mitchell had claimed the first perfect Pac-Man score and the world's highest on Donkey Kong. Who was the CEO?
context: Jace Hall is a Hollywood producer, founder of Monolith Productions (No One Lives Forever, F.E.A.R.), and Twin Galaxies' owner from 2014. The Mitchell investigation used reverse-engineering of arcade-board level-load patterns vs MAME's level-load patterns — a frame-by-frame signature analysis the original Twin Galaxies referees couldn't have done in 2003.

question: Warren Robinett buried a hidden credit reading 'Created by Warren Robinett' inside a home console game in 1979, the first known video-game Easter egg, after his company refused to credit designers on cartridges. In the game a small square hero carries keys and a sword between three castles while dodging three dragons. What was the game called?
context: Robinett's hidden credit was placed in the Black Castle, accessible by carrying a pixel-thin 'gray dot' across multiple screens to a specific spot. Atari executives at first wanted Robinett fired for the secret, then realized players loved discovering it. The term 'Easter egg' was coined by Atari Director of Software Steve Wright in 1980 to describe the phenomenon.

question: Howard Scott Warshaw made his first big hit with Yars' Revenge in 1982, before his E.T. disaster. A fly-like hero, Yar, battles the Qotile cannon behind a force field, and a scrolling band of random colors and pixels runs down the middle of the screen. What is that central band called?
context: The Neutral Zone was a randomly-painted strip of memory bytes — Warshaw used the game's ROM itself as the visual texture. The Yar character was a yellow eight-legged fly-creature; the Qotile alternated between a stationary cannon and a swirly killing-projectile called the Swirl. Yars' Revenge sold over a million copies for the 2600, an enormous hit for the era.

question: Midway hid a secret roster in NBA Jam Tournament Edition, sent to arcades in 1994, which players unlocked by typing certain dates and initials at the title screen. It held TV stars, the developers themselves and even American politicians dunking alongside NBA pros. One hidden player was the person in the White House at the time. Which sitting US president was on the list?
context: NBA Jam TE's hidden characters: Bill Clinton, Al Gore, Tipper Gore, the Beastie Boys, Frank Thomas, Tonya Harding, several Mortal Kombat fighters, and the entire Midway development team. The Mortal Kombat unlocks featured stretchy-arm versions of Sub-Zero, Scorpion, and Raiden. Many cheat codes were leaked in Electronic Gaming Monthly print articles.

question: An American semiconductor company in Pennsylvania released a cheap, fast 8-bit processor chip, easy to program, in the late 1970s. It became the brain of the Apple II, the Commodore 64 and, in a Ricoh-manufactured version with its decimal mode locked out, the Nintendo NES. Almost every classic home computer and console of that era ran on this chip family. Which chip was it?
context: The 6502 was designed by Chuck Peddle's team at MOS Technology in 1975 — explicitly to compete with Motorola's 6800 at one-fifth the price. The 6502 dominated 8-bit personal computing of the late 1970s and the entire NES era.
