Iron Man leads the pro-registration side; Captain America leads the anti-registration side. The series ends when Cap surrenders and is assassinated on the courthouse steps. Who fires the shot?
answer: Crossbones (Brock Rumlow), then Sharon Carter under mind control
choices: Crossbones (Brock Rumlow), then Sharon Carter under mind control
Bullseye (Lester) hired by Norman Osborn for the Thunderbolts
The Punisher (Frank Castle) caught between sides
The Red Skull personally with a Cosmic Cube
context: Crossbones fires the initial sniper round; Sharon Carter (Cap's girlfriend, brainwashed by Doctor Faustus) delivers the killing shot. Cap's body is shown on the steps of the Federal Courthouse in Manhattan. Bucky Barnes (Winter Soldier) takes up the shield. The 2007 Captain America #25 sold out within hours.

question: In Ed Brubaker's Captain America run, Bucky Barnes came back. Bucky was Cap's sidekick in World War II and was thought dead since 1945. The Soviets had found his body, given him a metal arm, and used him as a frozen assassin for years. What was his code name?
context: Brubaker's Winter Soldier arc, with Steve Epting on art, ran in Captain America (vol. 5) #1–14 (2005). The Russos adapted it as Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014), starring Sebastian Stan as Bucky. The metal arm in the comic was originally bionic-Cyborg; the films changed it to vibranium with kinetic-pulse functions.

question: Jeff Smith self-published Bone from 1991 to 2004 through his own Cartoon Books — a 1,300-page black-and-white epic following three cartoon-looking cousins lost in a sword-and-sorcery world. The three cousins are Fone Bone, Smiley Bone, and what greedy schemer?
answer: Phoney Bone (real name Phoncible P. Bone)
choices: Phoney Bone (real name Phoncible P. Bone)
Sneaky Bone (real name Sneakford P. Bone)
Cranky Bone (real name Crankford T. Bone)
Bouncy Bone (real name Boungo T. Bone)
context: Smith was inspired by Walt Kelly's Pogo, Carl Barks's Donald Duck, and Tolkien's Lord of the Rings in roughly equal parts. The series won a record-setting 11 Eisner Awards and 10 Harvey Awards. Scholastic later released the books in color.

question: American comics writer Frank Miller launched his black-and-white crime series Sin City in 1991. It is set in a violent, rain-soaked town called Basin City. The very first Sin City story follows a huge man covered in scars — an ex-convict just out of prison — who wakes up one morning next to a beautiful woman named Goldie. When Goldie is murdered in the night beside him, he vows to hunt down her killer and tear the city apart to do it. What is the ex-convict's name?
context: Mickey Rourke played Marv in Robert Rodriguez and Frank Miller's 2005 Sin City film, with Bruce Willis as Hartigan and Clive Owen as Dwight. Miller's hand-drawn high-contrast art with selective color washes (yellow Roark Jr., red Goldie blood) became the film's visual signature.

question: Frank Miller's 1998 graphic novel '300' retells the ancient Greek Battle of Thermopylae, in which King Leonidas of Sparta and his three hundred elite warriors held a narrow mountain pass against a massive Persian invasion army led by King Xerxes. In the 2006 movie based on the comic, a Persian messenger comes to Leonidas' throne room demanding Sparta's surrender. Leonidas kicks the messenger backward into a bottomless pit while shouting a line that became a famous internet meme. What is the line?
context: The actual ancient quote, from Plutarch and Herodotus, was 'Molon labe' — 'Come and take them' — Leonidas's reply when Xerxes demanded the Spartans surrender their weapons. Gerard Butler played Leonidas in the film. The 'spartan kick' meme of dropkicking someone into darkness became one of the most reused 2000s internet jokes.

question: DC Comics' 1996 miniseries Kingdom Come, written by Mark Waid with painted art by Alex Ross, imagines a near-future where an older, retired Superman comes out of hiding to lead the old heroes against a reckless new generation of super-people. The story is narrated by a small-town American Christian pastor named Norman McCay, who suffers terrifying end-of-the-world visions. A grim, ghostly DC hero with a Bible-sounding name walks beside him as his supernatural escort through those visions. Which hero?
choices: Doctor Fate (with the Helmet of Nabu)
context: Alex Ross painted every page; Mark Waid wrote. The visual style — fully painted realistic figures — was inspired by Norman Rockwell. Pastor Norman McCay is modeled on Ross's father, a real-life Methodist minister. The series ended with Superman returning to a normal life and Wonder Woman pregnant.

question: In Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix, the Ministry of Magic sends a pink-clad new teacher named Dolores Umbridge to Hogwarts. She bans real spellwork in Defense Against the Dark Arts class — students may only read theory from a textbook. With Voldemort actively rising again outside, Harry, Hermione, Ron, and their friends decide to defy her. They meet secretly in the hidden Room of Requirement to practice real defensive spells, and they give their student study-group a proud name. What do they call it?
context: The group meets in the Room of Requirement, a magically-revealed chamber on the seventh floor. Hermione enchants a list of members so anyone who betrays them has 'SNEAK' magically appear on the traitor's face — Marietta Edgecombe gets the curse when she reports them.

question: Sirius Black dies in Order of the Phoenix during the Battle of the Department of Mysteries, killed by his cousin Bellatrix Lestrange. He falls backward through an ancient stone archway draped with a tattered veil. What's the in-universe name for this artifact in the Death Chamber?
answer: The Veil of Death (or simply 'the Veil')
choices: The Veil of Death (or simply 'the Veil')
context: The Veil is studied by the Department of Mysteries; characters report hearing voices from behind it. Whether the dead can be reached has been a source of fan theorizing for decades. Sirius's last words before he falls: 'Nice one, James!' — to Harry, who looks just like his father.

question: In Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, Dumbledore takes Harry into a Pensieve of memories and reveals a terrible piece of Voldemort's past. As a young student, Tom Riddle had used the darkest branch of magic to split his own soul into seven pieces, then hid each fragment inside a physical object (a diary, a ring, a locket, and more) so no killing curse could ever finish him for good. To create one, he first had to commit a murder. What is the wizarding term for each of these dark soul-fragment containers?
context: Creating a Horcrux requires committing murder, the act that splits the soul. Horace Slughorn, the new Potions Master, explains the concept to a young Tom Riddle decades earlier — a memory Harry retrieves with Dumbledore's help. The book's title 'Half-Blood Prince' refers to Snape, whose mother Eileen was a Prince and father Tobias was a Muggle.

question: In J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, Hermione Granger reads aloud an old wizard fairy tale called The Tale of the Three Brothers. In the story, three wizard brothers meet Death on a lonely bridge and each demand a gift. The first asks for the mightiest wand ever made, the second for a Resurrection Stone to bring back the dead, and the third for a Cloak of Invisibility. The gifts together are the Deathly Hallows. What is the first brother's wand called?
context: The Elder Wand passes between owners by being mastered, not gifted — which is why Voldemort dies in the final book when the wand recognizes Harry as its true master via Draco's disarming of Dumbledore. Harry already owned the Cloak (a Potter family heirloom). The Resurrection Stone was hidden in Dumbledore's gift Snitch.

question: In J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, Voldemort's Death Eaters storm Hogwarts castle in the final Battle of Hogwarts. The Weasleys, a red-headed wizarding family, defend the school alongside Harry and Hermione. One of the family's identical twin pranksters is fighting beside his older brother Percy — who has just rejoined the family after years of estrangement — and is laughing at a rare joke Percy has just cracked when an exploding wall crashes down on them mid-laugh. Which twin dies?
context: Rowling has said she deliberated long over which twin to kill; she chose Fred because she felt readers would find it more shocking. Fred dies mid-laugh, having just made up with his estranged brother Percy. George survives and eventually marries Angelina Johnson, naming their first son Fred II.

question: Near the end of J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (2007), Harry dips his face into a stone basin called the Pensieve to view Severus Snape's private memories. He discovers that Snape has quietly loved Harry's mother, Lily Potter, since they were children playing together. In one memory the headmaster Albus Dumbledore gently asks Snape whether he still loves Lily after all these years. Snape replies with a single, one-word answer. What word does he say?
context: The one-word answer 'Always' became one of the most quoted lines from the series, especially after Alan Rickman delivered it in the 2011 film. Snape's silver doe Patronus matches Lily's, confirming the depth of his love. Harry names his second son Albus Severus Potter in tribute.

question: In the Harry Potter books by J.K. Rowling, four friends attended Hogwarts School together in the 1970s: James Potter, Sirius Black, Remus Lupin, and Peter Pettigrew. They called themselves the Marauders. Because Remus was a werewolf, the other three secretly learned to become Animagi — wizards who can turn into a chosen animal at will — so they could keep him company on full-moon nights. They also made the Marauder's Map, signing it with each Animagus nickname. James was Prongs, a stag. What form did Sirius take?
answer: A large black dog (he was nicknamed Padfoot)
choices: A large black dog (he was nicknamed Padfoot)
A grey wolf (he was nicknamed Greybeard)
A black panther (he was nicknamed Shadowpaw)
A great horned owl (he was nicknamed Nightwing)
context: Remus Lupin was a werewolf — 'Moony' — but not an Animagus. James, Sirius, and Peter became unregistered Animagi during their Hogwarts years specifically to keep Lupin company during his monthly transformations. Peter's form was a rat — 'Wormtail' — and he hid as Ron's pet Scabbers for twelve years.

question: In J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, thirteen-year-old Hermione Granger has somehow been attending more classes than her Hogwarts timetable should allow. Finally she pulls a tiny gold hourglass on a chain out from under her robes and shows it to Harry and Ron. Professor McGonagall had lent it to her so she could quietly take two classes at the same hour. What is the necklace called?
context: The Ministry of Magic strictly regulates Time-Turners. Hermione uses hers to take extra classes including Ancient Runes and Muggle Studies. At the climax, she and Harry use it to rescue Buckbeak and Sirius. Rowling has admitted writing Time-Turners into the series was a mistake — it creates plot holes the rest of the books have to work around.

question: Newt Scamander's textbook Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them is referenced throughout the Harry Potter series. The Yule Ball in Goblet of Fire (book 4) features two student musicians performing — the in-universe wizarding rock band whose drummer wears a kilt. What's the band called?
context: Despite the name, the Weird Sisters are an all-male band (their name is a Macbeth reference). In the film, members were played by real musicians including Jarvis Cocker of Pulp and Jonny Greenwood of Radiohead. Pulp's Jarvis Cocker wrote and performed the band's original song 'Do the Hippogriff.'

question: In Order of the Phoenix, Dolores Umbridge takes over Hogwarts as the Headmistress and inquisitor. She forces Harry to write lines with a magic quill that carves the words into his hand. What clever plan does Hermione use to get Umbridge removed from the school?
answer: Tricking Umbridge into the Forbidden Forest where centaurs carry her off
choices: Tricking Umbridge into the Forbidden Forest where centaurs carry her off
Spiking her tea with Veritaserum to expose her Ministry blackmail
Convincing Peeves to flood her office with permanent corridors
Setting Hagrid's Blast-Ended Skrewts loose in her classroom
context: Umbridge had insulted centaurs as 'filthy half-breeds.' Firenze and his herd capture her after Hermione lures her in claiming Dumbledore has a hidden weapon there. Umbridge appears again in Deathly Hallows persecuting Muggle-borns at the Ministry; Harry punches her to retrieve Slytherin's locket from her.

question: The 2011 Marvel movie Captain America: The First Avenger opens during World War Two. A frail young man from Brooklyn named Steve Rogers volunteers for a secret U.S. Army project run out of a hidden basement lab. A kindly German-born scientist there gives Steve a special super-soldier serum that turns him into a super-strong hero. Right after Steve is transformed, a Hydra spy shoots the scientist dead so his formula can never be made again. What was the scientist's name?
context: Stanley Tucci played Erskine. The serum's formula dies with him — which is why Hulk (gamma) and Iron Man (technology) become the closest other 'super' Avengers. Erskine had previously experimented on Johann Schmidt (the Red Skull) with an imperfect version that left Schmidt deformed. The serum amplifies a man's character.

question: In Marvel's The Avengers (2012), the Asgardian trickster god Loki stands atop Stark Tower in New York City holding a glowing blue-tipped scepter. He raises it, and a swirling rift opens in the sky. Through the portal, the alien Chitauri army pours down onto Manhattan. The scepter secretly hides one of the six Infinity gems, and the glowing cube Tesseract on the roof is what powers the portal itself. Which item in Loki's hand opened the sky?
answer: Loki's scepter (containing the Mind Stone, with the Tesseract powering the portal)
choices: Loki's scepter (containing the Mind Stone, with the Tesseract powering the portal)
The Casket of Ancient Winters, repurposed by Frost Giants
The Eye of Agamotto, stolen from Kamar-Taj before Doctor Strange
The Reality Stone, infused in Mjolnir's hilt
context: The Tesseract is the Space Stone in disguise (revealed in later films). Loki's scepter contains the Mind Stone, which is later extracted to power Vision. Tony Stark's iconic 'I have a nuclear missile' redirect at the end — flying it through the closing portal — establishes his arc toward sacrifice.

question: The 2014 Marvel movie Guardians of the Galaxy stars a ragtag team of space heroes led by Star-Lord. One of them is a giant walking, talking tree-alien, voiced by actor Vin Diesel, who can speak only the same three words over and over. At the movie's climax he sacrifices himself to save his friends, and is later regrown from a cutting into a tiny dancing sapling in a flower pot. What is the tree-alien's name?
context: Groot first appeared in Marvel Tales #13 (November 1960) as a one-off alien menace. Diesel records 'I am Groot' in dozens of languages. The character's sacrifice at the end of GotG — 'We are Groot' — was scripted by James Gunn specifically to subvert expectations of disposable comic-relief sidekicks.

question: Age of Ultron introduced two new heroes from Sokovia, twins who were experimented on with the Mind Stone by Baron Strucker. Because Fox held the X-Men rights, the film couldn't call the twins mutants, but their comic-book codenames were used. What codenames were used for Wanda and Pietro Maximoff?
context: Marvel had a complicated rights situation with Fox's X-Men franchise. Fox could call them 'mutants'; Marvel could not. Fox's X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014) also featured Quicksilver, played by Evan Peters. Aaron Taylor-Johnson played Quicksilver in Age of Ultron; the character dies saving Hawkeye and a Sokovian child.

question: Captain America: Civil War (2016) features the first MCU appearance of Black Panther and Spider-Man (Tom Holland). The Russos' film climaxes at Berlin Airport with a massive 'team Cap vs team Iron Man' battle and then a private fight in Siberia. What does Tony learn there that destroys his alliance with Cap?
answer: Bucky (the Winter Soldier) murdered Tony's parents on Hydra's orders in 1991
choices: Bucky (the Winter Soldier) murdered Tony's parents on Hydra's orders in 1991
Cap knew about Bucky's brainwashing from 1948 and never told Tony
Zemo was actually Loki's variant and brokered the entire Sokovia Accords
S.H.I.E.L.D. had killed Tony's father to seize the Howling Commandos' files
context: Helmut Zemo (Daniel Brühl) engineers the entire Civil War from grief over his Sokovian family's death in Age of Ultron. The 1991 footage of Bucky killing Howard and Maria Stark is from Hydra's archives; Zemo's whole plan is to make Tony see it in Cap's presence. Civil War's last shot — Cap dropping his shield — frames Endgame's final reconciliation.

question: Doctor Strange was released by Marvel Studios in 2016. Stephen Strange is a world-famous neurosurgeon — brilliant, wealthy, and unbearably arrogant. A car crash smashes his hands and ends his career. Desperate, he travels to Kamar-Taj in Nepal to study sorcery under a master called the Ancient One. In the film's climax, one enchanted magical item in the Sanctum Sanctorum actually chooses him — flying to his shoulders and helping him fight when he cannot. What is this relic?
context: Cumberbatch broke his vocal cords during training. The Cloak of Levitation is sentient and chooses Strange in the climactic Kamar-Taj fight. Strange's signature relic the Eye of Agamotto contains the Time Stone — used to trap Dormammu in a bargaining loop in the film's climax: 'Dormammu, I've come to bargain.'

question: The 2018 Marvel film Black Panther is set mostly in Wakanda, a hidden high-tech African kingdom protected by a costumed superhero called the Black Panther. When the old king dies, his son T'Challa takes the throne. Then a fierce American challenger appears — Erik Killmonger, a former U.S. special-forces soldier — who reveals he is actually T'Challa's cousin, born abroad and long exiled from Wakanda. He fights T'Challa for the crown. Which actor played Killmonger?
context: Coogler had previously directed Jordan in Fruitvale Station (2013) and Creed (2015). Killmonger's name Erik 'Killmonger' Stevens grew up in Oakland, the same city where Coogler grew up and where the Black Panther Party was founded in 1966. Killmonger's death line — 'Bury me in the ocean with my ancestors that jumped from ships' — is one of the most-quoted MCU lines.

question: Avengers: Endgame (2019) features the Avengers staging a 'time heist' to retrieve the six Infinity Stones from various points in their MCU history. In the heist, two of the Avengers — a Russian-trained super-spy and a bow-wielding S.H.I.E.L.D. archer, longtime partners — both volunteer to die on Vormir for the Soul Stone. Who actually makes the sacrifice?
choices: Both at once (the Red Skull permitting two souls)
Neither (they trick the Stone into accepting Loki's earlier death)
context: Natasha and Clint struggle for who gets to make the sacrifice — both believing themselves more expendable. Natasha wins the fight and falls. Scarlett Johansson had filmed her own death scene; the character was given a posthumous Black Widow film (2021). Endgame doesn't include a funeral for her, though Hawkeye laments her loss throughout the post-snap scenes.

question: Bob Kane took full credit for Batman from 1939 until his death in 1998, signing every cover and deal. His overlooked co-creator actually wrote the first Batman story, drew the cape-and-cowl look that replaced Kane's ski-mask sketches, named Bruce Wayne, made up Commissioner Gordon, and gave Bruce the orphan backstory. The publisher finally added his credit in 2015. Who was this co-creator?
context: Finger died penniless in his Manhattan apartment in January 1974. Jerry Robinson, an artist on early Batman, had created the Joker; Robinson spent decades publicly campaigning for Finger's recognition. The 2017 documentary Batman & Bill traces the long fight by Finger's family and Marc Tyler Nobleman to get the credit added.

question: Matt Murdock is Marvel Comics' Daredevil — a blind lawyer from New York's Hell's Kitchen who fights crime as a costumed hero at night. In writer Frank Miller's 1986 story arc 'Born Again,' the crime boss Kingpin learns Matt's secret identity and slowly ruins his life step by step: his money, his home, his law license, everything. Broken and half-dead, Matt is nursed back to health by a kind Catholic nun who turns out to be his own mother, long thought dead. What is her name?
context: Born Again ran in Daredevil #227–233 with David Mazzucchelli on art. The story is widely considered one of the greatest superhero narratives ever published. The Netflix Daredevil show (2015–18) drew heavily from this run; Joanne Whalley played Sister Maggie in season three. Miller and Mazzucchelli followed Born Again with Batman: Year One in 1987.

question: Alan Moore first pitched Watchmen using heroes his publisher had just bought from a folded rival called Charlton, including The Question, Captain Atom, Blue Beetle, and Nightshade. The publisher blocked Moore from using them because it still wanted those heroes in its own books. So Moore made stand-in characters instead. Which Charlton hero inspired Rorschach?
context: Rorschach is Moore's deconstruction of The Question, a Steve Ditko hero who shared Ditko's Randian objectivist outlook. Dr. Manhattan is Captain Atom; Nite Owl is Blue Beetle; The Comedian is Peacemaker; Silk Spectre is Nightshade; Ozymandias is Thunderbolt. DC's Charlton heroes were rolled into the post-Crisis DC universe in 1986. Watchmen ran for 12 issues, September 1986 to October 1987.

question: British writer Neil Gaiman wrote the acclaimed comic book The Sandman for DC Comics from 1989 to 1996. It followed Dream, the immortal lord of stories. Issue #19, called 'A Midsummer Night's Dream,' showed William Shakespeare and his acting troupe performing that very play on a hillside for a real audience of fairy folk led by Titania and Oberon. That single issue made Gaiman the first comics writer ever to win a major literary prize. Which award did it take home in 1991?
answer: The World Fantasy Award for Short Fiction (1991)
choices: The World Fantasy Award for Short Fiction (1991)
The Hugo Award for Best Short Story (1991)
The Nebula Award for Best Novelette (1991)
context: The World Fantasy Convention amended its rules after the win, banning comic-book stories from future consideration. Gaiman was 30 at the time. Charles Vess illustrated the issue, drawing on classical fairy iconography for Titania and Oberon. The issue's premise — that Dream commissioned Shakespeare to write multiple plays in exchange for talent — remains one of the most-cited single comics ever produced.

question: Mark Millar wrote Kick-Ass in 2008, drawn by John Romita Jr., about a Brooklyn teenager who becomes a real-life costumed vigilante despite having no powers. The 2010 Matthew Vaughn film adaptation made an 11-year-old actress a star for playing a small foul-mouthed knife-wielding murder-vigilante in a purple wig. What was the character's name?
context: Chloë Grace Moretz played Hit-Girl at age 11. Her father Big Daddy was played by Nicolas Cage in full Adam West Batman voice. The 'C-word' scene caused a media firestorm; Roger Ebert wrote that he was 'morally outraged' by the film. Mark Millar's original comic ran for eight issues in 2008–09 from Marvel's Icon imprint.

question: The 1993 Batman: Knightfall storyline ran across 19 issues over six months and famously broke Batman's back. The breaking takes place in Batman #497 (July 1993) at the hands of a hulking villain genetically enhanced by a steroid called Venom. The villain was created by Doug Moench and Chuck Dixon expressly to defeat Batman. What's his name?
context: Bane is born in the fictional Caribbean prison of Peña Duro. He's intelligent — speaks multiple languages, a chess master — as well as physically overwhelming. Tom Hardy played him in The Dark Knight Rises (2012); Robert Swenson played him in Batman & Robin (1997). After breaking Batman, Jean-Paul Valley takes over the cowl as Azrael-Batman in a brutal, gun-using mode for over a year.

question: Garth Ennis and John McCrea's 1990s DC/Vertigo comic Hitman ran for 60 issues (1996–2001) starring a gun-for-hire who could read minds and see through walls because of an alien parasite incident. The character was named after a famous American film starring Sylvester Stallone. What's the character's name?
context: Tommy was a Gotham-set hitman, originally introduced in a Bloodlines crossover annual in 1993. The series is famous for issue #34, 'Of Thee I Sing,' a heartfelt Superman story where Tommy meets Supes on a rooftop. Ennis cited the issue as one of his proudest moments. Tommy dies in the final issue (#60) in a deliberately downbeat ending.

question: Brian Michael Bendis's Ultimate Spider-Man, launched in 2000, rebooted Spider-Man for a new audience with Mark Bagley on art. The series ran for 200+ issues with Bendis as sole writer. In 2011's Ultimate Comics: Spider-Man, Bendis introduced a Black Latino teenager who takes over the Spider-Man mantle after Peter Parker's Ultimate-universe death. What's the new Spider-Man's name?
context: Miles debuted in Ultimate Fallout #4 (August 2011). Sara Pichelli co-created him with Bendis. He became the lead character of the 2018 animated film Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, voiced by Shameik Moore. Miles's signature ability is a 'venom blast' bio-electric shock, which Peter Parker's Spider-Man can't do. His uncle Aaron Davis is also the Prowler.

question: In the comic 100 Bullets, Agent Graves finds people who have been wronged. He hands them a case with a gun, 100 bullets that can't be traced, and a folder naming the person who wronged them. Graves works for a secret group that has run American crime through 13 families. What is the group called?
context: The Trust is presented as the founding investors of America — 13 European families that funded the colonial expansion in exchange for ongoing dominance of American organized crime. The Minutemen are their enforcement arm; Graves is their former leader. The series won an Eisner for Best Continuing Series. Eduardo Risso's noir-influenced shadow-heavy artwork is considered some of the best in the medium.

question: Bill Watterson drew the American newspaper comic strip Calvin and Hobbes, about a wild six-year-old boy named Calvin and his stuffed tiger Hobbes, who came to life whenever the two of them were alone. The strip ran in papers for ten years, from 1985 to 1995. Watterson turned down a licensing deal that would have earned him hundreds of millions of dollars, and every other cartoonist was baffled. What did he refuse to do?
answer: License the characters for merchandise (no plush Hobbes, no shirts, no commercials)
choices: License the characters for merchandise (no plush Hobbes, no shirts, no commercials)
Allow Sunday strips to expand beyond the standard four-panel grid
Permit foreign-language translations after the 1991 Italian incident
Hand off the strip to a successor cartoonist after his 1989 sabbatical
context: Watterson believed licensing would cheapen the strip — Hobbes had to remain ambiguous (real tiger? stuffed toy?), which was impossible if you could buy a plush. Charles Schulz had given different advice (Peanuts merchandising made Schulz hundreds of millions). The ubiquitous Calvin-peeing decals on pickup trucks are all unlicensed, illegal bootlegs.

question: Hergé's Tintin comics ran from 1929 to 1976 (with the unfinished Tintin and Alph-Art posthumous in 1986). The Belgian cartoonist's real name was Georges Remi; 'Hergé' comes from reading his initials R.G. in French. The series features Tintin's white fox terrier whose name in the original French is 'Milou.' What was the dog's name in English translations?
context: Hergé's Tintin has been translated into 70+ languages and sold over 200 million copies worldwide. The character's iconic cowlick, red plus-fours, and blue sweater were finalized by 1934. Steven Spielberg directed the 2011 motion-capture film The Adventures of Tintin starring Jamie Bell. Hergé took some hits postwar for collaborationist Belgian newspaper Le Soir publication under Nazi occupation.

question: Cartoonist Berkeley Breathed drew the newspaper comic strip Bloom County from 1980 to 1989, and won the Pulitzer Prize for editorial cartooning in 1987. Two of its characters became giant merchandise hits — Opus, a gentle wide-eyed penguin with a big beak, and a scruffy, cigar-chomping, tongue-hanging-out cat whose face ended up on so many T-shirts, lunch boxes, and plush toys that Breathed grew to resent the little monster. What was the cat's name?
context: Breathed designed Bill specifically to mock Garfield's commercialization. The 'Ack! Thbbft!' catchphrase appeared on millions of T-shirts and mugs. Bill once ran for president in 1984 and 1988 on the Meadow Party ticket. Breathed walked away from Bloom County in 1989, did Outland (1989–1995) and Opus (2003–2008), then revived Bloom County on Facebook in 2015.

question: J.K. Rowling famously sketched out the seven-book Harry Potter plan on a napkin in 1990 during a delayed Manchester-to-London train ride. She spent five years developing it before writing began. The first publisher to accept Philosopher's Stone after rejection from twelve houses was a small London independent. Their initial print run was just 500 hardcover copies. Which publisher took the gamble?
context: Nigel Newton, Bloomsbury's chair, had his eight-year-old daughter Alice Newton read the opening chapter — she demanded the rest of the manuscript and refused to be put off. Bloomsbury offered Rowling £2,500 advance. Scholastic later acquired US rights for $105,000 — a then-record for a children's book. Today, surviving first-edition Bloomsbury hardcovers sell for $20,000–$50,000.

question: The Mirror of Erised, first encountered by Harry in Philosopher's Stone (book 1, 1997), shows the viewer their deepest, most desperate desire. The inscription on its frame reads 'Erised stra ehru oyt ube cafru oyt on wohsi' — a mirror-reversed sentence. What does the English original say?
answer: I show not your face but your heart's desire
choices: I show not your face but your heart's desire
Mirror of dreams, show me my heart's hidden joy
Within these depths a wish is granted unseen
What you seek the most you shall not find unspoken
context: 'Erised' is 'Desire' reversed. Dumbledore tells Harry: 'It does not do to dwell on dreams and forget to live.' The Philosopher's Stone is hidden inside the Mirror at the climax — only someone who wants to find the Stone but not use it can retrieve it. This is the test Harry passes and Quirrell/Voldemort fails.

question: J.K. Rowling built the four houses of Hogwarts School around the four classical elements of ancient thought — fire, water, air, and earth. Gryffindor is fire, and prizes courage. Slytherin is water, and prizes ambition. Ravenclaw is air, and prizes wit. Each of the four houses was founded a thousand years ago by one witch or wizard, who left behind a personal relic that later became a treasured heirloom. What element and virtue does Hufflepuff represent, and what heirloom did its founder leave behind?
answer: Earth, loyalty, and Helga Hufflepuff's gold-and-badger-engraved cup
choices: Earth, loyalty, and Helga Hufflepuff's gold-and-badger-engraved cup
Wood, patience, and Helga Hufflepuff's oak-and-honey-bee-engraved horn
Stone, kindness, and Helga Hufflepuff's silver-and-mole-engraved chalice
Mist, humility, and Helga Hufflepuff's pewter-and-fox-engraved goblet
context: The Cup is one of Voldemort's seven Horcruxes — stolen from Hepzibah Smith, an elderly heiress murdered by young Tom Riddle in the 1950s. Bellatrix Lestrange hides it in her vault at Gringotts; Harry, Ron, and Hermione break in during Deathly Hallows. Hufflepuff's badger symbol is a 'sett' (badger family group) — JK Rowling chose badgers in part because the Old English 'huff' means 'pant.'

question: Cedric Diggory's death in Goblet of Fire (2000) was a turning point — the first major character death in the series. The killing curse is delivered by Peter Pettigrew on Voldemort's command in a graveyard in Little Hangleton. Voldemort's revival in the same scene requires three ritual ingredients. The first is bone of the father, unknowingly taken. The second is flesh of the servant, willingly given (Wormtail's hand). What's the third?
answer: Blood of the enemy, forcibly taken (from Harry, with a silver dagger)
choices: Blood of the enemy, forcibly taken (from Harry, with a silver dagger)
Tear of the betrayer, freely shed (from Bellatrix, atop the cauldron)
Hair of the rival, secretly clipped (from Snape, during the gathering)
Tongue of the prophet, unwilling spoken (from Trelawney's grand-niece)
context: Voldemort uses Harry's blood because it carries Lily's protective magic. The act binds Harry and Voldemort more deeply — Harry survives Voldemort's killing curse in the Forest in Book 7 partly because Voldemort's body contains Harry's blood, anchoring Harry to life. Pettigrew sacrifices his own hand and Voldemort restores it as a silver hand of immense strength.

question: In J.K. Rowling's fourth Harry Potter book, Goblet of Fire, Hogwarts hires a scarred old ex-Auror called Mad-Eye Moody to teach Defense Against the Dark Arts. He acts strange and paranoid all year, but he quietly steers Harry toward victory in the Triwizard Tournament. At the very end of the book it is revealed that this 'Moody' is actually a hidden Death Eater who kidnapped the real Moody, stuffed him inside a magical trunk, and drank Polyjuice Potion every hour all year to look like him. Who was the imposter?
context: Barty Crouch Jr. is a Death Eater whose Ministry-official father (Barty Crouch Sr.) had imprisoned him in the family home under the Imperius Curse after Azkaban. Voldemort frees him to engineer Harry's delivery to the graveyard. Brendan Gleeson played Moody; David Tennant played Crouch Jr. in the 2005 film. Crouch Jr. is later given the Dementor's Kiss by Cornelius Fudge, who refuses to believe Voldemort has returned.

question: In Order of the Phoenix (book 5), Dolores Umbridge takes over Hogwarts as 'High Inquisitor' on Cornelius Fudge's orders. Her cruel disciplinary methods include a magical detention quill that uses the writer's blood as ink, carving the words 'I must not tell lies' into the back of Harry's hand. The scar remains permanent on Harry's hand for the rest of the series. What has Rowling said Umbridge is modelled on?
answer: A composite of authoritarian schoolteachers and middle-management bureaucrats Rowling had encountered
choices: A composite of authoritarian schoolteachers and middle-management bureaucrats Rowling had encountered
Margaret Thatcher's later-cabinet posture in the 1980s Education Ministry
Mary Whitehouse, the British media-decency campaigner of the 1970s and 80s
Enid Blyton's headmistress Miss Grayling from the Malory Towers series
context: Imelda Staunton played Umbridge in the 2007 film. Rowling has said Umbridge is her most-hated character in the series; she modeled her on a real-life teacher who 'bullied' Rowling's friend. The pink cardigan, the kitten plates, the saccharine voice — every detail is calibrated for maximum domestic-tyrant menace. Umbridge appears again in Deathly Hallows as a Ministry official under the Voldemort puppet regime.

question: Hogwarts has a poltergeist named Peeves who plagues students and even staff. Peeves answers to one authority at the school besides Dumbledore. Filch hates Peeves. But the only one who can actually keep Peeves in line short of Dumbledore is who?
answer: The Bloody Baron (the Slytherin House ghost)
choices: The Bloody Baron (the Slytherin House ghost)
Nearly Headless Nick (the Gryffindor House ghost)
The Grey Lady (the Ravenclaw House ghost)
The Fat Friar (the Hufflepuff House ghost)
context: The Bloody Baron's bloodstains came from killing the Grey Lady (Helena Ravenclaw) in life — a backstory revealed in Deathly Hallows. Peeves was cut from all eight films. Rik Mayall (of The Young Ones) filmed scenes as Peeves for the first film, but all were ultimately cut by Chris Columbus. Mayall publicly groused about it for years.

question: In Deathly Hallows, Harry, Ron, and Hermione spend much of the book on the run, hunting Horcruxes while wearing Slytherin's locket Horcrux in turns. The locket exerts a corrupting psychological influence on its wearer. Harry, Ron, and Hermione each have different reactions. Ron's reaction in particular causes him to abandon Harry and Hermione for weeks before returning. What artifact does Ron use to find his way back to them?
answer: The Deluminator left to him by Dumbledore in his will
choices: The Deluminator left to him by Dumbledore in his will
A Howler from his mother delivered through Apparition
Hermione's enchanted DA Galleon she kept on her wrist
The Marauder's Map redirected through the Floo Network
context: The Deluminator (Dumbledore's silver cigarette-lighter device that absorbs light from a room) gains a special enchantment that lets Ron hear Hermione's voice and Apparate to her location when he speaks her name. Dumbledore had foreseen Ron's defection — Ron's three bequests in Dumbledore's will are the Deluminator (a tool to come back), the Sword of Gryffindor (for destroying Horcruxes), and the children's book The Tales of Beedle the Bard.

question: The Battle of Hogwarts in Deathly Hallows takes place on May 2, 1998 (a date Rowling has confirmed). Voldemort kills Snape in the Shrieking Shack to claim mastery of the Elder Wand. Voldemort believes Snape is the Wand's master because Snape killed Dumbledore. Why is Voldemort wrong about who really mastered the Elder Wand?
answer: Draco disarmed Dumbledore atop the Tower before Snape's curse, then Harry later disarmed Draco at Malfoy Manor
choices: Draco disarmed Dumbledore atop the Tower before Snape's curse, then Harry later disarmed Draco at Malfoy Manor
Dumbledore had quietly passed mastery to Aberforth in a sealed will days before the Tower confrontation
Snape's killing curse was a mercy killing that Dumbledore requested, which voids any wand-mastery transfer
Gellert Grindelwald never actually lost mastery of the Wand to Dumbledore back in their 1945 confrontation
context: The Elder Wand's mastery passes when its current owner is disarmed, not when killed. Draco's disarming of Dumbledore on the Astronomy Tower in Half-Blood Prince — moments before Snape's killing curse — quietly transferred mastery to Draco. Harry's later disarming of Draco at Malfoy Manor (Deathly Hallows) transferred it to Harry. When Voldemort fires the killing curse in the climactic duel, his own spell rebounds off the Wand and kills him.

question: J.K. Rowling has confirmed multiple deliberate dates throughout the series. Harry was born on July 31, 1980 (matching Rowling's own birthday). Voldemort attacked the Potters on Halloween — October 31, 1981 — killing James and Lily and giving Harry his lightning scar. The Potters were betrayed by their Secret-Keeper, switched at the last minute from Sirius to whom?
choices: Caradoc Dearborn (an early Order of the Phoenix member)
context: The Fidelius Charm hides a location/secret in a single chosen person; even those who already knew can no longer find it. Sirius convinced James and Lily that swapping him for the seemingly weak Peter would fool Voldemort. Peter immediately betrayed them. Sirius then went after Peter; Peter cut off his own finger, blew up a street, killed 12 Muggles, and transformed into Scabbers — leaving Sirius framed for the murders.

question: The 2008 movie Iron Man kicked off the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Tony Stark, a billionaire weapons maker, secretly builds a red-and-gold flying suit of armor and becomes a hero. The villain is Obadiah Stane, played by bald and bearded actor Jeff Bridges — Stark's father-figure business partner who has been quietly selling Stark weapons to terrorists behind Tony's back. At the film's climax, Stane builds his own giant, hulking, gray version of the Iron Man armor and attacks Tony in the Stark Industries parking lot. What was Stane's oversized suit called?
context: Stane reverse-engineers the original Mark I suit Tony built in the cave. The Iron Monger is roughly twice Iron Man's size. Bridges shaved his head for the role; the bald look surprised audiences expecting his Big Lebowski-era hair. The film was 2008's third-highest-grossing US release behind The Dark Knight and Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull.

question: Joss Whedon's The Avengers (2012) opened to $207.4 million in its US opening weekend — at the time the biggest opening in cinema history. The film established Marvel's three-act team-up template. A famous one-shot circling tracking-shot during the Battle of New York shows each Avenger fighting Chitauri in sequence. Who closes the shot, leaping off a ruined taxi to fire a single arrow that destroys an oncoming Leviathan beast?
context: The tracking shot was extensively reshot in post-production to add the camera weave-and-pan, then finished in CGI. Jeremy Renner had been in the MCU since a Thor (2011) cameo but Avengers gave him his first major screen time. The cinematic 'one-shot Avengers showcase' became a recurring Marvel device repeated in Age of Ultron's opening and Endgame's portal sequence.

question: Iron Man 3 (2013) features the apparent return of Iron Man's long-foreshadowed comics archnemesis the Mandarin. The character was teased throughout the first two films via the Ten Rings terrorist group. In Iron Man 3, Ben Kingsley plays the Mandarin as a terrifying bin-Laden-styled mastermind. The mid-film twist is that Kingsley's Mandarin is actually what?
answer: A drug-addled British actor named Trevor Slattery, hired by the real villain to be a public face
choices: A drug-addled British actor named Trevor Slattery, hired by the real villain to be a public face
An AIM holographic projection driven from a hidden submarine docked off the Miami coastline
Aldrich Killian's hallucination created by the Extremis virus injected into Tony Stark's bloodstream
A shapeshifting Skrull infiltrator using a technology that would later be revealed in Captain Marvel
context: The real villain is Aldrich Killian (Guy Pearce), CEO of Advanced Idea Mechanics (AIM), who hired Slattery as the public face of the Mandarin while he experimented with the Extremis virus. Iron Man 3 was Shane Black's directorial entry into the MCU, his first feature since Kiss Kiss Bang Bang (2005). The film angered some comics fans furious about the Mandarin twist; a 2014 Marvel One-Shot (All Hail the King) walked back the implication that the 'real' Mandarin doesn't exist.

question: In Marvel's Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015), the Avengers accidentally give birth to a synthetic android whose forehead holds the yellow Mind Stone. The being calls himself Vision. At a Stark Tower party he casually reaches out and lifts Thor's enchanted hammer Mjolnir, a feat only someone deemed worthy can perform — no one else in the room except Thor himself can even budge it. Which British actor plays Vision?
context: Bettany had voiced JARVIS (Tony's AI butler — 'Just A Rather Very Intelligent System') since 2008's Iron Man. The actor wore prosthetic-and-face-paint pink-and-green Vision makeup that took hours each day. Paul Bettany is married to actress Jennifer Connelly. The hammer-lifting scene was filmed but kept under wraps from the cast until released.

question: Avengers: Infinity War (2018) marked the end-act of Phase 3 with the Russos' first Avengers film. The film opens with Thanos killing Loki and Heimdall aboard the Asgardian refugee ship, then progressively collecting six Infinity Stones. The Soul Stone requires a soul-for-soul sacrifice on a remote planet called Vormir. Who does Thanos sacrifice?
answer: Gamora, his adopted daughter, by throwing her off a cliff
choices: Gamora, his adopted daughter, by throwing her off a cliff
Nebula, his adopted daughter, in a duel-to-the-death ritual
Ebony Maw, his most loyal Black Order servant, with a spell
Drax's daughter, returned to him through Ravager negotiations
context: Zoe Saldana played Gamora. Endgame later resurrects a 2014-era Gamora through the time heist. The Red Skull, banished from Earth by the Tesseract's Space Stone in Captain America: The First Avenger (1945), guards the Soul Stone on Vormir. Ross Marquand voices Red Skull (Hugo Weaving, who played him in 2011, declined). The 'soul for a soul' rule pays off again with Black Widow's Endgame sacrifice.

question: Captain Marvel (2019) is set primarily in 1995, before any of the other MCU films chronologically except parts of Captain America: The First Avenger. Brie Larson stars as Carol Danvers, a US Air Force pilot who gains photon-blast powers from the Tesseract's Space Stone. The film's chief twist concerns the Skrulls — the green shapeshifting aliens. What turns out to be true about them, contradicting comics canon?
answer: They are sympathetic refugees fleeing genocide, not the evil empire they appear to be, and the Kree are the true villains
choices: They are sympathetic refugees fleeing genocide, not the evil empire they appear to be, and the Kree are the true villains
They are revealed to be the source of all human mutation genes throughout history, retconning the X-Men's mutants
They are revealed to have created the Asgardians using genetic engineering, retconning the entire Bifrost system
They are revealed to be Phyla-Vell variants from another dimension entirely, brought through by Captain Mar-Vell
context: Ben Mendelsohn plays Talos, a Skrull refugee leader, with cheek-pouch prosthetics. The Kree — purple/blue antagonists in Guardians of the Galaxy and elsewhere — are framed as the genocidal imperialists. Jude Law plays Yon-Rogg, Carol's mentor-turned-traitor in the Kree Starforce. The de-aging tech used on Samuel L. Jackson for the 1995 Fury sequences was a milestone in MCU VFX.

question: Avengers: Endgame (2019)'s 'time heist' splits the surviving Avengers into teams traveling to specific points in the MCU's past. Captain America, Iron Man, Hulk, and Ant-Man travel to 2012 New York during the Battle for the Tesseract. Cap fights an alternate-timeline version of himself. The fight ends with the present-day Cap whispering two words that throw the past Cap off-guard. What does he say?
context: The 'Hail Hydra' line plays off a then-recent comics storyline (Secret Empire, 2017) where Captain America was retconned into a lifelong Hydra agent — a much-controversial Nick Spencer storyline. The Russos winked at the controversy. The line briefly stuns 2012 Cap (who at that point believed Bucky dead since 1945) long enough for present-Cap to win the elevator fight.

question: Tom Holland's Spider-Man debuted in Captain America: Civil War (2016) but got his first solo MCU film with Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017), directed by Jon Watts. The film's villain is a Brooklyn-based salvager who has been illicitly building tech from Battle of New York debris into a winged armored suit. Michael Keaton plays him. What's the character's comics name?
context: Keaton's casting was a meta-joke — he'd played Batman (1989, 1992) and the actor Birdman in the 2014 Best Picture winner Birdman, both winged characters. Adrian Toomes first appeared in Amazing Spider-Man #2 in 1963. Homecoming was a Sony-Marvel co-production made possible by the 2015 deal that put Spider-Man in the MCU after years of Sony's solo Andrew Garfield films flopping.

question: Action Comics #1 (April 1938) introduced Superman with a cover by Joe Shuster showing the Man of Steel lifting a green car over his head while terrified onlookers flee. The cover became one of the most-imitated images in comics history. The original cover painting was reportedly lost by DC's offices for decades, but Joe Shuster's original interior pencils for the issue did survive. A pristine Certified Guaranty Company (CGC)-graded 9.0 copy of Action Comics #1 sold at Heritage Auctions on April 4, 2024 for a record-shattering amount. What was the final price?
context: The previous record was $3.2 million for a 9.0 in 2021. Action Comics #1 had a print run of about 200,000; experts estimate fewer than 100 copies survive today in any condition. The cover price was 10 cents. Heritage Auctions's $6M was the highest-ever paid for a single comic book. The Vincent Zurzolo / Stephen Fishler company ComicConnect tracks pricing in detail.

question: In 1970, Jack Kirby left Marvel for DC after a fight over credit and ownership. At DC he built a huge cosmic saga across four titles known as the Fourth World. Two warring planets sit at its heart: Apokolips, ruled by Darkseid, and what paradise world?
choices: Themyscira (ruled by Queen Hippolyta of the Amazons)
Olympus Major (ruled by Zeus of the New Olympians)
Krypton II (ruled by the survivors of the original Krypton)
context: Kirby's Fourth World saga ran 1970–73 at DC before all four titles were cancelled. Darkseid is the most enduring creation — a New York-accent space tyrant whose face is carved from blackened stone. He has been used as the primary cosmic villain in Crisis on Infinite Earths, Final Crisis (2008), and the Zack Snyder Justice League cut. Steppenwolf and the Parademons are also from this saga. Kirby returned to Marvel in 1976.

question: In 1984, Marvel Comics ran a huge twelve-issue crossover story that pulled almost every one of its heroes and villains — the Avengers, X-Men, Spider-Man, the Fantastic Four, Doctor Doom, Magneto and more — off Earth and dumped them all onto a stitched-together patchwork planet called Battleworld. There they were forced to fight each other for the amusement of a godlike, near-omnipotent alien known as the Beyonder. It was the first modern comics 'event' and became the template every big publisher would copy for decades. What was it called?
context: Mike Zeck and John Beatty drew the bulk of Secret Wars. The 12-issue series was tied directly to a Mattel toy line; Mattel had wanted a Marvel branded event to push action figures, the same toy-driven approach DC's Super Powers line was using. The Beyonder's appearance, a glowing white humanoid, wouldn't be revealed until issue 11. Spider-Man also got his black costume in Secret Wars, which later became Venom.

question: Artist Steve Ditko worked with Marvel writer Stan Lee in the early 1960s and, alongside Lee, co-created and drew The Amazing Spider-Man before quietly walking away from the book in 1966. Beyond Spider-Man, Ditko and Lee together also created another iconic Marvel hero — a former surgeon turned mystical Sorcerer Supreme who protects Earth from magical threats, wears a red Cloak of Levitation, and carries the all-seeing Eye of Agamotto around his neck. Which hero?
context: Ditko was 90 years old when he died on June 29, 2018. He was found two days later. He had lived a famously private life — refusing interviews, publishing essays only through small press. His objectivism led him to create Mr. A (1967), a black-and-white-morality character published outside Marvel. John Romita Sr. took over Spider-Man and softened the visual style. Ditko also co-created Doctor Strange (Strange Tales #110, 1963).

question: Alan Moore's Watchmen ran 12 issues from September 1986 to October 1987. Issue #5, 'Fearful Symmetry,' is famous for being structured as a literal mirror — the panels in the first half of the issue are reflected by the second half, with the centerfold (pages 14–15) being the visual fulcrum. Each page mirrors its opposite. The chapter title comes from a William Blake poem. What's the poem called?
context: The opening lines: 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night; / What immortal hand or eye, / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?' Each Watchmen issue closes with a literary epigraph from sources including Nietzsche, Genesis, Einstein, Carl Jung, and Bob Dylan. Moore is famously meticulous about issue construction; he wrote full prose-style scripts running 40+ pages per issue for Dave Gibbons.

question: Neil Gaiman's Sandman issue #50 (June 1993), titled 'Ramadan,' is a self-contained story about Haroun al-Rashid, the 8th-century Abbasid caliph of Baghdad. Al-Rashid summons Dream to make a bargain: in exchange for Dream's protection, he will preserve the golden age of Baghdad forever in a sealed bottle. The story addresses real grief over the modern destruction of the city. P. Craig Russell drew the issue in a deliberately illuminated-manuscript style. The story made its print debut at what is widely seen to be a politically tragic moment. What was happening at the time?
answer: The first months after the 1991 Gulf War and the 1990s Iraq sanctions regime were intensifying
choices: The first months after the 1991 Gulf War and the 1990s Iraq sanctions regime were intensifying
The 1979 Iranian Revolution had toppled the Shah and stranded American hostages in Tehran
The 1982 Israeli action in Lebanon was destroying Beirut's reputation as Paris of the East
The 1986 Chernobyl disaster had displaced Eastern European writers across multiple cultures
context: Sandman #50 sold significantly above its usual run — many comics shops cited it as a 'lifetime favorite' single issue. Gaiman has spoken about the personal grief he had over reports of Baghdad's modern destruction; the issue's ending, where Dream tells the story to a small boy crouching against a wall in modern Baghdad, has become a much-shared image among Iraqi diaspora writers. P. Craig Russell would later adapt The Sandman into multiple opera librettos.

question: Mike Mignola's Hellboy #1 (March 1994) was published by Dark Horse Comics after Mignola left Marvel and DC, where he had been a high-profile interior artist for over a decade. Hellboy was conceived as a 1994 Comic-Con sketch Mignola did during downtime. The character's full name — given by Trevor Bruttenholm — is a riff on a Bavarian demon-name. What is Hellboy's actual birth-name in the comics' mythos?
context: Anung Un Rama means 'and upon his brow is set a crown of flame.' Hellboy's destiny in the comics is to bring about the end of days — the Right Hand of Doom (his oversized stone right hand) is the literal key to releasing the seven Dragon-gods of the Ogdru Hem. Mignola revealed Hellboy's true heritage gradually over decades. Ron Perlman played him in the 2004 and 2008 del Toro films; David Harbour did the 2019 reboot. Mignola's spare brushwork was directly influenced by Mike Kaluta and Bernie Wrightson.

question: From 2004 to 2008 the Irish comics writer Garth Ennis wrote a long, brutal series called The Punisher MAX (Marvel's mature-readers imprint) for Marvel Comics. The Punisher is Frank Castle, a Vietnam veteran turned vigilante whose wife and children were gunned down in New York's Central Park in 1976 after they stumbled onto a mob hit. The first six-issue arc, called In the Beginning, sends an older Castle back to hunt the men responsible. Whom is he tracking?
answer: The Gnucci family, then back to Bruno Costa and ultimately the original Costa hit team
choices: The Gnucci family, then back to Bruno Costa and ultimately the original Costa hit team
Jigsaw (Billy Russo) operating out of the Hudson Hospital ICU ward
The Kingpin in his Hell's Kitchen real-estate office on the 25th floor
Barracuda's old crew including the original Microchip from Cape May
context: Ennis's Punisher MAX is widely considered the definitive take on the character — Frank as a hollowed-out Vietnam vet, the mob as petty cruel men, no redemption. The Frank Castle Sr. flashbacks were drawn with deliberate visual flatness compared to the gritty present-day scenes. Tim Bradstreet did most of the painted MAX covers. Ennis followed up with The Punisher: Born (2003, with Darick Robertson) about Frank in Vietnam.

question: Bucky Barnes was Captain America's teenage sidekick in Marvel Comics of the 1940s, killed off in a plane explosion at the end of World War II. For six decades editors held firm that Bucky must stay dead. Then in 2005, writer Ed Brubaker brought him back as a brainwashed Soviet assassin called the Winter Soldier. Marvel Editor-in-Chief Joe Quesada had famously said only three deaths in comics should stay real forever. Which three?
answer: Uncle Ben, Jason Todd, and Bucky Barnes himself
choices: Uncle Ben, Jason Todd, and Bucky Barnes himself
Uncle Ben, Gwen Stacy, and Tony Stark Sr. (Howard Stark)
Aunt May, Jason Todd, and the original Captain Marvel (Mar-Vell)
Doctor Strange's mentor, Jean Grey, and Bucky Barnes himself
context: Brubaker's pitch focused on Bucky as a tortured agent kept frozen between hits — emphasizing his lost humanity rather than reversing the death cheaply. Quesada approved. Jason Todd would later be brought back in 2005 via Judd Winick's Under the Red Hood arc; Uncle Ben has stayed dead but appeared in Spider-Verse alternate-realities. Brubaker continued his Cap run through 2012 with Marcos Martin, Mike Perkins, and Butch Guice. The Winter Soldier arc was adapted as the 2014 Russo Brothers film.

question: Bone, Jeff Smith's self-published 55-issue series (1991–2004), tells the story of three cousins exiled from the town of Boneville after a Phoney Bone scheme goes wrong. They find themselves in a sword-and-sorcery valley where they encounter a young woman named Thorn. Thorn's grandmother is the elderly Gran'ma Ben, who turns out to be the deposed queen of the valley. What was Gran'ma Ben's real name as queen?
context: Gran'ma Ben's daughter Briar Harvestar is the saga's villain — sister-turned-Lord of the Locusts. Jeff Smith published the entire series himself through Cartoon Books, refusing offers from Marvel and DC. The full series is 1,332 pages. Scholastic released the entire run in 9 color volumes from 2005–2009, exposing a generation of younger readers to the saga. Smith followed up with RASL (2008–12) and the 2018 Tüki: Save the Humans series.

question: Frank Miller was the American comic-book star behind gritty crime and superhero books at Marvel and DC. His then-wife Lynn Varley painted the colors for his most famous late-1980s work. In 1989 the pair released Daredevil: Love and War, a Marvel graphic novel Varley colored in bright, painterly tones. She had also colored two other Miller books in that same decade that would later become cinema legends. Which two?
choices: Sin City: The Hard Goodbye (1991) and Sin City: A Dame to Kill For (1993)
Elektra: Assassin (1986) with Bill Sienkiewicz and Ronin (1983)
Daredevil: Man Without Fear (1993) and Batman: Year One (1987)
context: Lynn Varley was Miller's wife from 1980–2005. Her painted color work was a major departure from comics' usual flat-color print processes; The Dark Knight Returns featured halftone gradients and Sun Yat-Sen yellow flecks that gave Gotham an apocalyptic warmth. Varley also colored Miller's Ronin (1983), Elektra Lives Again (1990), and 300 (1998). Varley and Miller divorced in 2005 after Miller's All-Star Batman & Robin began.

question: DC Comics's Crisis on Infinite Earths (April 1985 to March 1986) ran 12 issues, drawn entirely by George Pérez. The series consolidated DC's tangled parallel-Earth continuity into a single universe and killed dozens of legacy characters. Pérez personally drew over 1,200 pages. The maxi-series's most-iconic single image — used on Crisis #7's cover (October 1985) — depicts Superman cradling a fallen character whose face is in shadow. That cover image has been repeatedly homaged in DC comics for forty years. Who is Superman cradling?
choices: Lois Lane in her Earth-2 incarnation
context: Supergirl dies in Crisis #7 attacking the Anti-Monitor on his throneworld. Pérez's cover composition — Superman in mid-cry, holding the broken body — was inspired by a Pieta motif (the Madonna cradling the dead Christ). Pérez told interviewers he drew the cover at his kitchen table the morning after his mother had passed away. The cover has been parodied in The Simpsons, Family Guy, multiple anniversary covers, and Justice League: Earth 2 (2002). Kara would not return to the main DC continuity until 2004.

question: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone was rejected by twelve publishers before Bloomsbury accepted it in 1996. J.K. Rowling has named several of the rejecting publishers in interviews over the years. The first major US-rights bid came from Arthur A. Levine Books, an imprint of Scholastic, at the 1997 Bologna Children's Book Fair. The advance Scholastic paid Rowling was the highest amount ever paid for a children's book at that point. What was the advance?
context: The Bloomsbury UK advance was £2,500 — about $4,000 USD at the time. The Scholastic deal in spring 1997 was specifically to publish under the new 'Arthur A. Levine Books' imprint. Levine had to convince Scholastic's board on the gamble; he flew to Frankfurt in October 1996 to read the manuscript over a weekend. Levine personally edited the first several books and named the imprint after himself. He retired in 2019; the imprint was folded.

question: In J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter, the dark wizard Lord Voldemort split his soul into seven magical objects called Horcruxes so that he could not truly die. One Horcrux was Helga Hufflepuff's golden cup, hidden in a wizarding bank vault. In Deathly Hallows, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger sneak down into the flooded ancient hall deep beneath Hogwarts — the very place Harry had entered in his second year — to finish the cup off. Hermione does the deed. What weapon does she use?
answer: A basilisk fang from the Chamber of Secrets
choices: A basilisk fang from the Chamber of Secrets
Godric Gryffindor's Sword pulled from the Sorting Hat
Fiendfyre conjured by Vincent Crabbe in the Room of Requirement
Ravenclaw's Diadem-shard fragment of Voldemort's split soul
context: Hermione retrieves the basilisk fangs in Deathly Hallows from the Chamber of Secrets — she'd memorized the way after Ron 'opens' it by mimicking Parseltongue. Each Horcrux requires a specific weapon-or-poison powerful enough to overcome the dark magic. The Sword of Gryffindor (impregnated with basilisk venom from Harry's stabbing it in Chamber of Secrets) destroys the locket. Fiendfyre destroys the Diadem (Crabbe's curse going out of control). Neville destroys Nagini with the Sword.

question: In Half-Blood Prince (book 6, 2005), Harry obtains a used Potions textbook with marginal annotations from a previous owner. The annotations dramatically improve every potion Harry brews. The previous owner had also invented original spells written in the book — including 'Sectumsempra,' a slashing curse Harry uses against Draco Malfoy in a bathroom duel that nearly kills him. The book is signed 'Property of the Half-Blood Prince.' Whose book was it?
answer: Severus Snape (his mother was Eileen Prince)
choices: Severus Snape (his mother was Eileen Prince)
Sirius Black (his mother was a 'prince' in family fiction)
Tom Riddle (a Slytherin Prefect during his Hogwarts years)
Regulus Black (a young man called R.A.B. in Sirius's letters)
context: Snape's father Tobias was a Muggle; his mother Eileen Prince was a pure-blood witch. 'Half-Blood Prince' is Snape's invented self-styled title, combining his mother's surname and his mixed heritage. The book is buried in Snape's adolescent diary-prose handwriting. Harry hides the book in the Room of Requirement at the end of Book 6. Rowling has admitted the book's reveal felt thinner than she wanted — many readers had figured out Snape was the Prince by issue #1's mid-publication speculation.

question: The Order of the Phoenix (book 5, 2003) headquarters is 12 Grimmauld Place, the ancestral London townhouse of the Black family. Sirius's nightmarish childhood home is filled with Black family tapestries, dark-arts artifacts, and the portrait of his portrait-shrieking mother Walburga Black. The house is protected by the Fidelius Charm with Dumbledore as Secret-Keeper. The house elf attached to the property is a disgruntled, generations-old half-mad servant who at first betrays the Order before reconciling with the protagonists. What's the elf's name?
context: Kreacher's loyalty to the Black family — particularly to Sirius's brother Regulus — explains his initial bitterness toward Sirius (who detested the family). Regulus had been a Death Eater before turning on Voldemort and retrieving the locket-Horcrux; Regulus took Kreacher into the cave-trap with Voldemort and ordered Kreacher to retrieve the locket. Kreacher kept Regulus's secret for years until Harry, Ron, and Hermione earn his trust in Deathly Hallows. The earlier book introduced Dobby and Winky.

question: In J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, the Hogwarts groundskeeper Rubeus Hagrid has kept a giant intelligent spider named Aragog as a pet in the Forbidden Forest since he was a boy. Aragog finally dies of old age. In tears, Hagrid begs Harry and Ron to sneak out of the castle at night and help him with the funeral. Aragog is enormous -- much too heavy for Hagrid to manage alone. What help does Hagrid need?
answer: Lifting the body to bury it (Aragog is the size of a small elephant)
choices: Lifting the body to bury it (Aragog is the size of a small elephant)
Brewing a memorial potion using Aragog's venom for the funeral guests
Distracting Mosag and the offspring spiders during the burial ceremony
Translating Latin funerary phrases Hagrid had memorized for the eulogy
context: Slughorn becomes drunk on Hagrid's homemade wine at the funeral, which is when Harry uses Felix Felicis (Liquid Luck) to extract the unaltered Horcrux memory from him. Aragog had been Hagrid's secret 'pet' since his Hogwarts expulsion in 1943 — when Tom Riddle framed Hagrid for Aragog's release. Rubeus Hagrid is half-giant — his mother Fridwulfa was a giantess; his father was a wizard. Robbie Coltrane played Hagrid in all eight films.

question: Harry Potter's wand contains a phoenix tail feather from Dumbledore's bird Fawkes — the same source feather that's in Voldemort's wand. This 'brother wand' connection causes the Priori Incantatem (golden cage of light) effect when Harry and Voldemort directly attack each other in the Goblet of Fire graveyard scene. Both wands were made by Ollivander, the legendary wandmaker. What is his first name?
context: Mr. Ollivander runs Ollivanders, the wand shop at 1 Diagon Alley, founded 382 BC. He's the leading wand expert in wizarding Britain. The phoenix-feather brother wands ('twin cores') are unusually rare; only Fawkes ever donated feathers to wandmakers. Voldemort kidnaps Mr. Ollivander early in Deathly Hallows seeking knowledge of wand mastery, leading Voldemort to track down the Elder Wand. John Hurt played Ollivander in films 1 and 7-8. The shop's signature line: 'The wand chooses the wizard.'

question: Hermione Granger's parents — both dentists in London — appear briefly in Chamber of Secrets and Goblet of Fire. In Deathly Hallows, Hermione casts a memory-charm on them and sends them off so they cannot be tortured for her location. She erases their memory of having a daughter and gives them new identities. What new names does she give them?
context: Hermione plants in her parents' minds the idea that they've always wanted to retire to Australia. She intends to find and restore them after the war. Rowling has stated in interviews that Hermione successfully reunites with her parents and restores their memories after Voldemort's fall. The Granger-parents subplot didn't make it into the film of Deathly Hallows. The scene where Hermione enchants the family photos to erase herself is one of the most emotional moments in the book.

question: The Marauders — James, Sirius, Remus, and Peter — became secret Animagi at Hogwarts to keep Lupin company on full-moon nights. Becoming an Animagus is very hard magic and takes years. As part of the process, what plant's leaf must you keep in your mouth for a full month without a break?
answer: A leaf from the Mandrake plant
choices: A leaf from the Mandrake plant
A leaf from the Aconite plant (wolfsbane)
A leaf from the Belladonna plant (nightshade)
A leaf from the Mistletoe plant (Druidic origin)
context: If the leaf is dislodged before the full month, the wizard must start over. The full ritual involves further potion-brewing during a specific lightning storm. The Marauders accomplished the transformation in fifth year — about three years of work. McGonagall (registered Animagus, tabby cat) is the only known legal Animagus in the modern era. Rita Skeeter (beetle) is an unregistered Animagus exposed by Hermione in Goblet of Fire.

question: The Battle of Hogwarts ends with Voldemort firing the killing curse at Harry in the Great Hall — and the curse rebounding to kill Voldemort because Voldemort has been the unwitting master of his own death. Harry survives the prior killing curse in the Forest because of the soul-anchor effect of Voldemort containing Harry's blood. Harry's blood was taken in 1995 to revive Voldemort. The 'King's Cross' chapter between forest-death and Great Hall return features Harry in conversation with Dumbledore. What does Harry see lying under a bench during this dream-sequence?
answer: A flayed, child-sized creature that represents the broken remnant of Voldemort's soul
choices: A flayed, child-sized creature that represents the broken remnant of Voldemort's soul
A silver phoenix feather lying alongside a perfect green basilisk egg
A tarnished mirror reflecting the Forest of Dean's protective enchantments
A torn fragment of the Resurrection Stone wrapped in Harry's mother's handkerchief
context: The King's Cross dream-sequence is one of Rowling's most-debated chapters — whether Harry is dead, dreaming, in limbo, or somewhere else. The flayed creature represents the soul-fragment of Voldemort attached to Harry as the seventh Horcrux, now severed. Dumbledore's appearance allows him to explain the entire Hallows-and-Horcruxes plan to Harry. After the conversation, Harry chooses to return to life; the Forbidden Forest scene plays out with Voldemort believing he'd just killed Harry.

question: Iron Man (2008) was directed by Jon Favreau and made for $140 million on a film that had been in development hell since New Line Cinema acquired the rights in 1992. The film's casting was a public gamble; Robert Downey Jr. was uninsurable due to past drug arrests, and Marvel Studios had to pay for his insurance bond personally. The pivotal cave-escape scene was largely improvised by Downey and Jeff Bridges as Obadiah Stane. The film's opening sequence with the Stark Industries weapons convoy in Afghanistan ends with a now-iconic AC/DC song — the band's name comes from AC (Alternating Current) and DC (Direct Current) — playing as Tony Stark gets into the lead Humvee. What's the song?
context: Favreau picked Back in Black to immediately signal Tony's rock-star personality. The film's score by Ramin Djawadi (later of Game of Thrones) features blues-rock guitar reminiscent of AC/DC throughout. The original cut had Iron Maiden's 'Iron Man' over the same scene, but rights issues forced the change. Stan Lee has a cameo as 'Hugh Hefner' at the Vegas charity event near the film's opening, mistaken by Tony for the real Hef.

question: Joss Whedon's The Avengers (2012) features one of the most-quoted lines in superhero film history during the Stuttgart cathedral scene: Loki commands a frightened crowd of gala-attendees to kneel, asking 'Is not this simpler? Is this not your natural state?' An elderly German man stands up alone in defiance. What's the line the old man delivers, alluding to a specific historical period?
answer: There are always men like you.
choices: There are always men like you.
We have been ruled by tyrants before.
I have stood in stadiums while men like you raved.
You speak with the voice of those we buried.
context: The full exchange: Loki orders the crowd to kneel. An old German man (played by Kenneth Tigar) stands and says 'Not to men like you.' Loki replies 'There are no men like me.' The old man responds 'There are always men like you.' Captain America arrives at the moment Loki is about to execute the old man, deflecting the blast with his shield. The line and shield-arrival sequence is one of the MCU's most-quoted moments.

question: The Russos' Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014) was inspired heavily by 1970s political-thriller films -- particularly Alan J. Pakula's paranoia thrillers, Sydney Pollack's Three Days of the Condor (1975), and The Parallax View (1974). The Russos cast veteran actor Robert Redford as the senior S.H.I.E.L.D. official Alexander Pierce specifically because of his association with that era. What was Redford's iconic 1970s political-thriller role that directly informed the Pierce casting?
answer: Bob Woodward in All the President's Men (1976) and Joseph Turner in Three Days of the Condor
choices: Bob Woodward in All the President's Men (1976) and Joseph Turner in Three Days of the Condor
Sundance in Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969) and Jeremiah Johnson title role
Bill McKay in The Candidate (1972) and his Oscar role as Norman in Ordinary People
Hubbell Gardner in The Way We Were (1973) and Roy Hobbs in The Natural (1984)
context: Redford reportedly took the part for $1 to do something his grandchildren could see. Pierce is revealed to be a Hydra operative — Hydra having quietly subverted S.H.I.E.L.D. from within since 1945. The film's helicarrier-takedown finale (Cap leaping between three falling helicarriers) was practically choreographed before becoming CGI. Captain America: The Winter Soldier opened to $95M domestically and is widely cited as one of the best-reviewed Marvel films, sitting at 90% on Rotten Tomatoes.

question: Marvel's Black Panther (2018), directed by Ryan Coogler, is set in the fictional African nation of Wakanda, hidden from the world and ruled by young King T'Challa. The Dora Milaje are Wakanda's elite all-female bodyguard, shaven-headed warriors in red armor and spears, led by General Okoye. The filmmakers based them on a real all-female army from West African history. Which real regiment?
answer: The Agojie of the Kingdom of Dahomey, an all-female military regiment that existed from the 17th to the late 19th century
choices: The Agojie of the Kingdom of Dahomey, an all-female military regiment that existed from the 17th to the late 19th century
The Mino of the Zulu Kingdom under Shaka's reign in the early 19th century, before colonial dissolution
The Nubian Queens' Guard of ancient Meroe, which trained women warriors from the 5th century BC onward
The Carthaginian Women's Auxiliary that defended the city during the Third Punic War, 149-146 BC
context: The Agojie (also called 'Dahomey Amazons' by European writers) numbered up to 6,000 women at their peak. They were officially disbanded in 1894 after the French conquest of Dahomey. The 2022 film The Woman King with Viola Davis dramatized the Agojie. Ryan Coogler consulted Boston University Africanist scholars during pre-production. Florence Kasumba played Ayo and Danai Gurira played Okoye as the most-prominent Dora Milaje in Black Panther.

question: Thor: Ragnarok (2017) was Taika Waititi's first major-studio film. Waititi approached Marvel with a pitch focused on lightening the previously-serious Thor films. The film's iconic 'Immigrant Song' opening fight scene -- Thor swinging Mjolnir as the classic rock track blasts -- required Marvel to pay one of the largest single-song licensing fees in studio history. The fee was negotiated personally with whom?
answer: Jimmy Page and Robert Plant, the surviving members of Led Zeppelin
choices: Jimmy Page and Robert Plant, the surviving members of Led Zeppelin
The estate of John Bonham via his son Jason Bonham, who acted as agent
Atlantic Records, the band's master-recording rights holder since 1968
Peter Grant Estate, since the band's original manager owned the rights
context: Led Zeppelin almost never grants song licenses. Page and Plant personally approved Ragnarok after watching an early cut Waititi sent them. The 'Immigrant Song' (1970, from Led Zeppelin III) plays both in the opening sequence and in the climactic Asgard-battle. Waititi's gambit was that the song's Norse mythology lyrical content ('We come from the land of the ice and snow') was uniquely thematic. The licensing fee has been variously reported at $1-2 million.

question: In Marvel's Avengers: Endgame (2019), the surviving Avengers have just lost half of all life in the universe to the Mad Titan Thanos, who wiped it away with a snap of the Infinity Gauntlet. Weeks later they track him to a small retirement farm on a distant planet, hoping to seize the Infinity Stones back and undo the Snap. In the ambush, Thor does something to Thanos that most of the cast were not told about ahead of time. What does he do?
answer: Thor decapitating Thanos with Stormbreaker, going for the head this time
choices: Thor decapitating Thanos with Stormbreaker, going for the head this time
Thor binding Thanos in adamantine chains for Doctor Strange to extract Stones
Thor smashing Thanos's gauntlet to destroy the stones before they can be recovered
Thor calling lightning to teleport Thanos back to Vormir where Gamora could be returned
context: Thor's 'I went for the head' opening of Endgame is meta-commentary on his Infinity War failure (Stormbreaker stab to chest, didn't kill Thanos because Thanos completed the snap first). Hemsworth shot the scene with a stunt-double Brolin rather than the real Thanos. The Asgardian armor for the scene was a 60-pound suit. The film's opening was filmed last in the production schedule. The Russos kept the scene out of all marketing — opening night audiences experienced it cold.

question: Avengers: Endgame (2019)'s portal scene features the on-screen return of every previously dusted hero. Sam Wilson (Falcon) is the first to appear from a portal, contacting Captain America by radio with a specific two-word line callback to The Winter Soldier (2014). What does Sam say?
context: 'On your left' is the line Sam used in Winter Soldier when he repeatedly lapped a running Steve Rogers on the National Mall before introducing himself. The Endgame portal-scene callback turns the joke into one of the franchise's most emotional moments — Steve is alone, exhausted, facing Thanos's full army; the radio crackles; the portals open. Co-director Joe Russo has spoken about the line in multiple interviews as a deliberate emotional payoff.

question: Marvel's Clone Saga ran across five Spider-Man titles from 1994 to 1996. The story claimed the Spider-Man readers had followed since 1975 was really a clone. The 'real' Peter, called Ben Reilly, had spent years wandering the country under a different name. What name?
context: The Clone Saga was initially planned as a six-month story but expanded under executive pressure into a two-year crossover that sold millions but alienated longtime readers. Ben Reilly took over as Spider-Man for the better part of a year (1996) before Marvel reversed everything in 1997's Spider-Man #75.
