The Saga is widely considered the most-disliked Spider-Man storyline ever. Writer J.M. DeMatteis has spoken candidly about the editorial chaos that drove the storyline.

question: In J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter books, Fawkes is Headmaster Albus Dumbledore's pet phoenix — a bird that bursts into flame and is reborn from its own ashes. In Chamber of Secrets, Fawkes flies down to Harry in the underground chamber, drops him the Sword of Gryffindor, and blinds the giant basilisk. Two books later, in Order of the Phoenix, Fawkes appears in the middle of a duel in the Ministry of Magic between Dumbledore and the dark wizard Voldemort. To save Dumbledore's life, Fawkes swoops in front of him and physically swallows one specific spell Voldemort has just cast. Which spell?
choices: Voldemort's Crucio that would have shattered the Fountain statues
A controlled Fiendfyre conjured during the duel's middle phase
A Mind-Probing curse from Bellatrix that targeted Dumbledore's memory
context: Fawkes intercepts the green killing-curse beam at the Battle of the Department of Mysteries and dies, then is reborn from the ashes — a phoenix can absorb an Avada Kedavra. The atrium duel between Dumbledore and Voldemort is one of the most-cinematic moments in the entire series. The Order's name itself comes from Fawkes — Dumbledore's Patronus and personal-protector phoenix. The phoenix-feather wands of Harry and Voldemort both come from Fawkes's tail.

question: In a 1937 children's book, a small hairy-footed creature called a hobbit named Bilbo Baggins gets lost in a dark goblin-cave under the Misty Mountains. Groping through a tunnel, he picks up a gold ring without knowing what it is, then meets Gollum, a slimy pale-eyed creature, and plays a riddle contest for his life. Who wrote the book?
context: John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an Oxford philology professor. The Hobbit was published in September 1937 by Allen & Unwin in London. Tolkien's sequel grew into the three-volume Lord of the Rings (1954-55).

question: In J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, a young hobbit of the Shire inherits a magic gold ring from his cousin Bilbo, learns it is the Dark Lord's One Ring, and agrees to carry it to the volcano where it was forged. What is his name?
context: Frodo is Bilbo's cousin, though he is often called his nephew, and he sets out from the Shire carrying the One Ring. The first volume, The Fellowship of the Ring, was published in July 1954.

question: J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit tells of a giant fire-breathing dragon who long ago drove the dwarves out of the Lonely Mountain in Middle-earth. He now sleeps curled over their stolen treasure — a mountain of gold coins, jewels, and armor — inside the mountain's hollow halls. A small hobbit named Bilbo Baggins sneaks in to see him. What is the dragon's name?
context: Smaug captured the Lonely Mountain (Erebor) and its dwarven gold-hoard centuries before The Hobbit begins. Tolkien drew Smaug himself for the book's illustrations. Benedict Cumberbatch voiced Smaug in Peter Jackson's 2013 film adaptation.

question: The American writer Edgar Allan Poe published his most famous poem, The Raven, in 1845. In it, a lonely man sits up late one December night grieving his lost love Lenore. A black raven flies in through the window, lands on a marble bust of Pallas Athena above the chamber door, and croaks the same single word again and again in reply to the man's questions. What word does the raven say?
context: The Raven appeared in the New York Evening Mirror on January 29, 1845. It made Poe instantly famous but earned him only $9. The bust the raven perches on is of Pallas Athena. The narrator's lost love is named Lenore.

question: In 1912, American writer Edgar Rice Burroughs sold a pulp magazine a story about an English baby whose parents, Lord and Lady Greystoke, died in the African jungle. A gentle female ape found the orphan and raised him as her own child. He grew up climbing trees, wrestling leopards, and swinging on vines with the great apes as his family. What is this jungle-raised hero's name?
context: Tarzan of the Apes debuted in All-Story Magazine in October 1912. His ape name Tarzan means White-Skin in the language of the great apes Burroughs invented. He inherits the title Lord Greystoke from his father.

question: Throughout the 1930s, American pulp magazines and a hit weekly radio show followed a mysterious crime-fighter who prowled the night in a slouch hat, red scarf, and long black cloak, with twin .45 automatic pistols hidden under his coat. His radio show opened with a chilling laugh and his famous catchphrase, 'Who knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men?' Who is this pulp hero?
context: The Shadow debuted in Detective Story Hour radio in 1930 and as a pulp character in 1931 (written mostly by Walter Gibson under the pen name Maxwell Grant). The radio tagline finished: 'The Shadow knows!'

question: The American horror writer H. P. Lovecraft invented the most famous monster of cosmic horror in a 1928 short story pieced together from a dead professor's notes and a sailor's diary. The creature is a giant green horror the size of a mountain, with an octopus-like face full of writhing tentacles, huge dragon wings, and enormous claws. He is said to sleep beneath the Pacific Ocean in the sunken stone city of R'lyeh, waiting to wake. What is the creature called?
context: Cthulhu debuted in The Call of Cthulhu in the February 1928 issue of Weird Tales. The sunken city is called R'lyeh. Lovecraft admitted no human mouth could properly pronounce the name; he suggested 'Khlûl'-hloo.'

question: In the 1930s, American writer Robert E. Howard invented a black-haired warrior born in the cold northern land of Cimmeria. He wanders the ancient Hyborian world as a thief, a pirate, and a mercenary before finally seizing a crown for himself and ruling the kingdom of Aquilonia. What is this Cimmerian warrior-king's name?
context: Conan first appeared in Weird Tales in December 1932 in the story 'The Phoenix on the Sword.' Howard wrote 21 Conan stories before his suicide in 1936. Arnold Schwarzenegger played him in the 1982 John Milius film Conan the Barbarian.

question: In 1930s Los Angeles, the American writer Raymond Chandler created a tough, wisecracking private detective who walks the mean streets in a rumpled trench coat, chasing crooks and rich clients who lie to him. He first appeared in the 1939 novel The Big Sleep and became the model for the hard-boiled detective in every book and movie that followed. What is this private eye's name?
context: Marlowe appears in seven Chandler novels. Humphrey Bogart played him in the 1946 film of The Big Sleep. Chandler's other novels include Farewell My Lovely (1940), The Long Goodbye (1953), and The Lady in the Lake (1943).

question: The Russian-American science-fiction writer Isaac Asimov wrote a book series set thousands of years in the future. A vast Galactic Empire is beginning to collapse, and a mathematician named Hari Seldon invents psychohistory — math that predicts the behavior of huge populations — to shorten the coming dark age from 30,000 years to just 1,000. What is the series called?
context: Asimov began the Foundation stories in Astounding Science Fiction in May 1942. The mathematician's name is Hari Seldon; his predictive science is called psychohistory. The original trilogy was published as books between 1951 and 1953.

question: In a 1965 science-fiction novel by American writer Frank Herbert, a young noble named Paul Atreides is thrown into the deserts of a distant planet called Arrakis. Giant sandworms hundreds of feet long slide unseen beneath the dunes, and a rare spice called melange lets starship pilots fold space and jump between stars. What is the book called?
context: Herbert based the desert ecology on his research on Oregon coastal dunes for an unfinished article. The book was rejected by 20 publishers before Chilton Books (a manuals publisher) bought it. Sandworms can be over 400 meters long.

question: In 1953, the American author Ray Bradbury wrote a chilling story set in a future where all books are outlawed and firemen no longer put out fires -- they start them, burning any book they find. Bradbury titled the novel after the temperature at which paper catches fire and burns. What is the title of the book?
context: Bradbury wrote the original novella in nine days on a rented typewriter in the basement of UCLA's Powell Library at ten cents per half-hour. The fireman protagonist is Guy Montag; his wife is Mildred. The title's temperature isn't quite accurate — paper actually ignites around 480°F.

question: In the Middle-earth stories of J. R. R. Tolkien — The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings — a wise old wizard travels the roads in gray robes with a long gray beard, a pointy blue hat, and a walking staff. He sends the hobbit Bilbo Baggins off on his quest for the dragon's treasure, and years later he leads Frodo Baggins and the Fellowship of the Ring against the dark lord Sauron. What is the wizard's name?
context: Gandalf is called Mithrandir by the Elves and Tharkûn by the Dwarves. He is one of the Istari, sent to Middle-earth as a Maia (angelic being) in the shape of an old man. Ian McKellen played him in Peter Jackson's films.

question: Poe's 1843 story is told by a narrator who swears he is not mad. He has hidden an old man's body under the floorboards, and with police in the room he thinks he hears its heart beating. What is the story?
context: First published in The Pioneer in January 1843, the story is told by an unnamed narrator who is undone by the sound he believes is the dead man's beating heart.

question: In a 1912 story by the American writer Edgar Rice Burroughs — the same author who would later create Tarzan — an ex-Confederate cavalry officer is mysteriously transported to the planet Mars. The green-skinned four-armed Martians call their world Barsoom. Mars's lower gravity makes the Earthman leap huge distances and fight like a superhero, and he falls in love with a red-skinned princess named Dejah Thoris. What is his name?
context: A Princess of Mars debuted in All-Story Magazine in February 1912, six months before Tarzan. Carter is a Virginia gentleman. Burroughs wrote eleven Barsoom novels through 1948. The 2012 Disney film John Carter was a famous box-office bomb.

question: In J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, a dark lord in the shadowy land of Mordor once forged the One Ring in secret, planning to use it to rule all the other rings of power. His body was destroyed long ago, but his spirit lives on as a huge flaming Eye that watches from the top of a black tower called Barad-dur. What is this dark lord's name?
context: Sauron was originally a Maia (servant of the Valar) under Morgoth, the first Dark Lord. His tower is Barad-dûr. His Eye is fashioned in the Eye of Sauron iconography by Peter Jackson; in the books it is more metaphorical. The One Ring contains a fragment of his power.

question: In Dashiell Hammett's 1930 novel, crooks chase a jewelled black bird statue said to be from the Knights of Malta, and private eye Sam Spade is caught in the middle. What is it called?
context: The novel was serialized in Black Mask in 1929-30. John Huston's 1941 film, with Humphrey Bogart as Spade, is a landmark of film noir.

question: In 1937 the British writer J. R. R. Tolkien published a children's book about a small hairy-footed creature named Bilbo Baggins. Thirteen dwarves led by Thorin Oakenshield knock on Bilbo's round green door and hire him as their burglar. They want to take back their stolen mountain of gold from a fire-breathing dragon named Smaug, who sleeps curled on top of it deep inside the Lonely Mountain. What is the book called?
context: Full title: The Hobbit, or There and Back Again. The thirteen dwarves are led by Thorin Oakenshield. The first edition was 1500 copies and sold out by Christmas 1937. C.S. Lewis was one of the first reviewers and praised it warmly.

question: In 1947, the American writer Mickey Spillane introduced readers to a brutal, hard-drinking, fast-shooting private eye who works the tough streets of New York City. In his first novel, I, the Jury, this detective hunts down the killer of his best friend and swears violent revenge. What is this private eye's name?
context: Spillane wrote the first Hammer novel in 19 days. By 1980, seven of the top fifteen best-selling fiction titles of all time were Mike Hammer novels. Spillane himself starred as Hammer in the 1963 film The Girl Hunters.

question: In 1968, the British science fiction author Arthur C. Clarke teamed up with the American film director Stanley Kubrick to create both a novel and a movie about astronauts flying to Jupiter, an eerie black stone monolith left on the Moon by aliens, and a talking spaceship computer named HAL 9000 that suddenly turns on its human crew. What is the shared title of this story?
context: Clarke and Kubrick developed the novel and film concurrently. The book came out four months after the film's April 1968 release. The story expands Clarke's 1948 short story The Sentinel. HAL stands for Heuristically programmed ALgorithmic computer.

question: In 1897, the Irish author Bram Stoker published a horror novel about a mysterious ancient nobleman from Transylvania in eastern Europe. This vampire count buys a ruined estate in England, sails there aboard a ghostly ship where the crew mysteriously die one by one, and begins hunting young English women at night for their blood. Who is the count?
context: Stoker partly modeled Dracula on the 15th-century Wallachian prince Vlad III, Vlad the Impaler. The novel is epistolary — diary entries, letters, telegrams. Bela Lugosi's 1931 film performance defined the screen image of the vampire.

question: Starting in 1933, an American pulp magazine printed 181 novels about a bronze-skinned scientist and adventurer and his five brilliant helpers — a lawyer, an engineer, a chemist, an electrical wizard, and a giant strongman. The team traveled the world in a private plane fighting evil masterminds. Fans and every magazine cover called their hero the Man of Bronze. His stories directly inspired Superman and Indiana Jones. What is his name?
context: Doc Savage (Clark Savage Jr.) debuted in March 1933. Lester Dent wrote most of the novels under the house pen name Kenneth Robeson. Doc's headquarters were on the 86th floor of a Manhattan skyscraper modeled on the Empire State Building.

question: In J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, the hobbit Frodo Baggins carries the evil One Ring across many dangerous lands to destroy it. The Ring cannot be broken with any weapon; it can only be unmade by casting it into the fiery lava of the volcano in Mordor where the dark lord Sauron first forged it. What is this volcano called?
context: Mount Doom (Orodruin in Sindarin, Amon Amarth) is an active volcano in central Mordor. Sauron forged the Ring there in the Second Age. The Ring can be unmade only in the same fires that forged it. The mountain stands within sight of Sauron's tower Barad-dûr.

question: Robert E. Howard, the Texan who created Conan, spent most of his short life in one small town in central Texas, writing his stories in his parents' house. He took his own life there in June 1936, at thirty. The house is now a museum and a pilgrimage site for pulp fans. Which town was his lifelong home?
context: Howard spent most of his life in Cross Plains, with some years in nearby Brownwood, and his home there is now the Robert E. Howard Museum. He died on 11 June 1936, aged 30; his mother died the next day.

question: The American horror writer H.P. Lovecraft, who invented the tentacled sea-god Cthulhu and wrote weird cosmic tales in the 1920s and 1930s, lived almost his entire life in one small New England city. He was born there in 1890. He briefly left for a short, miserable marriage in New York City, then hurried home and spent his last years writing in his attic study. What city was his lifelong home?
context: Lovecraft was born in Providence on August 20, 1890 and died there March 15, 1937 of intestinal cancer. He briefly lived in Brooklyn 1924-26 after marrying Sonia Greene; the experience deepened his xenophobia and informed The Horror at Red Hook. Many of his fictional towns (Arkham, Innsmouth, Kingsport) are based on real New England locations.

question: In March 1923, a new pulp magazine went on sale on Chicago newsstands — cheap paper, lurid covers, packed with tales of horror, wizards, and monsters. Over the next thirty years it printed the best work of Texan sword-and-sorcery writer Robert E. Howard, cosmic-horror master H.P. Lovecraft, and California poet-fantasist Clark Ashton Smith. The magazine finally folded in 1954. What was it called?
context: Weird Tales was founded by Jacob Henneberger. Farnsworth Wright edited it through its 1930s golden age. The signature triumvirate — Lovecraft, Howard, and Clark Ashton Smith — anchored the magazine in the early 1930s while corresponding with each other constantly.

question: J.R.R. Tolkien, the author of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, served as a young British signals officer at the Battle of the Somme in 1916. Two of his closest school friends, fellow members of a little club they called the T.C.B.S., were killed in that battle. Tolkien later said one loyal, brave hobbit reflected the ordinary British soldiers he served with. Which hobbit?
context: Tolkien described his Sam as a reflection of the English soldier, of the privates and batmen he knew in the First World War. Two of the four friends at the heart of the T.C.B.S. (Tea Club and Barrovian Society), Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Bache Smith, were killed in 1916; Tolkien caught trench fever and was invalided home on 8 November 1916.

question: In 1841 the American writer Edgar Allan Poe published a short story called 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue.' A brilliant French gentleman-detective in Paris solves the seemingly impossible killings of two women found inside a locked upstairs apartment. He uses pure reasoning to crack a case the police cannot. Critics call this the very first modern detective story — Sherlock Holmes and Hercule Poirot both grew out of it decades later. What is the French detective's name?
context: The Murders in the Rue Morgue (April 1841 in Graham's Magazine) introduced detective fiction's foundational conventions: the brilliant amateur sleuth, the slower narrator-companion, the locked-room mystery, the dramatic reveal. Conan Doyle named Poe's stories as the direct ancestor of Sherlock Holmes.

question: John W. Campbell took over an Astounding magazine in 1937 and launched what is now called the Golden Age of science fiction, publishing Asimov, Heinlein, Sturgeon, and van Vogt. One of his own 1938 novellas became the basis for John Carpenter's 1982 horror film. What was the novella?
context: Who Goes There? appeared in the August 1938 issue under Campbell's pen name Don A. Stuart. The story features Antarctic researchers and a shape-shifting alien. It was first adapted as The Thing from Another World (1951) and then Carpenter's The Thing (1982). Campbell edited Astounding (renamed Analog in 1960) until his death in 1971.

question: In October 1912, a New York pulp magazine ran the first story of Tarzan, a boy raised by apes in the African jungle. In the tale, Tarzan's parents were English nobles marooned on the African coast by mutineers on their ship. They died in a jungle cabin before their baby son could speak — but the boy would later learn he was heir to a proud English family title. What was that title?
context: John Clayton, the 7th Lord Greystoke (Tarzan's father). The 'Clayton' surname is family; Greystoke is the peerage title. The mother ape Kala raises Tarzan. The Tarzan-of-the-Apes book appeared in 1914. Johnny Weissmuller's 1932 MGM film cemented the iconic image.

question: In 1928, Rhode Island writer H.P. Lovecraft wrote a story for the pulp magazine Weird Tales. It was about a giant tentacled monster older than mankind, sleeping in a sunken stone city called R'lyeh at the bottom of the Pacific Ocean. Cults around the world dreamed of the day the creature would wake. The story became one of the most famous horror tales ever written. What was it called?
context: Published in the February 1928 Weird Tales. The story is told in three parts via the papers of Professor George Gammell Angell of Brown University. The Cthulhu mythos vocabulary — R'lyeh, the Necronomicon, the cult phrase 'In his house at R'lyeh dead Cthulhu waits dreaming' — all enter the canon here.

question: The American science fiction writer Frank Herbert spent years shopping around a strange desert epic novel. Twenty publishers turned him down before Chilton Books — a company mostly known for printing car repair manuals — took a chance and published it in 1965. It became one of the most famous science fiction books ever written. The hero is a young noble boy named Paul Atreides, whose family is sent by the galactic emperor to rule a scorching, waterless desert planet full of gigantic sandworms. What is the desert planet's name?
context: Arrakis is colloquially called Dune. The desert is the only source of spice melange — the substance that enables faster-than-light navigation across the Imperium. The native Fremen people drink water-of-life and ride sandworms called Shai-Hulud.

question: In 1894 the Welsh writer Arthur Machen published a short horror novel that shocked Victorian readers. A doctor performs a brain operation that opens a young woman's mind to a glimpse of a wild pagan nature-god, and she loses her reason. Years later a mysterious woman drifts through London society, and the gentlemen who know her begin to die. What is the story called?
context: Arthur Machen (1863-1947) published The Great God Pan with John Lane in 1894, to a storm of scandal. Lovecraft praised it in his 1927 essay Supernatural Horror in Literature, and it shaped his own cosmic horror.

question: J.R.R. Tolkien, the author of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, spent nearly his whole life writing the ancient creation myths, elf-songs, and origin stories of Middle-earth. He died in 1973 with the manuscript unfinished. In 1977, his son gathered the mountain of unfinished notes and drafts and shaped them into a published book called The Silmarillion. Who was this son and editor?
context: Christopher Tolkien (1924-2020) was J.R.R.'s third son and literary executor. He spent the rest of his life editing his father's papers — twelve volumes of The History of Middle-earth (1983-1996) plus Unfinished Tales (1980), The Children of Húrin (2007), Beren and Lúthien (2017), and The Fall of Gondolin (2018). Guy Gavriel Kay assisted on The Silmarillion.

question: In August 1939 Fritz Leiber's first published story introduced two swords-for-hire. One was a giant barbarian from the north. The other was a small thief and magician's apprentice. Together they roam a corrupt city of thieves and wizards. What were the two heroes called?
context: The story appeared in Unknown in August 1939. Leiber went on writing about the pair, the tall barbarian and the small thief, until his death in 1992.

question: In 1961 Michael Moorcock wrote a novella in Science Fantasy magazine. It starred an albino sorcerer-emperor from a dying magical race. He leaned on drugs and a black sword that drank souls. He became a founding anti-hero of dark fantasy. What is his name?
context: Elric's sword is Stormbringer. Moorcock developed the larger concept of the Eternal Champion (Elric, Corum, Hawkmoon, Erekosë, etc.) — different incarnations of the same hero across multiple worlds. The original Elric stories ran 1961-1964 in Science Fantasy; Moorcock has returned to the character repeatedly since.

question: In 1843, American horror writer Edgar Allan Poe published a short story set in a torture chamber during the Spanish Inquisition. A prisoner is strapped flat to a wooden board while a huge razor-sharp blade swings closer and closer overhead. Around him, the red-hot iron walls of the room slowly slide inward to crush him. What is Poe's story called?
choices: The Masque of the Red Death
context: The story first appeared in the 1843 edition of the annual The Gift. Its narrator is a prisoner of the Spanish Inquisition in Toledo, tormented first by a pit in the dark and then by the swinging blade.

question: In 1959 the American science fiction writer Robert Heinlein published a novel about future soldiers who fight in powered exoskeleton armor that lets them jump like grasshoppers. It follows a young recruit named Johnny Rico through brutal boot camp and into an interstellar war against giant intelligent bug-like aliens from a planet called Klendathu. The book won the Hugo Award, science fiction's top prize. In 1997 the Dutch director Paul Verhoeven turned it into a famously satirical movie. What was Heinlein's novel called?
choices: The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress
context: Heinlein conceived powered armor (the Mobile Infantry suits) in the novel, influencing every mecha and powered-armor concept since. The book's political philosophy — full citizenship earned only through federal service — provoked decades of debate. Verhoeven's 1997 film satirized the politics; Heinlein's text plays them straight.

question: In 1928 Robert E. Howard put a new hero in the pulp magazines. He was a Puritan in a slouch hat, armed with a rapier. He wandered the world fighting evil and avenging the innocent. He was Howard's grim religious answer to the pagan Conan. What is his name?
context: Solomon Kane first appeared in Red Shadows in Weird Tales in August 1928, four years before Conan. Howard made him a grim Puritan swordsman who roams the world righting wrongs.

question: In the 1930s and 1940s, J.R.R. Tolkien, C.S. Lewis, and a handful of other Oxford scholars met once or twice a week — sometimes at a pub called The Eagle and Child (nicknamed 'The Bird and Baby'), sometimes in Lewis's college rooms at Magdalen — to read their unfinished works aloud to each other. Drafts of The Hobbit, The Lord of the Rings, and the Chronicles of Narnia were all first heard by this small circle of friends. What did they call themselves?
context: The Inklings included Lewis, Tolkien, Charles Williams, Owen Barfield, Hugo Dyson, and Lewis's brother Warnie. They met at the Eagle and Child pub (nicknamed the Bird and Baby) on St. Giles' Street, Oxford. Tolkien read drafts of LOTR to the group; Lewis read drafts of Narnia and Out of the Silent Planet.

question: From 1920 to 1951, the American pulp magazine Black Mask was the top home for hardboiled crime fiction — tough, gritty detective stories set in mean city streets. It ran early work by Dashiell Hammett (creator of Sam Spade) and Raymond Chandler (creator of Philip Marlowe). Hammett's most famous early Black Mask hero, though, was a short, tubby, unnamed private-eye who worked as an agent for a big detective agency in San Francisco. What did readers call him?
context: The Continental Op (short for 'Operative') works for the Continental Detective Agency, modeled on Hammett's real Pinkerton service. The Op appeared in 36 stories and the novels Red Harvest (1929) and The Dain Curse (1929). He is short, stout, middle-aged, and unnamed throughout.

question: H.P. Lovecraft invented a fake ancient book of forbidden magic and mentioned it in so many stories that many readers believed it was real. He said it was written long ago by a poet he called the Mad Arab, Abdul Alhazred, who went insane from what he learned. What is this made-up book called?
context: Lovecraft invented the Necronomicon for his story The Hound (1922) and wrote a mock History of the Necronomicon in 1927. Several real books have since been published under the name as hoaxes, and libraries still get requests for the original.

question: In 1939 two young writers who had been H.P. Lovecraft's devoted correspondents started a small book press in the Wisconsin town of Sauk City. Their goal was simple: keep the horror stories of their late friend, who had died two years earlier, in hardcover print. The press took its name from Lovecraft's fictional New England town. What is that press called?
context: August Derleth and Donald Wandrei founded Arkham House to publish The Outsider and Others (1939), the first big Lovecraft collection. Derleth also wrote Cthulhu Mythos stories of his own.

question: In 1962, American science fiction writer Philip K. Dick published a novel set in an alternate 1962 where Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan had won World War II and carved up North America between them — the Reich holds the East Coast, Japan the West, with a neutral zone in the Rockies. Inside the book is a second, forbidden novel-within-the-novel called 'The Grasshopper Lies Heavy,' which imagines that the Allies actually won. Dick's outer book won the Hugo Award. What is its title?
answer: The Man in the High Castle
choices: The Man in the High Castle
Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said
context: Won the 1963 Hugo Award. Dick used the I Ching to make plot decisions while writing. The story is set in 1962 in a Japanese-occupied West Coast (PSA), with a German-occupied East and a neutral Rocky Mountain States buffer. Hawthorne Abendsen is the in-novel author of Grasshopper, the inverse alternate-history showing an Allied victory.

question: In 1922 the English civil servant Eric Rucker Eddison published a huge, gloriously old-fashioned fantasy novel written in mock-Elizabethan English. Its story of noble Demons and treacherous Witches locked in endless war is set — bizarrely — not on Earth but on the planet Mercury. J.R.R. Tolkien later admired the sheer force of Eddison's ringing prose but disapproved of the cruel morals of his aristocratic characters. What is the novel called?
context: Eddison's prose imitates the cadence of Jacobean drama; he had translated Egil's Saga from the Old Norse. Tolkien wrote that Eddison was 'the greatest and most convincing writer of invented worlds I have read' but disliked his Nietzschean ethics. The 'worm' (Old English word for dragon) circles back on itself — the story's ending loops to its beginning.

question: Robert E. Howard wrote his Conan stories in his parents' house in Cross Plains, Texas, and poured his ideas into long letters to other writers. From 1930 until his death in 1936 his chief correspondent was a horror writer in Providence, Rhode Island, whom he never met in person; the two argued for years over whether civilisation or barbarism was the better state for mankind. Who was that correspondent?
context: Howard and Lovecraft began writing to each other in 1930 and kept it up for the rest of Howard's life, arguing over civilisation and barbarism. Their letters were later collected by Hippocampus Press as A Means to Freedom.

question: In 1936 the American horror writer H.P. Lovecraft published his longest single tale, a novella of cosmic dread. It follows an expedition of professors and graduate students from the fictional Miskatonic University in Massachusetts, who fly deep into Antarctica. There, buried in the ice at the foot of a vast unknown mountain range taller than the Himalayas, they find the frozen corpses of star-headed alien beings that built enormous stone cities on Earth millions of years before humans existed. What is the story called?
choices: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward
context: Astounding ran the novella in its February, March and April 1936 issues. Its Antarctic expedition echoes the real flights of Richard Byrd's 1928-1930 expedition, and the barrel-shaped Elder Things it finds built their cities long before humanity.

question: In December 1932, the pulp magazine Weird Tales printed Texan writer Robert E. Howard's first Conan the Barbarian story. Howard built the tale by rewriting an unpublished story about his earlier hero, King Kull — an Atlantean warrior who seized a decadent throne and became the king of a dying, pre-human kingdom on a lost continent long before Conan's time. What was Kull's fallen kingdom called?
context: Kull debuted in 'The Shadow Kingdom' (Weird Tales, August 1929). Valusia is the most powerful of the Seven Empires of Howard's pre-Cataclysm world. Kull and the snake-people of Valusia inspired numerous later writers including Lin Carter and L. Sprague de Camp. Conan's Hyborian Age is technically a later epoch after Kull's Atlantis sinks.

question: California writer Clark Ashton Smith was the third pillar of the pulp magazine Weird Tales in the 1930s, sharing its pages with H.P. Lovecraft and Robert E. Howard. Unlike them, Smith spent most of his life as a near-hermit, living in a rough cabin in the Sierra Nevada foothills of northern California, writing dark-fantasy poems and stories in near-poverty. In which small California town did he live most of his life?
context: Smith (1893-1961) lived in a self-built cabin near Auburn, California. He was a teenage prodigy poet first, then turned to weird fiction in the late 1920s. His Zothique, Hyperborea, Averoigne, and Xiccarph cycles each represent different fantastic milieus. Smith ground his own pigments and carved fantastic stone heads in his last years. His correspondence with Lovecraft was nearly as substantial as Howard's.

question: Tolkien's invented Elvish languages — which he developed for decades before The Lord of the Rings (LOTR) was even conceived — fall into two main branches. The high-speech of the Noldor Elves (used in formal contexts in LOTR) was meant to sound like Latin or Finnish. The everyday speech of the Sindar Elves (used for most Elvish names in LOTR) was meant to sound like Welsh. Name those two languages.
context: Tolkien was a philology professor at Oxford whose academic work centered on Old English and the West Midlands dialect. He created Quenya around 1915 based on Finnish phonology after reading the Kalevala. Sindarin's Welsh-style consonant mutations come from Tolkien's love of Welsh place-names. Khuzdul (Dwarvish, modeled on Semitic languages) is heard rarely; the Black Speech of Mordor was created by Sauron.

question: Edgar Allan Poe wrote a short poem in 1849 that was first printed two days after his mysterious death in Baltimore. The poem opens 'It was many and many a year ago, in a kingdom by the sea, that a maiden there lived whom you may know by the name of...' — the title is the maiden's name. What is it?
context: Poe's young wife Virginia had died of tuberculosis in January 1847, and the poem is widely read as a memorial to her. Poe died in Baltimore on 7 October 1849, and the poem was first published two days later.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs invented a series of subterranean novels about a hollow Earth accessed near the North Pole, where dinosaurs survive and primitive humans wage wars with stone tools. The world is lit by an inner sun and has no concept of time. What did Burroughs call this hollow-Earth realm?
context: At the Earth's Core (1914) opens the Pellucidar series; Burroughs wrote seven Pellucidar novels through 1944. David Innes and his mentor Abner Perry tunnel down into the inner world in a mechanical 'iron mole.' The Caspak series (The Land That Time Forgot, 1918) is a separate Burroughs lost-world setup involving a Pacific island, not hollow Earth. Tarzan visits Pellucidar in a 1929 crossover.

question: Isaac Asimov began his first robot story in June 1939: a robot named Robbie who works as a little girl's nanny, the seed of all his later robot tales and their Three Laws. John W. Campbell turned it down for Astounding, and it finally sold to Frederik Pohl, who printed it in Super Science Stories in September 1940 under a new title that Asimov thought distasteful. What was that title?
context: Pohl renamed the story Strange Playfellow for Super Science Stories (September 1940), a title Asimov disliked; Asimov restored his own title, Robbie, when he collected it in I, Robot in 1950.

question: Tolkien's essay On Fairy-Stories, first given as a lecture in 1939, is his main statement about how fantasy writing works. In it, he coined a special word for the happy ending of a story — the sudden turn of joy that lifts everything. What is that word?
context: Eucatastrophe = 'good catastrophe.' Tolkien argued the Gospels are the eucatastrophe of human history — Christ's resurrection being the supreme unexpected turn from death to life. The essay also developed 'sub-creation' (the artist as imitator of God's creative act) and the primary/secondary world distinction. It first appeared in the 1947 Essays Presented to Charles Williams memorial volume.

question: In a story printed in 1929, Lovecraft takes readers into the decaying hill country of Massachusetts around a village called Dunwich. The strange Whateley family lives in a lonely farmhouse there, and young Wilbur Whateley grows at a frightening rate and goes looking for a forbidden book. What is the story called?
context: Published in Weird Tales in April 1929, the story sends Wilbur Whateley to the library of Miskatonic University in search of the Necronomicon. Its Massachusetts hill country is one of Lovecraft's invented corners of New England.

question: Doc Savage, the pulps' Man of Bronze, was raised from birth by trainers his father hired to make him a superman in body and mind. In 1973 the science-fiction writer Philip José Farmer wrote a mock biography of Doc that treats the pulp novels as fictionalised memoirs of a real man, and it even fixes his birthplace. Where was Doc born, according to Farmer?
answer: Aboard a schooner off Andros Island in the Bahamas
choices: Aboard a schooner off Andros Island in the Bahamas
In Hidalgo, his secret Central American haven
In Manhattan, in his father's hospital suite
In the Yucatan, in his father's Mayan refuge
context: Philip José Farmer's Doc Savage: His Apocalyptic Life (1973) places Doc's birth on 12 November 1901, aboard the schooner Orion in a cove off the northern tip of Andros Island in the Bahamas. Doc's full name is Clark Savage Jr.

question: During World War II, Robert Heinlein worked as a civilian engineer for the US Navy at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard, and he recruited two fellow science-fiction writers, Isaac Asimov and L. Sprague de Camp, to join him there. Among other jobs, the three brainstormed unconventional defences against kamikaze attacks. What was the Navy facility called?
context: Heinlein worked as a civil servant at the Navy Aircraft Materials Center at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard and brought in Asimov and de Camp to work there too. He had left the Navy in 1934 because of tuberculosis.

question: In 1839 Edgar Allan Poe published a Gothic horror story. A visitor rides up to a crumbling old family mansion that stands beside a still, dark pond, and notices a thin crack running down its wall. Inside, the nervous last heir of the family lives with his pale, sickly twin sister, and the house itself seems to share their gloom. What is the story called?
answer: The Fall of the House of Usher
choices: The Fall of the House of Usher
The Masque of the Red Death
context: Published in Burton's Gentleman's Magazine in September 1839, the story ties the Usher family to the house itself, so that the House of the title means both the mansion and the bloodline. Roger Corman filmed it in 1960 with Vincent Price.

question: After Robert Howard died in 1936, L. Sprague de Camp and Lin Carter kept the Conan stories alive for decades, editing old manuscripts, completing unfinished pieces and writing new Conan tales of their own. The very first Conan books came from a small New York publisher that began putting the stories between hard covers in 1950, starting with Conan the Conqueror. Which publisher put them out?
context: Gnome Press published Conan the Conqueror in 1950 as the first Conan book, in hardcover, and later volumes carried L. Sprague de Camp's edits. The Lancer paperbacks of 1966 to 1971, with Frank Frazetta covers, later made Conan a cultural phenomenon.

question: Tolkien made up a writing system for his elf languages Quenya and Sindarin. It has 24 basic letters grouped by the sounds they make, not by ABC order. You see it on the One Ring and on the west gate of Moria ('Speak, friend, and enter'). What is the script called?
context: Tengwar means 'letters' in Quenya. Tolkien invented it in the 1930s. Cirth is a separate runic alphabet used by the Dwarves for stone-cutting. The One Ring inscription is in Tengwar letters but renders the Black Speech of Mordor — 'Ash nazg durbatulûk, ash nazg gimbatul...' Tolkien also invented the Sarati (an earlier elvish script) and various tengwar modes for different languages.

question: Edgar Allan Poe died in Baltimore on October 7, 1849, four days after he was found delirious, wearing someone else's clothes, outside Ryan's Tavern. His death has remained mysterious for over 175 years. He was repeatedly heard to call out a name in his hospital delirium. What name?
context: No 'Reynolds' connected to Poe has ever been definitively identified — Jeremiah Reynolds, the Antarctic explorer Poe had once championed, is one candidate. The 'cooping' theory holds that Poe was kidnapped by political operatives, plied with alcohol, and forced to vote multiple times at different polls (election day was October 3); the 'rabies' theory was proposed in 1996 by R. Michael Benitez. Whitman, Baudelaire, and Mallarmé all wrote in defense of Poe's reputation after attacks by his literary executor Rufus Griswold.

question: Walter Gibson wrote The Shadow pulps under the pen name Maxwell Grant, starting in 1931. On the radio the Shadow is the wealthy Lamont Cranston, but in the pulps Cranston is a real millionaire playboy whose identity the Shadow borrows while Cranston is off travelling the world. The pulp Shadow's real name was only revealed in 1937, in The Shadow Unmasks: he is a famed First World War aviator. What is the pulp Shadow's true identity?
context: In the pulps the Shadow is really Kent Allard, a famous aviator who flew for the French in the First World War and was nicknamed the Black Eagle; his name was revealed in The Shadow Unmasks (1937). Lamont Cranston is a rich playboy whose identity he borrows, and the radio show made Cranston the Shadow himself.

question: Tolkien wrote a short story around 1939, first published in the Dublin Review in January 1945, about a painter named Niggle whose great picture of a tree, with a forest in the distance, is forever being interrupted by chores for his lame neighbour Parish. Many readers take it as a picture of Tolkien's own struggle to finish his work, though Tolkien said it was more mythical than allegorical. What is the story called?
context: Leaf by Niggle first appeared in the Dublin Review in January 1945 and was collected with On Fairy-Stories in Tree and Leaf (1964). Tolkien said the story came to him one morning in 1939 and that he wrote it out almost in a single sitting.

question: Lord Dunsany was an Anglo-Irish baron who wrote fantasy in a formal, old-fashioned style modelled on the King James Bible. His 1905 book of invented gods, describing a whole pantheon and its creation of the world, was a major influence on H.P. Lovecraft. What was that book called?
context: The Gods of Pegana (1905) was followed by Time and the Gods (1906) and many story collections. Lovecraft's Dream Cycle stories, such as The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, are open homages to Dunsany.

question: Edgar Allan Poe published his only complete novel in 1838 — a strange seafaring adventure full of mutiny, starvation, and a voyage toward the southern polar region. Jules Verne later wrote a sequel to it, and Lovecraft drew on it for his own work. What was the novel called?
answer: The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym
choices: The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym
context: Pym was published by Harper & Brothers in July 1838. The novel's last lines describe a white shrouded figure in the polar sea — Lovecraft used the cry 'Tekeli-li!' from the novel as the cry of the shoggoths in Mountains of Madness. Jules Verne's 1897 sequel was An Antarctic Mystery (Le Sphinx des glaces). Borges wrote that Pym's final whiteness was the model for Moby-Dick's whiteness chapter.

question: H.P. Lovecraft's 1931 novella follows a young traveller to a decaying Massachusetts seaport whose people have a strange, staring, fish-like look, and whose fishermen haul in more than they should from a black reef offshore. The traveller stays one night too many. What is the town called?
context: The Shadow over Innsmouth was written in 1931 and published as a small book in 1936, one of the very few Lovecraft books printed in his lifetime. The black reef offshore is Devil Reef.

question: In 2007 Christopher Tolkien edited and released The Children of Húrin, a long tale from his father's papers about Túrin, a doomed hero of Men in Middle-earth's First Age, with paintings by Alan Lee. J.R.R. Tolkien named one old source for that cursed hero: the hapless Kullervo, whose story he had retold in prose as an Oxford undergraduate in 1914. From which national epic did Kullervo come?
context: Tolkien wrote The Story of Kullervo, a prose version of a cycle from Elias Lönnrot's Kalevala, as an undergraduate at Exeter College, Oxford, in 1914 and 1915, and it became one of the sources for Túrin Turambar. The Children of Húrin came out in April 2007 with illustrations by Alan Lee.

question: Robert E. Howard took his own life on 11 June 1936 in Cross Plains, Texas, as his mother lay in her final coma. He left behind a typed couplet: 'All fled, all done, so lift me on the pyre; the feast is over and the lamps expire.' The lines were not his own. Where did they come from?
choices: An original couplet Howard composed for his own grave
A line from Howard's own 1929 poem 'The King and the Oak'
An anonymous couplet from a 1934 issue of Weird Tales
context: The couplet comes from Viola Garvin's poem The House of Caesar; accounts differ on whether it was found in Howard's typewriter or in his wallet. Howard was 30, and his mother died the following day.

question: H.P. Lovecraft died in Providence on March 15, 1937, of cancer, with his stories scattered across old issues of pulp magazines. Two young readers who had corresponded with him were determined not to let his work vanish. In 1939 they founded a small Wisconsin press for the sole purpose of keeping it in print, and that year they published his first big hardback collection. Who were the two founders?
choices: Frank Belknap Long and Clark Ashton Smith
Lin Carter and L. Sprague de Camp
context: August Derleth and Donald Wandrei founded Arkham House in 1939, and its first book, The Outsider and Others, gathered stories they selected themselves. Derleth later wrote many Mythos tales of his own.

question: John W. Campbell took over as editor of Astounding with its October 1937 issue and renamed it Astounding Science-Fiction in March 1938. Campbell wrote fiction too, under the pen name Don A. Stuart, taken from his wife's maiden name, and as Stuart he published Who Goes There? that August. That June, a Brooklyn teenager studying at Columbia University had walked into Campbell's office to hand over a story in person, and Campbell talked with him for more than an hour; in July 1939 the young man's story Trends appeared in Astounding. Who was he?
context: Asimov delivered a story to Campbell in person in June 1938, and Campbell spent more than an hour with him. His first sale went to Amazing Stories (Marooned Off Vesta, March 1939), and Trends appeared in Astounding in July 1939. Campbell's Don A. Stuart stories include Twilight (1934) and Who Goes There? (1938).

question: The American writer who created Tarzan took control of his own work in 1923 by setting up a company and printing his own books through it. His ranch north of Los Angeles, which he had named Tarzana, later gave its name to the community that grew up around it. What was the company officially called?
context: In 1923 Burroughs set up Edgar Rice Burroughs, Inc., and through the 1930s it printed his own books. He had bought his ranch in 1919 and named it Tarzana, and the people of the community that grew around it voted to take the same name.

question: Tolkien served in the Lancashire Fusiliers as a signals officer in 1916. He sailed for France in early June, reached the Somme in early July, and fought on until trench fever sent him home to England on November 8, 1916. Four schoolboys had been at the heart of the T.C.B.S. (Tea Club and Barrovian Society), the little club Tolkien and his friends formed at King Edward's School in Birmingham, and two of the four died in the Somme campaign that same year. What were those two friends' names?
answer: Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Bache Smith
choices: Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Bache Smith
Hugh Cary Gilson and Edward Williams
context: Rob Gilson was killed on 1 July 1916, the first day of the Somme, and Geoffrey Bache Smith died that December of wounds from a shell. The fourth member, Christopher Wiseman, survived the war, and Tolkien later edited Smith's poems as A Spring Harvest (1918). Charles Williams and Owen Barfield were later Inklings friends, not T.C.B.S. members.

question: Frank Herbert worked for years on Dune before its 1965 hardcover publication by Chilton Books, a Philadelphia firm best known for auto-repair manuals. The seed of the project was a magazine article Herbert researched about Oregon's shifting sand dunes and the effort to tame them with grass. Long before the finished novel, he wrote an outline of a simpler version of the story, and in 2005 his son Brian Herbert and Kevin J. Anderson turned it into an alternate Dune story for the book The Road to Dune. What is that story called?
context: Spice Planet, written by Brian Herbert and Kevin J. Anderson from Frank Herbert's original outline for Dune, appeared in The Road to Dune in September 2005.

question: Philip K. Dick wrote 44 novels between 1955 and his death in March 1982, a few months before Ridley Scott's Blade Runner premiered. His 1981 novel about a divine encounter grew out of a mystical episode Dick lived through in 1974 and his idea that reality is a 'Black Iron Prison'. The novel takes its title from a five-letter acronym for a godlike intelligence. What was the 1981 novel called?
context: VALIS stands for Vast Active Living Intelligence System. The novel grew from what Dick called his 2-3-74 experiences of February and March 1974, which he spent years trying to explain in a private journal later published as the Exegesis.

question: Tolkien wrote The Hobbit largely between 1930 and 1932 during his time as Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford. The book famously opens with a line he scribbled on the back of an exam paper he was grading. He didn't know what a 'hobbit' was at the time — the word came first. The exam paper was for the School Certificate Examination in English. What was the opening line he scribbled?
answer: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit
choices: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit
Far over the misty mountains cold
There was once a hobbit who lived in a hole
Bilbo Baggins of Bag End was no ordinary hobbit
context: Tolkien said the line came to him 'out of nowhere' while he was looking at a blank examination booklet. He set it aside and only returned to writing the book around 1932. He read drafts aloud to his children. C.S. Lewis read it in manuscript around 1933 and pushed him to finish it. Susan Dagnall at George Allen & Unwin recommended publication. The first edition (September 21, 1937) had a print run of 1,500 copies.

question: Manly Wade Wellman started out as a 1930s pulp writer. Later he became the top American folklore-horror writer. From 1951 on he wrote the John the Balladeer stories, also called 'Silver John,' set in the Appalachian Mountains of North Carolina. Silver John is a Korean War veteran with a silver-stringed guitar who battles witches, devils, and dark fae drawn from real Appalachian folk tales. Where did his first Silver John story appear in 1951?
answer: The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction
choices: The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction
Weird Tales after the Wright era end
Unknown Worlds, the Campbell sister title
Beyond Fantasy Fiction, the Galaxy spinoff
context: Wellman's 'O Ugly Bird!' appeared in F&SF in December 1951. The Silver John stories are characteristically narrated in first-person mountain dialect. Wellman won the British Fantasy Society's August Derleth Award (1975) for Worse Things Waiting; he also won the World Fantasy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1980. He died in 1986 in Chapel Hill, North Carolina at age 82. His Silver John novels include After Dark (1980) and The Lost and the Lurking (1981).

question: Karl Edward Wagner trained as a psychiatrist in North Carolina before he became a writer, and from 1980 he edited the long-running anthology The Year's Best Horror Stories. He created an immortal red-haired swordsman who is the Cain of Genesis, marked by God after killing his brother and doomed to wander the Earth forever. The hero debuted in a small-press novel in 1970 and appeared in about fifteen stories before Wagner died in 1994. What was the hero's name?
context: Kane first appeared in Wagner's novel Darkness Weaves (1970). Wagner held a degree in psychiatry, mixed sword-and-sorcery with horror, and edited The Year's Best Horror Stories from 1980 to 1994.

question: William Hope Hodgson wrote four big weird-fiction novels in the early 1900s before dying at Ypres in 1918. His most cosmic novel came out in 1912. It is set far in the future on an Earth where the sun has gone dark. The last humans live in a huge pyramid-fortress called the Last Redoubt, ringed by monsters from the black outside. What was the novel called?
choices: The Boats of the Glen Carrig
context: The Night Land's prose imitates 17th-century English deliberately — Hodgson considered it formal scriptural style appropriate to the eschatological subject. The novel was reviewed unenthusiastically in 1912 but became a major influence on Lovecraft (who called it 'one of the most potent pieces of macabre imagination ever written'), Clark Ashton Smith, and later Gene Wolfe. Hodgson was a former merchant-marine officer; the sea-horror in his earlier novels The Boats of the Glen Carrig (1907) and The Ghost Pirates (1909) drew from his own North Atlantic experience.

question: Algernon Blackwood, an English author of supernatural fiction, published a 1907 novella widely considered one of the finest weird stories ever written. Two friends canoeing down the Danube camp on a tiny island of sand choked with low, endlessly rustling bushes, and slowly sense that the plants themselves are watching them. Lovecraft later ranked it as the single best weird story he had ever read. What was the story called?
context: The Willows was published in The Listener and Other Stories (1907). Blackwood himself had canoed the Danube in 1900. His other major weird stories include The Wendigo (1910, the source of the modern North American Wendigo mythos in popular culture) and the John Silence stories — proto-psychic-investigator tales. Blackwood lived 1869-1951 and became a BBC radio personality in his later years, reading his own ghost stories on Christmas broadcasts.

question: M.R. (Montague Rhodes) James was a Cambridge medieval scholar who wrote ghost stories to read aloud to friends at Christmas. He published four collections between 1904 and 1925, and his tales defined what is now called the antiquarian ghost story: bookish scholars, ancient objects and slow-building dread. His first collection, in 1904, includes a story about a Cambridge professor who finds an old bronze whistle in the ruins of a Templar preceptory on the East Anglian coast, blows it, and finds that something is now following him. What is the story called?
answer: Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad
choices: Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad
The Treasure of Abbot Thomas (1904 tale)
Count Magnus and the Black Pilgrim Tale
context: The story first appeared in Ghost Stories of an Antiquary (1904); James had read it to a King's College Christmas gathering in 1903. The whistle bears the Latin words Quis est iste qui venit, 'Who is this who is coming?', and the professor, Parkins, is staying at the Globe Inn in Burnstow.

question: H.P. Lovecraft wrote one of his most science-fictional horror tales between February and September 1930, and Weird Tales printed it in August 1931. A Miskatonic University instructor trades letters with a lonely Vermont farmer after the great floods of 1927 wash strange bodies down the rivers, and the hills turn out to hide fungoid, crab-like miners from the planet Yuggoth, who can carry a human brain to the stars inside a metal cylinder. What is the story called?
choices: The Dreams in the Witch House
context: The Whisperer in Darkness was written between February and September 1930 and first printed in Weird Tales in August 1931. Its aliens, the fungoid Mi-Go from Yuggoth, mine the Vermont hills and can carry a human brain through space in a metal cylinder, and the story opens in the wake of the real Vermont floods of November 1927.

question: Khuzdul is the secret language Tolkien invented for the Dwarves, its sounds modeled on Semitic languages like Hebrew rather than on the Indo-European roots of his Elvish tongues. Only a few Khuzdul phrases appear in The Lord of the Rings. At the Battle of the Hornburg, Gimli cuts down orcs to the Dwarves' ancient war-cry. What is that war-cry?
context: The cry translates as 'Axes of the Dwarves! The Dwarves are upon you!' Tolkien designed Khuzdul phonetically to feel angular and stone-like, matching the Dwarves' culture. The Dwarves' true names (in Khuzdul) are kept secret from outsiders; the names we know (Thorin, Balin, Gimli, etc.) are Mannish translations from a related Northern-Mannish tongue. Tolkien based the secret-language idea partly on Hebrew traditions about the Tetragrammaton.

question: Edgar Allan Poe launched the detective genre in April 1841 with a tale in Graham's Magazine. In it, a brilliant French thinker solves the locked-room killing of two women in Paris. Conan Doyle later called the story the direct ancestor of Sherlock Holmes. What was the family name of the two murdered women?
context: Madame L'Espanaye and her daughter are the two women murdered in The Murders in the Rue Morgue, the first Dupin story. Poe followed it with The Mystery of Marie Roget (1842) and The Purloined Letter (1844), and Conan Doyle acknowledged Dupin as an ancestor of Sherlock Holmes.

question: Beyond Conan, Robert Howard wrote about many other heroes, and one of the best is the last king of the Picts, who leads his dwindling people against Rome's armies in Britain and even strikes at Hadrian's Wall. The Picts were a real ancient people of northern Britain, and most of his stories ran in Weird Tales between 1930 and 1932. What was this character's name?
context: Bran Mak Morn is the last king of Howard's romanticized Picts and fights the Romans in Britain; his final story, Worms of the Earth, ran in Weird Tales in November 1932. Howard's friend and correspondent Lovecraft slipped a reference to Bran into The Whisperer in Darkness.

question: In late 1951 Tolkien wrote an enormous letter to the publisher Milton Waldman, explaining how The Silmarillion and The Lord of the Rings fit together into one mythology. In it he said that all of this material is mainly concerned with three things, and he warned that the urge to make and sub-create, once it turns possessive, ends in the lust for power. Which three things did he name?
context: In his letter to Milton Waldman (Letter 131 in the published Letters), Tolkien wrote that the legendarium is mainly concerned with Fall, Mortality and the Machine. By the Machine he meant using outside plans or devices instead of developing inner powers and talents.

question: In March 1942, the American science-fiction writer Isaac Asimov published a short story called 'Runaround' in the magazine Astounding Science Fiction. In it, he laid out his famous Three Laws of Robotics in full for the first time: laws that told fictional robots never to harm humans, always to obey orders, and always to protect themselves. Asimov later said that the magazine's editor had actually helped him shape the laws into their final form while editing his earlier robot stories. Who was that editor?
context: John W. Campbell edited Astounding Science Fiction from 1937 to 1971 and was a towering — if controversial — influence on the Golden Age of SF. Asimov's earliest robot stories ('Liar!' 1941, 'Robbie' 1940) hinted at the rules; Campbell pushed Asimov to formalize them. The Three Laws first appear in named form in 'Runaround' (March 1942 Astounding). Campbell also discovered and developed Robert Heinlein, A.E. van Vogt, Theodore Sturgeon, and Lester del Rey. Frederik Pohl edited Galaxy and If; Anthony Boucher edited F&SF; H.L. Gold founded Galaxy.

question: Poe's 1841 story 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' gave the world its first fictional detective. It also gave the genre its toolkit: the odd genius amateur, the slow-witted friend who tells the story, the locked-room puzzle, and the big reveal at the end. Dupin solves the case with a method Poe named. The same word was later borrowed for code-breaking, crime science, and the study of the mind. What did Poe call it?
context: Poe used 'ratiocination' as a noun for systematic, reasoning analysis. He published three Dupin stories — Rue Morgue (1841), Marie Rogêt (1842), and The Purloined Letter (1844). Dupin's method blends induction from physical clues, deduction from behavior, and what we would now call profiling. Conan Doyle adopted nearly all of Poe's apparatus for Sherlock Holmes. Poe's term 'ratiocination' was the closest the 1840s came to articulating what twentieth-century cognitive science would call 'analytical reasoning.'

question: In Part III of Lovecraft's 1928 story The Call of Cthulhu, the sailor Gustaf Johansen lands on a strange island newly risen from the South Pacific. Its geometry is non-Euclidean — angles that should be convex appear concave to the eye, and a massive door swings inward and outward simultaneously. The passage became a literary reference point for impossible geometry in horror. What did Lovecraft famously call the geometry of R'lyeh?
answer: 'Loathsomely redolent of spheres and dimensions apart from ours'
choices: 'Loathsomely redolent of spheres and dimensions apart from ours'
'Made of corners that opened sideways from sanity itself'
'A geometry of impossible curvature that bent the gaze of the beholder'
'Carved against the laws of Euclid by a mathematics older than men'
context: Lovecraft had been reading popular accounts of Einstein and Riemann throughout the 1920s. His 1928 phrase 'spheres and dimensions apart from ours' was a science-aware way of conveying that R'lyeh's geometry obeyed rules incompatible with our spacetime. The Emma's voyage starts in New Zealand in March 1925 and ends with Johansen alone, surviving to write the manuscript in Oslo. The story's three-part structure — the professor's papers, the New Orleans cult raid, and the Norwegian's account — gives it a documentary feel Lovecraft would refine throughout his career.

question: Tolkien first wrote the Riddles in the Dark chapter of The Hobbit for the 1937 edition, then rewrote it substantially in 1947 to fit the newly finished Lord of the Rings. In that book, the Ring needed to be a sinister object Gollum would never willingly surrender. What was the most important plot change between the two versions of the chapter?
answer: In 1937 Gollum cheerfully offered the Ring as the prize for losing the riddle game; in 1947 Tolkien rewrote it so Gollum lied and tried to murder Bilbo when he lost
choices: In 1937 Gollum cheerfully offered the Ring as the prize for losing the riddle game; in 1947 Tolkien rewrote it so Gollum lied and tried to murder Bilbo when he lost
In 1937 the cave was located in the Misty Mountains; in 1947 Tolkien moved it to the Iron Hills
In 1937 Bilbo defeated Gollum in single combat; in 1947 Tolkien revised the contest to a true riddle exchange
In 1937 Gollum had no name; in 1947 Tolkien gave him the Sméagol backstory and the river-folk origin
context: Tolkien justified the 1947 rewrite as a textual correction — within the in-story conceit, Bilbo had originally told the Riddles chapter wrongly in the Red Book of Westmarch, then later told the true version to Frodo and Gandalf. The 1951 second edition of The Hobbit reflects this rewrite; copies of the 1937 first edition with the original benign Gollum are extremely valuable to collectors. Tolkien himself wrote in a 1959 letter that the original chapter 'gave a wholly different impression of the chief character.'

question: Robert E. Howard's Conan stories ran in Weird Tales from December 1932 to October 1936. Howard wrote only one full-length Conan novel, in 1934, for a British book publisher that went bankrupt before printing it, so Weird Tales ran it as a five-part serial from December 1935 to April 1936, the last months of Howard's life. In it King Conan of Aquilonia loses his throne to a sorcerer raised from the dead and must find a jewel called the Heart of Ahriman. What was the novel titled?
answer: The Hour of the Dragon (later republished as Conan the Conqueror)
choices: The Hour of the Dragon (later republished as Conan the Conqueror)
The Phoenix on the Sword (the original Conan debut)
Beyond the Black River (the frontier-Pictish horror)
context: Howard wrote The Hour of the Dragon in 1934 for the British publisher Denis Archer, which went bankrupt before printing it, so it first appeared as a Weird Tales serial from December 1935 to April 1936. It was his only full-length Conan novel; its villain is Xaltotun of Acheron, and Gnome Press first published it as a hardcover book, Conan the Conqueror, in 1950.

question: Two of H.P. Lovecraft's young correspondents founded Arkham House in 1939 for one purpose: to keep his work in print after his death in 1937. Their first book that year was a thick hardback of his best stories, The Outsider and Others, which they chose themselves. Advance orders were taken at $3.50 a copy against a list price of $5, and the book sold slowly but steadily until it went out of print early in 1944. Today a first edition is a prize for horror collectors. How many copies were printed?
context: The Outsider and Others was printed in 1,268 copies in 1939. Advance orders were taken at $3.50 each against a planned price of $5, and the book went out of print early in 1944.

question: Philip K. Dick, suspicious of the Blade Runner project, saw a 20-minute rough cut at Warner Bros. in October 1981 and was deeply moved. He died of a stroke on March 2, 1982, three months before the film's June release. One writer later set down the making of the film, Rutger Hauer's 'Tears in Rain' speech included. Who recorded Hauer's full account of writing it?
answer: Paul M. Sammon, author of Future Noir
choices: Paul M. Sammon, author of Future Noir
Jerry Pournelle, in his Galaxy column
Roger Ebert, in his 1992 Great Movies
Pauline Kael, in the 1982 New Yorker
context: Sammon's Future Noir (1996, revised 2007) remains the definitive making-of book on Blade Runner. Hauer reduced what was a longer scripted speech to its iconic core: 'I've seen things you people wouldn't believe. Attack ships on fire off the shoulder of Orion. I watched C-beams glitter in the dark near the Tannhäuser Gate. All those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain. Time to die.' The original script lines (which Hauer kept) were technical descriptions of off-world warfare; Hauer transmuted them into poetry. Ridley Scott has called it the single most moving line ever written for him.

question: The Silmarillion, published by Christopher Tolkien in 1977, four years after his father's death, tells of three holy jewels, the Silmarils, made by the Elf Feanor of the Noldor in the Blessed Realm. They are stolen by the first Dark Lord, Morgoth, set in his iron crown, and become the cause of long wars. What did Feanor put inside the Silmarils that no other jewel could ever hold?
answer: The light of the Two Trees of Valinor (Telperion and Laurelin), captured before the Trees were destroyed by Morgoth and Ungoliant
choices: The light of the Two Trees of Valinor (Telperion and Laurelin), captured before the Trees were destroyed by Morgoth and Ungoliant
The first stars Varda had kindled in the sky during the elves' awakening at Cuiviénen
A drop of the blood of the Vala Aulë, shed during the forging of the Dwarven Seven Fathers
The compressed essence of Eru Ilúvatar's first creative thought before the Music of the Ainur
context: Yavanna made the Two Trees, silver Telperion and golden Laurelin, which lit Valinor before the Sun and Moon. When Morgoth and the great spider Ungoliant destroyed them, the Silmarils held the only light of the Trees left in the world.

question: On the night of September 19, 1931, C.S. Lewis walked along Addison's Walk at Magdalen College, Oxford with Tolkien and Hugo Dyson. Tolkien argued that the pagan myths Lewis loved were splintered lights pointing toward the one true myth that had actually happened in history. The conversation eventually converted Lewis to Christianity, and Tolkien captured its argument in a poem Lewis called personally important. What is the poem called?
choices: The Lay of Aotrou and Itroun
context: Mythopoeia is a 148-line poem written for Lewis. Its key argument: man is a 'sub-creator' bearing 'the refracted Light through whom is splintered from a single White / to many hues, and endlessly combined / in living shapes that move from mind to mind.' Lewis's account of the conversation is in Surprised by Joy (1955) and in a letter to Arthur Greeves dated 18 October 1931. Lewis converted to theism in 1929 and to Christianity specifically after the Addison's Walk conversation. Mythopoeia was published posthumously in Tree and Leaf (1964) with 'On Fairy-Stories' and 'Leaf by Niggle.'

question: On October 3, 1849, Edgar Allan Poe was found dying outside Ryan's Tavern in Baltimore, delirious and wearing stained clothes that were not his own. Over four days in the hospital he refused the alcohol he was offered and kept calling out one name that no biographer has ever identified. He died at age 40. In 1996 one doctor argued Poe had died of an illness carried by animals, not of drink. Who was that doctor?
answer: Dr. R. Michael Benitez, the University of Maryland cardiologist who proposed rabies as the cause
choices: Dr. R. Michael Benitez, the University of Maryland cardiologist who proposed rabies as the cause
Dr. John Carlson, the medical historian who proposed encephalitis
Dr. Marie-Claude Caron, the French academic who proposed brain tumor
Dr. Peter Kennedy, the Edinburgh neurologist who proposed Lyme disease
context: Benitez presented the rabies hypothesis at a 1996 medical history conference and published it in the Maryland Medical Journal. His argument: Poe's symptoms (delirium, hydrophobia-like aversion to drink, perspiration, hallucinations) match rabies's presentation; alcoholism alone does not explain the four days of symptoms before death. Competing theories include cooping (election-day kidnapping for repeated voting), brain tumor, syphilis tertiary, and heavy-metal poisoning. The mystery of who clothed Poe, where he had been, and who 'Reynolds' was remains unsolved.

question: John W. Campbell, editing Astounding Science-Fiction from 1937 through 1971, published in the August 1938 issue a novella that became the basis for two classic Hollywood films — Howard Hawks's 1951 The Thing from Another World and John Carpenter's 1982 The Thing. Campbell wrote the novella himself under his Don A. Stuart pseudonym. The story is set at a fictional Antarctic research station. Twelve men discover a frozen alien spacecraft and the still-frozen body of its pilot, which they thaw out in the lab. The alien turns out to be a shape-shifting predator. The novella's title literally asks the sentry's challenge; what does that title phrase reveal about the survivors' climactic problem?
answer: Asks 'Who Goes There?' — by the climax no one can tell who is human and who is the alien wearing a human's face
choices: Asks 'Who Goes There?' — by the climax no one can tell who is human and who is the alien wearing a human's face
Asks 'Who Goes There?' — the alien is identified by being unable to give the proper sentry response in English
Asks 'Who Goes There?' — the alien is detected when it answers incorrectly in clipped Norwegian dialect
Asks 'Who Goes There?' — the alien is found out when it cannot reply with the radio operator's call sign
context: Campbell's novella appeared in Astounding in August 1938 under the pen name Don A. Stuart. Its alien can imitate any living thing it absorbs, memories and all, which is why no one at the station can trust anyone else. John Carpenter's 1982 film The Thing stays closer to the novella than the 1951 version did.

question: Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings came out in three volumes from George Allen & Unwin between July 1954 and October 1955; Tolkien had planned one long book in six parts, but the publisher split it up. Tolkien was unhappy with the title chosen for the final volume, The Return of the King, because he felt it gave away too much of the story. What title did he prefer for it?
context: Tolkien felt The Return of the King revealed too much and preferred The War of the Ring, but the publisher kept its own title, and the third volume appeared on 20 October 1955. In his six-book plan, Book Five was to be called The War of the Ring and Book Six The End of the Third Age.

question: Lord Dunsany, an Anglo-Irish baron and war veteran, was a major influence on the young H.P. Lovecraft. He wrote in a deliberately archaic, scriptural style modelled on the King James Bible. His 1924 fantasy novel about a king's son and an elven princess is widely considered his masterpiece. What was that novel called?
choices: The Curse of the Wise Woman
context: Lord Dunsany (1878-1957) published The King of Elfland's Daughter in 1924, and his dreamlike invented mythologies were a model for Lovecraft's Dream Cycle stories.

question: The paranoid science-fiction novelist behind Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? experienced a series of religious-mystical events in February and March 1974 -- what he called the '2-3-74 experiences' -- that consumed the rest of his life and shaped his last six novels. He spent the next eight years writing an enormous private journal of philosophical speculation about what had happened to him. The journal eventually ran over 8,000 pages. A selection was published posthumously in 2011, twenty-nine years after his death. What was the published selection called?
answer: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
choices: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
context: The Exegesis is over 1,000,000 words in total. The 2011 published selection (edited by Pamela Jackson and Jonathan Lethem) ran 944 pages, a 10% selection of the available archive. Dick's experience began with a delivery driver wearing a Christian fish-symbol necklace; from there Dick believed he was receiving 'pink light' transmissions from a Vast Active Living Intelligence System (VALIS). His diagnoses ran from schizophrenia to temporal lobe epilepsy to vitamin overdose to genuine gnostic revelation, depending on his mood. Dick died in March 1982 in Santa Ana, California, of a stroke.

question: Tolkien's Middle-earth mythology began as private writing during the First World War (WWI). The earliest surviving fragments are pencil drafts in notebooks he kept while recovering from trench fever in late 1916. One of the very first stories he drafted was the tragic doomed love between an elf-maiden and a mortal man — the seed of what became the Beren and Lúthien legend. In 1917, in Roos Wood, Yorkshire, Tolkien's wife Edith danced for him among the hemlock blossoms; he immediately connected the moment to his story. What names appear on the joint Tolkien gravestone in Wolvercote Cemetery, Oxford?
choices: Galadriel and Celeborn, the immortal couple
Arwen and Aragorn, the mortal-elven pair
Eärendil and Elwing, the lovers of the Sea
context: Edith Bratt had been Tolkien's secret fiancée since his teens. After his hospitalization in late 1916 with trench fever, Edith danced for him among the hemlock blooms of Roos Wood in East Yorkshire. They married March 22, 1916 (before his deployment to France). Edith died November 29, 1971; J.R.R. died September 2, 1973. Their joint grave in Wolvercote Cemetery, North Oxford bears the names Christopher Tolkien arranged: 'Edith Mary Tolkien, Lúthien, 1889-1971' and 'John Ronald Reuel Tolkien, Beren, 1892-1973.'

question: On August 15, 1977, the Big Ear radio telescope at Ohio State recorded a 72-second signal from the direction of Sagittarius, roughly 30 times louder than the surrounding background noise, and it has never been detected again. The telescope that heard it is gone too: in 1998, after developers bought its site from the university, the giant instrument was taken apart. What did the developers use the land for?
answer: To expand a nearby golf course
choices: To expand a nearby golf course
To build a regional shopping mall
To lay a new interstate highway
To house a college football stadium
context: Big Ear was disassembled in 1998 after developers bought the site from the university, and they used the land to expand a nearby golf course. The telescope had searched the sky for alien signals since the 1970s; Jerry Ehman circled the 1977 signal on its printout and wrote 'Wow!' beside it.

question: Hal Foster's medieval-knight comic strip launched in 1937 and ran continuously in Sunday newspapers for over 80 years. The hero is a young Norse prince from Thule who joins King Arthur's Round Table and later weds an Asian princess named Aleta. What is the strip called?
context: Foster drew Prince Valiant himself from February 1937 until 1971. The strip is set in 5th-century Arthurian Britain but ranges across Europe, Africa, and even North America. King Features Syndicate distributes it. Foster had previously drawn the Tarzan Sunday strip from 1931 to 1937 before launching Valiant as his own creation. Aleta of the Misty Isles becomes Val's wife in 1946.

question: Lee Falk created a costumed jungle hero in 1936, considered the first hero in a purple bodysuit and eye-mask. He lives in a Skull Cave deep in the African jungle and is treated as immortal by the locals. Really, each generation is a new son taking over from his father. Who is this hero?
context: The Phantom debuted in newspaper strips on February 17, 1936 — predating Superman (1938) by two years, making him arguably the first costumed superhero. Lee Falk also created Mandrake the Magician (1934). The current Phantom is the 21st in line. The Skull Cave is in the fictional African country of Bangalla. Native tribes call him 'the Ghost Who Walks.'

question: In 1844 Edgar Allan Poe wrote what may be the most famous detective story of the 1800s. In it, a letter is stolen and the Paris police cannot find it, even after tearing the suspect's apartment apart. Dupin cracks the case by seeing the letter is hidden in plain sight on the mantel, turned inside out and re-addressed. Later thinkers like Lacan and Derrida made the story famous in literary theory. What is it called?
choices: The Murders in the Rue Morgue
