context: Published in The Gift annual in 1844. The 'Minister D—' steals a compromising letter from the Queen and hides it in plain sight; Dupin recovers it. Jacques Lacan's 1956 seminar on the story and Jacques Derrida's response ('Le facteur de la vérité') are landmark texts of post-structuralist literary theory. Borges, Eco, and Auster have all written homage-stories. The phrase 'hiding in plain sight' is sometimes credited to Poe.

question: From 1920 to 1943, Tolkien wrote letters each year to his own children, signed as if from Father Christmas at the North Pole. The letters were illustrated and had a running cast -- polar bears, gnomes, and a bumbling helper. Who is the accident-prone North Pole sidekick in the letters?
choices: Snow Bear (the rival of Father Christmas)
context: Tolkien wrote the letters for his children John, Michael, Christopher and Priscilla and illustrated each one himself; the bumbling Polar Bear causes most of the trouble at the North Pole. Baillie Tolkien edited the published collection in 1976.

question: Sherlock Holmes debuted in A Study in Scarlet in 1887. Readers saw him as a descendant of Poe's Dupin, and Doyle later admitted the debt in his 1924 memoir. But Doyle also based Holmes on a real Edinburgh medical professor whose way of reading a patient had stunned him as a student. Doyle worked under him as a clinical clerk in 1877 and 1878. The professor could name a patient's job, home region, illness, and recent travels at a glance. Who was he?
context: Joseph Bell (1837-1911) taught at Edinburgh's medical school and amazed students by reading a patient's job and history from small physical clues. Conan Doyle worked for him as a clerk and later acknowledged him as the model for Holmes.

question: Robert Howard's 1935 Conan story Beyond the Black River takes the barbarian to a log fort on the edge of a forest held by the Picts, and critics have called it a transplanted Western. For the setting of that Pictish wilderness, Howard drew on a frontier novel by an American writer who is better known today for the eerie stories of The King in Yellow. Who was the novelist?
context: The critics Cerasini and Hoffman call Beyond the Black River a transplanted Western, and say Howard modelled his Pictish wilderness on the setting of Robert W. Chambers's frontier novel The Little Red Foot. The story first ran in Weird Tales in May and June 1935.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs invented several lost-world settings besides Tarzan and John Carter. In 1918 he ran a magazine serial about a captured German U-boat captain and a stranded American who find a strange island in the South Pacific. On the island, life gets more modern as you travel north. The 1975 Amicus film series was based on it. The island has one odd feature: a single river cuts through the steep cliffs that ring it. What did Burroughs call the island?
context: The Caspak trilogy comprises The Land That Time Forgot (1918), The People That Time Forgot (1918), and Out of Time's Abyss (1918), all originally serialized in Blue Book Magazine. Caspak's spatial-evolutionary scheme — life evolves as it migrates north — is one of pulp's most original cosmologies. The 1975 Kevin Connor film adaptation The Land That Time Forgot starred Doug McClure. Maple White Land is the setting of Conan Doyle's The Lost World (1912); Skull Island is King Kong's home.

question: Tolkien's Catholic faith shaped his fiction at every level. He brought his fiancee Edith Bratt from the Anglican church to the Catholic church in 1913 (she resented it for decades). He went to daily Mass most of his adult life. In a 1953 letter he called The Lord of the Rings 'fundamentally religious and Catholic' -- but said he had cut nearly all direct religion out so the story would not read as clumsy allegory. Which medieval devotional dream-narrative did Tolkien translate from Middle English into modern English? It is one of the few verse works he completed for publication.
choices: Caedmon's Hymn, the earliest known Old English poem
The Dream of the Rood, the cross-as-narrator Crucifixion poem
Christ III, the Cynewulf eschatological poem
context: Tolkien's translation of Pearl (along with Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and Sir Orfeo) was published posthumously by Christopher Tolkien in 1975. Pearl is by the same anonymous 14th-century Pearl Poet who wrote Sir Gawain. The poem features a grieving father who has lost his two-year-old daughter and dreams of meeting her, now a grown maiden in heavenly bliss. The Pearl Poet's other surviving works are Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (Tolkien co-edited the standard scholarly edition with E.V. Gordon, 1925) and Patience and Cleanness.

question: T.H. White's 1958 single-volume omnibus The Once and Future King combined four novels (The Sword in the Stone, 1938; The Queen of Air and Darkness, first published as The Witch in the Wood, 1939; The Ill-Made Knight, 1940; The Candle in the Wind, 1958) into the most-read 20th-century Arthurian work, following Arthur from boyhood under Merlyn's teaching to old age. In 1960 Alan Jay Lerner and Frederick Loewe turned the book into a stage musical, with Richard Burton as Arthur and Julie Andrews as Guenevere. What was the musical called?
context: Camelot, adapted from The Once and Future King, opened at Toronto's O'Keefe Centre on 1 October 1960 before moving to Broadway, with music by Frederick Loewe and book and lyrics by Alan Jay Lerner. Richard Burton played Arthur, Julie Andrews Guenevere and Robert Goulet Lancelot.

question: Sir Thomas Malory finished Le Morte d'Arthur around 1470, apparently while in prison, weaving French and English sources into one story of Arthur's rise, the Grail quest and the fall of the Round Table. The oldest surviving handwritten copy only turned up in June 1934, when a schoolmaster found it at Winchester College. Before that, every reader knew Malory through one printer's 1485 edition. Who printed it?
context: Le Morte d'Arthur was completed around 1469 or 1470 and first printed by William Caxton in 1485. Walter Oakeshott discovered the Winchester Manuscript, an earlier handwritten copy, in June 1934.

question: Isaac Asimov introduced his Three Laws of Robotics in a 1942 story called Runaround. Four decades later, in 1985, he added a Zeroth Law that supersedes the original three, first stated in a novel that united his Robot, Empire, and Foundation series into a single timeline. In the plot, the robot R. Daneel Olivaw realizes the Three Laws are not enough to protect humanity as a whole. What novel introduced the Zeroth Law, and what does it state?
answer: Robots and Empire (1985) — 'A robot may not harm humanity, or by inaction allow humanity to come to harm'
choices: Robots and Empire (1985) — 'A robot may not harm humanity, or by inaction allow humanity to come to harm'
Foundation and Earth (1986) — 'A robot must protect the long-term flourishing of all human society'
The Robots of Dawn (1983) — 'A robot must place collective good above individual welfare'
Forward the Foundation (1993) — 'A robot may serve humanity even at the cost of an individual'
context: Robots and Empire (1985) joined Asimov's Robot and Empire series into one timeline. In it the robots R. Daneel Olivaw and R. Giskard Reventlov reason their way to a Zeroth Law that puts humanity as a whole ahead of any single human.

question: A young writer from Sauk City, Wisconsin, sold his first story to Weird Tales in 1926 while still a teenager, corresponded with H.P. Lovecraft for years, and co-founded the press that kept Lovecraft's stories in print. Yet he considered his most serious work to be something else entirely: an ambitious cycle of novels, stories, journals and poems about his own corner of Wisconsin. What did he call it?
context: August Derleth considered the Sac Prairie Saga, his long series of novels, stories, journals, poems and nonfiction about the Sac Prairie region, his most serious work. He sold his first story, Bat's Belfry, to Weird Tales in 1926.

question: Tolkien's 1936 lecture Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics transformed academic Beowulf studies. He argued the poem is a coherent literary work, not a quarry for historical data. He said the monsters were the heart of its meaning, and he named a tragic-heroic worldview from Old English at the poem's center. What did Tolkien call this outlook?
answer: The Northern courage of resistance — fighting on though the cause is hopeless and defeat is certain
choices: The Northern courage of resistance — fighting on though the cause is hopeless and defeat is certain
The Anglo-Saxon doctrine of wyrd — fate as the ultimate arbiter of all human endeavor
The Heroic Code of dryht — the warband loyalty above family or kin
The Pagan-Germanic concept of doom — the certainty of cosmic destruction at Ragnarok
context: In his 1936 British Academy lecture, Tolkien argued that the monsters are central to Beowulf's meaning and praised the poem's Northern courage: fighting on even when defeat is certain. The lecture changed how scholars read the poem.

question: Robert E. Howard launched Conan in the December 1932 Weird Tales with The Phoenix on the Sword, in which King Conan of Aquilonia fights off a plot against his throne. He built it by rewriting an unsold story about his earlier hero, the Atlantean warrior-king Kull, and long passages of the two are identical. What was the rejected Kull story called?
context: The Phoenix on the Sword, Conan's debut in Weird Tales in December 1932, is a rewrite of the unpublished Kull story By This Axe I Rule!, with long passages identical.

question: Mary Stewart's Merlin Trilogy — The Crystal Cave (1970), The Hollow Hills (1973), The Last Enchantment (1979) — retold the Arthur story from Merlin's point of view. Stewart drew on the 9th-century Welsh Historia Brittonum, Geoffrey of Monmouth's 1136 History of the Kings of Britain (which invented most of the Arthur legend the West knows), and the 12th-13th-century French Vulgate Cycle. Her Merlin is a half-divine boy raised in 5th-century Wales after Rome pulled out. The trilogy's title points to a real place in Wales tied to Merlin's youth. Where is the actual Crystal Cave?
answer: Bryn Myrddin near Carmarthen in southwest Wales, the legendary home of Myrddin Wyllt, the Welsh Merlin
choices: Bryn Myrddin near Carmarthen in southwest Wales, the legendary home of Myrddin Wyllt, the Welsh Merlin
Cadbury Castle in Somerset, the leading archaeological candidate for the historical Camelot
Tintagel Castle on the Cornish coast, the traditional birthplace of Arthur in Geoffrey of Monmouth
Glastonbury Tor in Somerset, the leading candidate for the location of the Isle of Avalon
context: Bryn Myrddin, Merlin's Hill, rises just outside Carmarthen, whose Welsh name, Caerfyrddin, was long read as 'Myrddin's fort', and local legend places Merlin's cave there. The Welsh Myrddin appears in early Welsh poetry, and Geoffrey of Monmouth Latinised the name as Merlinus.

question: Marion Zimmer Bradley's 1983 bestseller The Mists of Avalon retells the Arthur legend from the women's side, as a struggle between the goddess religion of the island of Avalon and the rising Christian church. Its narrator is a priestess of Avalon and Arthur's own half-sister, a woman the old romances remember as a dangerous sorceress and his enemy. Who narrates the novel?
answer: Morgaine, known in older tales as Morgan le Fay
choices: Morgaine, known in older tales as Morgan le Fay
Viviane, the Lady of the Lake herself
Igraine, the mother of Arthur himself
context: The Mists of Avalon (1983) is narrated by Morgaine, a priestess defending the old religion of Avalon as Christianity threatens to destroy it; Viviane is the High Priestess of Avalon for most of the story. The novel was a bestseller and was made into a TNT miniseries in 2001.

question: Robert E. Howard died in 1936, but his Conan tales of muscle, magic and doomed cities founded a whole genre, and later writers piled in after him. For decades the genre had no name. In 1961 the British writer Michael Moorcock asked fellow fans what to call this kind of story, and an American author of barbarian-and-thief adventures answered in a fanzine with a catchphrase that stuck. Who coined the term sword and sorcery?
context: Fritz Leiber suggested sword-and-sorcery in the fanzine Ancalagon in April 1961, answering Michael Moorcock, who had proposed epic fantasy, and he expanded on it in Amra that July. The genre grew out of Howard's early-1930s work, and his 1929 Kull story The Shadow Kingdom is often called the first true sword-and-sorcery tale.

question: Robert Heinlein worked on Stranger in a Strange Land through the 1950s, building it on one idea: a human baby raised by Martians and brought back to Earth as a grown man. Putnam published it in June 1961, and it became a touchstone of the 1960s counterculture. Heinlein's hero, Valentine Michael Smith, founds a religious movement based on Martian ways, and his followers learn to understand things so completely that they become part of what they understand. What Martian word did Heinlein invent for this, a word that has since entered the English language?
context: Grok literally means 'to drink' in Heinlein's invented Martian, but it stands for understanding something so thoroughly that the observer becomes part of the observed. Stranger in a Strange Land won the Hugo Award, and a longer uncut version was published in 1991.

question: For over a hundred years, hikers, hunters, and Native American tribes have told stories of a giant hairy ape-like creature -- called Bigfoot or Sasquatch -- that walks upright on two legs and hides deep in thick evergreen forests. Almost all of the famous sightings happen in the misty, rainy woods of the northwestern United States. Which region of the US is this?
context: Sasquatch lore is concentrated in Washington, Oregon, and northern California. The name 'Bigfoot' was coined by a journalist after construction worker Jerry Crew found large prints in Humboldt County in 1958.

question: For centuries, people have claimed to see a huge, long-necked, plesiosaur-like water monster swimming in a deep, dark freshwater lake in the misty Highlands. The lake is called Loch Ness. It is a lake in one of the four countries of the United Kingdom. In which of those countries is Loch Ness found?
context: Loch Ness is a 23-mile freshwater lake in the Scottish Highlands. The 'Surgeon's Photograph' from 1934 was the most famous image until a 1994 deathbed confession revealed it was a hoax using a toy submarine.

question: The Yeti, sometimes called the Abominable Snowman, is a legendary shaggy, ape-like giant said to leave enormous footprints in the snow high up on the roof of the world. The Sherpa people, who guide climbers to the top of Mount Everest, have told stories about seeing it for hundreds of years. In which mountain range is the Yeti said to live?
context: Sherpa folklore long predates Western reports. Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reported strange large footprints on the 1953 Everest expedition, fueling Western Yeti enthusiasm for decades.

question: The Loch Ness Monster is Scotland's most famous cryptid -- a huge, long-necked creature said to live in a deep, dark freshwater lake in the Scottish Highlands. Over the years, tourists, locals, and even some scientists have grown so fond of the creature that they gave her a warm, playful, one-word nickname now used around the world. What is that nickname?
context: The nickname became standard in Scottish newspapers in the 1930s and now appears on everything from souvenir T-shirts to Inverness pub signs.

question: In 1966 and 1967, people in a small river town near the Ohio River began seeing a huge dark winged creature with glowing red eyes. They called it the Mothman. The town, called Point Pleasant, sits right on the border between two US states, but only one of those states can call the Mothman its own. In which state is Point Pleasant located?
context: Sightings ran from November 1966 through December 15, 1967, when the Silver Bridge collapsed and killed 46 people. A 12-foot polished-steel statue of the creature stands in downtown Point Pleasant today.

question: The Jersey Devil is a legendary winged monster with hooves, a horse-like head, bat wings, and a forked tail. In the old colonial-era legend, it was born in 1735 to a poor woman with twelve children who cursed her thirteenth baby. It is said to haunt a vast, dark pine forest known as the Pine Barrens. Which US state contains that forest?
context: The Pine Barrens is a million-acre stretch of pinelands in southern New Jersey. The legend dates to the 18th century and the creature is said to be the cursed 13th child of one Mother Leeds.

question: The Bermuda Triangle is a mysterious stretch of open sea whose three corners are Miami in Florida, the island of Bermuda, and the island of Puerto Rico. Over the past hundred years, dozens of ships and airplanes are said to have vanished inside this triangle without a trace. Wreckage is often never found. In which body of water does this triangle lie?
context: The triangle is roughly bounded by Miami, Bermuda, and Puerto Rico. The lore was popularized by a 1964 Argosy Magazine article. Statistical reviews find no higher disappearance rate than other busy ocean lanes.

question: An ancient Greek philosopher wrote of a huge lost island empire called Atlantis around 360 BC. He said this proud sea-power grew so wicked that the gods sank it in a single day and night. Which ancient Greek thinker first told the tale?
context: Atlantis appears in two of Plato's dialogues, Timaeus and Critias, around 360 BC. Most classicists read it as a moral parable invented by Plato; modern enthusiasts have nevertheless searched for it for centuries.

question: Prehistoric people raised a ring of huge stone slabs, some over 20 feet tall, on the grassy plain of Salisbury more than 4,000 years ago. That ring, Stonehenge, stands in the south of one of the four countries of the United Kingdom. In which country?
context: Stonehenge stands on the Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire. The inner bluestones were quarried in the Preseli Hills of Wales and transported roughly 150 miles to the site.

question: John White, governor of the English colony founded on Roanoke Island in 1587, sailed home for supplies. When he finally returned in 1590, all 115 settlers had vanished. The only clue was a single word carved into a wooden post. What was it?
context: The Roanoke Colony was established in 1587 on the coast of present-day North Carolina. The 115 colonists vanished entirely before White's resupply ship returned. 'Croatoan' was the name of a nearby island and tribe.

question: In the summer of 1947, a rancher named Mac Brazel found strange metallic debris scattered across his sheep pasture in the American southwest. The local Army Air Field first told newspapers they had recovered a crashed 'flying disc.' A day later they took the story back and called it a weather balloon. Some people still believe it was a spaceship. In which US state did the crash happen?
context: The crash site was near Roswell, New Mexico. The Army Air Forces initially reported recovering a 'flying disc,' then retracted to call it a weather balloon. A 1990s declassification revealed it was a Project Mogul nuclear-test-detection balloon.

question: Area 51 is a highly secret US military base in the middle of a hot, dry desert in the American Southwest. The Air Force has used it for decades to test experimental spy planes and other classified aircraft. Locals have long claimed to see strange lights, disc-shaped craft, and flying saucers in the night sky above the base. In which US state is Area 51 located?
context: The base sits at Groom Lake, about 80 miles north of Las Vegas. The Air Force only officially acknowledged its existence in 2013, after decades of public records and even tour-bus jokes about it.

question: Women bathe in green pools among star charts and plants that match no known species, in a handwritten book about six hundred years old. A swirling script captions it all. What has nobody ever managed to do with the book?
context: The 240-page illustrated book dates to the 15th century. It contains an unknown script and drawings of plants nobody can identify. It now lives in Yale University's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library.

question: The Yowie is a hairy, ape-like beast from the folklore of the world's driest inhabited continent — a sort of southern-hemisphere Bigfoot. Aboriginal people of that country have told stories for many generations of a tall, shaggy creature walking the deep bush and the red-earth outback. In which country is the Yowie usually placed?
context: Yowie traditions appear across many Aboriginal nations under different names. European settlers in the 19th century recorded their own 'hairy man' sightings, and modern Yowie hunters concentrate in eastern Australia.

question: Khufu had the Great Pyramid of Giza built as his tomb around 2560 BC. It rose 481 feet on the west bank of the Nile, and its size and precision led to wild theories about who built it. In which country does it stand?
context: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC as a tomb for Pharaoh Khufu. Mainstream Egyptology attributes it to Egyptian laborers; alternative theories from Erich von Däniken to modern internet conspiracies persist.

question: A Polynesian carver on Rapa Nui, the South Pacific island outsiders call Easter Island, cut a giant figure from volcanic rock, with a blocky head, long ears and a stern face. His people made nearly 900. What Polynesian word do the islanders use for them?
context: Easter Island, called Rapa Nui by its people, lies in the South Pacific. The 887 monolithic moai were carved between roughly 1250 and 1500 AD. 2012 experimental archaeology showed they could be 'walked' upright with ropes.

question: In 1934 a London paper ran a photo of a long neck rising from Loch Ness, and Nessie became world-famous. Sixty years later a dying man confessed it was a toy submarine with a putty neck. What is the photo called?
context: Robert Kenneth Wilson, a London gynaecologist, put his name to the 1934 photograph, which is why it is called the Surgeon's Photograph. In 1994 Christian Spurling confessed on his deathbed that his stepfather Marmaduke Wetherell had staged it with a toy submarine and a sculpted putty neck, as revenge on the Daily Mail.

question: In the American Southwest, one Native American nation tells fearful stories of the skinwalker -- an evil witch who can shape-shift into a coyote, a wolf, or a crow, and walk unseen at night. Many members of this nation will not say the creature's name out loud, believing that just speaking it can call it near. Which Native American people first told the stories of the skinwalker?
context: In Navajo language the figure is called yee naaldlooshii, 'by means of it, it goes on all fours.' Speaking the name is widely considered taboo. The modern 'Skinwalker Ranch' in Utah inherits the name without inheriting the religious context.

question: In the freezing forests of northern North America and Canada, a group of related Native American peoples told stories of the wendigo -- a tall, gaunt spirit of hunger and ice that hunts lonely travelers in winter and eats human flesh. These related peoples included the Cree, the Ojibwe, and the Innu, all speaking languages from one great family. What is the shared name of this family of related tribes?
context: The wendigo legend belongs to Algonquian-speaking peoples across what is now Canada and the northern United States. The figure is associated with winter, famine, and the moral horror of cannibalism — never with hunger you can satisfy.

question: The gods sink the proud island empire of Atlantis in a single day and night, in a Greek tale written down around 360 BC. The tale sets the island beyond the Pillars of Heracles, now the Strait of Gibraltar. Which body of water swallows Atlantis?
context: Plato placed Atlantis 'beyond the Pillars of Heracles,' i.e. beyond the Strait of Gibraltar in what we now call the Atlantic. The very name 'Atlantic' derives from the Greek 'sea of Atlas,' which the Atlantis story helped cement.

question: On November 24, 1971, a quiet man in a dark suit and sunglasses boarded a Boeing 727 airliner in Portland, Oregon, and gave his name as Dan Cooper. In midair, he handed a flight attendant a note claiming his briefcase held a bomb, and demanded $200,000 in cash and four parachutes. After the plane landed in Seattle and he was handed the money and parachutes, the plane took off again with only Cooper and the crew aboard. Somewhere over the dark forests of Washington state, what did Dan Cooper do?
choices: Stowed away on the next flight
context: The hijacking happened on Thanksgiving Eve, November 24, 1971. He jumped from the rear airstair of a Northwest Orient Boeing 727 over southwestern Washington and was never identified. The press misheard 'Dan' as 'D.B.,' and the nickname stuck.

question: On the morning of June 30, 1908, deep in the wild pine forests of Siberia in the old Russian Empire, a monstrous fireball tore across the dawn sky and burst in mid-air above the Podkamennaya Tunguska River. The airburst flattened roughly 2,000 square kilometers of forest -- about 80 million trees knocked flat like matchsticks -- but left no crater. Scientists believe a comet or small asteroid exploded overhead. In which country did this Tunguska Event happen?
context: The blast occurred above the Stony Tunguska River basin in Siberia on June 30, 1908. Most scientists attribute it to the airburst of a 50-meter meteoroid or comet fragment. No impact crater was ever found.

question: In 2009, a man named Eric Knudsen entered a Photoshop contest on the internet forum Something Awful and posted two faked black-and-white photos of a tall, faceless figure in a black suit standing behind groups of children. The character caught on so hard on internet horror sites that he soon had his own video games, comics, and a 2018 horror movie. What is he called?
context: Created by Eric Knudsen (handle 'Victor Surge') for a Something Awful Photoshop contest about supernatural images. Entrants were asked to alter photos to look like real paranormal documents. Slender Man's documents were photoshopped to look like archive shots of children with a faceless tall figure in the background. The character became a viral creepypasta, then the 2012 indie game Slender: The Eight Pages, then a 2018 movie. A tragic Wisconsin case in May 2014 brought the character to national news and a documentary, Beware the Slenderman.

question: In August 1995, a rancher in the town of Moca found eight of his sheep dead in the field with no meat eaten -- only two small puncture wounds on each neck and every drop of blood drained. Frightened locals blamed a strange upright creature with spikes down its back, and a radio host coined the Spanish name chupacabra, meaning 'goat-sucker.' The panic spread across the whole Caribbean island where the killings began. On which island were the first chupacabra attacks reported?
context: The first sightings were near the town of Canóvanas, Puerto Rico. Witness Madelyne Tolentino later told folklorists she had recently seen the alien-creature film Species, whose monster strikingly resembles her chupacabra description.

question: On the night of August 15, 1977, astronomer Jerry Ehman was reviewing computer printouts from Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope. One column of readings jumped so far above the background hum that Ehman circled it in red pen and scrawled 'Wow!' in the margin -- a strong, narrow-band radio burst that has never been explained. The Big Ear had been built by the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) project to listen for one specific thing. What was it listening for?
context: Astronomer Jerry Ehman, working on Ohio State's 'Big Ear' radio telescope SETI program, circled the printout in red pen and wrote 'Wow!' beside it. The 72-second signal has never been heard again.

question: In December 1872, a British merchant ship was found drifting empty across the Atlantic Ocean between the Azores and Portugal. Her sails were still set. Her cargo of alcohol was untouched below decks. But her lifeboat was gone, and so were the captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife Sarah, their little two-year-old daughter Sophia, and all seven crewmen. What is this famous ghost ship called?
context: The American brigantine Mary Celeste was found by the British ship Dei Gratia east of the Azores on December 4, 1872. Captain Briggs, his wife Sarah, daughter Sophia, and all seven crew were never seen again. The cargo of 1,701 alcohol barrels was intact; the lifeboat was missing. Modern theory: Briggs feared a hold-fire from leaking alcohol vapor and ordered evacuation; the ship sailed away from them. The archetypal ghost ship, referenced by Conan Doyle, Doctor Who, and countless others.

question: In 1958, a worker named Jerry Crew discovered huge footprints at his logging site in California. He made plaster casts of the prints and took them to a local newspaper. The reporter's story gave the unknown creature a memorable new name. What was that name?
context: 'Sasquatch' was already in use, anglicized from the Halkomelem Salish word sasq'ets. 'Bigfoot' was the journalist's invention and quickly became the dominant North American name. The Crew casts are still on display in Willow Creek, California.

question: On October 20, 1967, two friends named Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin were riding on horseback through the woods at Bluff Creek in northern California, hoping to spot a Bigfoot. They ended up filming what they said was a female one — a big, dark, hairy figure walking across a sandbar and glancing back at the camera. It became the most famous piece of Bigfoot footage ever shot. What nickname did Patterson give the creature in the film?
context: The film was shot on October 20, 1967. Patterson named the subject 'Patty.' Hollywood costume designers and biomechanics researchers have studied the gait, the muscle movement, and the unusual proportions of the figure for decades without consensus.

question: On December 15, 1967, the Silver Bridge — a suspension bridge crossing the Ohio River between Point Pleasant, West Virginia and Gallipolis, Ohio — collapsed during rush-hour traffic. Cars and trucks plunged into the freezing river below. For over a year before the disaster, locals in Point Pleasant had reported a winged, red-eyed creature they nicknamed 'the Mothman' haunting the town at night. About how many people died when the bridge fell?
context: The 1928 eyebar suspension bridge failed because of a cracked I-bar in a single eyebar; rush-hour cars and trucks plunged into the freezing Ohio River. John Keel's 1975 book The Mothman Prophecies tied the disaster to the cryptid sightings.

question: The 1934 'Surgeon's Photograph' of the Loch Ness Monster — a grainy shot of a long-necked shape rising from the Scottish lake — was said to have been snapped by a respectable London physician named Robert Kenneth Wilson. Because a real Harley Street specialist had put his name on the picture, people trusted it for sixty years. Wilson's actual medical field, though, had nothing to do with lakes or monsters — he was a specialist in women's health. What kind of doctor was he?
context: Robert Kenneth Wilson said he had stopped to look at the loch on a road trip and snapped the photo. He kept his name out of newspaper credits for decades. The image was finally exposed as a hoax in a 1994 deathbed confession.

question: Greek sponge divers exploring an ancient Roman shipwreck pulled up a lump of corroded bronze about the size of a shoebox in 1901. Decades later, X-rays showed what the lump really held. What is this 2,000-year-old device called?
context: Divers recovered it in 1901 off the small island of Antikythera. The lump soon broke into pieces, and on 17 May 1902 Valerios Stais found a gear wheel embedded in one of them; X-ray studies in 1971 and CT scans in 2005 later mapped its gears. The mechanism dates to around the 2nd century BC.

question: Someone in Central Europe filled a 240-page book by hand in the early 1400s with strange plants, star charts and women bathing in green pools, all captioned in a swirling script. A Polish book dealer bought it in Italy in 1912. Which American university keeps it today in its rare-book library?
context: The manuscript lives in Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library. Polish-American antique dealer Wilfrid Voynich bought it in 1912. The script has resisted every cryptographic, linguistic, and AI-assisted attempt to decode it.

question: Ancient people in the desert of southern Peru scraped away the dark surface stones to reveal lighter soil, drawing a hummingbird, a monkey and long straight lines that stretch for miles. Some of these Nazca figures are hundreds of feet long. What puzzling feature makes them so strange to anyone standing on top of them?
answer: They are only fully visible from the air
choices: They are only fully visible from the air
They glow brightly at sunrise and sunset
They move slowly over the course of a year
They are invisible from less than a mile away
context: The geoglyphs were made by the Nazca culture between roughly 500 BC and 500 AD, by removing the dark surface stones to reveal lighter sand. They cover 450 km² in the Nazca Desert. Theories about purpose include religious ritual and astronomical calendar.

question: In the summer of 1947, ranch foreman Mac Brazel found strange metal debris scattered across his sheep pasture near Roswell, New Mexico. The nearby Roswell Army Air Field first told newspapers they had recovered a crashed 'flying disc' — front-page news across America. A day later, the Army took the story back and called it a plain weather balloon. In which month of 1947 did this famous flip-flop happen?
context: The press release went out July 8, 1947 from Roswell Army Air Field. A 1990s declassification revealed it was actually wreckage from Project Mogul, a high-altitude balloon array meant to detect Soviet nuclear tests.

question: On August 15, 1977, an astronomer named Jerry Ehman was reviewing a computer printout from Ohio State University's giant 'Big Ear' radio telescope, which had been listening for possible signals from alien civilizations. He noticed one column of numbers that looked far stronger than the background noise — a narrow-band signal that seemed to come from deep space near the constellation Sagittarius. Astonished, he circled it in red pen and scrawled 'Wow!' next to it. Roughly how long did the signal last?
context: The signal lasted exactly the length of the telescope's beam-pass across a single sky position, suggesting an extraterrestrial source. It came from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius. Despite repeated listening campaigns, the signal has never been heard again.

question: In February 1959, a team of nine skilled Soviet hiking students on a winter cross-country trek slashed their way out of their tent in the middle of the night and died in the freezing forest below. Some had crushed ribs but no bruises. The event became known as the Dyatlov Pass Incident, after the group's twenty-three-year-old leader Igor Dyatlov. In the northern part of which Russian mountain range did all this happen?
context: Group leader Igor Dyatlov and his eight companions cut their way out of their tent from the inside and fled into a sub-zero blizzard inadequately dressed. Some bodies showed crushing injuries without external wounds. A 2019 reinvestigation favored a katabatic-snowslab avalanche as the most likely trigger.

question: On December 5, 1945, five US Navy torpedo bombers took off from a base in Fort Lauderdale, Florida for a routine training flight over the Atlantic Ocean. All five aircraft — and later a large Martin Mariner flying-boat rescue plane sent after them — vanished without a trace over the stretch of ocean now called the Bermuda Triangle. The lost squadron became known as 'Flight 19,' the Triangle's most famous disappearance. What kind of aircraft were the five bombers?
context: The five Avengers left Fort Lauderdale on December 5, 1945. Lt. Charles Taylor reported being lost over featureless water. A PBM Mariner flying boat sent to search for them also vanished, very likely from a known onboard fuel-fume explosion problem.

question: The phrase 'Bermuda Triangle' was coined in a 1964 pulp-magazine article by writer Vincent Gaddis to describe a stretch of Atlantic Ocean between Miami, Bermuda, and Puerto Rico where ships and planes were said to vanish. Ten years later, in 1974, an American language-school founder and paranormal author wrote a bestselling paperback titled 'The Bermuda Triangle' that made the mystery a household name. Who wrote that 1974 bestseller?
context: Vincent Gaddis coined the term in Argosy Magazine in February 1964. Berlitz's 1974 book sold five million copies. Larry Kusche's 1975 The Bermuda Triangle Mystery — Solved went through individual cases and showed many had been misrepresented or exaggerated.

question: One lonely night, a married American couple named Betty and Barney Hill were driving through the White Mountains of New Hampshire when, they said, a bright disc-shaped craft followed their car and landed in the road. Under hypnosis they described short gray beings and a strange medical exam aboard. Theirs became the first widely publicized alien-abduction case in America. In which decade did the Hills say it happened?
context: The encounter took place in the White Mountains of New Hampshire on September 19, 1961. Betty and Barney were an interracial couple — she was a social worker, he was a postal worker — whose detailed hypnotic-regression accounts shaped almost every later abduction narrative.

question: In November 1975, an Arizona logging crew driving out of a work site reported that one of their men, twenty-two-year-old Travis Walton, had been struck by a bright beam of light from a hovering flying saucer and had vanished into the woods. Walton turned up dazed on a highway five days later. He later wrote a book about the experience, and Paramount Pictures turned it into a 1993 Hollywood film. What is the film called?
context: Walton's six fellow loggers passed lie-detector tests about the incident. The 1993 Robert Lieberman film stars D.B. Sweeney as Walton, Robert Patrick as the foreman, and Peter Berg as a young James Garner type. The film's onboard-craft scenes terrified a generation of kids.

question: Through the 1950s and 1960s, one American spy agency ran a secret program called MKUltra to test whether drugs, hypnosis, and psychological torture could break people's minds and turn them into controllable puppets. Its chief chemist, Sidney Gottlieb, dosed unwitting citizens and soldiers with the hallucinogen LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide). Most files were destroyed in 1973, but in 1977 a Senate hearing led by Ted Kennedy dragged the whole program into public view. Which American agency ran MKUltra?
context: MK Ultra ran roughly from 1953 to 1973 under chemist Sidney Gottlieb. It involved LSD experiments on unwitting subjects, including Boston-area drug addicts and a US Army biochemist named Frank Olson, who died in a fall from a 13th-story New York hotel window during a dosing.

question: Skinwalker Ranch is a 512-acre cattle spread in the high desert of the Uintah Basin, a wide sagebrush valley ringed by mountains and bordered by the Ute Indian reservation. The Sherman family bought the ranch in 1994 and quickly reported glowing orbs floating over the pasture, cattle carved up with surgical cuts, and tunnels of light opening in the sky. Local Ute tribal lore had already warned the land was cursed by shape-shifting witches. Which US state contains the Uintah Basin?
context: The Sherman family bought the ranch in 1994 and reported a wave of livestock mutilations, light phenomena, and bipedal-creature sightings. Aerospace billionaire Robert Bigelow bought it in 1996. The History Channel's 2020 series brought it to mainstream attention.

question: On the morning of June 30, 1908, deep in the remote Siberian taiga of Russia near the Tunguska River, a huge fireball streaked across the sky and something exploded with the force of a large nuclear bomb. The blast flattened roughly 80 million trees in a butterfly-shaped pattern across hundreds of square miles of forest. Yet when scientists later reached the site, they could not find any impact crater at all. What does the missing crater tell us about how the object hit?
context: The airburst occurred above the Stony Tunguska River on June 30, 1908. Eyewitnesses 300 miles away saw a fireball brighter than the sun. No crater was ever found. Most scientists attribute it to a 50-meter stony asteroid airburst at about 8 kilometers altitude.

question: On the night before Thanksgiving 1971 (November 24), a soft-spoken man who bought his ticket under the name 'Dan Cooper' hijacked a Northwest Orient Boeing 727 flying over the state of Washington. He handed a stewardess a note saying his briefcase held a bomb, demanded a ransom paid in unmarked $20 bills, and then parachuted out the back stairs of the plane into a storm. He was never caught. How much cash did he take with him?
context: The FBI photographed every serial number before delivery. In February 1980, an eight-year-old boy named Brian Ingram found about $5,800 of the bills on a sandbar of the Columbia River near Vancouver, Washington. The rest has never surfaced.

question: A baby girl vanished with the 115 English colonists of Roanoke Island between 1587 and 1590. Her grandfather, John White, returned to discover the entire colony gone. She became famous as the first English child born in what is now the United States. What was her name?
context: Virginia Dare was born August 18, 1587 — nine days after the colony's arrival. She was the daughter of Ananias and Eleanor Dare and granddaughter of Governor John White. When White returned to England for supplies, the Spanish Armada delayed him three years; he returned in August 1590 to find the colony abandoned, fortifications dismantled, no bodies, and the word CROATOAN carved on a fence post. A storm prevented his search of nearby Croatoan Island. Virginia Dare's name remains an American mystery icon.

question: In May 2007, a three-year-old British girl named Madeleine McCann disappeared from her family's holiday apartment while her parents were eating dinner at a nearby restaurant. The apartment was located in a small seaside resort village called Praia da Luz on the southern Algarve coast. She has never been found, and the case became one of the most famous missing-child mysteries in the world. In which country was she taken?
context: The disappearance happened on the night of May 3, 2007, in the Algarve region. Her parents, Kate and Gerry McCann, were dining nearby. The case became one of the most-covered missing-child investigations in history. German national Christian Brückner is the current prime suspect.

question: In the spring of 1483, twelve-year-old King Edward V of England and his nine-year-old brother Richard, Duke of York — sons of the late King Edward IV — were placed for their 'protection' in the royal apartments of the Tower of London under the care of their uncle, the Lord Protector. Within months the uncle had seized the crown for himself, and the two boys, the famous 'Princes in the Tower,' were never seen alive again. Who was that uncle who became king in their place?
context: Twelve-year-old Edward V and his nine-year-old brother Richard of Shrewsbury vanished from the Tower in 1483 after Richard III had them declared illegitimate and seized the throne. In 1674, workmen at the Tower found a chest containing the bones of two children of the right ages.

question: In June 2009 an amateur artist named Eric Knudsen entered an online Photoshop horror contest, posting under the handle Victor Surge. He edited two old black-and-white playground photos and pasted into the background a very tall, faceless figure in a black suit with long, drooping arms -- the first images of Slender Man. The mythos exploded from that single forum thread. Which website ran the contest?
context: Knudsen posted two altered black-and-white photos of children with a faceless tall figure in the background. The character spread across YouTube alternate-reality games like Marble Hornets and inspired the 2014 Waukesha, Wisconsin stabbing case carried out by two 12-year-old girls.

question: In May 2019, an anonymous user posted a single grainy photograph of an empty yellow-carpeted office corridor with buzzing fluorescent lights, and a reply soon imagined slipping through the world into endless rooms exactly like it. The internet ran with the idea. Fans call this scary made-up place 'The Backrooms.' Which image board was the original photo first posted on?
context: The photo went up on 4chan's /x/ board, and a reply added the line: 'If you're not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you'll end up in the Backrooms.' The mythos has since exploded into YouTube series, the Kane Pixels short films, and a Lionsgate film deal.

question: The SCP Foundation ('Secure, Contain, Protect') is a shared online wiki where thousands of writers pretend to work at a top-secret organization that captures and studies strange objects — items that break the laws of nature. Each entry is written like a dry, redacted government science report. The whole project began with a single 2007 post on the image board 4chan about a concrete statue that only moves when no one is looking directly at it. What SCP number was that first statue given?
context: The original post was about SCP-173, a roughly humanoid concrete sculpture by Japanese artist Izumi Kato. The Foundation lore now spans over 8,000 'SCP files' written by thousands of contributors under a Creative Commons license. It is one of the largest fiction projects in internet history.

question: Robert Bauval, a Belgian engineer and amateur Egyptologist, published a controversial idea in the 1990s. He argued that the ground plan of the three Great Pyramids of Giza matched, star for star, three bright stars as they stood around 10,500 BC, a match most Egyptologists reject. Which trio of stars did he mean?
context: Bauval's 1994 book The Orion Mystery argued the three pyramids — Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure — match the spacing and angle of Orion's Belt. Mainstream Egyptologists reject the precision claim but acknowledge the sky played a role in pyramid alignment.

question: The 1934 'Surgeon's Photograph' of the Loch Ness Monster ran in the Daily Mail as authentic evidence for sixty years. In 1994, Christian Spurling gave a deathbed confession. He revealed his stepfather had directed the hoax using a toy submarine with a putty 'neck' attached. Who was that stepfather?
context: The Daily Mail had previously hired Wetherell to find Nessie. He produced footprints, but the British Museum identified them as hippopotamus tracks from an umbrella stand, embarrassing the paper. Wetherell built the toy-submarine hoax as revenge and had family friend Wilson, a respectable doctor, front the image.

question: The Patterson-Gimlin Bigfoot film was shot at Bluff Creek in northern California on October 20, 1967 by cowboys Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin. It's less than a minute of shaky footage of what they said was a large hairy female creature, nicknamed 'Patty.' One single frame from the film is reproduced more than any other in books, magazines, and websites about Bigfoot — the moment where Patty pauses mid-stride and glances back over her shoulder directly at the camera. What frame number is it?
context: The 53-second 16mm film runs at 24 frames per second. Frame 352 has been analyzed by Hollywood costume designers, biomechanics researchers, and gait analysts for decades. Patterson died of cancer in 1972 still maintaining the film was authentic; Gimlin maintained that position until his death in 2024.

question: Journalist John A. Keel investigated the Point Pleasant winged-creature sightings of 1966-67 and the December 15, 1967 Silver Bridge collapse, tying them together in a 1975 book that became a classic of high-strangeness literature. What is its title?
choices: Strange Creatures From Time and Space
context: The book is titled The Mothman Prophecies. Keel had spent most of 1967 in Point Pleasant interviewing witnesses. He also documented Men in Black encounters and prophetic dreams reported by townspeople. Mark Pellington adapted the book into a 2002 film starring Richard Gere.

question: In 1994, the Sherman family bought a 512-acre ranch in Utah. They soon reported dead cattle, strange lights, and creatures walking on two legs. Two years later they sold it to an aerospace billionaire. His group studied it for over ten years. Who bought it?
context: Bigelow runs Bigelow Aerospace, known for inflatable space habitats. He sold the ranch to real-estate developer Brandon Fugal in 2016. The Pentagon's later AAWSAP advanced-aerospace UFO study program included Skinwalker Ranch as a site of interest.

question: In February 1959, nine experienced Soviet hikers from the Ural Polytechnic Institute were found dead in the snowy Ural Mountains after fleeing their tent in the middle of the night in only their underclothes. The place is now called Dyatlov Pass, after the group's leader Igor Dyatlov. Several of the hikers had crushed skulls and broken ribs with no cuts on their skin at all. One young woman, Lyudmila Dubinina, was missing a body part when searchers finally reached her body months later. What was missing?
context: Dubinina's tongue, eyes, and parts of her lips were missing — most likely from scavenger activity after she died face-down in the creek. Some of the recovered clothing showed elevated radioactivity, which a 1959 investigation chalked up to thorium gas-mantle lantern impregnation rather than nuclear activity.

question: A museum archaeologist in Athens examined a broken fragment of corroded bronze in 1902, a year after Greek sponge divers pulled the lump up from a Roman-era shipwreck about 2,000 years old. X-rays in 1971 and CT scans in 2005 later showed it to be the oldest known analog computer ever found. What did this device do?
choices: Calculated tax revenues from temple holdings
Computed harbor tides for trading vessels
context: The mechanism modeled the irregular motion of the moon, predicted solar and lunar eclipses, and tracked the cycle of ancient Greek athletic games. Valerios Stais noticed its first gear in 1902; Derek de Solla Price and Charalampos Karakalos X-rayed the fragments in 1971, and a Cardiff University team led by Mike Edmunds CT-scanned them in 2005.

question: Klaus Schmidt, a German archaeologist, led excavations at a hilltop in southeastern Turkey in 1995. He found huge carved T-shaped stone pillars arranged in rings, older than Stonehenge by about seven thousand years, and argued that the place hinted at worship coming before fields. What is the site called?
context: Göbekli Tepe dates to roughly 9500 BC, predating settled agriculture in the region. Some pillars are carved with leopards, vultures, scorpions, and snakes. Schmidt argued it was a ritual site rather than a settlement, suggesting religion may have preceded organized food production rather than followed from it.

question: In February 1980, an eight-year-old boy named Brian Ingram was digging on a sandbar of the Columbia River near Vancouver, Washington. He uncovered a rotting bundle of waterlogged $20 bills whose serial numbers matched the ransom from a 1971 hijacking. About how much money did Brian find?
context: The hijacker, who called himself Dan Cooper, had jumped from Northwest Orient Flight 305 over southwestern Washington on Thanksgiving Eve 1971 with $200,000 in $20 bills. The 1980 find was the only piece of the ransom ever recovered. Brian's family was awarded a portion of the bills after a court fight with the FBI and the airline insurer.

question: Two English cousins, Elsie Wright and Frances Griffiths, produced five remarkable photographs between 1917 and 1920. The pictures showed them posing with what they claimed were tiny winged figures in a Yorkshire glen. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle himself championed the photographs as authentic evidence. In 1983 the elderly cousins finally confessed. What had they actually used?
answer: Paper cutouts traced from a children's book and held up with hatpins
choices: Paper cutouts traced from a children's book and held up with hatpins
Glass-plate exposures of dragonfly wings glued to dolls
Carved beeswax figures Frances's mother had sewn from velvet
context: The Cottingley Fairies images first appeared in Doyle's 1920 Strand Magazine article 'Fairies Photographed: An Epoch-Making Event.' Doyle, despite his Holmes, was a committed spiritualist. Frances maintained until her death that the fifth photograph was genuine, while admitting the other four were faked.

question: Throughout the 1980s, huge geometric patterns kept appearing overnight in English wheat fields, and true believers claimed only aliens or plasma vortices could possibly make them. Then, in September 1991, two retired artists from Southampton walked into the offices of the Today newspaper and demonstrated to reporters exactly how they had been making the crop circles since 1978 — using a wooden plank, two lengths of rope, and a baseball cap with a wire sight to aim by. What were their names?
context: Bower had gotten the idea from a 1966 Australian 'flying-saucer nest' news story. He and Chorley made hundreds of circles in fields around Wessex over thirteen years, often watching the next morning as cerealogists earnestly explained them as alien craftwork. Other circle-makers continued — the Wessex Triangle is still a hotbed.

question: A 109-mile-long freshwater lake stretches along the border between Vermont, New York, and the Canadian province of Quebec. For over four centuries, people living on its shores have reported seeing a serpent-like creature living in its deep, cold waters — the American cousin of Scotland's Loch Ness Monster. The French explorer Samuel de Champlain himself reported spotting a strange creature in the lake in 1609, when he first mapped it. What is the modern nickname for the cryptid?
context: Lake Champlain is the sixth-largest natural freshwater lake in the United States. The 1977 'Mansi photograph' by Sandra Mansi is the Champ equivalent of the Surgeon's Photograph. Vermont and New York both passed legislation in the 1980s protecting any unknown creature in the lake.

question: In a long, narrow, fjord-like lake in the interior of the Canadian province of British Columbia is said to live a serpent-like cryptid called Ogopogo. It is the Canadian cousin of Scotland's Loch Ness Monster and Vermont's Champ. The Indigenous Syilx people of the region knew the figure as N'ha-a-itk — the 'lake demon' — long before European settlers arrived, and left offerings before crossing the water. The lake is 135 kilometers long. In which lake does Ogopogo live?
context: Lake Okanagan is in interior British Columbia, between Kelowna and Penticton. The name 'Ogopogo' came from a 1924 British music-hall song that locals applied to the creature in jest. There is now a Kelowna statue of Ogopogo and an annual sighting log maintained by tourism authorities.

question: The Mary Celeste was found drifting east of the Azores on December 4, 1872 by the British brigantine Dei Gratia. The captain, his wife Sarah, their two-year-old daughter Sophia, and all seven crew were gone, but the ship was seaworthy and well-stocked. What was the captain's name?
context: Briggs was a devout New England seaman. The Dei Gratia crew found the binnacle damaged, a sounding rod left on deck, and one lifeboat missing. The most-defended modern theory is that Briggs feared a hold explosion from fumes off the alcohol cargo and ordered an evacuation by lifeboat, then the lifeboat parted from the ship.

question: In December 1900, the relief vessel Hesperus arrived at a remote lighthouse on Eilean Mòr in the Outer Hebrides and found the three keepers gone. The clock was stopped, one oilskin coat was missing, the table was set for a meal, and one of two sets of lighthouse gates had been left open during a storm. What was the lighthouse called?
context: Keepers James Ducat, Thomas Marshall, and Donald McArthur disappeared sometime between December 7 and December 15, 1900. The most-defended theory is that a freak wave from a westerly storm struck them while they were securing equipment on the landing platform 110 feet below the cliff edge.

question: In December 1948, an unidentified man was found dead on Somerton Beach near Adelaide, Australia, with all clothing labels removed. In a hidden pocket of his trousers was a tiny scrap of paper torn from the final page of a specific book. The scrap read 'Tamam Shud' — Persian for 'ended' or 'finished.' What book was it torn from?
context: The matching copy of Edward FitzGerald's translation of the Rubaiyat was found six weeks later in the back seat of an unlocked car parked near the beach. Inside it was an indented coded message. In 2022, University of Adelaide researcher Derek Abbott proposed Carl 'Charles' Webb, an electrical engineer from Melbourne, as the man — based on DNA from a strand of hair preserved in a 1949 plaster bust.

question: A Polish-born antique dealer bought a 240-page illustrated volume from a Jesuit college near Rome in 1912, and the book has carried his surname ever since. Its pages hold strange plant drawings, star charts and women bathing in green pools, all in a script no one recognizes. What is this manuscript called?
context: Carbon-dated to 1404-1438. ~240 pages of vellum. Its 'script' has consistent statistical properties suggesting a real language or constructed cipher, but cryptographers from WWII codebreakers to modern AI researchers have all failed to crack it. Some plants depicted may match New World species — predating Columbus impossibly. Currently held at Yale's Beinecke Library as MS 408. Theories: medieval cipher, hoax, lost language, even alchemical code. The Codex Seraphinianus (1981, Luigi Serafini) is a modern art-book cousin.

question: The 'Zodiac Killer' murdered at least five people in northern California during 1968 and 1969. He tormented newspapers with taunting letters and coded cryptograms. In 2020, three amateur code-breakers finally solved his famous 340-character cipher from November 1969. What did the message actually say?
answer: A taunting message about not being afraid of the gas chamber
choices: A taunting message about not being afraid of the gas chamber
A coded set of map coordinates pointing to a buried weapon
A list of seven victim names the police had not yet connected
An anagram of the killer's real name and street address
context: The team — David Oranchak, Jarl Van Eycke, and Sam Blake — published their solution on December 11, 2020. The Zodiac's identity has never been confirmed. The FBI formally closed its investigation in 2023. Robert Graysmith's books and David Fincher's 2007 film Zodiac drew on the case's enduring grip on the American imagination.

question: The 'Jack the Ripper' murders terrorized Whitechapel in East London during the autumn of 1888. Historians generally accept five women as the canonical victims. The first canonical victim, killed on August 31, 1888, was a woman named Mary Ann Nichols. What was her familiar nickname?
context: The other four canonical victims were Annie Chapman ('Dark Annie'), Elizabeth Stride ('Long Liz'), Catherine Eddowes, and Mary Jane Kelly. The 'From Hell' letter, sent in October 1888 to George Lusk of the Whitechapel Vigilance Committee, included half a preserved human kidney. No suspect was ever charged.

question: An Egyptian priest told the tale of Atlantis to Solon, the Athenian lawgiver, or so said the philosopher who wrote it down centuries later. He recorded the account in two related dialogues near the end of his life, around 360 BC. What are those two dialogues called?
context: Timaeus is the dialogue that gave the West its later theory of the four classical elements. Critias was left unfinished — it breaks off mid-sentence as the gods are about to punish Atlantis for its hubris. Most classicists read the Atlantis story as Plato's invention to illustrate the dangers of an overreaching maritime empire — likely modeled on contemporary Athens itself.

question: In 1674, workmen tearing down a staircase at the Tower of London found a wooden chest holding the bones of two children — long assumed to be the missing 'Princes in the Tower.' Their uncle Richard III died at Bosworth Field in 1485. Who defeated him and took the crown as Henry VII?
context: Richard III lost his crown and his life to Henry Tudor at Bosworth Field on August 22, 1485, ending the Plantagenet dynasty and beginning the Tudor. The Princes were never publicly seen alive after the summer of 1483. The Westminster Abbey bones were briefly examined in 1933; the Abbey has refused subsequent DNA testing.

question: Under hypnosis in 1964, Betty Hill drew a 'star map' from memory. She said her alien abductors had shown it to her three years before. It had twelve dots with lines she called trade routes. In 1969, an Ohio teacher named Marjorie Fish used a 3D star catalog. She matched the map to a real place near Earth. Which star system did Fish pick?
context: The Hill–Fish star-map hypothesis became the foundation of 'Greys from Zeta Reticuli' as a UFO subculture. Critics later argued the dot pattern could be matched to many random three-dimensional star arrangements with sufficient effort. Carl Sagan was an early and sharp critic; Fish defended her analysis until her death in 2013.

question: Since the 1940s, shortwave radio hobbyists tuning across the airwaves have picked up eerie broadcasts from mysterious transmitters no government will ever admit to running. A man's, woman's, or child's voice reads out long strings of numbers in a flat, robotic tone, sometimes preceded by strange music, chimes, or bursts of Morse code. Radio fans call these transmissions 'numbers stations.' What are they most widely believed to actually be doing?
answer: Sending one-way messages to deployed intelligence agents
choices: Sending one-way messages to deployed intelligence agents
Broadcasting weather data to maritime fishing fleets
Triangulating positions for early ballistic-missile tests
context: Numbers stations broadcast one-time-pad ciphers, which are mathematically unbreakable if used correctly. The Cuban 'Atención' station was caught in 1998 when FBI agents arrested several Cuban intelligence officers in Miami whose decryption pads matched recent transmissions. The Lincolnshire Poacher (UK) and the Swedish Rhapsody are among the most famous.

question: The Black-Eyed Kids modern legend involves mysterious children with solid black eyes who approach strangers and ask to be let inside. The story began with a 1996 internet posting by a Texas journalist describing two such boys at his car window in Abilene. What was that journalist's name?
context: Bethel posted to a paranormal mailing list. The story spread to other internet boards through the late 1990s. It is one of the earliest 'creepypasta-shaped' urban legends to spread through the internet rather than through oral tradition. Bethel still maintains the encounter actually happened.

question: The 2019 4chan post that started the Backrooms showed one photo, an empty room with yellow walls and buzzing lights, and a reply added a few lines about 'noclipping out of reality' into that place. Beyond the yellow walls, which two details did that caption make key to the story?
answer: The endless fluorescent hum and faint smell of damp carpet
choices: The endless fluorescent hum and faint smell of damp carpet
The visible blood spatter on the back wall
The dim outline of a figure in the doorway
The reflection of a window without a sun outside
context: The May 2019 caption described the Backrooms as the stink of old moist carpet, the madness of mono-yellow, and the endless background noise of fluorescent lights at maximum hum-buzz. Kane Pixels' 2022 YouTube films later set the modern visual standard, and fans have since built hundreds of 'levels' by collaborative fiction.

question: On August 20, 1966, two Brazilian electronics technicians were found dead on a hill in Niterói, wearing matching homemade lead masks like those used to protect welders' eyes. A small notebook near them listed steps including 'be at agreed place, swallow capsules, await signal.' What is that hill called?
context: Vintém means 'penny' in Portuguese. The masks were the kind worn to look directly at strong light without harm. No drugs or poison were found in the men's bodies at autopsy, but Brazilian forensic technology in 1966 was limited and the case remains officially unsolved. Theories range from suicide pact to UFO contact ritual to corporate-espionage murder.

question: On the evening of September 12, 1952, three local boys and a group of adults from Flatwoods, West Virginia hiked up a farm to check what they thought was a downed aircraft. They said they met a 10-foot creature in the woods, with a glowing head and a skirt-shaped lower body. What name did newspapers give the creature?
context: The 'aircraft' the witnesses had seen overhead was a fireball — possibly a meteor that night. Some skeptics later argued the 'monster' was a startled barn owl in a tree, with its heart-shaped face glowing in flashlight beams. Locals call the creature the Braxton County Monster or 'Braxxie'; there is a small Braxxie museum in Sutton today.

question: Loch Ness, the cold dark freshwater lake in the Scottish Highlands that gave the Western world its most famous cryptid, is roughly 23 miles long and a mile wide. Its deepest measured point is so deep that the lake holds more freshwater than every other lake in England and Wales combined. How deep is Loch Ness at its deepest?
context: 754 feet is roughly 230 meters — deeper than most of the North Sea. The loch's water is stained black by peat from the surrounding hills, which limits underwater visibility to a few feet even in daylight. Sonar surveys in 1987 and 2003 found no large object resembling a Nessie-shaped creature.

question: The Patterson-Gimlin Bigfoot film, shot at Bluff Creek on October 20, 1967, has been the subject of repeated 'I was in the suit' claims over the decades. The most-publicized claim came from a man named Bob Heironimus in 2004, who described being paid by Patterson to wear a suit. What did Heironimus claim the suit was made of?
answer: A modified horsehide costume he wore over a football helmet
choices: A modified horsehide costume he wore over a football helmet
A bear pelt sewn over a wetsuit lined with foam padding
A gorilla costume rented from a Hollywood studio prop house
A cloth-and-fur suit hand-stitched by Patterson's wife Patricia
context: Heironimus's brother corroborated the broad outline of the story but never the specifics. Bigfoot researchers including Daniel Perez and Bill Munns have pushed back on the suit hypothesis, citing visible muscle movement in the subject and the difficulty of replicating the gait. The Bluff Creek site is now part of the Six Rivers National Forest.

question: In 2003, sculptor Bob Roach unveiled a 12-foot polished stainless-steel Mothman statue in downtown Point Pleasant, West Virginia — red reflective eyes, outstretched wings. What abandoned World War II munitions site outside town was ground zero for the original 1966-67 sightings?
context: Roach's statue stands in front of the Mothman Museum, run by Jeff Wamsley. The annual Mothman Festival started in 2002 — partly to capitalize on the Richard Gere film. The Silver Bridge collapse memorial sits a few blocks away, with the names of all 46 dead engraved on a granite slab.

question: The Pentagon ran a UFO (unidentified flying object) study called the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP) from 2008 to 2010. It cost $22 million and looked into Skinwalker Ranch. People often mix it up with the name the same effort went by later, which a New York Times story made famous in December 2017. What is that later name?
answer: AATIP, the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program
choices: AATIP, the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program
UAPTF, the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force
AARO, the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office
AAPAO, the Advanced Aerospace Phenomena Analysis Office
context: AAWSAP was the original name of the Defense Intelligence Agency effort; it later went by AATIP, the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program, which reached the public through a New York Times story on December 16, 2017. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid arranged the funding, and Robert Bigelow's company BAASS held the contract. The Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force (2020) and the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (2022) came years after that story.

question: The 1959 Soviet report on the Dyatlov Pass deaths logged a strange detail. Three of the nine victims had elevated beta radiation on their clothing. Investigators in later decades have argued this is not really as unusual as it initially sounds. What is the leading ordinary explanation for the radiation?
answer: Impregnation from thorium-coated gas-mantle camping lantern parts the hikers had handled
choices: Impregnation from thorium-coated gas-mantle camping lantern parts the hikers had handled
Atmospheric fallout drift from an open-air Soviet nuclear test that week
Background radon decay product accumulation in the closed tent fabric
Industrial radium-paint contamination from glow-in-the-dark wristwatches
context: The 1959 investigation recorded elevated beta radiation on some of the clothing but left it unexplained. A leading ordinary explanation is thorium from the cloth mantles of gas lanterns, which leave detectable residue on anyone who handles them; Yuri Krivonischenko's earlier work at the Mayak nuclear plant is another possible source. The 2019-2020 reinvestigation found no radiation anomaly and named a snow-slab avalanche as the trigger.

question: Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo built a 4.4-ton replica in 2012 to test an old Rapa Nui tradition, which held that Easter Island's giant statues 'walked' from the volcanic quarry of Rano Raraku to their stone platforms. The two anthropologists demonstrated the technique in a now-famous test. How did they move the statue?
answer: Three teams of ropers rocking the statue side-to-side while pulling it forward
choices: Three teams of ropers rocking the statue side-to-side while pulling it forward
A wooden sledge dragged over a track of greased palm logs
A counterweighted A-frame lever swung step by step down the slope
A team rolling the statue on its back over inflated leather bladders
context: The Hunt-Lipo demonstration walked the replica several hundred yards in a few hours with about 18 people on three ropes. Older theories required massive deforestation to provide roller logs and had long been used to argue Rapa Nui civilization 'committed ecocide.' The Hunt-Lipo work undercut that narrative significantly. Their book is titled The Statues That Walked.

question: Captain Dimitrios Kontos and his Greek sponge divers discovered a Roman-era shipwreck off a small island in 1900. The following spring they recovered marble statues, bronze objects and a single corroded mass of metal that nobody noticed at first. Months later, museum staff in Athens watched the mass split open as it dried. What did they see inside?
answer: A wooden case with bronze gears and Greek inscriptions visible on the edges
choices: A wooden case with bronze gears and Greek inscriptions visible on the edges
A silver-leaf astrolabe etched with Egyptian hieroglyphic constellations
A box of carved obsidian disks fitted into a hollow lead cube
A nested set of iron-rod orreries linking five painted clay planets
context: Athens National Archaeological Museum curator Valerios Stais first recognized the gears in 1902. The internal structure was finally mapped by Derek de Solla Price in the 1970s using X-rays and Michael Wright in the 1990s using improved tomography. The Antikythera Mechanism Research Project's 2006 Nature paper laid out the full gear-train. A second device may still be on the seabed — recovery operations continued through 2024.

question: Dan Cooper escaped by lowering the rear airstair of a Boeing 727 in mid-flight and stepping off into the dark. After copycat hijackers used the same exit in 1972, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered every 727 fitted with a small spring-loaded wedge that the rushing air shoves under the stairs, so they cannot drop open while the plane flies. The part carries the hijacker's name. What is it called?
context: The Cooper vane is an aerodynamic wedge: once the plane is moving, airflow pushes a spring-loaded plate under the 727's ventral airstair so the stairs cannot be lowered in flight. The FAA ordered it fitted to Boeing 727s after Cooper's jump and several copycat hijackings in 1972.

question: The Wow! Signal reached Earth in August 1977. Big Ear, a radio telescope in Ohio, picked it up. It came in right near a natural radio frequency in space. For years, scientists said a smart alien race would pick that exact frequency to send messages. Which one is it?
answer: The 1420 MHz hydrogen line, sometimes called the 'water hole'
choices: The 1420 MHz hydrogen line, sometimes called the 'water hole'
The 1665 MHz hydroxyl line, the 'second water hole' marker
The 4830 MHz formaldehyde line typical of dark molecular clouds
The 22000 MHz water-maser line associated with stellar nurseries
context: The neutral hydrogen 21-centimeter line at 1420 MHz is the most ubiquitous emission in the universe. Cornell University's Frank Drake and others have argued any radio-using civilization would discover it early and likely use frequencies near it for beacon transmissions. The Big Ear was dismantled in 1998 to make way for a golf course expansion. Jerry Ehman, the astronomer who circled the printout, has been notably cautious about extraterrestrial conclusions.

question: Betty and Barney Hill said aliens took them one night in September 1961. It happened on a road in New Hampshire as they drove home from a Niagara Falls trip. Later, a Boston doctor named Benjamin Simon hypnotized them so they could remember. Their story became the model for later alien abduction tales. Which one of them had the first dreams that led to the hypnosis?
context: Betty was a social worker; Barney was a postal worker. Their interracial marriage was unusual for the era and they were active in the NAACP. John G. Fuller's 1966 bestseller The Interrupted Journey introduced the case to the public. James Earl Jones starred as Barney in the 1975 TV film The UFO Incident. A roadside historical marker now stands on Route 3 in Lincoln, New Hampshire.

question: On March 13, 1997, thousands of Arizona residents saw a silent V-shape of lights drift across the night sky above Phoenix and other nearby cities. Governor Fife Symington publicly mocked the incident at the time. Ten years later, he admitted he had personally seen the lights himself. What is the leading ordinary explanation for at least part of the event?
answer: A formation of A-10 Warthogs from the Maryland Air National Guard on a training run, plus later flare drops
choices: A formation of A-10 Warthogs from the Maryland Air National Guard on a training run, plus later flare drops
A high-altitude flock of Sandhill cranes lit by city lights from below
A research balloon carrying a chemiluminescent atmospheric sensor array
A multi-vehicle laser-projection art installation conducted from Camelback Mountain
context: The Air Force later identified the second wave of lights, around 10 pm, as LUU-2B/B parachute flares dropped during a training exercise at the Barry Goldwater Range south of Phoenix. The earlier 'V formation' has never been fully explained. Symington, in his 2007 reversal, said he saw something he believes was non-terrestrial. He compared the experience to his earlier service as an Air Force officer.

question: On the morning of August 4, 1892, in Fall River, Massachusetts, banker Andrew Borden and his wife Abby were killed with a hatchet in their family home. Andrew's 32-year-old unmarried daughter was tried for the murders the next year and acquitted. The case generated a famous American skipping-rope rhyme. What is the daughter's name?
context: The rhyme: 'Lizzie Borden took an axe / And gave her mother forty whacks / When she saw what she had done / She gave her father forty-one.' (The actual count was 18 blows to Abby and 10 or 11 to Andrew.) Lizzie was acquitted by an all-male jury in June 1893 and lived on in Fall River until her death in 1927. Her Fall River house is now a bed and breakfast and museum.

question: Six-year-old beauty queen JonBenét Ramsey was found beaten and strangled in her family's basement in Boulder, Colorado on December 26, 1996. A handwritten ransom note asked for the unusually specific sum of $118,000 and was left on a back staircase. Whose yearly bonus was reported to have matched that amount almost exactly?
answer: Her father John Ramsey's recent Access Graphics bonus
choices: Her father John Ramsey's recent Access Graphics bonus
Her older brother's college tuition deposit for spring semester
A donation pledge her mother had made to a local charity
A previous home-improvement contractor's outstanding invoice
context: The ransom note ran two and a half pages, an unusual length for an actual kidnapping. No arrest has ever been made. A 2008 DNA test on the victim's clothing technically cleared her parents and brother as primary contributors, but the case has remained officially open with Boulder Police. Patsy Ramsey died of cancer in 2006; the family never returned to their Boulder home.

question: The most infamous individual MKUltra case is the November 1953 death of Army biochemist Frank Olson. Days earlier, CIA chemist Sidney Gottlieb had secretly dosed his drink with the hallucinogen LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide) at a Maryland retreat. Olson later fell or was pushed from a New York City hotel window. From which hotel did he fall?
answer: The Hotel Statler (now the Hotel Pennsylvania)
choices: The Hotel Statler (now the Hotel Pennsylvania)
The Plaza Hotel on Central Park South
The Algonquin Hotel on West 44th Street
The Waldorf Astoria on Park Avenue
context: Olson fell from the 13th-floor window at the Hotel Statler across from Penn Station on November 28, 1953. The CIA paid the family a settlement in 1976 after the death was reclassified. A 1994 exhumation by forensic pathologist James Starrs found injuries consistent with a blow to the head before the fall. Olson's son Eric pursued the case until his own death in 2024.

question: Three teenage boys on Oak Island, Nova Scotia, found a depression in the ground in 1795, with heavy tackle hanging from a tree above it, and started digging. Treasure hunters have been at the Money Pit ever since. The early diggers reported hitting distinctive wooden platforms at regular intervals down the shaft. About how often were those platforms spaced?
context: Daniel McGinnis, John Smith, and Anthony Vaughan dug the original shaft.
