By the early 1800s, syndicates were excavating and reporting layers of oak logs, coconut fiber, putty, and charcoal at depths of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 80, 90, and 100 feet. The pit floods catastrophically at about 90 feet. The History Channel's The Curse of Oak Island debuted in 2014 and has run for over a decade since.

question: Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 was a Boeing 777 with 239 people on board. It vanished from radar early on March 8, 2014, on a trip from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing. Later, satellite pings tracked the plane to a far part of one ocean. Pieces of it washed up on islands and on the African coast the next year. In which ocean did the plane go down?
choices: The Java Sea south of Sumatra
The Philippine Sea east of Mindanao
The Andaman Sea north of Sumatra
context: British satellite firm Inmarsat used the small frequency shifts in the hourly handshake pings to compute a 'seventh arc' along which the plane was when its fuel ran out — somewhere in the southern Indian Ocean west of Perth, Australia. A 100,000-square-kilometer Australian-led search ended in 2017. A second 2018 search by US firm Ocean Infinity also failed. Confirmed debris pieces include a flaperon recovered on Réunion Island in 2015.

question: The disappearance of three-year-old Madeleine McCann from a Praia da Luz apartment in Portugal's Algarve on May 3, 2007 became one of the most-covered missing-child cases in history. In 2020, German federal prosecutors named a primary suspect. Who is he?
answer: Christian Brückner, a convicted German sex offender
choices: Christian Brückner, a convicted German sex offender
Robert Murat, a British-Portuguese local resident
Gonçalo Amaral, the original lead Portuguese investigator
Goncalves dos Santos, the McCanns' apartment cleaner
context: Brückner was living in a camper van near Praia da Luz at the time of Madeleine's disappearance and had a long record of break-ins and sexual offenses in the region. He is currently serving a separate seven-year sentence in Germany for the 2005 rape of an elderly American woman in Praia da Luz. German prosecutors said in 2022 that they were confident he had killed Madeleine but lacked enough physical evidence to charge him. He was acquitted in October 2024 in a separate trial.

question: The 'Lincoln-Kennedy coincidences' list came out in the late 1960s. It claims the two shot presidents had many things in common. Today it is used as a classic example of seeing patterns that are not really there. Which one from the list is actually true as people usually tell it?
answer: Both were succeeded by vice presidents named Johnson
choices: Both were succeeded by vice presidents named Johnson
Both were shot from behind in the head on a Friday by a man with three names
Both assassins were themselves killed in a brick warehouse before trial
Both presidents had secretaries who warned them not to go to the theater
context: Andrew Johnson (1865) and Lyndon Johnson (1963) is one of the few genuinely accurate items. Lincoln's secretary was named John Nicolay, not 'Kennedy'; Kennedy's was named Evelyn Lincoln — but neither warned about a theater. Lee Harvey Oswald was killed in a parking garage, not a brick warehouse. The list became a popular illustration of cognitive bias in skeptical literature; Martin Gardner devoted a 1989 column to debunking it.

question: The 'Mandela Effect' is when many people share the same false memory. Some 'remember' the Berenstain Bears spelled 'Berenstein.' Some 'remember' the Monopoly Man with a monocle. Fiona Broome named the effect around 2010. She met many people who 'remembered' Nelson Mandela dying in prison years before he really did. When did the real Nelson Mandela die?
context: Mandela was released from Robben Island in 1990, elected South African president in 1994, and died as a private citizen in Johannesburg on December 5, 2013 at age 95. Broome coined the term in 2009-2010 conversation at a Dragon Con paranormal event. The most-defended explanation is mundane: confabulation, conformity in retelling, and the brain reconstructing rather than retrieving memories.

question: Mike Parker Pearson's team used chemical and structural fingerprints in 2015 to identify the quarries behind Stonehenge's smaller 'bluestones'. The outer ring is built from huge local sarsen sandstone blocks, but the bluestones of the inner horseshoe come from a much more remote source. Where did they come from?
answer: The Preseli Hills of southwest Wales
choices: The Preseli Hills of southwest Wales
The Cumbrian Mountains of northwest England
The Mourne Mountains of Northern Ireland
context: The bluestones come specifically from Carn Goedog and Craig Rhos-y-felin. They are roughly 150 miles from Salisbury Plain by the most direct route. Parker Pearson's team has argued the stones may originally have stood as a complete monument in Wales centuries before being dismantled and dragged to Stonehenge — turning Stonehenge into a kind of second-hand monument.

question: The 'Bunny Man' is a Virginia local legend connected to a railroad overpass in Fairfax County. Beginning in the 1970s, teenagers reported encounters with an axe-wielding figure in a rabbit suit hanging skinned rabbits from the bridge. Investigators have traced the story back to two actual 1970 police reports of a man in a rabbit suit. What is the local nickname for the underpass?
choices: Hop Hollow Trestle on Burke Lake Road
Rabbit Run Tunnel in Clifton Hollow
context: Brian Conley, then a Fairfax librarian, traced the legend's origin to two confirmed 1970 incidents: on October 19, an Air Force cadet and his fiancée reported a man in a bunny costume throwing a hatchet through their car window in Burke; ten days later a security guard found a man in a rabbit suit chopping at a roof column. Neither suspect was ever identified. The bridge sits in Clifton, Virginia and the local-legend pilgrimage continues every Halloween.

question: The 'Pope Lick Monster' is a Kentucky urban legend of a goatman who lives under a 90-foot active railroad trestle in eastern Louisville. The legend is dangerous in a non-supernatural way: people climb the trestle hoping to see the monster, and the active freight-rail line still uses it. How many people have been killed climbing the Pope Lick Trestle to date?
context: The trestle was built in the late 1800s and is still in active freight use. The deaths typically involve people who climb the trestle to look for the goatman, get caught by an oncoming train, and either jump 90 feet to escape or are struck. Local prosecutors have repeatedly tried to deter trespassers through public-safety campaigns. The legend was the subject of the 1988 short horror film The Legend of the Pope Lick Monster.

question: In 1908, a huge blast in central Siberia flattened about 2,000 square kilometers of forest. It left no crater. The blast hit on June 30, but Russian scientists did not reach the site for nearly 20 years. Which Soviet mineral scientist led the first big trip to Tunguska in 1927?
context: Kulik led four expeditions between 1927 and 1939. He documented the radial 'butterfly' pattern of fallen trees with the apex at the airburst location and the trees nearest ground zero left standing but stripped of branches — the classic signature of an air-burst shock wave from above. Kulik died of typhus as a Soviet partisan in 1942 during World War II. No major fragment has ever been recovered, supporting a stony asteroid airburst at about 8 km altitude.

question: Spyridon Marinatos, a Greek archaeologist, argued in 1939 that a colossal Bronze Age eruption had shattered the Minoan civilization of Crete. He later suggested that the tale of sunken Atlantis grew out of memories of the blast, and in 1967 he began uncovering Akrotiri, a whole town buried in the volcano's ash. Which island's volcano erupted?
answer: Thera, the island now called Santorini
choices: Thera, the island now called Santorini
Stromboli, off the north of Sicily
context: Marinatos argued in 1939 that the eruption of Thera (Santorini) devastated Minoan Crete, and later proposed that the Atlantis legend came from oral memories of it. His dig at Akrotiri, begun in 1967, uncovered a Bronze Age town sealed under the ash. Scholars still debate how much the eruption had to do with the Minoans' decline.

question: Logger Travis Walton vanished in front of six fellow crewmen on November 5, 1975, near Heber, Arizona while their company's logging contract was running behind schedule. He reappeared five days later beside a roadside phone booth in nearby Heber. Walton's brother passed lie-detector tests; so did all six crewmen. Which federal-lands thinning contract were the crew working under?
answer: A US Forest Service thinning contract in the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest
choices: A US Forest Service thinning contract in the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest
A Bureau of Land Management juniper-clearing contract in Coconino County
A National Park Service hazard-tree removal contract in Grand Canyon North Rim
A US Fish & Wildlife meadow-restoration contract in the Kaibab National Forest
context: Walton's foreman Mike Rogers was the only crew member who failed a polygraph (results were 'inconclusive'). Walton has stuck with his story for fifty years and runs a UFO conference in his hometown. Robert Lieberman's 1993 film Fire in the Sky takes substantial creative license with the details — most notably, the harrowing on-craft sequence is invented; Walton's actual memory described a far more clinical experience.

question: In 1934 the famous 'Surgeon's Photograph' showed the Loch Ness Monster. It became the most reproduced cryptid image in history. In 1994 a ninety-three-year-old man named Christian Spurling confessed on his deathbed. His stepfather Marmaduke Wetherell had constructed the hoax using a clockwork toy submarine with a putty neck attached. From which famous London department store did the hoaxers buy the toy submarine?
context: Wetherell had been publicly humiliated by the Daily Mail in 1933 after his 'Bigfoot' Nessie footprint find turned out to be hippopotamus tracks from an umbrella stand. The toy-submarine hoax was his revenge: he had his stepson Spurling rig the toy with putty, his other son Ian shoot the photograph, and his friend Maurice Chambers approach gynecologist Robert Kenneth Wilson to front the image as a respectable witness. The 1994 confession ran in the British Journal of Photography and in Sunday Telegraph. The Loch Ness Centre at Drumnadrochit displays the toy-submarine reconstruction today.

question: The Patterson-Gimlin film was shot at Bluff Creek in northern California on October 20, 1967. It shows what many think is a Bigfoot walking. In 2014, a Hollywood creature-suit expert who had worked on Star Wars, Predator, and Total Recall put out a book about the film. He used sharp scanned frames to argue no 1967 costume could have looked like that. Who was he?
context: Munns's book When Roger Met Patty (2014) catalogs frame-by-frame measurements of muscle movement, fur dynamics, and gait against costume design references from the late 1960s. Bigfoot researchers including Daniel Perez and Jeff Meldrum cite the work; skeptics like Donald Prothero have published rebuttals. Roger Patterson's 1973 widow Patricia confirmed in interviews that her husband had never owned a costume of the kind required. The high-resolution scans were made from the original first-generation film print, which the Patterson family preserved.

question: The Silver Bridge between Point Pleasant, West Virginia and Gallipolis, Ohio collapsed at 5:04 pm on December 15, 1967, dropping 46 people into the freezing Ohio River and ending thirteen months of Mothman sightings. The 1928 eyebar suspension bridge failed because of a single 1.5-millimeter crack that had grown undetected for years in an irreplaceable structural element. In what part of the bridge did the crack form?
answer: A single eyebar in the north chain on the Ohio side
choices: A single eyebar in the north chain on the Ohio side
A south anchorage pin in the West Virginia abutment
A vertical hanger cable between the deck and chains
A stiffening truss panel near the central tower
context: The post-collapse National Bureau of Standards investigation identified eyebar number 330 on the north chain as the failure origin. The crack had grown through stress corrosion in a high-carbon heat-treated steel that had no redundancy: every eyebar's failure took down the bridge. The disaster led to the 1968 National Bridge Inspection Standards and a mandate that suspension bridges have redundant cable systems. The replacement Silver Memorial Bridge opened in 1969 just downstream. John Keel's later The Mothman Prophecies tied the sightings to the disaster; whether locals had a true premonition or pareidolia in retrospect remains one of high-strangeness literature's central debates.

question: The black clip-on tie left on seat 18-E by the hijacker known as D.B. Cooper became the FBI's primary physical evidence after the November 24, 1971 hijacking of Northwest Orient Flight 305. In 2011, a citizen sleuth team led by paleontologist Tom Kaye published electron-microscope analysis of trace particles trapped in the tie's fabric. The team found microscopic shards of titanium, cerium, and other rare-earth elements not commonly co-located in 1971 except in one very specific industry. What industry?
answer: Aerospace manufacturing, particularly chemical-plant equipment for titanium production
choices: Aerospace manufacturing, particularly chemical-plant equipment for titanium production
Petrochemical refining for high-temperature catalytic cracking units
Naval submarine reactor cladding and pressure-vessel welding work
Photographic-film coating production for color-process labs
context: Kaye's analysis was published in collaboration with FBI cooperation. The Boeing plants in Renton, Washington and the SR-71 program at Skunk Works in Burbank were two of the few US sites in 1971 routinely handling titanium aerospace alloys; the Pittsburgh-area chemical plant of Crucible Steel also made the list. The geographic pull is suggestive but not conclusive. The FBI suspended active investigation in July 2016 after 45 years; over 1,000 suspects had been named, none confirmed. The bills Brian Ingram found on a Columbia River sandbar in February 1980 totaled about $5,800 — the only piece of the $200,000 ransom ever recovered.

question: Whoever built the ancient Greek instrument raised from a Roman-era shipwreck in 1901 based its spiral eclipse dial on the old Babylonian 'saros' cycle. The saros is a long cycle with eclipses scattered through it. How long is the cycle, and how many eclipses does the dial cover?
context: The saros dial occupies the back of the mechanism. The Babylonian astronomers had recognized that after 223 synodic months, the relative positions of the sun, moon, and lunar nodes repeat, so a list of eclipses in one saros lets you predict eclipses in the next. Around 51 of the 223 months in the cycle contain eclipses. Mike Edmunds's Antikythera Mechanism Research Project published the saros analysis in Nature in 2008. Tony Freeth's team modeled the gear-trains and continues to publish — including a 2021 paper proposing a reconstruction of the mechanism's lost front panel.

question: William Friedman, the US Army cryptanalyst who broke the Japanese Purple cipher, spent decades on the script of a mysterious medieval book full of unknown plants and star charts. He hid his conclusion inside an anagram until his death. What did Friedman conclude about the manuscript's language?
answer: It was an early attempt at a constructed synthetic 'philosophical' language
choices: It was an early attempt at a constructed synthetic 'philosophical' language
It was Czech written in a phonetic substitution cipher
It was Hebrew with vowels removed and consonants reversed
It was an Arabic dialect with Mongol-script numerals
context: Friedman published his anagram in 1959: 'The Voynich MSS was an early attempt to construct an artificial or universal language of the a priori type.' He never lived to see it confirmed or refuted. Modern statistical analyses lean toward the manuscript being either a genuine constructed language or a sophisticated hoax with structural features mimicking real language. A 2025 paper using transformer-based language modeling found the text has word-frequency distributions consistent with real language, not random gibberish. The Beinecke Library catalogs it as MS 408 and has digitized all 240 pages freely online.

question: Louis Hammond of California brought Emory University a 21-pound stone in 1937 and claimed to have discovered it near Edenton, North Carolina. The carving seemed to be a message from Eleanor Dare, one of the lost Roanoke colonists. Forty-eight more 'Dare Stones' surfaced over four years, telling a detailed survival story, until a 1941 magazine investigation exposed nearly all as fraudulent. Who had actually been producing the later stones?
answer: A stonecutter named Bill Eberhardt, who sold them to Brenau College in Georgia
choices: A stonecutter named Bill Eberhardt, who sold them to Brenau College in Georgia
A traveling carnival ventriloquist named Howard 'Pop' Dawson
A Methodist preacher named Edgar Cayce as part of a séance practice
A southern aristocrat named Elizabeth Cabbell as a literary prank
context: Eberhardt and his accomplice 'Pop' Dawson sold the later stones to Haywood Pearce Jr. of Brenau College in Gainesville, Georgia, who paid bounty for new finds. Sparkes's 1941 magazine exposé documented Eberhardt manufacturing 'authentic' new stones for cash. The first 1937 stone is still considered possibly genuine by some specialists. The historical mystery — what actually happened to the 115 colonists left at Roanoke in 1587 — remains open. Recent archaeological work led by the First Colony Foundation has found Elizabethan-era artifacts at Site X on the western shore of Albemarle Sound, consistent with at least some colonists having moved 50 miles inland.

question: Big Ear's computer printed each radio channel as a column of characters, one reading every ten seconds. A blank meant plain background hiss, the digits 1 through 9 meant louder readings, and letters meant louder still, with A for 10, B for 11 and so on up the alphabet. On August 15, 1977, one column climbed to about thirty times the background over six readings and then faded. Jerry Ehman circled the whole run in red ink. What six characters did he circle?
context: The string 6EQUJ5 is not a message but a record of the signal's strength over six ten-second readings: 6, then E (14), Q (26), U (30, the peak), J (19) and 5. Ehman circled it and wrote 'Wow!' beside it, which gave the signal its name.

question: Frank Olson was a US Army biochemist. In November 1953, he fell from a 13th-floor New York hotel window. His death became the best-known case tied to MK-Ultra, the CIA's Cold War mind-control program. He had been doing secret bioweapons work at Fort Detrick. In 1994, a body exam by James Starrs found a bruise on his skull that looked like a blow before the fall. What secret bioweapons work had Olson done that may have made him a risk?
answer: The Army's anthrax and other aerosol-weapon dispersion field tests in Florida and the Caribbean
choices: The Army's anthrax and other aerosol-weapon dispersion field tests in Florida and the Caribbean
The Navy's Project Aquarius nuclear-isotope detection program at Norfolk
The Air Force's high-altitude thorium-photolysis research at Wright-Patterson
The Marine Corps' polonium-210 acoustic-weapon testing in California
context: Olson worked on aerosol biological-weapon dispersion, including 1950 sea-spray tests off Norfolk and tests in Caribbean waters that may have involved live anthrax simulant in populated areas. He had reportedly grown morally distressed in the weeks before his death. The CIA, under chemist Sidney Gottlieb, secretly dosed him with LSD at a Deep Creek Lake retreat on November 19, 1953, then sent him to a New York psychiatrist who, declassified files later showed, was a CIA contractor. Eric Olson sued the federal government in 2012; the case was dismissed for sovereign immunity but produced major document releases. Errol Morris's six-episode 2017 Netflix series Wormwood dramatized the saga.

question: In 2008, the Pentagon gave a $22 million UFO contract to a firm owned by billionaire Robert Bigelow. The program was called AAWSAP. Its main field site was a remote Utah cattle ranch famous for paranormal reports. The team wrote a few inside documents. One was over 100 pages long and was all about that ranch. What was that main report often called?
context: AAWSAP overlapped with and is often confused with AATIP, the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program, which later focused on military UFO encounters like the 2004 USS Nimitz 'tic-tac' incident. Former Pentagon official Luis Elizondo became the public face of AATIP after a December 2017 New York Times article by Helene Cooper, Ralph Blumenthal, and Leslie Kean. Skinwalker Ranch has been owned since 2016 by real-estate developer Brandon Fugal, who funds the History Channel's ongoing series with physicist Travis Taylor as the lead investigator. The 2021 book Skinwalkers at the Pentagon by James Lacatski (the AAWSAP program manager), Colm Kelleher, and George Knapp made the program's existence undeniable.

question: The nine hikers who died at Dyatlov Pass in February 1959 were almost all students at a Soviet university known for nuclear-physics and metallurgy programs. Their leader Igor Dyatlov was a radio-engineering student there. Others studied fields tied to the strange 'radiation on clothing' detail. Where were the Dyatlov hikers students?
answer: The Ural Polytechnic Institute in Sverdlovsk (now Ekaterinburg)
choices: The Ural Polytechnic Institute in Sverdlovsk (now Ekaterinburg)
context: The hikers studied at the Ural Polytechnic Institute in Sverdlovsk, now part of Ural Federal University, and one of them, Yuri Krivonischenko, had worked at the Mayak nuclear plant. The 1959 investigation noted the radiation on some clothing without explaining it; later writers have pointed to thorium lantern mantles or to contamination from that nuclear work. The 2019-2020 reinvestigation found no radiation anomaly and blamed a snow-slab avalanche.

question: In early July 1947, an Army officer said a 'flying disc' had crashed near Roswell, New Mexico. The Army took it back the next day and said it was a weather balloon. In 1994, an Air Force report finally named the real cause: parts from a secret high-altitude balloon program. The balloons were made to spot one kind of Soviet activity from far away. What were they trying to find?
answer: Atmospheric pressure waves from Soviet atomic-bomb tests
choices: Atmospheric pressure waves from Soviet atomic-bomb tests
Long-wave radio communications from Soviet submarines
Aerosol fallout from Soviet biological-weapons trials
Magnetic-field anomalies from Soviet missile-silo construction
context: Project Mogul ran from 1947 to 1949 under the Office of Naval Research and the Army Air Forces. Engineer Maurice Ewing of Columbia University proposed using long balloon trains carrying low-frequency microphones at the constant-altitude sound channel in the upper atmosphere to listen for distant atomic-test pressure waves. The Roswell debris was likely from Flight 4, a Mogul launch that went missing in early June 1947. The 1994 Air Force report (and its 1997 follow-up on 'flying disc' bodies) credited Project Mogul plus crash-test-dummy parachute experiments as the most-defended mundane source for the persistent Roswell aliens story. Walter Haut later co-founded the International UFO Museum and Research Center in downtown Roswell, which now draws over 200,000 visitors a year.

question: Two anthropologists took on the popular 'ecocide' story of Easter Island in a 2011 book. That story said the Rapa Nui destroyed their own island by building too many statues. Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo argued that the islanders adapted well and were later ruined by imported diseases and Peruvian slave raids. A strange feature of the statues themselves gave the book its title. What is the book called?
choices: Collapse: How Societies Choose to Fail or Succeed
context: Hunt and Lipo's 2011 book at Free Press is a direct response to Jared Diamond's 2005 Collapse, which used Easter Island as a parable of self-destructive resource exploitation. Hunt and Lipo demonstrated the 'walking' technique with a 4.4-ton replica moai and three rope teams; their experiment is now standard in the literature. Rapa Nui's population may have peaked at 15,000 or higher before contact; after Peruvian slave raids in 1862-63 and subsequent smallpox, the native population dropped to roughly 110 in 1877. The island is today a Chilean special territory with a population of about 7,750. The 887 moai are protected as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

question: On June 30, 1908, the Tunguska airburst flattened roughly 80 million trees over 2,000 square kilometers of Siberian forest yet produced no ground crater. In 1927 mineralogist Leonid Kulik documented the classic radial 'butterfly' pattern: trees blown outward from a central point, with the central trees left standing but stripped of branches. That signature indicates a specific kind of impact event. At what altitude above the surface did the airburst occur?
answer: About 5 to 10 kilometers above the surface
choices: About 5 to 10 kilometers above the surface
About 100 to 200 meters above the surface
About 30 to 50 kilometers above the surface
Directly at the surface in a shallow lake
context: Modern modeling places the airburst at 5 to 10 kilometers altitude, with a yield equivalent to 10 to 15 megatons of TNT — comparable to the largest US thermonuclear test. The most-defended cause is a 50-to-80-meter stony asteroid that fragmented and exploded in mid-air before reaching the ground. The standing 'telegraph pole' trees directly beneath the burst escaped because the shock wave came straight down rather than sideways. The 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor airburst — also over Russia — produced a similar but smaller signature and provided a modern reference. Russian academic expeditions to the Tunguska site continue; the area is now part of the Tunguska Nature Reserve.

question: The 'Mansi photograph,' considered the Champ equivalent of the Surgeon's Photo, was taken on July 5, 1977 by Sandra Mansi at St. Albans Bay on the Vermont side of Lake Champlain. The Polaroid instant image shows a long-necked dark shape rising from the lake while Mansi's children played at the shore. What aspect of the photograph's history has frustrated subsequent skeptical analysis?
answer: Mansi lost the camera and the exact location, and the original negative is a Polaroid with no preserved negative
choices: Mansi lost the camera and the exact location, and the original negative is a Polaroid with no preserved negative
Multiple later photographs from the same vantage point showed an obvious sandbar formation
A second witness immediately disputed Mansi's account and was later disowned by the family
Sandra Mansi confessed in 1995 that the figure had been added with a darkroom double exposure
context: Polaroid SX-70 photographs are single-shot positives — there is no negative to enlarge or re-examine. Mansi waited several years to publicize the photo and then could not relocate the exact spot on the lake's edge, frustrating bathymetric comparison studies. University of Arizona optical-physics analysis in 1981 found no signs of double exposure or manipulation. Champ-spotter websites still cluster sightings around Burlington and Plattsburgh Bay. Lake Champlain is 12 miles wide at its widest and reaches 400 feet deep — plenty of room for sturgeon, gar pike, schools of fish, log mats, and creative wave-and-light effects.

question: The Mary Celeste was discovered drifting east of the Azores on December 4, 1872 by the British brigantine Dei Gratia. Captain Briggs, his family, and the entire seven-man crew had vanished, though the vessel was seaworthy and the cargo untouched. The most defended modern explanation focuses on a peculiar property of the specific cargo she carried. What was the cargo, and what was the suspect property?
answer: 1,701 barrels of denatured industrial alcohol; nine empty barrels in the hold suggest a partial fume leak Briggs feared could explode
choices: 1,701 barrels of denatured industrial alcohol; nine empty barrels in the hold suggest a partial fume leak Briggs feared could explode
Several thousand pounds of guano fertilizer that may have produced toxic ammonia fumes in the closed hold
Stacked crates of black-powder fireworks heated by sunlight after a glass skylight cracked open
Live ostrich eggs and a calf whose distress led the crew to abandon their stations to investigate
context: The barrels were red oak rather than the more typical white oak. Red oak is more porous, and modern researchers including Anne MacGregor have argued the porous barrels could have leaked alcohol vapors as the ship traveled through warm seas. A pressure-vapor incident — possibly a brief but loud overpressure rupture from the hold — may have convinced the devout Briggs his ship was about to explode, prompting him to order an immediate evacuation by lifeboat. The lifeboat then parted from the ship, leaving the empty Mary Celeste to drift. The 'cargo evaporated' hypothesis was demonstrated experimentally by MacGregor and naval architects in a 2007 Channel 5 documentary. The Mary Celeste itself was eventually deliberately wrecked on a Haitian reef in 1885 by its last owner, a Boston merchant captain trying to commit insurance fraud.

question: The Somerton Man was found dead on a beach in Adelaide, Australia on December 1, 1948. He had no ID. All his clothing labels had been cut off. In a hidden pocket was a scrap of Persian text reading 'Tamam Shud.' In 2022, University of Adelaide scientist Derek Abbott named him at last. He used DNA from a hair saved in a 1949 plaster bust of the dead man's face. Who did Abbott say the Somerton Man was?
answer: Carl 'Charles' Webb, an electrical engineer from Footscray, Melbourne
choices: Carl 'Charles' Webb, an electrical engineer from Footscray, Melbourne
H.C. Reynolds, a wartime British seaman with a 1918 American merchant marine card
Solomon Hayim, a Hungarian-Jewish refugee dentist who had vanished from Sydney
Alfred Boxall, an Australian intelligence officer linked to a nurse named Jestyn
context: Abbott and forensic genealogist Colleen Fitzpatrick used Y-chromosome DNA from the bust hair to identify Webb, born November 16, 1905. Webb was an electrical engineer estranged from his wife Dorothy in 1947; he had a documented love of poetry and gambling. The 1949 indented coded message found inside the matching Rubaiyat copy has still not been decrypted — Webb may have been working through a personal cipher rather than spy traffic. The case is one of the longest-running cold-case identifications in Australian history. South Australia Police accepted Abbott's identification in 2022 but did not formally close the case, as the cause of death (a digitalis-like poison was suspected but never confirmed) remains undetermined.

question: King Richard III is the uncle blamed for the missing Princes in the Tower back in 1483. He died at Bosworth Field on August 22, 1485. He was buried in a rush at Greyfriars in Leicester. That building was torn down later, and his grave was lost for over 500 years. In 2012, a team from the University of Leicester found his bones under what odd modern spot?
answer: A municipal car park behind Leicester city council offices
choices: A municipal car park behind Leicester city council offices
The basement of a Victorian-era Wesleyan chapel
The west tower of Leicester Cathedral
The kitchen garden of a 19th-century almshouse
context: The car park was the Social Services Department's staff lot. Buckley's team chose the dig site from a 19th-century map overlay onto modern Leicester streets. Within hours of breaking the asphalt they uncovered articulated leg bones; within a week the full skeleton was exposed with severe scoliosis and battle wounds consistent with Tudor accounts of Richard's death. DNA matched living maternal-line descendant Michael Ibsen, a London cabinetmaker. Richard III was reinterred in Leicester Cathedral on March 26, 2015 in a ceremony attended by Benedict Cumberbatch, the king's third cousin sixteen times removed. The Westminster Abbey 'Princes' bones from the 1674 staircase find have still not been DNA-tested.

question: Prehistoric people quarried Stonehenge's smaller 'bluestones' about 150 miles from Salisbury Plain. Mike Parker Pearson's team named two exact outcrops in a 2015 paper, and each outcrop gave a different kind of rock. What is either of those two quarries called?
answer: Carn Goedog (spotted dolerite) or Craig Rhos-y-felin (rhyolite)
choices: Carn Goedog (spotted dolerite) or Craig Rhos-y-felin (rhyolite)
Pen y Fan (limestone) or Carn Llidi (basalt)
context: Carn Goedog and Craig Rhos-y-felin sit about three kilometers apart in the Preseli Hills of Pembrokeshire. At Craig Rhos-y-felin, Parker Pearson's team found a Neolithic quarry floor with hammer-stones and stone-extraction wedges still in situ. Parker Pearson has argued the Welsh stones may originally have stood as a complete monument in Wales for several centuries before being dismantled and dragged to Salisbury Plain around 2900 BC — making Stonehenge in part a 'second-hand monument' assembled from imported Welsh material. The proposed original Welsh stone circle, identified at Waun Mawn, would have been roughly the same diameter as Stonehenge's bluestone circle.

question: 'Wendigo psychosis' was a strange case: people became sure they were turning into a wendigo, craved human flesh, and sometimes acted on it. It was noted in Cree, Ojibwe, and other Algonquian groups from the 1800s into the early 1900s. A missionary named Paul Le Jeune wrote the first close look at it in 1635-37. Scientists have argued about the best way to label it. Which label fits best?
answer: A culture-bound syndrome shaped by famine, isolation, and a powerful Algonquian moral framework about cannibalism
choices: A culture-bound syndrome shaped by famine, isolation, and a powerful Algonquian moral framework about cannibalism
An infectious encephalitis transmitted by undercooked moose meat in winter
A neuroactive ergotism from contaminated grain stores during harsh winters
A genetic prion disorder analogous to kuru in Papua New Guinea cannibals
context: The 1907 case of Swift Runner, a Cree trapper hanged in Fort Saskatchewan after killing and eating most of his family during a winter famine, is the most-cited single case. Anthropologist Robert Brightman's influential 1988 paper argued the syndrome was real but inseparable from Algonquian cosmology — kids grew up hearing wendigo stories the way Western kids grow up hearing about devils. The Native American academic Basil Johnston wrote elegantly about the wendigo as a metaphor for greed and consumption — the monstrous transformation a person who eats other people for material gain undergoes morally even without a literal cannibal act. Modern Algonquian writers including Joseph Boyden have continued to use the figure in literary fiction.

question: On May 31, 2014 in Waukesha, Wisconsin, two 12-year-old girls attacked a friend in a wooded park, saying they wanted to please the internet folk figure Slender Man. Their friend survived. Both girls were tried as adults in Wisconsin and pleaded not guilty by reason of mental illness. To what kind of secure facility were both eventually committed?
choices: Wisconsin's Lincoln Hills Juvenile Detention Center
Wisconsin's Mendota Mental Health Institute Juvenile Wing
Wisconsin's Copper Lake School for Girls
context: One girl was committed to Winnebago for 40 years in December 2017, the other for 25 years in 2018. Slender Man had been invented in June 2009 by Eric Knudsen ('Victor Surge') on the Something Awful forum. The Waukesha stabbing became a national news story and a HBO documentary, Beware the Slenderman (2016). Knudsen himself published a statement of grief and shock and stepped back from much of his public Slender Man involvement. The girl they attacked later said publicly that she had forgiven them.

question: Librarians at an American university put every page of a six-hundred-year-old manuscript of unknown plants and star charts online in 2004, free to view, so that people all over the world could try to crack the code. The book had reached their rare-book library in 1969. Under what catalog number does the library file it?
context: Hans Kraus, a New York antiquarian book dealer, bought the manuscript from Voynich's daughter Anne Nill in 1961 and donated it to Yale in 1969 after failing to sell it. The Beinecke's 2004 digitization was led by curator Raymond Clemens. The publicly available high-resolution images have fueled a new round of cryptanalytic attempts including Stephen Bax (2014, partial), Greg Kondrak's University of Alberta team (2018, 'Hebrew' hypothesis), and a growing number of transformer-based language-model attempts since 2022. None has produced a generally accepted decryption. The Beinecke has refused to allow destructive sampling of the vellum beyond the original Arizona carbon dating.

question: The Jersey Devil legend dates to the eighteenth century in the Pine Barrens of southern New Jersey. Most versions name a 'Mother Leeds' who in 1735 cried 'let this one be a devil!' while pregnant with her thirteenth child. At birth the infant reportedly transformed and flew up the chimney. Historian Brian Regal traced the tradition to a real colonial New Jersey family with a controversial religious history. What was the family's name, and what was their actual occupation?
answer: The Leeds family of Burlington County; Daniel Leeds was a Quaker surveyor and almanac-maker turned colonial heretic
choices: The Leeds family of Burlington County; Daniel Leeds was a Quaker surveyor and almanac-maker turned colonial heretic
The Leigh family of Cape May; Charles Leigh was a colonial sea captain known for marsh smuggling
The Pennington family of Cumberland County; Joshua Pennington was an itinerant Methodist circuit preacher
The Logan family of Atlantic County; James Logan was an indentured-servant overseer at a Pine Barrens iron forge
context: Historian Brian Regal, in work that led to the 2018 book The Secret History of the Jersey Devil (with Frank J. Esposito), traced the 'Leeds Devil' name to Daniel Leeds, a Burlington County surveyor whose 1687 almanac carried astrology. His Quaker meeting condemned it; after he turned Anglican and attacked the Quakers in print, a 1700 Quaker tract accused him of serving the devil. His son Titan later printed the family crest, a bat-winged wyvern much like later descriptions of the Jersey Devil.

question: The 'Philadelphia Experiment' is a long-running lore claim -- first promoted in 1955-56 letters to unidentified-flying-object (UFO) researcher Morris K. Jessup by a writer using the name 'Carlos Allende' (real name Carl M. Allen) -- that in October 1943 the US Navy made the destroyer escort USS Eldridge briefly invisible and teleported it from a Philadelphia shipyard to Norfolk, Virginia. The US Navy and the actual logs of the Eldridge and the Naval Reserve both make a specific factual problem for Allende's story. What is the problem?
answer: The Eldridge was not at the Philadelphia Navy Yard in October 1943 and never had any classified invisibility experiment
choices: The Eldridge was not at the Philadelphia Navy Yard in October 1943 and never had any classified invisibility experiment
The Norfolk Navy Yard logs show no record of any ship arriving by sea or otherwise that month
Carlos Allende was a known German-American radio engineer with espionage convictions in 1942
Jessup himself confessed in a sealed 1959 letter that he had invented the story
context: USS Eldridge's actual logs, declassified and digitized by the National Archives, place the ship in New York and Bermuda during the time Allende claimed it was in Philadelphia. The 'experiment' lore was largely amplified after Charles Berlitz and William Moore's 1979 book The Philadelphia Experiment: Project Invisibility. The 1984 Stewart Raffill film starring Michael Pare turned the lore into a low-budget sci-fi staple. Morris Jessup did die in 1959 in an apparent suicide in a Florida park — a fact that fed the rumor mill but had no demonstrated connection to the Eldridge story. The Office of Naval Research has occasionally published statements debunking the experiment because so many letters from the curious continue to arrive.

question: On August 21, 1955, the Sutton and Taylor families near Kelly, Kentucky reported a five-hour siege of their farmhouse. Small silvery humanoids with pointed ears and clawed hands kept appearing outside. The men told reporters they emptied their shotguns and rifles, and that the creatures toppled from trees and the roof, then floated away unhurt. It became one of the most-documented 'close encounter' cases in US history. Some researchers now argue the creatures were really a local animal behaving strangely. Which animal?
answer: Great horned owls defending their nest from human intruders
choices: Great horned owls defending their nest from human intruders
A small troop of escaped capuchin monkeys from a defunct carnival
An unusual nighttime mass of barn-stored bats roused by gunfire
Wild young raccoons made luminous by phosphorescent fungus on their fur
context: The Hopkinsville Goblin case is sometimes referred to as the Kelly Green Men case. Air Force investigators in Project Blue Book closed the case as 'monkeys escaped from circus' but local zoos and traveling shows reported no escaped primates that week. UFO researcher Joe Nickell's 2006 article in Skeptical Inquirer made the great-horned-owl case in detail: the silvery 'glow' was reflected moonlight on the owls' lighter belly feathers; the pointed 'ears' were ear tufts; the floating motion was wing-glide; the imperviousness to gunfire was simply that, at night, scared men with shotguns rarely connected. The Kelly area still hosts an annual Little Green Men Festival, and the original Sutton farmhouse, long since demolished, stood near State Route 41A.

question: Popobawa is a modern shape-shifting monster from the islands of Zanzibar, off Tanzania. It was first reported on Pemba Island in 1965. More waves of sightings hit in 1970, 1995, and 2007. People say it looks like a bat-winged creature with one eye that attacks sleepers. Anthropologist Martin Walsh studied the sightings. He thinks the modern panics are best seen as one kind of community event tied to political worry. What kind of event?
answer: A culture-bound mass-anxiety phenomenon that intensifies during elections and political tension on the islands
choices: A culture-bound mass-anxiety phenomenon that intensifies during elections and political tension on the islands
A coordinated village-level hoax to deflect blame from village-elder land disputes
A pattern of nocturnal home invasions by economic migrants from the mainland
A misidentification wave triggered by the appearance of large flying fox bats during fruiting seasons
context: Walsh's 2005 paper in Journal of Religion in Africa documents that Popobawa panic waves cluster around Zanzibar's politically charged election cycles, when the ruling CCM party and the opposition CUF have repeatedly clashed. The cryptid's name means 'bat-wing' in Swahili. Belief in the creature is widespread enough that village men have sometimes slept outside in courtyards during panic waves rather than risk being attacked indoors. The phenomenon shares features with sleep-paralysis traditions worldwide — including the Old Hag of Newfoundland, the Mara of Scandinavia, and the kanashibari of Japan — but the political timing on Zanzibar makes it locally distinct. The 2007 wave even produced reports of Popobawa attacking the secular Tanzania president's motorcade aides during a campaign stop on Pemba.

question: Deep in the dungeons of Dungeons and Dragons lurks a purple villain with an octopus-shaped head and four writhing face tentacles. It fires powerful psychic blasts to stun heroes, then wraps its tentacles around a victim's skull and eats the brain inside. Adventurers know it by a fitting common name. What is it called?
context: Also called an Illithid. First appeared in Strategic Review #1, Spring 1975. Mind flayers eat brains. Elder Brains rule each illithid colony from a brine pool. The Far Realm is their suspected origin in later lore.

question: Two friends in the American Midwest put out a strange new game in 1974, a small white box with three little rulebooks inside, and called it Dungeons and Dragons. One of them, Gary Gygax, had founded a tiny Wisconsin company to publish it. What was the company called?
context: The 1974 White Box was published by TSR in Lake Geneva, Wisconsin. Chainmail (1971) was the medieval-wargame seed. The Monster Manual (1977) was the first AD&D hardcover.

question: In the early 1970s, Dungeons & Dragons co-creator Gary Gygax was writing up his first list of dungeon monsters when he bought a bag of cheap plastic beast toys made in Hong Kong. One weird figure looked like a bear crossed with an owl -- brown feathers, a hooked yellow beak, huge black claws -- so Gygax kept the shape and put it in the game exactly as it appeared. What did he name this now-iconic D&D monster?
context: Gary Gygax based the owlbear on a cheap plastic Chinese-toy monster sitting on his desk in the early 1970s. The same toy bin gave him the bulette and the rust monster. Owlbears first appeared in the 1975 Greyhawk supplement.

question: In Dungeons & Dragons, one whole race of elves fled the sunlit world long ago and now lives far below ground in a vast lightless cavern network called the Underdark. Their skin is coal black, their hair snow white, and they worship a cruel spider goddess named Lolth who demands blood, betrayal, and human sacrifice. What are these dark elves called in D&D?
context: Drow first appeared in 1978's D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, but were fully detailed in D3 Vault of the Drow (1978). Their goddess Lolth, the Demon Queen of Spiders, was introduced in the same module trilogy.

question: Gary Gygax and a childhood friend founded a little game company in 1973 to publish a fantasy war game, and its first boxed sets came together in 1974 in Gygax's basement. The company was based in the Wisconsin town where he lived all his adult life. Which town was it?
context: Gary Gygax lived in Lake Geneva his entire adult life. The first Gen Con convention was held there in 1968, in his basement and the local Horticultural Hall. The TSR office was on Sage Street.

question: A 10-foot cube of clear jelly slides silently down D&D dungeon corridors, filling them wall to wall. It dissolves anything organic and leaves coins and metal behind, and heroes rarely see it until they walk into it. What is it called?
context: The gelatinous cube first appeared in the original 1974 boxed set. It is a ten-foot cube of transparent ooze, the width of a standard corridor, whose acidic juices dissolve everything organic and leave indigestible matter such as metal behind.

question: Gary Gygax bought a bag of plastic monster figures at a dime store and turned one bug-like creature into a Dungeons and Dragons monster made to horrify players. It is small, has two long antennae, and destroys any metal weapon or armor on contact — a mighty +5 magic sword crumbles to dust at its touch. What is it called?
context: The rust monster came from the same bag of cheap Chinese plastic toys as the owlbear and the bulette. Gary Gygax saw their potential as a player-character nightmare. Touching armor or weapons disintegrates them instantly.

question: In Dungeons and Dragons, deep in the misty land of Barovia stands the mountain fortress Castle Ravenloft. Its lord is a legendary vampire whose name sounds distinctly Czech. Long ago he betrayed and killed his own brother for the love of a woman, and he was cursed forever to haunt the castle. Who is he?
context: Strahd was created in 1983 by Tracy and Laura Hickman for the module I6 Ravenloft. Strahd murdered his brother Sergei on the wedding day and tried to claim Sergei's bride Tatyana. The curse turned him into the first vampire.

question: A Minneapolis wargamer ran the very first Blackmoor campaign in 1971, a homebrew fantasy game set around a wizard's tower on an island. He liked to swing a real hand-axe at medieval reenactments, and he shared the Dungeons and Dragons co-creator credit for the rest of his life. Who was he?
context: Arneson developed Blackmoor as a Chainmail variant starting around 1971. He brought the dungeon-crawl concept and the referee role to Gygax, who systematized the rules. Arneson died in 2009, one year after Gygax.

question: In the world of Dungeons & Dragons, the drow are dark-skinned elves who live in vast underground cities in a huge cave-world called the Underdark. They worship a cruel goddess who appears as a huge black spider with a woman's face. She rewards priestesses who murder rivals, feeds enemies to her spider children, and demands blood sacrifices. What is her name?
context: Lolth (also spelled Lloth in some Forgotten Realms novels) rules the 66th layer of the Abyss — the Demonweb Pits. She was introduced in 1978's D-series, then made the centerpiece of Q1 Queen of the Demonweb Pits in 1980.

question: Drizzt Do'Urden is the most beloved player-character in all of Dungeons & Dragons fiction: a good-hearted dark elf ranger who fled his cruel underground people, taught himself to wield twin scimitars, and made a home in the frozen valleys of Icewind Dale. Millions of paperbacks have sold about him. Which American novelist created Drizzt and has written his adventures since 1988?
context: Salvatore introduced Drizzt in 1988's The Crystal Shard, the first Icewind Dale novel. Drizzt's companions — Bruenor Battlehammer, Wulfgar, Regis, and Catti-brie — became the most-published heroes in D&D fiction history.

question: A fourth hero slips into Dungeons and Dragons with the 1975 supplement Greyhawk, joining the three classes of the first box. He hides in shadows, climbs walls and strikes enemies from behind for double damage. What is this new class called?
context: The original 1974 White Box had only three classes: fighting-man, magic-user, cleric. Greyhawk (1975) added the thief and the critical-hit rule. Eldritch Wizardry (1976) added the druid and psionics.

question: Gary Gygax put the Monster Manual, the Player's Handbook and the Dungeon Master's Guide under one new brand, shortened to AD&D. The three big rulebooks came out between 1977 and 1979. What did AD&D stand for?
context: AD&D's three core hardcovers were the Monster Manual (1977), Player's Handbook (1978), and Dungeon Master's Guide (1979). Gygax wrote the 500-page DMG, considered his magnum opus.

question: In Dungeons & Dragons, good knights and paladins sometimes ride into battle on a splendid white winged horse pulled straight from Greek myth -- the same steed the hero Bellerophon tamed to slay the fire-breathing Chimera. In the game it can carry an armored rider through the air and kick monsters with its hooves. What is this legendary winged horse called?
context: The pegasus is the winged horse of Greek myth, Bellerophon's mount against the Chimera. In D&D it's the classic good-aligned aerial mount. Hippogriffs (eagle-front horse-back) and griffins (eagle-front lion-back) are related.

question: The tabletop horror game Call of Cthulhu, where investigators slowly lose their sanity facing cosmic monsters, takes its name and its tentacled god from a 1928 story by a horror writer from Providence. Who wrote it?
context: Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu (1981) is built on H.P. Lovecraft's story of the same name, first printed in Weird Tales in February 1928, and on the wider Cthulhu Mythos. Lovecraft wrote the story at home in Providence, Rhode Island.

question: Gary Gygax opened his rebuilt game in 1977 with the Monster Manual, a thick illustrated book of every dragon, demon and beast in Dungeons and Dragons. It broke with every earlier product of the game. What did that make the Monster Manual?
context: The 1977 Monster Manual was the first hardcover rulebook ever published for a tabletop roleplaying game. It set the production-quality standard for the entire RPG industry, with its iconic Erol Otus, David Sutherland, and David Trampier art.

question: In D&D, a blue-black panther with six legs and two barbed shoulder tentacles always seems to stand a few feet from where it really is, so heroes swing and miss. Gygax borrowed it from a 1939 science-fiction story. What is it called?
context: The displacer beast's name comes from its magical displacement — it always appears a few feet from where it actually is. Gygax adapted it from the 'coeurl' in A.E. Van Vogt's 1939 sci-fi story 'Black Destroyer.'

question: The 1974 Dungeons and Dragons white box offers players only three classes. The Fighting-Man swings a sword, the Magic-User casts spells, and the third prays to a god for holy power, heals wounded friends and drives back skeletons and zombies with a raised holy symbol. What is this healer class called?
context: The original 1974 White Box had three classes: Fighting-Man, Magic-User, and Cleric. The cleric was a mash-up of medieval crusader-knight and Van Helsing the vampire-hunter, designed to keep one of Arneson's vampire monsters in check.

question: Conan the Barbarian -- the muscle-bound wandering warrior of the imagined Hyborian Age, who first stalked the pages of the pulp magazine Weird Tales in 1932 -- became the model for generations of fantasy barbarians. His creator was a young Texas writer who lived most of his short life in the tiny farm town of Cross Plains and typed his stories on a rickety desk in his parents' house. Who was this pulp author?
context: Howard's Conan stories ran in Weird Tales from 1932 until Howard's suicide in 1936. Gygax cited Howard, along with Tolkien, Vance, and Leiber, as a primary inspiration for D&D in the original DMG's Appendix N reading list.

question: In Dungeons & Dragons, some ancient evil wizards perform a horrible ritual to escape death forever. They tear their own soul out of their body and lock it inside a small magical jar called a phylactery, then hide the jar somewhere secret. Their body rots away to a skeleton — but as long as the phylactery survives, the wizard cannot really die. What is this kind of undead wizard called?
context: A lich's soul is bound to its phylactery — a small magic item, often a gemstone or amulet. Destroying the body only sends the lich back to its phylactery to regenerate. Acererak in Tomb of Horrors became a demilich.

question: In Greek myth, a monster with the body of a lion, the face of a woman, and huge feathered wings sat on a rock outside the city of Thebes and stopped every traveler with a riddle. Those who answered wrong she strangled and devoured. Only the hero Oedipus solved her puzzle. Dungeons & Dragons keeps her almost exactly. What is this riddling monster called?
context: The sphinx of Greek myth guarded Thebes and asked Oedipus the riddle 'What walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, three in the evening?' D&D has gynosphinxes (female, riddle-loving) and androsphinxes (male, warrior-like).

question: In Greek myth, one fire-breathing monster ravaged the kingdom of Lycia -- she had the body and forelegs of a lion in front, a second bleating head of a goat sprouting from her back, and a hissing serpent for her tail. The hero Bellerophon killed her from the air while riding Pegasus. Dungeons & Dragons uses her almost exactly. What is this three-in-one monster called?
context: The Greek-myth chimera had a lion-front body, a goat-head emerging from the back, and a serpent-tail. Bellerophon killed it with the help of Pegasus. In D&D, the standard chimera also has wings and three-headed breath weapons.

question: One of the most terrifying demon lords in all of Dungeons & Dragons has two hideous baboon heads that twist and hiss on long reptilian necks, tentacles for arms, and huge leathery bat wings. Called the Prince of Demons, he first crawled into the game in the 1976 supplement Eldritch Wizardry and returned as the ultimate villain in later editions. What is his name?
context: Demogorgon is the Prince of Demons in AD&D — the top of the demonic hierarchy. The two heads on his goat-shoulders are Aameul (left, deceitful) and Hethradiah (right, destructive). His name became a Stranger Things 2016 monster-name.

question: Gary Gygax's company put a ten-dollar price on its first Dungeons and Dragons boxes in 1974, with three thin booklets inside each. Early sets came together by hand in his basement. How many boxes did that first print run make?
context: TSR's first print run was 1,000 copies, made on a production budget of about $2,000. Gygax and his partners hand-assembled early sets in his basement, and the box sold for $10. It went through many more printings.

question: Gary Gygax, a Wisconsin insurance underwriter, co-wrote a medieval war game with his friend Jeff Perren in 1971. Its tiny lead miniatures were pushed around a tabletop, and a fantasy supplement added later put elves, dwarves, wizards and dragons on the battlefield. That ruleset was the seed of the first Dungeons and Dragons. What was the game called?
context: Chainmail was published by Guidon Games in 1971. The fantasy supplement, added late, drew on Tolkien — until the Tolkien estate's lawyers forced TSR to rename hobbits to halflings and balrogs to balors. The supplement was what Arneson built Blackmoor on.

question: A childhood friend of Gary Gygax put up $2,000 in 1973 to co-found the little company that would first sell Dungeons and Dragons. The friend died of a heart attack in 1975, months after the game shipped. Who was he?
context: Don Kaye was Gygax's childhood friend. He died of a heart attack in early 1975, age 36, just months after D&D shipped. Brian Blume, who had been brought in to help fund the 1974 print run, took over Kaye's share and ran TSR with Gygax.

question: In 1979 Gary Gygax finished the three core rulebooks of Advanced Dungeons & Dragons (AD&D) by releasing the Dungeon Master's Guide. It joined the Monster Manual from 1977 and the Player's Handbook from 1978. Near the back of the book, one appendix lists the fantasy and sword-and-sorcery fiction that inspired the game: Tolkien, Robert E. Howard, Jack Vance, Fritz Leiber and many more. What is that appendix called?
context: Appendix N of the 1979 Dungeon Master's Guide lists authors such as Lord Dunsany, H.P. Lovecraft and Jack Vance, along with series such as Howard's Conan and Leiber's Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser.

question: Gary Gygax wrote Tomb of Horrors for a 1975 convention, and TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) published it in 1978 as a module notorious for killing heroes instantly, often with no saving throw. At its heart lurks a demilich, a skull with glowing jeweled eyes floating in the dark of the final chamber. What is his name?
context: Gygax wrote Tomb of Horrors for the 1975 Origins convention to challenge players who claimed their characters were unkillable, and TSR published it in 1978 as S1. Its green devil face trap is a sphere of annihilation.

question: The Beholder is one of D&D's most recognizable monsters: a floating sphere with a fanged mouth, one great central eye that shuts down magic in front of it, and ten eyestalks that each fire a different deadly ray. Long before it starred in later rulebooks, it made its first appearance in print, and was even painted on the cover. Where did the Beholder first appear?
context: The beholder was introduced in Greyhawk (1975), the first supplement to the original Dungeons & Dragons rules, and it is pictured on that book's cover. Rob Kuntz's brother Terry Kuntz created it and Gary Gygax detailed it for publication; it appeared again in the 1977 Monster Manual.

question: The illithid, or Mind Flayer, is the tentacled brain-eating villain of Dungeons and Dragons. It first appeared in the spring of 1975 in a small magazine called Strategic Review — long before the Monster Manual. Its creator, one of D&D's founders, said he was partly inspired by H. P. Lovecraft's cosmic horror. Who made it?
context: Gygax has said the inspiration came from the cover of Brian Lumley's 1969 book The Burrowers Beneath, which shows a tentacled humanoid. The mind flayer's psionic combat and brain-eating diet established it as one of D&D's signature 'civilized' evil races. Elder Brains command each colony.

question: In 1983 TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) published a module for Advanced Dungeons and Dragons (AD&D) called I6 Ravenloft. It introduced the vampire-lord Strahd von Zarovich, his misty land of Barovia, and the whole gothic-horror setting known as the Demiplane of Dread. Designer Tracy Hickman co-wrote it with his wife. What is her name?
context: Tracy and Laura Hickman had been running Ravenloft as a Halloween home-game for years before TSR published it in 1983. It won the H.G. Wells Award in 1984. The card-drawn fortune-telling mechanic was revolutionary. The Ravenloft full campaign setting followed in 1990.

question: The American fantasy author R.A. Salvatore's most famous character is a dual-wielding dark-elf ranger who fled the underground drow city of Menzoberranzan to live on the surface world of the Forgotten Realms. He first appeared as a supporting character in Salvatore's 1988 novel The Crystal Shard, added at the last minute after an editor asked for a new companion for the human hero. He quickly stole the spotlight. What is his name?
context: Salvatore wrote Drizzt in as a placeholder when an editor said his original character wouldn't work — and the placeholder became the most popular character in Forgotten Realms history. Drizzt's twin scimitars Twinkle and Icingdeath are iconic. His panther companion is named Guenhwyvar.

question: Gary Gygax and Brian Blume packed Eldritch Wizardry, a 1976 supplement to Dungeons and Dragons, with two huge new toys for players. The first was the druid, a nature priest who could shapeshift into animals. The second was a brand-new game system that many referees banned. What was it?
context: Eldritch Wizardry was the third OD&D supplement after Greyhawk (1975) and Blackmoor (1975). The psionics system included disciplines like ego-whip, mind-blast, and psionic blast. Many DMs hated psionics and ignored them, but the system survived into AD&D 2e and beyond.

question: The 1986 fantasy trilogy Dragonlance Legends, by Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman, followed a pair of twin brothers on a perilous quest that took them backwards through time itself. One twin was a huge, cheerful warrior-knight named Caramon Majere. The other was a sickly, gifted, cynical wizard who wore the black robes of an evil order of mages and coughed constantly from a magical curse laid on him. What is the wizard twin's name?
context: Raistlin's golden hourglass eyes — he sees everyone he looks at aging — were a Hickman touch. The Legends trilogy runs Time of the Twins, War of the Twins, Test of the Twins. The character became a model for every brooding-wizard character since.

question: First printed at the end of 1979, Gary Gygax's classic starter adventure replaced B1 in the Basic Dungeons & Dragons box and then shipped in every copy of Tom Moldvay's 1981 edition. It sends new adventurers to a frontier fort beside caves where rival tribes of orcs, goblins and kobolds squabble. What is the module called?
answer: B2 The Keep on the Borderlands
choices: B2 The Keep on the Borderlands
B1 In Search of the Unknown
context: Gygax's B2 was first printed in December 1979, replaced Mike Carr's B1 in the Basic Set in early 1980, and shipped with the Moldvay Basic Set in 1981; at the height of the boom it sold about 750,000 copies a year. Its Caves of Chaos house orcs, kobolds, hobgoblins, gnolls, bugbears, ogres and a temple of evil chaos.

question: A California doctor, neurologist and science-fiction author trimmed the old Dungeons and Dragons rules down to a friendly 48-page book in 1977. It went into the Basic 'blue book' box, the version that taught the game to thousands of kids in libraries and hobby shops. Who was the editor?
context: TSR published the Holmes Basic Set in 1977. Dr. J. Eric Holmes, a neurology professor at USC, wrote it from Gygax and Arneson's original rules; it covered character levels 1 to 3 and pointed players to AD&D for higher levels. Tom Moldvay's 1981 revision replaced it, and Frank Mentzer's 1983 revision grew into the five-box BECMI line.

question: Gary Gygax's company answered an army of hungry fans in June 1976 with an official Dungeons and Dragons magazine, bringing adventure ideas, monster stats and rules debates to the mailbox every month. It ran for 359 issues, until the print run ended in September 2007. What was the magazine called?
context: Dragon was preceded by The Strategic Review (1975-1976), TSR's wargame newsletter, which is where the mind flayer made its debut. Dragon ran until WotC moved everything online in 2007. Sister mag Dungeon (1986-2007) published full ready-to-run modules each issue.

question: Gary Gygax personally brought a general manager into the company he had co-founded, and in 1985 she pushed him out. She had quietly bought up enough shares to become top shareholder and outvote him in the boardroom. What was her name?
context: Lorraine Williams ran TSR from 1985 until 1997, when the company nearly bankrupted and was acquired by Wizards of the Coast (founded by MtG's Peter Adkison). Gygax sued, lost, and went on to design Dangerous Journeys (1992) and Lejendary Adventure (2000). He never returned to TSR.

question: Gary Gygax's basement games in his world of Greyhawk gave Advanced Dungeons & Dragons its famous archwizards, Mordenkainen, Bigby, Tenser, Rary and Drawmij, and their names live on in spells like Bigby's Crushing Hand and Tenser's Floating Disc. Where did those wizards really come from?
answer: Characters from his home campaign, mostly run by his players
choices: Characters from his home campaign, mostly run by his players
Wizards borrowed from Jack Vance's Dying Earth tales
Fantasy authors from the DMG's Appendix N reading list
Saints from a medieval calendar on Gygax's desk
context: Mordenkainen was Gygax's own character, Tenser was played by his son Ernie, Rary was created by Brian Blume, and Drawmij belonged to Jim Ward, whose name it spells backward. Bigby began as an evil wizard in Rob Kuntz's dungeons before Gygax took him over as a player character.

question: In Dungeons and Dragons, Tiamat is the five-headed evil queen of the chromatic dragons (red, blue, green, black, white). Her good opposite rules the metallic dragons — copper, silver, gold, brass, and bronze. He is a platinum dragon god who sometimes disguises himself as an old man in flowing robes. What is his name?
context: Bahamut's name comes from Arabic mythology — a giant fish-leviathan in some Arabic cosmologies. In D&D he's the patron of dragonborn paladins and good-dragon families. His seven 'Great Wyrm' consorts and the platinum-dragon avatar both became core lore.

question: A young actor starred in Mazes and Monsters, a 1982 CBS made-for-TV movie, as a college student who got so absorbed in a Dungeons-and-Dragons-style game that he lost his grip on reality. The film became a key piece of the 1980s Satanic Panic, which accused D&D of driving kids toward suicide and witchcraft. Who was the actor?
context: Mazes and Monsters was Hanks' first leading film role, based on Rona Jaffe's 1981 novel inspired by the disappearance of James Dallas Egbert III. The film helped fuel the Patricia Pulling-led BADD (Bothered About D&D) panic. Hanks later said he was embarrassed by the project.

question: A gifted sixteen-year-old computer prodigy at Michigan State University vanished into the university's steam tunnels on August 15, 1979. His family hired a private investigator, William Dear, who told reporters he suspected Dungeons and Dragons had blurred the boy's grip on reality. The story fueled the 1980s Satanic Panic, though the boy had disappeared for very different personal reasons. What was the student's name?
context: Egbert was a depressed gay teenager who had attempted suicide before disappearing. He went into the steam tunnels but came out a few days later. Tragically he killed himself a year later, August 1980. Dear's 1984 book The Dungeon Master sensationalized the case, with no D&D-related findings.

question: In 1980, TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) wrote a four-module tournament series for the Origins wargaming convention, using Gary Gygax's Advanced Dungeons and Dragons (AD&D) rules. It sends a party of heroes deep into a coastal city to hunt slavers raiding the Wild Coast of Greyhawk. What is the first module, A1, called?
choices: Assault on the Aerie of the Slave Lords
In the Dungeons of the Slave Lords
context: The A-series ran A1 (1980), A2-A4 (1981). The fourth module is notorious for stripping the PCs of equipment and forcing escape from a cave-flooding chamber. The series was compiled as a single supermodule in 1986. Lawrence Schick and David Cook designed the originals.

question: In 1978 the Dungeons and Dragons co-creator Gary Gygax wrote a legendary trilogy of adventure modules called the G-series, or Against the Giants, in which a party of heroes hunts down three enemy chieftains one lair at a time. The first module, G1, sends adventurers raiding a wooden fortress-lodge where a chieftain of the crudest, lowest-elevation giant kind sits feasting with his brutish retinue at long tables. What is G1's full title?
answer: Steading of the Hill Giant Chief
choices: Steading of the Hill Giant Chief
Glacial Rift of the Frost Giant Jarl
Hall of the Fire Giant King
context: The G-series (G1, G2, G3 — all 1978) sends adventurers up the giant hierarchy. G1 is the hill giants, G2 the frost giants, G3 the fire giants. The trilogy connects directly to D1-D3 (the Drow series), which connects to Q1 (Queen of the Demonweb Pits). Together they're sometimes called the G-D-Q supermodule.

question: In 1981 TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) released the Expert-level Dungeons and Dragons rulebook, edited by David 'Zeb' Cook and Steve Marsh. Boxed with it came the very first Expert-level module — an adventure sending players to a far tropical island filled with dinosaurs and lost tribes. What is it called?
choices: X4 The Master of the Desert Nomads
context: X1 was modeled on King Kong's Skull Island. It established the default Known World (Mystara) setting that Basic and Expert D&D would use through the BECMI line. The island contains thunder lizards (dinosaurs), Aranea spider-mages, the lost cities of the Olman, and other classic pulp elements.

question: In the mid-1970s, Dungeons and Dragons co-creator Gary Gygax kept a bag of cheap plastic Chinese toy monsters on his desk. Two of them became famous D&D creatures: the owlbear and the bulette (pronounced 'boo-lay'). The bulette is a huge armored beast with a shark-like fin on its back, and it swims through solid earth, bursting up under adventurers' feet to bite them in half. Players took one look at that fin cutting through the dirt and gave the monster a nickname that stuck. What did they call it?
context: The bulette burrows fast through earth, surfaces with a dorsal-fin slice, and tries to bite player characters in half. The plastic-toy line that inspired it was sold cheap in Woolworth's bagged-monster bins. The same line gave Gygax the rust monster and the owlbear, three of D&D's most iconic creatures.

question: Ms. Frost, a game master, draws a teenage player into real witchcraft in the most widely distributed anti-D&D piece in history, a 1984 evangelical comic-book tract. It is the most famous artifact of the 1980s Satanic Panic. Whose work is it?
context: Jack Chick's tracts were tiny black-and-white comics handed out at Halloween, on church benches, and in bus stations. 'Dark Dungeons' depicts a fictional Ms. Frost recruiting a player named Debbie into real witchcraft via D&D. The tract became a meme; a 2014 indie film adapted it as a comedic short.

question: Gary Gygax's most famous character in his home Greyhawk game, from 1972 on, was a wizard who grew so strong that he led the Circle of Eight, Greyhawk's top group of mages. Several AD&D spells are named for him, including a magic mansion, a faithful hound, and a sword. Who is the character?
context: Mordenkainen was perhaps Gygax's most famous character and also his favorite. He first appeared in print in Eldritch Wizardry (1976), and spells such as Mordenkainen's Magnificent Mansion and Mordenkainen's Faithful Hound carry his name.

question: Lawrence Schick's 1979 module S2 White Plume Mountain sends adventurers into a wizard-built fun-house dungeon to recover three intelligent weapons stolen by the wizard Keraptis. The weapons are a flaming greatsword, a trident, and a war hammer. What are the names of the three weapons?
context: Blackrazor is a transparent homage to Stormbringer from Michael Moorcock's Elric saga — a soul-eating sword with chaotic alignment. The module is built around three distinct dungeon mini-environments: an inverted ziggurat, a series of bubbles in lava, and a flooded section with sirens. Schick wrote it as a job-application sample to TSR.

question: Gygax's 1978 D-series — D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, D2 Shrine of the Kuo-Toa, D3 Vault of the Drow — established the Underdark as a setting and depicted drow culture in detail for the first time. The series resolves in a 1980 module sending the PCs to confront Lolth herself on her home plane. What is the 1980 module called?
answer: Q1 Queen of the Demonweb Pits
choices: Q1 Queen of the Demonweb Pits
context: Q1 was written by David Sutherland (best known as the iconic D&D illustrator). The module sends the PCs through the entrance plane of the Abyss to Lolth's spider-shaped fortress. Demogorgon and Orcus get cameos. The G1-3, D1-3, Q1 series compiled as a single supermodule is sometimes called the most influential D&D campaign-arc ever.

question: Gary Gygax's home setting Greyhawk was first published as a TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) product in 1980 in a slim 32-page folio with a Darlene-drawn full-color map of Oerth. The folio was upgraded to a full hardcover boxed set in 1983. What was the boxed set's official title?
answer: World of Greyhawk Fantasy Game Setting
choices: World of Greyhawk Fantasy Game Setting
context: The Darlene map of the Flanaess is one of the most iconic fantasy-setting maps ever published. It hangs framed on countless gamers' walls. The boxed set described every nation, religion, and major NPC on Oerth's Flanaess continent. After Gygax's ouster, the From the Ashes (1992) reboot bombed and damaged the setting's reputation.

question: Gygax's 1979 module T1 The Village of Hommlet introduces a small farming village with a hidden moat-house, a smiling priest with secret loyalties, and a budding evil cult. Gygax promised the full sequel for years but only completed it in 1985 (with Frank Mentzer's help), as a 128-page supermodule. What's its title?
answer: T1-4 The Temple of Elemental Evil
choices: T1-4 The Temple of Elemental Evil
T2 The Forgotten Temple of Tharizdun
T1-4 The Caves of Chaos Expanded
context: The Temple of Elemental Evil was famously delayed for years. Gygax kept promising it in Dragon Magazine columns through the late 1970s and early 1980s. When it finally arrived in 1985, fans noticed the dungeon design was less ambitious than expected. The Troika 2003 computer-game adaptation by Tim Cain (Fallout) is well-regarded among CRPG fans.

question: Krynn — the world of the Dragonlance setting — has three moons, each tied to one of the three orders of wizards. The white moon Solinari serves good wizards (White Robes); the red moon Lunitari serves neutral wizards (Red Robes); the black moon, invisible except to its sworn wizards, serves the evil Black Robes. What's the black moon's name?
context: The three moons are also gods in the Krynn pantheon, children of the gods of magic. Raistlin Majere shifted from a Red Robe to a Black Robe over the course of the Chronicles trilogy. The Test of High Sorcery in the Tower of Wayreth is the formal initiation a wizard must survive to wear robes of any color.

question: The classic D&D Beholder is famous for its huge central anti-magic eye, which cancels magic in a sixty-degree cone in front of it. Ten smaller eyestalks around its body each fire a different magical ray. Which specific ray shoots from the topmost central eyestalk?
context: The classic 10 eyestalk rays in 1e Monster Manual: charm person, charm monster, sleep, telekinesis, flesh to stone, disintegrate, fear, slow, cause serious wounds, and death ray. The central anti-magic eye is the Beholder's signature defense — it cannot suppress its own eyestalks because they're 'inside' the cone's origin point.

question: Robert E. Howard wrote his Conan stories in his family's house in Cross Plains, Texas, between 1932 and 1936. His mother had been ill for years, and when she fell into her final coma in June 1936, Howard took his own life. How old was he?
context: Howard was born on 22 January 1906 and died on 11 June 1936, aged 30; his mother died the next day. He left a typed couplet beginning 'All fled, all done', borrowed from Viola Garvin's poem The House of Caesar.

question: Fritz Leiber's fantasy duo Fafhrd, a barbarian, and the Gray Mouser, a former wizard's apprentice turned thief, had been appearing in the pulps since 1939. Their adventures take place on the world of Nehwon, and most of their stories start or end in one sprawling, corrupt city of thieves and sorcerers. What city served as the duo's home base?
answer: Lankhmar, the city of black toga
choices: Lankhmar, the city of black toga
Sanctuary, the city of the Thieves' World
Cimmeria, the city of Conan's homeland
Carcosa, the city of the Yellow King
context: Lankhmar lies on the world of Nehwon, whose name is 'no when' spelled backwards. TSR published an official guide to the city for Advanced Dungeons & Dragons, Lankhmar - City of Adventure, in 1985.

question: H.P. Lovecraft was born August 20, 1890 and died March 15, 1937 in his hometown of Providence, Rhode Island, where he had lived nearly his entire life. He published 'The Call of Cthulhu' in Weird Tales in February 1928. Where in Providence is Lovecraft buried?
answer: Swan Point Cemetery, in the family plot under a small stone
choices: Swan Point Cemetery, in the family plot under a small stone
Saint John's Episcopal Cemetery, in his maternal grandparents' plot
Riverside Cemetery, beside his estranged father
North Burial Ground, in the Old Yankee section
context: Lovecraft's grave is a pilgrimage site. The original stone is small and lists him as 'Howard Phillips Lovecraft 1890-1937.' Fans have added a larger separate stone reading 'I AM PROVIDENCE,' a line from one of his letters. The cemetery is on the East Side of Providence near the Brown University campus.

question: Frank Mentzer edited the 1983 red box of Basic D&D, the third edition of the line after the 1977 blue book and the 1981 red box.
