His edition grew into a five-box set that took characters from beginner rules all the way to godhood in a final box. What was the five-letter acronym for the line?
context: BECMI stands for the five boxed sets Basic, Expert, Companion, Master and Immortals, which carried characters from level 1 to 36 and then on to play as gods. Aaron Allston's 1991 Rules Cyclopedia later gathered the Basic through Master rules into a single hardcover.

question: A designer gathered the Basic through Master boxes of Frank Mentzer's line into one 304-page hardcover, years after the 1983 red box that began them. Many fans still call that book the cleanest D&D rulebook ever. Who was the designer?
answer: Aaron Allston, of the 1991 Rules Cyclopedia
choices: Aaron Allston, of the 1991 Rules Cyclopedia
Tracy Hickman, of the Dragonlance setting
Bruce Heard, of the Voyage of the Princess Ark
David Cook, of the X1 Isle of Dread module
context: Aaron Allston (1960-2014) compiled and developed the 1991 Rules Cyclopedia, a 304-page hardcover that consolidates the Basic, Expert, Companion and Master sets. He was later best known for his Star Wars X-Wing novels.

question: Gygax's 1978 Tomb of Horrors module is studded with instant-death traps. The most infamous is the green devil-face carved into the entrance wall. The mouth appears purely decorative but is actually a Sphere of Annihilation. What happens when a character reaches into or steps into the mouth?
choices: Teleports the character to a random level of the Abyss
Drops the character into a 500-foot pit filled with green slime
Polymorphs the character into a green slime forever
context: Acererak's tomb has multiple devil-face Sphere of Annihilation traps. The tomb's famous false hallway with two false coffins leads to a real trap. Players who survive often find that Acererak himself, in his demilich form, is the LAST encounter. The legendary 'how to play Tomb of Horrors' wisdom: 'Test everything with a 10-foot pole.'

question: William Dear, a private detective, blamed Dungeons and Dragons when a sixteen-year-old student went missing in the steam tunnels at Michigan State in 1979, and the modern D&D Satanic Panic took off. The truth was sadder and more personal. The boy did emerge from the tunnels, but he took his own life a year later. When and where did the boy die?
context: Egbert was a depressed, suicidal, gay teenager from a high-pressure family. His D&D group was an outlet, not a cause. William Dear's 1984 book The Dungeon Master sensationalized D&D's role even though Dear's own findings contradicted that frame. The Egbert case directly inspired Rona Jaffe's novel Mazes and Monsters and the 1982 Tom Hanks film.

question: Rona Jaffe drew her 1981 novel Mazes and Monsters from a real disappearance at Michigan State, and CBS filmed it in 1982 as a made-for-TV movie. Its lead was a college student who lost touch with reality while playing a fictional game. What was the character's name?
context: Hanks played Robbie Wheeling, a college student whose character in the fictional game is the holy man Pardieu. The film calls the game Mazes and Monsters rather than Dungeons & Dragons.

question: One of D&D's most iconic villains is a lich-king reduced over centuries to a single severed hand and severed eye. Anyone who attaches them gains terrible magical powers. Brian Blume created him in the 1976 Eldritch Wizardry supplement. The name is an anagram of a famous fantasy author. What is his name?
context: Jack Vance's Dying Earth stories inspired the D&D 'fire and forget' spell system, which Gygax adopted directly. Vecna's Hand and Eye relics appeared as iconic AD&D magic items. The 1990 Vecna Lives! supplement and 1998 Die Vecna Die! both featured the lich's attempted ascension. Vecna joined the gods as the god of secrets in Greyhawk lore.

question: The 1983 Monster Manual II gave Advanced Dungeons & Dragons its doomsday beast: a scaly, horned, armored colossus that regrows from wounds that would kill anything else, and in the original rules could be finished for good only with a wish spell. Its name comes from a dragon of medieval Provençal legend that Saint Martha tamed with holy water and a cross. What is the monster called?
context: The tarrasque arrived in the 1983 Monster Manual II as the most destructive creature in the game's world. Its name comes from the Tarasque of Provence, a river dragon that legend says Saint Martha subdued near the town now called Tarascon. In the original rules only a wish could stop it regenerating after it was beaten down.

question: Six kids ride an amusement-park attraction into the Realm and must find their way home, menaced by Venger and his red dragon Tiamat. Their Saturday-morning cartoon, a partnership between Marvel Productions and Gary Gygax's company, runs on CBS from 1983 to 1985. What is the show called?
context: The animated series had voice talent including Don Most as Eric the Cavalier, Adam Rich as Presto the Magician, and Frank Welker as both Dungeon Master and Uni the baby unicorn. The series never aired its scripted finale ('Requiem'), which would have shown the kids returning home — leaving the show on an eternal cliffhanger. The script was finally produced as an audio drama in 2006.

question: Tactical Studies Rules (TSR)'s 1989 Spelljammer setting sent D&D into space. Ships sailed the 'phlogiston' between crystal balls that each held a solar system. The setting added a race of war-loving hippo-headed men who wear tricorn hats and red coats like an old army. What are they called?
context: Giff are widely beloved for their pure Napoleonic-era military aesthetic transplanted to a fantasy-space context. They use smokepowder firearms and prefer line-infantry tactics. The setting itself was a Jeff Grubb design and was famously divisive — beloved by some, rejected as silly by others. The 2022 5e Spelljammer reboot was widely panned.

question: Tactical Studies Rules (TSR)'s 1994 Planescape setting centers on Sigil, a torus-shaped city floating at the top of an infinite spire at the very center of the multiverse. The city's portals connect to every plane in existence. A silent goddess-like figure rules Sigil — tall and slender, with a corona of blades around her head. Anyone who speaks her name vanishes forever. What is she called?
context: The Lady of Pain (often shortened to 'the Lady') was created by designer David Cook. She never speaks; her shadow can flay anyone who threatens her city. The 1999 Black Isle Studios CRPG set in Sigil, with Chris Avellone leading the writing, brought the setting to wider fame. That game is considered one of the greatest RPGs ever written.

question: Tactical Studies Rules (TSR)'s 1991 Dark Sun setting was a post-apocalyptic desert world where metal was so scarce that obsidian and bone weapons became standard. Psionics replaced most divine magic. Arcane magic actually 'defiled' the surrounding land. The setting's signature visual look came from one fantasy artist. Who?
context: Brom's painted covers gave Dark Sun a unique 'Frazetta-on-Mars' aesthetic. The setting featured Thri-Kreen mantis warriors, halflings as primitive cannibals, half-giants, and the Sorcerer-Kings — wizard-tyrants of each city-state. The boxed set's first novel trilogy ('Prism Pentad') was written by Troy Denning. Dark Sun won the 1992 Origins Award for Best Roleplaying Supplement.

question: The 1990 Ravenloft box set expanded the 1983 module into a full demiplane of dread with many "Domains." Each Domain is ruled by a damned "Darklord" bound there for some signature evil, and Strahd rules Barovia. What is the name of the strange force that creates new Domains by pulling evil souls from across the multiverse?
context: The Dark Powers are deliberately never explained or stat-blocked — they're a meta-villain that exists to give the setting its premise. The 1994 Domains of Dread sourcebook lists dozens of Darklords. Vlad von Drakov, Vecna (briefly imprisoned there), Soth from Dragonlance, and Azalin Rex are all famous Darklords. The setting was the model for the 2016 Curse of Strahd 5e adventure.

question: Richard Garfield, a mathematics PhD, designed Magic: the Gathering and pitched it to a small Renton, Washington garage outfit called Wizards of the Coast in the early 1990s. The first set, Alpha, shipped in August 1993 with a print run of 2.6 million cards. Who was the WotC co-founder who agreed to the pitch?
context: Adkison ran WotC from Beth Moursund's garage in 1991, originally as a small RPG publisher. He greenlit Garfield's pitch when no one else in the industry would touch it — the 'collectible card game' was an unknown category. WotC bought a struggling TSR in 1997, ending TSR as an independent company. Adkison left WotC in 2001 to run Gen Con.

question: In 1977, TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) published the Holmes Basic Set — a blue-boxed introduction to Dungeons and Dragons for brand-new players, edited by Dr. J. Eric Holmes. From 1978 the box also held the very first Basic D&D adventure module ever printed. Its purpose was to teach new Dungeon Masters (DMs) how to fill a dungeon: the rooms come drawn and described, but the monsters and treasure are left blank on separate stocking tables so the Dungeon Master must fill them in by hand. What is this teaching module called?
answer: B1 In Search of the Unknown
choices: B1 In Search of the Unknown
B2 The Keep on the Borderlands
B3 Palace of the Silver Princess
context: Mike Carr wrote B1 as a teaching module, first printed in 1978 and packed into the Holmes Basic Set from that year. The Caverns of Quasqueton were built by two retired adventurers, Roghan the Fearless and Zelligar the Unknown. From 1979 the Basic box carried B2 The Keep on the Borderlands instead.

question: In Advanced Dungeons and Dragons, the Beholder is a floating spherical monster with one huge central eye and ten smaller eyestalks curling around the top of its body. Its central eye projects a magic-cancelling cone straight forward, shutting off any incoming spell that crosses it — and shutting off the Beholder's own eyestalk rays inside the same cone too. But that anti-magic cone only points one direction. From which direction is a Beholder still open to magic attack?
answer: Above and behind — the anti-magic cone covers only a sixty-degree forward arc
choices: Above and behind — the anti-magic cone covers only a sixty-degree forward arc
Below and forward — the rays travel upward only, leaving the floor exposed
Directly into the central eye — the anti-magic cone has a blind spot at zero range
From any direction — the central eye closes when it uses its bite attack instead
context: Tactically, the best way to fight a Beholder in classic AD&D is to attack from above and behind, outside the front-facing anti-magic cone. The Beholder must constantly rotate to keep the cone aimed correctly. Beholders are also famously paranoid — they consider all other Beholders heretics, leading to species-wide civil war.

question: The owner of Gary Gygax's old company sold it in 1997, when it was more than $30 million in debt, swamped by returned stock and unable to pay its printers. The buyer was a young publisher from Washington state, grown rich after launching a collectible card game at Gen Con in 1993. Which company took over Dungeons and Dragons?
context: Lorraine Williams sold TSR to Wizards of the Coast in 1997, and Wizards settled TSR's debts as part of the deal. Wizards had launched Magic: The Gathering at Gen Con in 1993, and the card game's success gave it the cash to buy the company that made D&D.

question: Tracy and Laura Hickman had been running a vampire-themed Halloween adventure for their home game for several years before TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) published it as the 1983 module I6 Ravenloft. The Hickmans submitted the manuscript to TSR's editing team, who polished it for the H.G. Wells Award-winning final form. One specific game-mechanical innovation became its most-copied feature, used to set the variable layout of the dungeon and the location of key items. What was it?
answer: A tarot-style fortune-telling card-draw system that randomized Strahd's plans
choices: A tarot-style fortune-telling card-draw system that randomized Strahd's plans
A real-time torch system tracking how long player light sources burned
A morale-tracking system causing the player party to suffer Fear penalties
A weather-cycle table that altered the castle's accessible rooms each round
context: The card-draw system used a custom 'Tarroka' deck (a Vistani fortune-teller character draws cards before play begins). The cards determine where the artifact 'Tome of Strahd' is hidden, where Strahd's spell-weapon is, where the Holy Symbol of Ravenkind is hidden, and Strahd's primary objective. This made every Ravenloft playthrough genuinely different. The 2016 5e Curse of Strahd kept the mechanic intact.

question: The Dragonlance Chronicles trilogy began as a series of modules — DL1 Dragons of Despair (1984) — and only became novels because TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) wanted to test whether 'game-fiction' tie-ins could sell. Tracy Hickman had pitched a series called 'Project Overlord.' TSR editor Margaret Weis was assigned to ghostwrite tie-in books; instead, she co-wrote the actual novels with Hickman. The first book outsold expectations massively. What was its title?
context: Autumn Twilight shipped in November 1984 and sold over 250,000 copies in its first year, stunning TSR. The Companions of the Lance — Tanis Half-Elven, Caramon Majere, Raistlin Majere, Sturm Brightblade, Flint Fireforge, Tasslehoff Burrfoot, Goldmoon, Riverwind, Tika Waylan — became iconic. The trilogy reshaped both D&D fiction and the broader fantasy paperback market. TSR launched several more novel lines off the Chronicles' success.

question: In 1977, after TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) put out an unlicensed board game based on The Hobbit, lawyers for the holders of the Tolkien rights sent the company a cease-and-desist notice that also took aim at Tolkien's names inside Dungeons & Dragons. TSR swapped in replacement names, and those substitutes became permanent D&D canon. Which three names replaced hobbits, ents and balrogs?
context: The legal threat followed TSR's unlicensed 1977 game The Battle of the Five Armies. Basic D&D changed hobbit to halfling and ent to treant, and the names have stayed in the game ever since.

question: Gary Gygax wrote Tomb of Horrors as a tournament module for the 1975 Origins convention in Baltimore. He was tired of players who bragged that their high-level characters were unkillable, so he engineered a dungeon designed to destroy them. The module was not published commercially until 1978. What was its S-series designation?
answer: S1 — first of the Special-series 'one-shot' modules
choices: S1 — first of the Special-series 'one-shot' modules
S0 — predating the formal Special-series numbering
T0 — initially classified with the T-series Temple modules
B1 — originally in the Basic line before being moved
context: The S-series followed: S1 Tomb of Horrors (1978), S2 White Plume Mountain (1979), S3 Expedition to the Barrier Peaks (1980 — the famous sci-fi crashed-starship module), S4 The Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth (1982). Tomb of Horrors has been revisited multiple times: as part of 1998's Return to the Tomb of Horrors, as a 2005 3.5e remake, and as the dungeon-finale of 2017's Tomb of Annihilation.

question: Gygax's 1978 module D3 Vault of the Drow gave AD&D its first detailed picture of dark-elf society. The adventurers visit the drow city of Erelhei-Cinlu, where they discover a crystalline cavern lit by glowing fungus and gem-covered stalactites. Gygax called it the most beautiful scene in any AD&D module. Where in the Underdark does D3 place Erelhei-Cinlu?
answer: In the Vault — a thirty-mile-long enclosed cavern with a glittering false-sky ceiling
choices: In the Vault — a thirty-mile-long enclosed cavern with a glittering false-sky ceiling
In the Pit — a vertical shaft descending three miles into volcanic depths
In the Spire — atop a needle-like stalagmite over a bottomless chasm
In the Web — a network of crystal bridges over the Demonweb itself
context: Erelhei-Cinlu is ruled by competing drow noble houses, each devoted to Lolth. The Fane of Lolth in the city is the religious center. The drow noble pyramid that Salvatore later developed into Menzoberranzan for the Forgotten Realms (1988) drew directly on Gygax's D3 framework. The Vault itself — that enclosed beautiful glittering cavern — is one of the most visually distinctive setting elements in D&D.

question: In Dragonlance, the world of Krynn suffered a divine disaster 350 years before the Chronicles trilogy. The Kingpriest of Istar demanded godhood from the gods, who answered by hurling a burning peak at his capital, wrecking the city and reshaping the land. Then the gods left the world. What has become the central image of that disaster?
answer: The fiery mountain that crashed onto Istar
choices: The fiery mountain that crashed onto Istar
The shadow of the Dragon Queen Takhisis
The shattering of the Graygem of Gargath
The silent fall of the Lostking's tower
context: After the Cataclysm, the gods of Krynn withdrew. True healing magic was lost, replaced by the false healing of Dragon Highlord-supplied charlatans. The Chronicles open in a world that believes its gods have abandoned it. Istar itself remained sunk beneath the Blood Sea — the new ocean created by the cataclysm.

question: R.A. Salvatore's 1988 novel The Crystal Shard launched the Icewind Dale trilogy and introduced Drizzt Do'Urden, who became the Forgotten Realms' most popular character. Drizzt was actually a last-minute pitch accepted on the spot. The primary hero was originally supposed to be the human barbarian at his side. What was that hero's name?
answer: Wulfgar, the young barbarian of the Tribe of the Elk
choices: Wulfgar, the young barbarian of the Tribe of the Elk
Bruenor, the dwarven king of Mithral Hall
Regis, the halfling burgomaster of Bryn Shander
Catti-brie, the adopted human daughter of Bruenor
context: Wulfgar's character arc — the young barbarian apprenticed to Bruenor — was the trilogy's main throughline. Drizzt was the gimmick character who walked away with the entire spotlight. Salvatore went on to write over 30 Drizzt novels through the early 2020s, plus film, comic, and game adaptations. The Crystal Shard, Streams of Silver (1989), and The Halfling's Gem (1990) form the original Icewind Dale Trilogy.

question: Gary Gygax wrote up the rules for the beholder, the floating orb with one great central eye, a fanged mouth and ten eyestalks, but he never claimed to have invented it. The idea came from another player at his Lake Geneva table: the brother of Gygax's co-Dungeon Master on Castle Greyhawk. Who dreamed up the beholder?
context: Terry Kuntz, brother of Gygax's co-Dungeon Master Rob Kuntz, created the beholder, and Gary Gygax detailed it for publication. It became one of the most famous monsters in the game.

question: In Gary Gygax's Greyhawk setting, the demigod cambion (half-demon) son of the demon Graz'zt and the human witch Iggwilv rules an evil kingdom in the northern Flanaess. He's the closest thing Greyhawk has to a Dark Lord of all evil — a recurring villain through dozens of modules. What's his name?
answer: Iuz, demigod ruler of the Empire of Iuz
choices: Iuz, demigod ruler of the Empire of Iuz
Vecna, lich-god of secrets and ambition
Tharizdun, the forgotten god of eternal darkness
Acererak, the demilich of the Tomb of Horrors
context: Iuz was created by Gygax in 1980. His mother Iggwilv had imprisoned the demon lord Graz'zt for 17 years using the legendary tome Demonomicon; she released him at the price of bearing his child. The 1991 'From the Ashes' Greyhawk reboot put Iuz at the center of a Cold-War-style standoff with the Kingdom of Furyondy. Gary Gygax himself appears in some Iuz lore as the rival 'Yrag,' an anagram of his name.

question: Dark Sun's most distinctive setting feature is its magic system. Arcane magic on Athas requires the caster to draw life energy from surrounding plant life to fuel each spell. Plants drained this way are destroyed; surrounding biology suffers. This is why Athas is a desert wasteland — millennia of unrestricted arcane magic stripped the planet. What name is given to this style of magic-use?
answer: Defiling — the source of Athas's environmental devastation
choices: Defiling — the source of Athas's environmental devastation
Channeling — drawing power from psionic spirits
Burning — siphoning power directly from the sun
Reaping — converting wasteland sand into temporary mana
context: A counter-school exists: 'preserving,' which draws the energy slowly without destroying plants. Defilers gain spells faster than preservers, creating a moral tension in every magic-user's career. The Sorcerer-Kings of each city-state are powerful defilers themselves, having spent millennia drawing life energy. The Sorcerer-King Nibenay rules from the city of Nibenay, surrounded by drained earth.

question: Dark Sun's setting features seven city-states across the Tablelands of Athas, each ruled by an immortal Sorcerer-King who has lived for over a thousand years. Their immortality has cost them their humanity. The first boxed set (1991) named all seven. Which Sorcerer-King rules the great city-state of Tyr — the city where the iconic Prism Pentad novel series begins?
answer: Kalak — the Sorcerer-King whose slaves build his ziggurat
choices: Kalak — the Sorcerer-King whose slaves build his ziggurat
Hamanu — the lion-headed warlord of Urik
Nibenay — the Shadow-King of his namesake city
context: Troy Denning's Prism Pentad (1991-1993) begins with The Verdant Passage, in which Kalak of Tyr drives his slaves to finish a great ziggurat meant to help him become an immortal dragon. The five novels are The Verdant Passage, The Crimson Legion, The Amber Enchantress, The Obsidian Oracle and The Cerulean Storm.

question: Ed Greenwood's Forgotten Realms setting began in Toronto in 1967, when he was about twelve years old, writing short stories about a wandering sage named Elminster of Shadowdale for his own amusement. His 1979 Dragon Magazine articles used the framing that Elminster dictated the tales through a magical portal. Greenwood sold the entire setting to Tactical Studies Rules (TSR) in 1986 for a 1987 release. What was the inaugural product?
answer: The 1987 Forgotten Realms Campaign Set, a gray boxed-set with two maps
choices: The 1987 Forgotten Realms Campaign Set, a gray boxed-set with two maps
The 1987 Forgotten Realms Player's Guide, a softcover rulebook
The 1988 Realms Sourcebook, a hardcover supplement
The 1988 Cyclopedia of the Realms, a single-volume reference
context: The gray box (sometimes called the Old Gray Box) is a beloved collector's item among Realms fans. Greenwood has continued writing Realms fiction and lore for nearly 40 years; he's the in-universe canonical authority. Elminster himself has appeared in over 20 novels — Greenwood writes them in first person from Elminster's voice in some volumes.

question: Magic: the Gathering's 1993 launch story is now industry legend. Richard Garfield pitched a 'collectible card game' concept (something that didn't exist as a category) to a small Renton, Washington outfit then operating out of Beth Moursund's basement. The company's founder agreed to publish it. Alpha (August 1993) shipped 2.6 million cards and sold through almost immediately. What was the company name?
answer: Wizards of the Coast, founded 1990 by Peter Adkison
choices: Wizards of the Coast, founded 1990 by Peter Adkison
Iron Crown Enterprises, founded 1980 in Charlottesville Virginia
Hero Games, founded 1981 by Steve Peterson and George MacDonald
FASA Corporation, founded 1980 in Chicago Illinois
context: Adkison was a Boeing software engineer when he co-founded WotC. The company's original products were small Greyhawk-style adventure modules and a sci-fi RPG called The Primal Order. Garfield had been pitching the card-game concept around the industry for years — only Adkison saw the potential. After Alpha sold out, WotC printed Beta (October 1993), Unlimited (December 1993), and Arabian Nights (December 1993).

question: Richard Garfield designed Magic the Gathering's five-color system as a deliberately rock-paper-scissors structure with five mana types. Each color has distinct commitments: white for order, blue for knowledge, black for ambition, red for emotion, and green for nature. This system is called the "color pie." Which colors sit diametrically opposed on the wheel?
answer: White and black, white and red, blue and red, blue and green, black and green
choices: White and black, white and red, blue and red, blue and green, black and green
Red and blue only; white and green only; black is allied with all four
Each color is enemy of the two next to it on the wheel; allies with the two opposite
All colors are equally allied with the others except colorless (gray)
context: The color-wheel relationships: white-black-red-green-blue-white. Each color is allied with two adjacent colors and enemy of the two non-adjacent ones. White-Black are enemies (order vs ambition); Blue-Red (knowledge vs emotion); Green-Blue (nature vs artifice). Garfield designed this for both flavor (each color's spells and creatures reflect its philosophy) and game balance (no color is universally superior).

question: Magic: the Gathering held its first formal professional tournament in February 1996 in New York City, with a prize pool of around $100,000 — substantial for the time. It marked MtG's transition from a 'gateway' card-game to a serious competitive game with paid professionals. Who won the first Pro Tour?
answer: Michael Loconto, a Massachusetts-based player using a White Weenie deck
choices: Michael Loconto, a Massachusetts-based player using a White Weenie deck
Mark Justice, the 1995 World Champion using Black Lotus combos
Zak Dolan, the 1994 World Champion playing power-mana ramp
Bertrand Lestree, the 1994 World Championship finalist
context: Loconto played 'Pat Chapin Black' — black-based control with Necropotence as the centerpiece. The 1996 Pro Tour New York established the format. Subsequent Pro Tours were held in Los Angeles, Atlanta, Dallas, Columbus, and Paris that year alone. The 1994 World Champion, Zak Dolan, had won the original Magic World Championship using a deck that included Black Lotus and several other Power Nine cards.

question: Robert E. Howard (1906-1936) and H.P. Lovecraft (1890-1937) never met in person but exchanged hundreds of letters from 1930 until Howard's June 1936 suicide. Their correspondence is one of the most important records of pulp-era fantasy thinking, discussing everything from Conan's cultural milieu to civilization's collapse. The letters survive and have been published as a two-volume scholarly edition by what specialist press?
answer: Hippocampus Press, dedicated to Lovecraft and pulp-era scholarship
choices: Hippocampus Press, dedicated to Lovecraft and pulp-era scholarship
Arkham House, the original Lovecraft estate publisher
Necronomicon Press, founded by Marc A. Michaud
Chaosium Press, the Call of Cthulhu RPG publisher
context: Hippocampus Press has published critical editions of nearly every major pulp-era fantasy author, including Clark Ashton Smith. The Howard-Lovecraft letters are titled A Means to Freedom: The Letters of H.P. Lovecraft and Robert E. Howard, edited by S.T. Joshi (the most prominent Lovecraft scholar living today). Arkham House was August Derleth's publisher, founded specifically to preserve Lovecraft's work after Lovecraft died in poverty.

question: Drizzt Do'Urden, R.A. Salvatore's most famous character, fights with two iconic magical scimitars. He took one from the treasure hoard of a white dragon he slew in Icewind Dale, and the blade took the dragon's nickname; the other is a magical elven blade. What are the names of Drizzt's two scimitars?
answer: Twinkle (the elven scimitar) and Icingdeath (from the dragon's hoard)
choices: Twinkle (the elven scimitar) and Icingdeath (from the dragon's hoard)
Frostmourne (the cold blade) and Sunrazer (the fire blade)
context: In The Crystal Shard, Drizzt found the scimitar Icingdeath in the hoard of the white dragon Ingeloakastimizilian, whose nickname was Icingdeath; the blade carries that name. Twinkle is an elven-made scimitar. Drizzt's companion is the onyx panther Guenhwyvar, summoned from a figurine.

question: Gary Gygax's 1980 module S3 Expedition to the Barrier Peaks sends heroes into a cave in the mountains of Greyhawk that leads somewhere no fantasy hero expects. Inside, robots still patrol the halls, colored cards open sealed doors, and the treasure includes blaster rifles and powered armor. What is the 'dungeon' really?
answer: A crashed spacecraft from the stars
choices: A crashed spacecraft from the stars
A buried dwarven forge of iron golems
A clockwork fortress of a mad archmage
A sealed vault of a lost wizard-empire
context: Gygax first ran Expedition to the Barrier Peaks as a 1976 tournament scenario, and TSR published it in 1980. The cave is the entrance to a downed spacecraft whose robots still work; players gather colored access cards to open its restricted areas and use futuristic gear such as blaster rifles.

question: Fritz Leiber kept writing about Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser for more than fifty years. In 1970 he finally told how the huge northern barbarian and the small grey-clad thief first met, on a night when both ambushed the same pair of Thieves' Guild burglars and decided to split the loot. The novella won both the Nebula and the Hugo. What is it called?
context: Ill Met in Lankhmar, first published in The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction in 1970, won the Nebula Award in 1970 and the Hugo in 1971 for Best Novella. In it Fafhrd and the Mouser both ambush two Thieves' Guild members, recognise kindred spirits, and agree to share the loot.

question: Tactical Studies Rules (TSR)'s 1995 Birthright setting did something new for D&D. Players ran kingdoms, not just wandering heroes. The rules covered taxes, armies, deals with other rulers, and even murder plots. The story followed the heirs of slain gods from an old pantheon. On the planet Aebrynis, which continent held its kingdoms?
choices: Faerûn, on the world of Toril
Oerth, on the world of Greyhawk
Krynn, the central continent of Ansalon
context: Birthright was designed by Richard Baker and Colin McComb. It ran from 1995-1997 in print but was canceled when TSR's financial troubles peaked. The bloodline-rulership system was unique — each ruler player character has 'blood points' that can be invested in spells, abilities, or kingdom actions. The 1995 boxed set is now a collector's item. Cerilia's nations include Anuire, the most populous human realm, and Vosgaard, the home of bestial Vos warriors.

question: Sigil sits at the top of the Spire in Tactical Studies Rules (TSR)'s 1994 Planescape setting. The city is shaped like an inside-out donut, so you live on the inside surface. Its portals are its most famous feature. Any door can be opened with a 'portal key' (an object, a gesture, a sound, or even a thought) and lead anywhere in the multiverse. About how many portals are open in Sigil at any one time?
answer: Tens of thousands, constantly opening and closing
choices: Tens of thousands, constantly opening and closing
Exactly nine, one matched to each Outer Plane
Three hundred sixty-five, one for each day of the year
Twelve thousand, one for each zodiac sign times five
context: Sigil's portals are central to its commerce and politics. The 15 factions of Sigil each have philosophical positions on the nature of the multiverse — the Athar deny the gods, the Doomguard worship entropy, the Bleak Cabal sees the universe as meaningless. The factions occupy specific neighborhoods and run specific institutions (the Athar run the Shattered Temple, the Doomguard run the Armory). The Lady of Pain doesn't take sides in faction politics.

question: The default world of Basic D&D and BECMI (Basic, Expert, Companion, Master, Immortal) was first called the Known World. It got a proper setting name in 1991. That same year, the Hollow World box added a hollow space in the planet's core, where 'preserved' cultures like the Romans, the Hutaakans, and the Aranea live just as they used to. What is the planet itself called?
answer: Mystara — the planet whose hollow interior contains preserved cultures
choices: Mystara — the planet whose hollow interior contains preserved cultures
Oerth — the planet of the World of Greyhawk Flanaess
Toril — the planet of Faerûn and Kara-Tur
Krynn — the planet of Ansalon and Taladas
context: The Known World rebranded as 'Mystara' in 1991 to give it a distinct identity. Aaron Allston's 1991 Rules Cyclopedia compiled BECMI rules around the Mystara setting. The 1996 Mystara D&D 'Black Box' was the last major boxed product before TSR collapsed. Mystara's nations — Karameikos, Glantri, Ylaruam, Thyatis — feature in many BECMI adventures. The Hollow World adventures explore lost-civilization tropes that wouldn't fit elsewhere.

question: Tom Moldvay edited the 1981 Basic Set of Dungeons & Dragons and designed several beloved Expert-line modules. His 1981 module X2 sends adventurers into a fog-shrouded chateau whose noble family has been carried off to a magical demiplane. The adventure is based directly on a weird-tales author whose stories of the medieval French province of Averoigne Moldvay loved. Whose stories inspired X2?
answer: Clark Ashton Smith, of Averoigne and Zothique fame
choices: Clark Ashton Smith, of Averoigne and Zothique fame
Lord Dunsany, of the Pegana cycle
Mervyn Peake, of the Gormenghast trilogy
James Branch Cabell, of the Biography of Manuel cycle
context: X2 Castle Amber takes its adventurers into Averoigne, the invented French province of Clark Ashton Smith's stories, and its villains are the decadent Amber family. Smith (1893-1961) was the third great Weird Tales writer of the 1930s beside Lovecraft and Howard.

question: Tactical Studies Rules (TSR)'s 1989 Forgotten Realms event, the Time of Troubles, told in the Avatar novels and modules, begins when the overgod Ao, angry at the gods' petty quarrels, casts almost the whole pantheon down to walk Faerûn as mortal avatars. The last straw is a theft: two gods have made off with the Tablets of Fate. Which two gods stole them?
context: In the Time of Troubles, which TSR's 1989 products used to carry the Forgotten Realms into a new edition, the overgod Ao cast the gods down to walk the world as mortal avatars after Bane and Myrkul stole the Tablets of Fate.

question: The Call of Cthulhu RPG, published by Chaosium in 1981, brought Lovecraft's cosmic-horror universe into the tabletop space. Its core mechanic is a sanity-score that decreases as characters witness cosmic-horror events. The game has been continuously in print since 1981. What system did Chaosium use as its foundation, also shared with its fantasy game RuneQuest?
answer: Basic Roleplaying (BRP), a d100 percentile-based skill system
choices: Basic Roleplaying (BRP), a d100 percentile-based skill system
Glory and Honor, a d20-based attribute-driven system
FUDGE, an open-source flexible dice-pool system
context: Basic Roleplaying (BRP) was first published by Chaosium in 1978 for RuneQuest. The system is percentile-based — skill checks roll d100 against a target. BRP became the foundation for Call of Cthulhu (1981), Stormbringer (1981), Pendragon (1985), and other Chaosium games. The latest Call of Cthulhu edition (7th edition, 2014) refined the system but kept the core d100 philosophy. Sandy Petersen designed CoC.

question: The classic AD&D Displacer Beast is a six-legged panther with two extra tentacle-limbs. It can appear shifted from its actual location. Gygax adapted it from a 1939 Astounding Stories novella about a tentacled cat that stalks a spaceship crew on an abandoned alien world. The creature in that novella was named "coeurl." Who wrote the original story, later collected in Voyage of the Space Beagle?
context: Van Vogt's 'Black Destroyer' (1939) is widely considered one of the foundational alien-monster stories. It directly influenced the 1979 film Alien — Dan O'Bannon and Ron Cobb cited Van Vogt as an inspiration alongside It! The Terror from Beyond Space. The Voyage of the Space Beagle (1950) fix-up collects four interconnected stories. Gygax cited Van Vogt explicitly in the original DMG's Appendix N reading list.

question: Gary Gygax had to reorganize his company in 1975 when the childhood friend who had founded it with him died. It had begun in 1973 as Tactical Studies Rules. The company changed its name late in 1975, and the new name lasted until a 1983 reorganisation split it into separate firms. What was the renamed company called?
answer: TSR Hobbies, Inc. — keeping the TSR acronym from the original
choices: TSR Hobbies, Inc. — keeping the TSR acronym from the original
Tactical Strategy Rules, Inc. — a slight rebrand
Tactical Studios Recreational, Inc. — emphasizing the hobby angle
Total Strategic Roleplaying, Inc. — claiming the full RPG space
context: The 1975 rename was forced by the death of Don Kaye that February, after which Brian Blume had bought into the company. Kaye had been the company treasurer; his death required a corporate reorganization. The new TSR Hobbies expanded beyond the original wargame focus into RPGs, novels, and (eventually) toys, games, and other licensed products. By 1982, TSR was the largest gaming company in the world by revenue. The 1985 crisis began when their over-expansion came home.

question: Gary Gygax co-founded the Gen Con convention in August 1968, hosting it in the Horticultural Hall and in his own basement in the Wisconsin town where he lived. The first one had 96 attendees, and by 1985 it had outgrown the town and moved to Milwaukee, then to Indianapolis in 2003. What was the name 'Gen Con' short for?
answer: Geneva Convention — a play on the international-law treaty
choices: Geneva Convention — a play on the international-law treaty
General Convention — a generic name for gaming gatherings
Generation Convention — a name for the new generation of gamers
Genuine Convention — emphasizing its hobby-gaming authenticity
context: The 'Geneva Convention' joke name was always Gygax's pun. The 1968 con featured the Castle & Crusade Society (precursor to Chainmail and D&D), Diplomacy tournaments, miniature wargames. The 1971 Gen Con was where Gygax met Dave Arneson and saw the Blackmoor campaign in action, sparking the OD&D collaboration. The 1975 Gen Con was the first formal D&D tournament (running Tomb of Horrors's prototype). Gen Con remains the largest tabletop gaming convention in North America.

question: The most famous fantasy map in tabletop history is the full-color hex map of the Flanaess, the east continent of Oerth. It came with the 1980 World of Greyhawk Folio and grew in the 1983 boxed set. A Tactical Studies Rules (TSR) mapmaker painted it. Her first name became a shorthand for the whole D&D map style of that era. What was her name?
answer: Darlene Pekul, credited as simply 'Darlene' on the published maps
choices: Darlene Pekul, credited as simply 'Darlene' on the published maps
Diesel LaForce, credited as just 'David Diesel' or 'D.D.'
Stephen Sullivan, credited as 'S.D. Sullivan' in TSR's catalog
Dennis Kauth, credited as 'D. Kauth' in art reviews
context: Darlene Pekul (1947-) joined TSR as a cartographer in the late 1970s. Her Flanaess map's distinct color palette (muted greens, browns, blues) and hand-lettered nation names became visual shorthand for 1980s D&D campaign settings. The map was reissued in poster form and remains a collector's item. Darlene also produced the maps for the 1983 World of Greyhawk hardcover boxed set and many TSR adventure modules. She returned to TSR/WotC for the 2007 Living Greyhawk Gazetteer.

question: After Gary Gygax was pushed out of Tactical Studies Rules (TSR) in 1985, he wrote a set of new sword-and-sorcery novels. The hero was a Greyhawk street thief who grew, book by book, into a strong adventurer. He was Gygax's own favorite character, and the novels (1985-1987, from New Infinities Productions) drew right from his home Greyhawk game. What was the hero's name?
answer: Gord the Rogue, of the City of Greyhawk
choices: Gord the Rogue, of the City of Greyhawk
Mordenkainen the Wizard, of the Circle of Eight
Robilar the Fighter, of the Bandit Kingdoms
Bigby the Hand, of the Greyhawk Academy
context: Gord the Rogue novels: Saga of Old City (1985), Artifact of Evil (1986), Sea of Death (1987), Night Arrant (1987), City of Hawks (1987), Come Endless Darkness (1988), Dance of Demons (1988). The series ends with Gord destroying the multiverse and being reborn as a new god — Gygax's literal authorial revenge on TSR for taking the world away from him. The Gord novels remain in print as PDFs through various small presses. Gygax's later original RPG settings (Dangerous Journeys, Lejendary Adventure) never reached the same audience.

question: Gygax's 1979 module T1 The Village of Hommlet shows a sleepy frontier village that hides an evil cult, with spies among its townsfolk. In the ruined moathouse outside town, the bandits answer to Lareth the Beautiful, a handsome young evil priest. The module warns that anyone who harms him had best not boast of it where word could reach the demon who favors him. Which demon is that?
answer: Lolth — the Demon Queen of Spiders
choices: Lolth — the Demon Queen of Spiders
Orcus — the demon prince of the undead
Demogorgon — the two-headed Prince of Demons
context: Lareth the Beautiful, a fifth-level cleric, is the new master of the moathouse bandits outside Hommlet. The module warns that whoever harms him had best not brag of it before anyone who might inform the demoness Lolth, the Demon Queen of Spiders, a thread that ties Hommlet to the drow and the later Q1 module.

question: The 1976 Eldritch Wizardry supplement added psionics to D&D, a second system of mental powers alongside magic. Gygax kept psionics in his 1978 Advanced Dungeons & Dragons Player's Handbook only as optional rules, open to characters who made lucky rolls, and many Dungeon Masters left them out entirely. What is the classic D&D psionic monster, a brain with bug-like legs that stalks dungeons and eats minds?
answer: The Intellect Devourer — a brain-shape with four crab-like legs
choices: The Intellect Devourer — a brain-shape with four crab-like legs
The Ulitharid — a giant elder-form mind flayer
The Cerebrilith — a demon-form psionic predator from the Abyss
The Thought Eater — an etherial creature that eats memorized spells
context: The intellect devourer first appeared in Eldritch Wizardry (1976), the supplement that introduced psionics, as a brain-shaped creature on four clawed legs that feeds on minds. In the first-edition Player's Handbook (1978) psionics were an optional appendix, available only to characters who qualified with lucky rolls.

question: Gary Gygax's 1979 Dungeon Masters Guide closes with Appendix N, his list of the authors whose books inspired Dungeons & Dragons. Many of the names are American pulp writers, such as Robert E. Howard and Fritz Leiber, but one is a titled Anglo-Irish nobleman who wrote dreamlike tales of elves and invented gods. Which lord made Gygax's list?
answer: Lord Dunsany, of the Pegana mythology and 'The King of Elfland's Daughter'
choices: Lord Dunsany, of the Pegana mythology and 'The King of Elfland's Daughter'
Lord Tennyson, of 'Idylls of the King' Arthurian poetry
Lord Macaulay, of 'Lays of Ancient Rome' historical poetry
Lord Byron, of 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage' Romantic poetry
context: Lord Dunsany (1878-1957) appears among the authors of Gygax's Appendix N, alongside series such as Howard's Conan and Leiber's Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser. Dunsany's 1924 novel The King of Elfland's Daughter is the classic picture of Faerie as a strange and beautiful realm.

question: A staff designer began answering readers' tricky rules questions in 1987 in 'Sage Advice', a monthly column in the official Dungeons and Dragons magazine. He stayed with it until 2004, through grappling, spell components, monster stats and every edge case gamers could invent, and he became the rules oracle for a whole generation. Who was he?
answer: Skip Williams, who later co-designed 3rd Edition D&D
choices: Skip Williams, who later co-designed 3rd Edition D&D
Roger E. Moore, who edited Dragon Magazine through the same era
Kim Mohan, who edited Dragon Magazine in the 1980s
Bruce Heard, of the Voyage of the Princess Ark Mystara column
context: Skip Williams started at TSR in 1976 as a part-time clerk in its Dungeon Hobby Shop and wrote Sage Advice from 1987 to 2004. He later worked on the 3rd Edition design team with Monte Cook and Jonathan Tweet.

question: Tactical Studies Rules (TSR)'s 1989 Spelljammer cosmology placed D&D solar systems inside vast crystal spheres, floating in a strange medium called the phlogiston. Ships travel the phlogiston using a magical helm, a chair-shaped device that turns the pilot's spell energy into ship motion. Helms range from cheap minor helms to powerful major helms. Which merchant race sells the high-end major helms in canonical Spelljammer lore?
answer: The Arcane — gigantic blue-skinned alien merchants who sell helms throughout the spheres
choices: The Arcane — gigantic blue-skinned alien merchants who sell helms throughout the spheres
The Scro — orc admirals who sell helms from their black shipyards
The Neogi — spider-slavers who manufacture helms via dark magic
The Giff — Napoleonic hippopotamus-mercenaries who fabricate helms
context: In Spelljammer the Arcane, towering blue-skinned humanoids, are the premier merchant race of wildspace, dealing in helms and other gear across the crystal spheres. Lore holds that they sell the major helms but do not build them, and they keep the helms' true source secret.

question: Before Ravenloft (1983), Tracy Hickman wrote a trilogy of 1982-1983 modules called the Desert of Desolation series, set in a fictional Arabian-inspired desert region of the Forgotten Realms. The three modules are I3, I4, I5. The middle module sends the PCs into a pyramid tomb of a long-dead Pharaoh, ultimately confronting his lich form. What was the lich-pharaoh's name?
answer: Amun-Re, sometimes spelled Amon-Re in different printings
choices: Amun-Re, sometimes spelled Amon-Re in different printings
Set-Anu, the Lord of the Black Lands of Athas
Khepri-Atum, the Sun Pharaoh of the lost dynasty
Imhotep-Ra, the Architect-King of the great pyramid
context: The Desert of Desolation trilogy: I3 Pharaoh (1982), I4 Oasis of the White Palm (1982), I5 Lost Tomb of Martek (1983). The series was popular enough that TSR compiled it as a single supermodule in 1987. The 'Pharaoh's Box' magic item from I3 is iconic among TSR collectors. Tracy Hickman has cited the modules as his proving-ground writing exercises before tackling Dragonlance and Ravenloft. The Egyptian-inspired Mulhorand region of the Forgotten Realms eventually absorbed the setting.

question: The 1974 Dungeons and Dragons box hands its buyer three small booklets: one for making characters and casting spells, one listing creatures and loot, and one for running games below ground and out in the wilds. Collectors still prize all three. What are the three booklets titled?
answer: Men & Magic, Monsters & Treasure, and The Underworld & Wilderness Adventures
choices: Men & Magic, Monsters & Treasure, and The Underworld & Wilderness Adventures
Heroes & Spells, Beasts & Gold, and The Dungeon & Outdoor Campaigns
Fighters & Wizards, Creatures & Loot, and The Labyrinth & Wilderness Guide
Characters & Sorcery, Dragons & Hoards, and The Castle & Countryside Book
context: The original 1974 set held three booklets: Men & Magic, Monsters & Treasure, and The Underworld & Wilderness Adventures. It sold for $10, and the first print run was 1,000 copies.

question: Mordenkainen's apprentice in Gygax's Greyhawk campaign was a wizard whose "hand" spells became iconic, including Bigby's Interposing Hand, Grasping Hand and Crushing Hand. Bigby did not start out as a hero: he was an evil low-level wizard living in another referee's dungeons until Gygax's Mordenkainen subdued him and forced him into service, and later Gygax played Bigby himself. In whose dungeons did Bigby begin?
answer: Rob Kuntz, Gygax's co-DM and an early TSR employee
choices: Rob Kuntz, Gygax's co-DM and an early TSR employee
Tim Kask, the original editor of Dragon Magazine
Brian Blume, Gygax's TSR business partner
James Ward, of Metamorphosis Alpha fame
context: Bigby started life as an evil low-level wizard in Rob Kuntz's dungeons of Greyhawk. Gygax's Mordenkainen subdued him and made him a servant, and after Bigby changed his ways Kuntz ruled that Gygax could take him over as a player character. Kuntz co-refereed the Greyhawk campaign and played the fighter Robilar.

question: A staff artist at Gary Gygax's company gave early-1980s Dungeons and Dragons its most distinctive look, with bright, strangely proportioned creatures and covers. He was one of a small group who set the game's visual identity around 1980, and his style was psychedelic, weird and slightly Gothic. Who was he?
answer: Erol Otus — cover painter of the 1981 Basic Set
choices: Erol Otus — cover painter of the 1981 Basic Set
David Trampier — DMG and Monster Manual interior art
Jeff Easley — covers of 1983-1989 AD&D hardcovers
context: Erol Otus joined TSR's art department in the late 1970s and was on staff by 1979; he was one of the two staff artists left after the May 1981 layoffs. He painted the cover of the first Deities & Demigods (1980) and the color cover of Tom Moldvay's 1981 Basic Set rulebook.

question: Rob Kuntz's home-campaign fighter Robilar became infamous in Greyhawk lore for breaking into Castle Greyhawk, Gygax's home-campaign mega-dungeon. Robilar slaughtered most of its monsters and traps during mid-1970s play. In a 1975 session, Robilar and Mordenkainen together explored the deepest level. They confronted its most powerful demonic ruler. Which demon-lord did they face?
answer: Zuggtmoy, the Demon Queen of Fungi
choices: Zuggtmoy, the Demon Queen of Fungi
Lolth, the Demon Queen of Spiders
Demogorgon, the Prince of Demons himself
Iuz, the cambion demigod of the Flanaess
context: Zuggtmoy was first mentioned in Gygax's Greyhawk play sessions in 1973-1975 before her formal publication in the 1985 Temple of Elemental Evil. Robilar and Mordenkainen 'defeated' her in the deepest level of Castle Greyhawk — though Gygax later said the encounter ended with the demon being imprisoned rather than destroyed, setting up her later return as the central villain of T1-4. The 'Castle Greyhawk' dungeon itself was the original D&D megadungeon, and Gygax's home-campaign play notes (later somewhat published) are sought-after collector's items.

question: Chaosium's 1981 Call of Cthulhu RPG translated Lovecraft's cosmic horror into a tabletop format with the iconic 'Sanity Score' mechanic. A character's Sanity points decrease as they witness cosmic horror; reach zero and the character goes permanently insane. The system spawned over 40 years of supplements and remains one of the longest-running RPGs ever. Who designed it?
answer: Sandy Petersen, who later did level design on id Software's Doom and Quake
choices: Sandy Petersen, who later did level design on id Software's Doom and Quake
Steve Perrin, the original RuneQuest fantasy-game system designer
Greg Stafford, the legendary creator of the Glorantha setting
Ken St. Andre, the irascible Tunnels and Trolls designer
context: Sandy Petersen (1955-) is a deeply religious Mormon designer who somehow became the world's foremost interpreter of cosmic-horror gaming. After Call of Cthulhu, he designed RuneQuest III and worked on id Software's Doom (1993) and Quake (1996). The 'level designer' role he pioneered at id influenced first-person shooter design forever. He returned to tabletop in the 2010s with his own company, Petersen Games, making Lovecraftian and historical board games.

question: Chaosium's 1978 RuneQuest was set in a Bronze Age fantasy world. It had cult-based religion, dragon-newts, dwarves who were living machines, talking ducks, and warring Lunar and Solar empires. Chaosium's founder made the whole setting. Who created Glorantha?
answer: Greg Stafford, founder of Chaosium and Glorantha mythologist
choices: Greg Stafford, founder of Chaosium and Glorantha mythologist
Steve Perrin, the RuneQuest rules designer
Sandy Petersen, the Call of Cthulhu designer
Lynn Willis, the Chaosium editor and designer
context: Greg Stafford (1948-2018) built Glorantha as a personal worldbuilding project starting in the 1960s — like Ed Greenwood with Forgotten Realms, but with a deeper anthropological framing. Glorantha drew on Eliade's Patterns in Comparative Religion as a structural inspiration. Stafford spent his entire life refining the setting; HeroQuest, Pendragon (1985), and the more recent 13th Age in Glorantha all drew on his core lore. Stafford was inducted into the Origins Awards Hall of Fame in 2013. He died in 2018.

question: Game Designers' Workshop published the sci-fi RPG Traveller in 1977, designed by Marc Miller, and it established many conventions of science-fiction roleplaying. Its character generation was famous for one specific innovation. Characters served careers (Navy, Marines, Scouts, Merchants, Army, Other) for four-year terms, gaining skills but risking death. If you 'died' at that stage, you actually rolled up a new character. What was this signature mechanic called?
answer: Survival rolls during chargen — characters could literally die before play began
choices: Survival rolls during chargen — characters could literally die before play began
Reincarnation tables — death meant a new body but the same character
Critical career failure — death meant career change, not actual death
Random aging effects — repeated terms reduced physical stats but not death
context: Traveller's death-during-chargen mechanic became famously controversial — some saw it as adding gritty realism, others as just frustrating. Later Traveller editions made the rule optional. The game's setting, the Third Imperium, has been a constantly-developing universe since 1977. Marc Miller still oversees the line, now published as Mongoose Traveller (2008+). Traveller is considered one of the most influential RPGs ever, alongside D&D, RuneQuest, and Call of Cthulhu.

question: Hero Games' 1981 superhero RPG Champions was the first big game built on 'point-buy' character creation. Players spent points to design custom powers, perks, and drawbacks. The same rules were later used for fantasy, spy, and sci-fi games. What was the shared system called?
answer: The Hero System, also called Champions Hero System
choices: The Hero System, also called Champions Hero System
The GURPS System, the Steve Jackson Games universal mechanic
The Storyteller System, the White Wolf World of Darkness mechanic
The FATE System, an early Fudge-derivative game
context: The Hero System reached its definitive form in 4th Edition (1989), with revisions through 6th Edition (2009). The system's signature feature is the granularity of power design — every superpower or magical effect could be deconstructed into 'mechanics' bought separately. Champions itself remains in print as the flagship Hero System game. Hero Games' tabletop RPG The Champions of New Olympus has appeared in superhero-RPG canon since 1981 alongside Mayfair Games' DC Heroes and TSR's Marvel Super Heroes.

question: West End Games' 1984 dystopian-comedy RPG Paranoia was designed by Greg Costikyan, Dan Gelber, and Eric Goldberg. It satirized Cold War paranoia through a future totalitarian complex run by an insane AI Computer. Players are Troubleshooters, whose job is finding traitors while being traitors themselves. Each carries a clearance color (Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet, Ultra-Violet). What was the player handbook's notorious cover slogan?
answer: 'Stay Alert! Trust No One! Keep Your Laser Handy!'
choices: 'Stay Alert! Trust No One! Keep Your Laser Handy!'
'You Are Safe! The Computer Is Your Friend! Report Everything!'
'Welcome To Alpha Complex! Have A Nice Day! Don't Die!'
'Service The Computer! Report All Mutants! Watch Out For Communists!'
context: Paranoia's tone was deliberately satirical — Costikyan was a libertarian-leaning author whose intent was a comedic critique of authoritarianism (the Computer thinks it's helping; the players are forced to lie and betray to survive). The game spawned multiple editions through Mongoose Publishing (2004 onwards). Greg Costikyan went on to write extensively about game design theory. The phrase 'The Computer is your friend' became a tongue-in-cheek meme outside the gaming hobby.

question: Gygax's 1978 S1 Tomb of Horrors module contains a famously specific trap involving the demilich Acererak's final form. After the PCs defeat his minions and pass through the tomb's puzzles, they reach Acererak's burial chamber. His skull rests on a pile of gems. When approached, the demilich rises and attacks. The skull has six gems set in its eye sockets, with very specific effects. What happens when a player tries to take one of the gems?
answer: Each gem holds the trapped soul of an adventurer Acererak previously defeated; touching releases the demilich's life-draining attack
choices: Each gem holds the trapped soul of an adventurer Acererak previously defeated; touching releases the demilich's life-draining attack
Each gem is a sphere of annihilation in disguise; touching disintegrates the PC instantly
Each gem is a wish-spell trapped in physical form; touching grants the wish but kills the PC
Each gem is an alternate timeline of the PC; touching merges the PC with the alternate, causing alignment loss
context: Acererak's gems include diamond, ruby, jet, fire opal, large opal, and emerald. Each represents a different soul-trapping mechanism — touching one drains levels, another forces a saving throw vs death, another permanently traps the PC's soul. The demilich form is a skull animated by the lich's residual willpower; it can only be defeated by destroying the gems AND the skull. Some 1e modules and later 5e adaptations have player characters who unsealed an Acererak gem decades earlier returning to the game as freed (but missing-souled) characters.

question: American writer Fritz Leiber and his college friend Harry Otto Fischer invented two sword-and-sorcery heroes in letters in the 1930s: Fafhrd, a giant red-haired barbarian of the north, and the Gray Mouser, a small thief and magician of the city. Then in August 1939 the first published Fafhrd-and-Mouser story appeared in Unknown, John W. Campbell's new fantasy pulp, and later collections renamed it The Jewels in the Forest. What was its original title?
context: Two Sought Adventure appeared in Unknown in August 1939 and was later retitled The Jewels in the Forest. Leiber went on writing about the pair until his death in 1992.

question: Gary Gygax's original home-campaign mega-dungeon, Castle Greyhawk, was the playtesting ground for D&D from 1972 onwards. The dungeon had multiple levels — Gygax himself ran it for years with his home group. The exact level count varies in different sources. According to Gygax's own 1979 Dragon Magazine retrospective and his later Castle Zagyg series, how many levels did Castle Greyhawk have in its mature form?
answer: Thirteen named levels, with sub-levels and dimensional pockets adding many more sections
choices: Thirteen named levels, with sub-levels and dimensional pockets adding many more sections
Ten levels of identical 20-by-20 hex rooms, with no significant deeper sections
Twenty-five themed levels, including elemental zones and a Far Realm gateway
Seven levels matching the classical seven-planet medieval astrology
context: Castle Greyhawk's design was idiosyncratic, with thematic levels (the Magic-User Level, the Trap Level, the Demonic Level), multiple stairways between levels, and dimensional pockets. The infamous 'Tomb of Tsojcanth' was one such pocket. Gygax began publishing partial Castle Greyhawk material via his post-TSR company Troll Lord Games in 2005 — Castle Zagyg (Yggsburgh + The East Mark of the Flanaess) before his 2008 death. The full mega-dungeon material was eventually published in 2008-2011 by Troll Lord, but the Gygax estate has restricted later printings.

question: R.A. Salvatore introduced Drizzt Do'Urden as a last-minute addition to The Crystal Shard (1988) — the publisher's book editor Mary Kirchoff needed a new sidekick for the young barbarian hero, and off the top of his head Salvatore offered a drow. The novel hadn't been pitched with Drizzt at the front, but he stole the entire trilogy and went on to anchor over thirty more Salvatore novels. Salvatore later wrote a separate prequel trilogy giving Drizzt's full origin in Menzoberranzan. What's that prequel trilogy called?
answer: The Dark Elf Trilogy: Homeland (1990), Exile (1990), Sojourn (1991)
choices: The Dark Elf Trilogy: Homeland (1990), Exile (1990), Sojourn (1991)
The Legacy Trilogy: Legacy, Starless Night, Siege of Darkness (1992-1994)
The Cleric Quintet: Canticle, In Sylvan Shadows, Night Masks, Fallen Fortress, Chaos Curse (1991-1994)
The Hunter's Blades Trilogy: Thousand Orcs, Lone Drow, Two Swords (2002-2004)
context: The Dark Elf Trilogy is widely considered Salvatore's best work and the definitive depiction of drow society. Homeland (1990) showed Drizzt's youth in House Do'Urden in Menzoberranzan; Exile (1990) showed his banishment into the Underdark wilderness; Sojourn (1991) showed his journey to the surface and the early friendship with the blind ranger Montolio DeBrouchee. Salvatore's portrayal of Menzoberranzan as a matriarchal drow city-state — with its noble houses, the Academy, and the constant intrigue against Lolth — became iconic Forgotten Realms canon.

question: Debbie, a fictional teenage girl, joins a D&D group under a 'Dungeon Master' named Ms. Frost in a 1984 evangelical comic tract. The group plays a session where Debbie's character earns levels of magic, and Frost then invites Debbie to a real witchcraft circle to learn 'real spells.' The tract names one spell Debbie casts on her father. What does she cast on him?
answer: A 'Mind Bondage' spell to get spending money from him
choices: A 'Mind Bondage' spell to get spending money from him
A 'Charm Person' spell directly copied from D&D
A 'Cause Disease' spell that makes him fall ill
A 'Curse of Failure' spell that destroys his business
context: In the tract Debbie casts a 'mind bondage' spell on her father to get spending money; the spell is Chick's invention, not a D&D spell. Her friend Marcie kills herself after her game character dies. A 2014 short film directed by L. Gabriel Gonda and written by JR Ralls took its plot and dialogue straight from the tract.

question: Tom Lazarus wrote the teleplay of Mazes and Monsters from Rona Jaffe's 1981 novel, the story of a college student who lost himself in a fantasy role-playing game. CBS aired the made-for-TV movie on December 28, 1982. Who directed it?
context: Steven Hilliard Stern directed Mazes and Monsters, which CBS aired on December 28, 1982. Tom Lazarus wrote it from Rona Jaffe's 1981 novel, and it was Tom Hanks's first lead role.

question: In the Pokemon world, Charmander is the small orange lizard starter Pokemon. Its most distinctive feature is a small flame that burns forever on the tip of its tail. According to the Pokedex (the trainer's Pokemon encyclopedia), if the flame ever goes out, what happens to Charmander?
choices: Charmander loses the ability to use Fire moves
context: The flame burns brighter when Charmander is healthy or excited and dims when he is weak or sick. Trainers shelter the tail from rain. It is the most iconic life-force symbol in the franchise.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, a trainer's little orange lizard Charmander grows up in two steps — first into the sturdier Charmeleon, then into the huge dragon-like Charizard, wings flared and tail blazing. Charizard's Pokedex entry lists two types, and one of those types is Fire. What is Charizard's other type?
context: Charizard is the only fully evolved Kanto starter with dual typing. Despite his dragon appearance, he was never Dragon-type until Mega Charizard X (Pokemon X/Y, 2013) granted him a Fire/Dragon alternate form.

question: In the Pokemon games for the Nintendo Game Boy, a young trainer walks through tall grass and suddenly runs into a wild creature like a Pikachu. To catch it, the trainer plucks a small red-and-white ball from their belt and throws it — the ball snaps open in a burst of light and pulls the Pokemon inside to become part of the trainer's team. What is this red-and-white capture ball called?
context: The standard Pokeball is the baseline catch device. The Master Ball is the rarest, with a 100% catch rate, and is famously given once in each main-line game.

question: In the 1997 Japanese anime Pokemon, a ten-year-old trainer named Ash Ketchum sets off with his Pikachu to catch monsters and become a Pokemon Master. He leaves his home in Pallet Town, battles gym leaders in Pewter City and Cerulean City, and finally competes in the Indigo League tournament — all inside one starting region modeled on real east-central Japan. What is this region called?
context: Kanto is the original 151-Pokemon region from Pokemon Red and Blue. Each later generation introduced a new region: Johto (Gold/Silver), Hoenn (Ruby/Sapphire), and so on.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, scientists on Cinnabar Island found a fossilized eyelash of Mew, an ancient myth Pokemon, and used its DNA to clone a new life-form in their secret lab. The result was a tall purple psychic Pokemon far more powerful than the original. He escapes, retreats to the Unknown Dungeon cave, and becomes the post-game boss the trainer must fight after beating the Elite Four. Name him.
context: Mewtwo's origin lore is told in journals scattered through the abandoned Cinnabar Island Mansion. He escapes captivity, destroys the lab, and is later found in Cerulean Cave by trainers who have already beaten the Elite Four.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, a young trainer from Pallet Town journeys across the Kanto region battling city Gym Leaders like Brock of Pewter City, Misty of Cerulean City, and Erika of Celadon City. Each defeated leader hands over a shiny metal Gym Badge. Only trainers who collect the full set of Kanto Gym Badges are allowed to travel to the Indigo Plateau and challenge the Elite Four. How many badges must a Kanto trainer earn to reach the Indigo League?
context: The Kanto gym badges, in order, are: Boulder (Brock), Cascade (Misty), Thunder (Lt. Surge), Rainbow (Erika), Soul (Koga), Marsh (Sabrina), Volcano (Blaine), and Earth (Giovanni).

question: In the Pokemon TV cartoon, Team Rocket is a bumbling trio of villains chasing Ash Ketchum's Pikachu. The three members — Jessie, James, and a talking cat Pokemon named Meowth — always show up reciting a rhyming motto together before every fight. What two-word phrase does Jessie use to open the motto?
context: The full opening is 'Prepare for trouble! / And make it double!' James follows Jessie, then they introduce themselves and Meowth caps it. The motto became one of the most recognizable bits of dialogue in 90s anime dubbing.

question: In February 1996 the tiny Japanese studio Game Freak released Pokemon Red and Green for the Nintendo Game Boy handheld console, ending six years of quiet development. Each Pokemon in the Kanto region got its own numbered entry in the trainer's Pokedex encyclopedia — starting with the grass-lizard Bulbasaur at number 001 and ending with the rare psychic legend Mew at the final slot. How many Pokemon appeared in that first Kanto Pokedex?
context: The 151 became the cultural canon. Mew was added in development as an Easter egg by programmer Shigeki Morimoto with only days left before the master disc shipped. The number 151 was later memorialized by the Pokerap.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, a starter Charmander grows through experience points earned by winning battles against wild Pokemon and other trainers. When a Charmander hits a set level, it glows white and reshapes itself into the tougher Charmeleon, and eventually into the huge winged Charizard. Every Pokemon species has an evolution level fixed in its stats. At what level does a Charmander first evolve into Charmeleon?
context: Charmander reaches Charmeleon at level 16 and the final-form Charizard at level 36, matching the other Kanto starters' evolution levels. Most players grind through Mt. Moon and Cerulean to hit level 16 before challenging Lt. Surge.

question: In an early Pokemon episode, Ash, Misty and Brock find a wild Charmander huddled on a rock in a rainstorm, shielding the tail flame his life depends on. His trainer had told him to wait there, then abandoned him with a cruel lie. What was the trainer's name?
context: Damian told Charmander to wait on the rock and would come back, knowing he would not. The Pokemon was too loyal to leave. Ash takes Charmander in, and the dynamic that produces Ash's most famous Pokemon arc begins right there in the rainstorm.

question: In the Pokemon anime, Ash Ketchum challenges the seventh Kanto gym leader — a bald old showman named Blaine who loves puzzles and stage-magic gags. In the deciding match Ash's newly evolved Charizard defeats Blaine's ace Magmar, and Ash walks away with the Volcano Badge. Blaine's home city, the entrance to his gym, and his Pokemon's element all match one very specific theme. Which Kanto gym leader is Blaine?
answer: The Cinnabar Island fire gym leader, hidden behind a riddle door
choices: The Cinnabar Island fire gym leader, hidden behind a riddle door
The Saffron City psychic gym leader of Silph Co. fame
The Fuchsia City poison gym leader who trains ninjas
The Vermilion City electric gym leader, an American soldier
context: Blaine's gym is hidden inside the Cinnabar Mansion through a secret-passage door requiring riddles to open. The mansion is also where Mewtwo was cloned. Blaine's iconic Pokemon are Magmar, Ninetales, and Rapidash.

question: In the Pokemon anime, Brock is the rock-type gym leader of Pewter City — the first city Ash Ketchum ever reaches on his Kanto journey, and the first gym he ever challenges. Ash loses to Brock on his first attempt. On his second try, Ash's Pikachu triggers the gym's overhead sprinklers, drenching Brock's ace Pokemon. That ace is a giant rock snake made of chained boulders, and once wet it becomes vulnerable to electricity — Pikachu zaps it and Ash finally earns the Boulder Badge. Name that rock-snake Pokemon.
context: Brock travels with Ash for most of the original anime as a cook and aspiring Pokemon breeder. He has many younger siblings whom he raises in Pewter City after his father Flint leaves. Brock's signature gag is fainting over every Nurse Joy and Officer Jenny he meets.

question: In the very first episode of the Pokemon anime, a wild Pikachu jolts a red-haired girl who is passing by on a two-wheeled vehicle, frying the vehicle to a smoking wreck. That girl is Misty, the water-type gym leader of Cerulean City, and she ends up traveling with Ash Ketchum as his first companion in the whole show. Across the early episodes she keeps chasing him and demanding he replace the vehicle her Pikachu incident ruined. What is the item Misty wants Ash to pay her back for?
context: Misty's flooded bike is the running gag of the early series. Pikachu fried it with a Thundershock that scared off a flock of Spearow chasing Ash and him. Misty follows them for repayment and never collects.

question: Pokemon Red and Green launched in Japan on February 27, 1996 as a pair of Game Boy cartridges. Nintendo re-released them worldwide as Red and Blue about two and a half years later, in September 1998 in North America. Each version's box cover features one of Kanto's three starter Pokemon in its fully-evolved form: Red shows the fire lizard, Green shows the plant dinosaur, and Blue shows the water starter — a giant blue turtle with cannons mounted on its shell. Name the fully-evolved Water starter that appears on the North American Blue cover.
context: Pokemon Red and Blue launched in the US on September 28, 1998 for the Game Boy. The English version was based on the Japanese Pokemon Blue revision, with the original Japanese Red and Green's color pair swapped to Red and Blue for the Western market.

question: In 1999, a special anime-tie-in version of Pokemon Red and Blue released in the US. It started the player with a Pikachu instead of one of the three Kanto starters, and Pikachu followed the player around outside its Pokeball. What was the game called?
context: Pokemon Yellow Version: Special Pikachu Edition launched in Japan on September 12, 1998 and in the US on October 19, 1999. Jessie, James, and Meowth replaced certain Rocket grunts. All three Kanto starters could be obtained over the course of the game.

question: The first Pokemon movie, released in 1998 in Japan and 1999 in the US, tells the origin of the lab-cloned Mewtwo. Mewtwo escapes the lab in a fit of psychic rage and broods about who he is. What rebuilt place does he blast to rubble before his big speech?
answer: The Cinnabar Island laboratory where Dr. Fuji cloned him
choices: The Cinnabar Island laboratory where Dr. Fuji cloned him
Team Rocket's Saffron City Silph Co. headquarters
Professor Oak's research lab in Pallet Town
The Indigo Plateau Pokemon League stadium
context: Dr. Fuji's journals (found in the abandoned Cinnabar Mansion in the games) describe the cloning experiment. The film's most famous moment is the climactic clone-versus-original showdown, halted by Ash leaping between Mewtwo and Mew and being turned to stone.

question: Pokemon Gold and Silver launched in Japan in 1999 and in North America in October 2000, on the Game Boy Color. They were the second generation of the Pokemon series and added 100 brand-new Pokemon to the original 151. Gold and Silver also introduced a real-time in-game day-and-night cycle, powered by the Game Boy Color cartridge's internal clock — the sky and the wild Pokemon really changed as the actual hours passed. Most importantly the games opened up a brand-new region located just west of Kanto. What is the name of that new region?
context: Johto introduced breeding via Day Care couples, the Pokegear watch device, and 16 gym badges (Johto's eight plus the original Kanto eight in the post-game). Crystal (2000-2001) added a female protagonist option named Kris.

question: In 2019, Warner Bros released Detective Pikachu, the first live-action Pokemon feature film. It stars American actor Justice Smith as Tim Goodman, a young man whose detective father has mysteriously vanished in Ryme City. Tim finds his father's Pikachu partner and, to Tim's shock, discovers the little electric mouse can suddenly talk to him — in the deadpan wisecracking voice of an adult man. That voice belongs to a Canadian-American actor best known for playing Deadpool. Who was the voice actor?
context: Detective Pikachu was directed by Rob Letterman, based on the 2016 Japanese 3DS spinoff game. It became the highest-grossing live-action video-game film at release. Reynolds's Pikachu drinks coffee, wears a deerstalker hat, and snarks his way through Ryme City's mysteries.

question: On July 6, 2016, Niantic launched a mobile augmented-reality game that turned real-world parks and landmarks into Pokemon hunting grounds. People walked into traffic, climbed fences, and gathered in parks at 2 a.m. by the thousands. What was the game?
context: Niantic had built the GPS-walking framework with its earlier game Ingress (2013). Pokemon GO hit 500 million downloads in its first eight months. The cultural sensation included serious news coverage of Lapras and Snorlax sightings in Central Park.

question: As a boy growing up in Machida, Japan, in the 1960s and 70s, Satoshi Tajiri obsessively collected beetles and stag beetles in the fields near his home — which decades later gave him the idea for a game about catching creatures. In 1989 he founded the game studio Game Freak in Tokyo with a talented young illustrator he had been co-publishing a Japanese fanzine with. Ever since Pokemon Red and Blue in 1996, that co-founder has personally drawn the concept art for every main-series Pokemon monster. Who is Tajiri's Game Freak co-founder?
context: Ken Sugimori is the lead character designer who has drawn the canonical art for every Pokemon since 1996. Junichi Masuda became the music director. Tsunekazu Ishihara runs The Pokemon Company, the licensing arm. Shigeru Miyamoto greenlit the project at Nintendo when no one else would.

question: Pokemon X and Y launched worldwide on the Nintendo 3DS in October 2013 as the sixth generation of the Pokemon series. Its headline new mechanic was Mega Evolution — a temporary in-battle super-form each Pokemon could enter if its trainer held the matching Mega Stone. Charizard was so popular the developers gave him two different Megas. Mega Charizard Y keeps his original Fire and Flying typing. But Mega Charizard X drops the Flying type entirely, turning his scales pitch black and his flames electric blue as he shifts into a completely new dual type. What is Mega Charizard X's dual typing?
context: Mega Charizard X was a fan-service nod to the long-running argument that Charizard 'should have been' Dragon-type. It exclusive to Pokemon X. Mega Charizard Y, exclusive to Pokemon Y, keeps the Fire/Flying typing and grows much larger wings. Both share a Charizardite stone.

question: In January 1999, the American game company Wizards of the Coast — the same publisher that already ran Magic the Gathering — released the English-language Pokemon Trading Card Game Base Set, a starter run of exactly 102 cards including sixteen holographic rares. The rarest, most valuable card in the whole set is the holographic Charizard, which schoolyard kids traded for lunch money and still trade for real money today. Collectors identify it by its exact slot in the numbered checklist. What is the Charizard card's number in the 102-card Base Set?
context: The Base Set is numbered alphabetically by Pokemon name within rarity groups, so Charizard's 4/102 reflects 'C-h-a-r' placement. The Base Set is the most reprinted TCG set in history. The card's 1st Edition Shadowless variant is the most valuable, currently selling at auction for hundreds of thousands of dollars.

question: In the Pokemon anime, Ash Ketchum's mother Delia lives back in Pallet Town while Ash travels the world. She keeps a strange helper around the house — a tall pink-haired clown Pokemon who cleans the house, cooks meals, and weeds the garden. What species is this Pokemon?
context: The Pokemon's nickname is Mimey. Delia adopts him after Ash and friends help out in an early-season episode. Mr. Mime's Pokedex skill is to project invisible walls, which Delia uses to keep dust out of the house. He is a household staple in the Ketchum home for the rest of the anime.

question: In the Pokemon anime's Orange Islands episode Charizard Chills, Ash's stubborn Charizard ignores his orders in a battle against a trainer named Tad.
